profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T12:10:04.483+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial decree.
Later Learning Heaven Tái
According to Xiāo Zǐxiǎn’s Qí Shū, in the biography of Cuī Zǔsī: In the early Sòng dynasty, it was initially proposed to enfeoff Tàizǔ as the Duke of Liáng.
Zǔsī presented to Tàizǔ, saying:
"The book of prophecies says: ‘A golden knife and sharp blade shall cut Qí.’
Now it is appropriate to be called Qí,
truly responding to Heaven's mandate."
Tàizǔ followed this,
and thus established the state of Qí.
Tàizǔ Gāo Huángdì’s
taboo name was Dàochéng,
his surname was Xiāo,
his courtesy name was Shàobó,
and his childhood name was Dòujiàng.
His original home was in Zhōngdū Lǐ, Zhōngdū Xiāng, Lánlíng Xiàn, Dōnghǎi.
When Jìn Huìdì divided Dōnghǎi to form Lánlíng Jùn,
he therefore became a native of Lánlíng Jùn.
His ancestor Zhěng crossed the river
and resided in Dōngchéng Lǐ, Wǔjìn Xiàn, Jìnlíng.
At that time, those who temporarily resided south of the Yangtze River [jiāngzuǒ] were all given "overseas" homesteads [qiáozhì běntǔ],
with the addition of "Nán" [South] to their names,
thus becoming Nán Lánlíng people.
Zhěng begot Jùn,
Jùn begot Lèzǐ,
Lèzǐ begot Chéngzhī,
and Chéngzhī begot the Emperor.
In the first year of Jiànyuán (Jǐwèi, 479),
in the fourth month of this year, he received the abdication,
and began to change the era name to Jiànyuán.
1 Spring,
first month,
Jiǎchén,
Xiāo Yí, the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, was appointed as Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of eight prefectures including Jīng and Xiāng, and Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
Wáng Yánzhī, Left Grandee Secretary, was appointed as Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
Xiāo Zǐliáng, Grand Astrologer of Ānnán, was appointed as Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of five commanderies including Kuàijī, and Grand Administrator of Kuàijī.
Last year, Xiāo Yìng and Xiāo Huǎng were already ordered to divide and garrison Yǎn and Yù.
Yí
was Dàochéng’s second son;
Zǐliáng
was Dàochéng’s grandson.
Among the forces south of the Yangtze River [jiāngzuǒ],
none was more important than the upper reaches,
and none was richer than the eastern lands.
Therefore, sons and grandsons were distributed to reside there.
Huì,
read as “wài” in reverse.
Shǒu,
read as “yòu” in reverse.
Initially, Shěn Yōuzhī wanted to gather a multitude,
and encouraged common people to inform on each other.
Many scholars and commoners were implicated and conscripted for labor;
when Yí arrived at the garrison,
he dismissed over three thousand people in one day.
The ceremonial objects of the府州 [fǔzhōu] [official residences and prefectures]
were managed with an emphasis on frugality.
With light punishments and low taxes,
his subordinates were greatly pleased.
2 Xīnhài,
Zé, the Heir Apparent of Jìnglíng, was appointed as Grandee Secretary,
and promoted to the title of General of the Central Army with the privilege of establishing a personal staff and enjoying the same ceremonial honors as the Three Ducal Ministers.
Dàochéng was promoted to the title of Duke of Jìnglíng Commandery,
hence Zé was the Heir Apparent of Jìnglíng.
Zé,
read as “qī gé” in reverse.
3 Grand Preceptor Dàochéng, considering Xiè Fěi to be of great renown,
was determined to draw him in to assist in his cause,
and appointed him as Left Grand Astrologer.
He once held a banquet and discussed stories of Wèi and Jìn with him,
and then said:
"Shí Bāo did not advise Jìn Wén early,
and only cried out sadly upon his death.
Compared to Féng Yì,
he was not someone who understood the opportune moment."
When King Wén of Jìn died,
Shí Bāo rushed from Yángzhōu to attend the mourning,
and wept bitterly, saying:
"The foundation of the enterprise is thus,
yet he ended his life as a subject!"
Féng Yì advised Hàn Guāng to ascend the throne.
Dàochéng said that Shí Bāo was unable to advise Jìn Wén early regarding the matter of abdication,
and comparing him to Féng Yì advising Hàn Guāng,
Bāo was not one who understood the opportune moment;
he wished to move Xiè Fěi with these words.
Fěi,
read as “fū wěi” in reverse.
"King Wén of Jìn served the Wèi court for generations,
and would certainly end his life facing north as a subject;
even if Wèi had followed the precedents of Táng and Yú,
he should still have refused three times to appear all the more virtuous."
This means that by yielding the empire three times,
his integrity and conduct would appear all the more noble.
Jiǎyín,
Fěi was appointed as Attendant at Court,
and Wáng Jiǎn was instead appointed as Left Grand Astrologer.
4 Bǐngchén,
Xiāo Chángmào, Palace Attendant and Yellow Gate Keeper, was appointed as Inspector of Yōngzhōu.
Chángmào
was Dàochéng’s eldest legitimate grandson.
5 Second month,
Bǐngzǐ,
Shàolíng Shāng Wáng Yǒu died.
6 Xīnsì,
the Empress Dowager and the Ruler of Wèi went to the Hot Springs in Dàijùn.
7 Jiǎwǔ,
an imperial edict reiterated the previous command,
ordering the Grand Preceptor to be excused from bowing by name.
Previous command,
see the previous year in the preceding volume.
8 Jǐhài,
the Empress Dowager and the Ruler of Wèi went to the West Palace.
The West Palace
was built by Wèi Tàizǔ in the first year of Tiāncì.
9 Third month,
guǐmǎo shuò,
there was a solar eclipse.
10 Jiǎchén,
the Grand Preceptor was appointed as Chancellor,
managing all state affairs,
enfeoffed with ten commanderies,
and made Duke of Qí.
At this time, he was enfeoffed with the ten commanderies of Qí Jùn in Qīngzhōu, Liáng Jùn in Xúzhōu, Lánlíng, Lǔ Jùn, Lángyé, Dōnghǎi, Jìnlíng, Yìxīng in Nánxúzhōu, Wú Jùn and Kuàijī in Yángzhōu.
His titles of General of Agile Cavalry, Governor of Yángzhōu, and Inspector of Nánxúzhōu remained as before.
Jǐ
sì,
an edict declared that the official ranks, titles, rites, and ceremonies of the state of Qí
should all imitate those of the imperial court.
Bǐngwǔ,
the Heir Apparent Zé was appointed concurrent Inspector of Nányùzhōu.
11 Yáng Yùncháng returned home from Xuānchéng Jùn,
and the Duke of Qí sent someone to kill him.
Yáng Yùncháng served as Grand Administrator of Xuānchéng,
see the first year of Sòng Shēngmíng in the preceding volume.
According to Xiāo Zǐxiǎn’s Qí Zhì: Línchuái Jùn had Líng Xiàn.
Yīng Shào said: The Líng River originates in the southwest of Líng Xiàn and flows into the Huái River.
Lì Dàoyuán said: The Líng River originates in Líng Xiàn,
flows eastward,
passes east of its old county seat,
then flows southeast into the Huái River.
He was the grandson of Yìqìng;
Yìqìng
was the second son of the King of Chángshā,
and inherited Dàoguī’s enfeoffment.
"You are a former intimate of the late emperor,
and a close relative of the imperial clan.
In such circumstances,
how can you long remain safe!
If you were to gather people from inside and outside,
many would likely follow.
The people within the imperial city often harbor this intention,
but unfortunately, there is no one to initiate it."
Zhì immediately reported this to the Duke of Qí.
Gēngxū,
Chuò and his brothers and their associates were executed.
12 Jiǎyín,
the Duke of Qí received the imperial mandate and strategy,
pardoned those within his territory,
and designated Shítou as the Heir Apparent’s palace,
entirely in accordance with the Eastern Palace.
Chú Yuān cited the precedent of Hé Céng, who went from Wèi Grand Commandant to Jìn Chancellor,
and sought to be an official of Qí,
but the Duke of Qí refused.
Wáng Jiǎn was appointed as Right Grandee Secretary of Qí,
concurrently Head of the Ministry of Personnel;
Jiǎn was twenty-eight years old at the time.
Summer,
fourth month,
Rénshēn shuò,
the Duke of Qí was promoted to King,
and enfeoffed with ten additional commanderies.
At this time, an additional ten commanderies were granted: Nánliáng, Chén, Yǐngchuān, Chénliú in Xúzhōu, Xūyí, Shānyáng, Qín, Guǎnglíng, Hǎilíng, Nánpèi in Nányǎnzhōu.
Jiǎxū,
King Zàn of Wǔlíng died,
not from illness.
Historians say that Qí killed him.
Bǐngxū,
the King of Qí was granted special rites,
and the Heir Apparent was promoted to Crown Prince.
On the xīn-mǎo day, Emperor Shùn of Sòng abdicated in favor of Qí [King Xiāo Dào-chéng].
On the rén-chén day,
the Emperor was supposed to appear at the imperial carriage porch,
but he refused to come out,
hiding under a Buddhist canopy.
Since the Jìn dynasty,
there had been a Buddhist chamber in the palace,
for the solemn worship of Buddhist statues.
A precious canopy was placed above to cover them.
The Sòng Emperor hid beneath it.
They used a palanquin to fetch the Emperor.
The Empress Dowager, afraid,
personally led eunuchs to find him.
Jìng-zé persuaded him to come out,
and led him to ascend the carriage.
The Emperor, wiping away tears, said to Jìng-zé:
"Are you going to kill me?"
Jìng-zé replied:
"You will merely move to another palace.
The government's previous taking of the Sī-mǎ family's [throne] was also like this."
The Emperor wept and snapped his fingers, saying:
"I wish that in my future lives, I will never again be born into an imperial family!"
Everyone in the palace wept.
The Emperor patted Jìng-zé's hand and said:
"Surely there's no need to worry excessively;
I will reward Fǔ-guó with a hundred thousand cash."
Jìng-zé was then Fǔ-guó Jiāng-jūn.
The historian said the Emperor was mediocre and dim-witted.
All the officials were present.
Shì-zhōng Xiè Fěi was on duty;
he was supposed to hand over the imperial seal and sash,
but pretended not to know,
saying:
"What public business is there?"
The messenger said:
"Hand over the imperial seal and sash to the King of Qí."
A messenger [chuán-zhào],
subordinate to the Zhōng-shū Shè-rén,
goes in and out to convey imperial decrees.
According to the Nán Shǐ,
in commanderies and prefectures, it was called chuán-jiào,
while in the capital, it was called chuán-zhào.
Xǐ [seal],
(Sī-shì fān).
Shòu [sash],
(sound shòu).
"Qí should have its own Shì-zhōng."
Then he took a pillow and lay down.
The messenger was afraid,
and made Fěi feign illness,
wanting to find an interim person,
wanting to find an interim Shì-zhōng.
"I am not ill,
what is there to say!"
So he walked out of the Dōng-yè-mén in court attire,
then boarded a carriage and returned home.
Then Wáng Jiǎn was appointed Shì-zhōng [to]
hand over the imperial seal and sash.
After the ceremony,
the Emperor rode in a huà-lún-chē.
A huà-lún-chē [painted-wheel carriage]
is a carriage with decorated wheels.
Jìn Zhì says: The huà-lún-chē
had four open views on top,
a green oil-cloth banner,
red silk cords,
the inside of the two side-panels adorned with gold brocade,
gilded,
and five colors.
Xiāo Zǐ-xiǎn says: A lacquered huà-lún-chē,
adorned with gold,
like an imperial carriage [niǎn],
but slightly reduced.
Dù Yòu says: The Jìn system: carriages used lacquered painted wheel hubs,
with four upright staffs on top,
four open views on the left and right,
green oil-cloth, scarlet, and blue silk interlocked above,
shaped like an imperial carriage [niǎn],
but below it was still a calf-carriage [dú-chē].
He asked:
"Why are the drums and wind instruments not played today?"
No one on his left or right responded.
Yòu Guāng-lù Dà-fū Wáng Kūn,
who was Huá's paternal cousin.
Wáng Huá had entered Sòng Gōng's administration early,
assisting in governance at the beginning of Yuán-jiā.
Chuī [wind instruments],
(chǐ-shuì fān).
Cóng [paternal cousin],
(cái-yòng fān);
same below.
At this point,
he clung to the otter-tail on the carriage and wept bitterly.
Otter fur can ward off dust,
so it was hung on carriages.
"People consider longevity a joy,
but this old official considers longevity a sorrow.
Since I could not be the first to [be trampled by] ants,"
meaning he could not die early.
He choked with sobs uncontrollably,
and all the officials wept like rain.
Meaning their tears flowed like rain.
Sòng received the abdication from Jìn in the first year of Yǒng-chū,
which was the gēng-shēn year;
eight rulers,
sixty years, and it perished.
Sī-kōng concurrently Tài-bǎo Chǔ Yuān and others presented the imperial seal and sash,
leading all officials to the Qí palace to urge the King to ascend the throne;
the King declined and did not accept yet.
Yuān's paternal cousin, the former Ān-chéng Tài-shǒu Zhào, said to Yuān's son Bēn:
"Where is Sī-kōng today?"
Bēn replied:
"He is presenting the imperial seal and sash at Qí Dà Sī-mǎ-mén."
Zhào said:
"I don't understand what your family's Sī-kōng means by giving one family's possessions to another!"
On the jiǎ-wǔ day,
the King ascended the imperial throne at the southern suburbs.
Returning to the palace,
a general amnesty was issued,
and the era name was changed.
Emperor Shùn of Sòng was enfeoffed as Rǔ-yīn Wáng,
and the rites of generous honoring [for him]
all imitated those at the beginning of Sòng.
A palace was built in Dān-yáng.
Dān-yáng,
Nán Shǐ writes
"Dān-tú".
Dān-yáng is correct.
Qí Shǐ says: A palace was built in the old county of Dān-yáng.
Sòng's ancestral spirit tablets were moved to Rǔ-yīn Temple,
and all other kings were demoted to dukes;
except for those who had exerted effort for the Qí house,
all others had their states abolished.
Only the three states of Nán-kāng, Huá-róng, and Píng-xiāng were retained,
to honor the descendants of Liú Mù-zhī, Wáng Hóng, and Hé Wú-jì.
Wáng Hóng's descendants did not have their states abolished
because Wáng Jiǎn assisted in the founding [of the Qí dynasty].
Píng,
same as píng.
Píng-xiāng County,
established in the second year of Wú Bǎo-dǐng.
Sòng Bái says.
King Zhāo of Chǔ crossed the Jiāng [Yangtze River]
and obtained a píng-shí [water caltrop] here.
Today, to the north of the county, there are Píng-shí-lǐ and Chǔ-wáng-tái,
thus the county was named after it.
Officials of the two administrations
temporarily assumed their duties according to their previous appointments;
the two administrations refer to the Sòng and Qí administrations.
A separate detailed discussion would follow.
Chǔ Yuān was appointed Sī-tú.
Guests congratulating him filled the seats.
Chǔ Zhào sighed and said:
"Yàn-huí established a good reputation and conduct in his youth,
how could he become so reckless!
Pī-chāng means to be unrestrained and rampant.
Pī,
(pǔ-pí fān).
Shào,
(shī-zhào fān).
Xíng,
(xià-mèng fān).
To actually receive an appointment like this today.
If Yàn-huí had died as a Zhōng-shū Láng,
wouldn't he have been considered a famous scholar?
A person of renowned virtue does not flourish,
yet [he] lives to the age of one hundred!"
Qū Lǐ says: A person's hundredth year is called qī-yí.
Zhèng's commentary says: Qī [期],
means "to require" [yào];
Yí [頤],
means "to nourish" [yǎng];
[at this age] one does not know about clothes, food, or taste,
and a filial son only needs to fulfill the duty of nourishment.
Fèngcháoqǐng Péi Yǐ of Hédōng submitted a memorial,
enumerating the emperor's transgressions and vices.
He hung up his cap and departed directly.
The emperor was enraged
and killed him.
Fèngcháoqǐng
meant merely being summoned for court assemblies;
it was not an official post.
Péi Yǐ, during the Sòng dynasty, had no official post
nor any outstanding and extraordinary integrity.
Yet, merely by refusing to eat Qí grain,
he managed to leave his name in the annals of history.
A gentleman dislikes dying without a name commensurate with his worth,
precisely for this reason.
Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo.
Yǐ,
pronounced yú qǐ.
Shǔ,
pronounced suǒ jù.
The emperor said,
"Killing him would just make his name,
so one should really tolerate him as beyond the pale."
After a long time,
due to an incident, he was dismissed and remained at home.
The emperor asked Liú Huán of Pèi-guó, formerly a staff officer to the Acting Military Governor, about governance.
He replied,
"Governance lies in the Classic of Filial Piety.
All the reasons why the Sòng family perished,
and why Your Majesty obtained the throne,
are found therein.
If Your Majesty learns from the mistakes of the past
and adds leniency and generosity,
even danger can be turned into safety;
but if you follow their disastrous path,
even safety will surely turn into danger."
The emperor sighed and said,
"The words of a scholar
are treasures for ten thousand generations!"
On the 13th day, bǐngshēn,
the Wèi ruler went to Guōshān.
On the 14th day, dīngyǒu,
Zhāng Xù, Prince Regent's Household Administrator, was appointed Central Secretariat Director;
Chén Xiǎndá, Left Guard General of Qí-guó, was appointed Central Protector-General;
Lǐ Ānmín, Right Guard General, was appointed Central Leader of the Army.
Xù
was the nephew of Dài.
On the 15th day, wùxū,
Yí, Inspector of Jīng-zhōu, was appointed Grand Master of Records, General of Agile Cavalry, Grandee Secretary with Ceremonial Privilege, and Inspector of Yáng-zhōu;
Yìng, Inspector of Nányǎn-zhōu, was appointed Inspector of Jīng-zhōu.
The emperor commanded his close officials to each speak of gains and losses.
Liú Shànmíng, Administrator of the two commanderies of Huáinán and Xuānchéng,
(the Huáinán Commandery in the Jiangzŭo region was provisionally established within the borders of Xuānchéng Commandery,
hence Shànmíng simultaneously governed both commanderies)
"requested the abolition of all harsh policies and minor regulations from the Dàmíng and Tàishǐ eras of the Sòng dynasty,
to promote simplicity."
He further believed that
"Jiāozhōu is treacherous and distant.
At the end of the Sòng dynasty, the government was harsh,
leading to resentment and rebellion.
(In the fourth year of Tàishǐ, during Emperor Míng of Sòng's reign,
Lǐ Chángrén occupied Jiāozhōu and rebelled.)
It is advisable to win them over with kindness and virtue.
Moreover, the products of that land
consist only of pearls and jewels,
which are not urgently needed by the imperial court.
Therefore, military expeditions
should, in my opinion, be temporarily halted."
Cuī Zǔsī of Qīnghé, Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, also memorialized,
stating,
"If people do not learn, they do not know the Way."
(Words from the Xúejì chapter of the Lǐjì.)
Shàng,
pronounced shí zhǎng.
"Currently, supernumerary officials
idly receive salaries and services,
exhausting the people's wealth.
(Supernumerary officials
are officials outside the regular quota,
what is later referred to as 'people beyond the limit'.)
Lù refers to
the salary received;
lì refers to
the people employed.
Order the supernumerary personnel in the central government, prefectures, and principalities, each according to their preference,
to engage in their respective professions.
(From the Jiǎshān Biographies in the Hànshū: 'make everyone pursue their profession and uphold their integrity.'
The commentary says: fāng
means 'way'.)
Yuè,
pronounced luò.
Send them back to their native commanderies.
Those excelling in classical arts
should be given irregular promotions.
Furthermore,
although Your Majesty personally practices frugality,
all your subordinates still comfortably indulge in extravagance.
It is advisable to commend and promote court officials who are modest, simple, and upright,
and to demote those who are arrogant, extravagant, dissolute, and licentious.
Then, customs can be changed."
In the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
all matters were entrusted to the commanderies and counties.
Emperor Shìzǔ, demanding things urgently, and finding the commanderies and counties slow,
began to dispatch central government envoys to supervise them.
From then on, envoys were everywhere,
vying to exert power and influence,
engaging in private gain and accepting bribes,
causing trouble for both public and private affairs.
Gōngzǐ Liáng of Wénxǐ, Administrator of Kuàijī, submitted a memorial extensively detailing these abuses,
believing that:
"If the central government has needs,
it should simply issue clear edicts,
setting a deadline,
then people will strive to exert themselves.
If there is any delay,
they should be punished according to the disciplinary code.
Although central government envoys now abound,
their accomplishments are attributed to the directly subordinate officials.
(Meaning, even if there are many envoys,
the work is still done by the subordinates.)
They merely cause further delays and idleness.
It is advisable to abolish all central government envoys."
Liú Sīxiào, Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary, memorialized:
"From the Dàmíng era of the Sòng dynasty onwards,
it gradually declined and became impoverished.
Taxes and levies increased, yet the imperial treasury became even poorer.
(Tiānfǔ refers to
the emperor's treasury.)
There was almost no vitality left;
yet the nobles and wealthy families
competed in luxury and extravagance,
to the extent that even people in the mountains and marshes
dared not gather food from their waters and grasses.
Your Majesty should completely renew the royal laws."
(Wángdù means
royal law.)
All these memorials were commended and rewarded,
or dispatched to the relevant departments
to deliberate on their suitability
and implement them.
On the day jǐhài,
an edict stated:
"The princes of the two palaces
are all forbidden from establishing agricultural estates
or enclosing mountains and lakes."
(The two palaces refer to
the upper palace and the eastern palace.
The upper palace refers to
the princes who are imperial sons;
the eastern palace refers to
the princes who are imperial grandsons.)
Dù Yù said: "Lüè means taking something not by the right way."
He also said: "Lüè
means boundary markers."
On the 17th day, the Wèi ruler returned to Píngchéng.
On the 18th day, Wèi Inspectors of Qín-zhōu Wèi Luòhóu and Yīndūwáng Mùchén, and General of Cháng'ān Garrison Chén Tí, among others, were all punished for greed, cruelty, and unlawful conduct.
Luòhóu and Mùchén were executed;
Tí was exiled to the frontier.
An edict was also issued stating that
"there are thousands of surveillance officers.
(Emperor Tàizǔ of Wèi established surveillance officers
to observe internal and external affairs.)
They raise even minor offenses by 'blowing on a hair' to find fault.
(Meaning, they quibble over trivial matters.)
Instead, several hundred careful and upright individuals should be appointed,
to patrol the streets
and only apprehend those who cause disturbances."
From then on, officials and common people began to live in peace.
On the 19th day, since the Tàishǐ era,
there had been many internal and external troubles.
Generals had each recruited their own units,
garrisoning them in Jiànkāng.
Lǐ Ānmín submitted a memorial,
believing that
"apart from the standing garrisons north of the Huái River,
all other armies should be disbanded
(Shū
means to send away),
and the number of people limited."
The emperor approved this;
in the fifth month,
on the day xīnhài,
an edict was issued to stop all private recruitment.
On the day of Rénzǐ in the 20th year,
the Emperor rewarded those who had assisted him in establishing the dynasty.
Chǔ Yuān, Wáng Jiǎn, and others were promoted in rank and granted increased households, each according to their merits.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Nán Shǐ*'s biography of Cuī Zǔsī states:
"When the Emperor was about to be granted the Nine Bestowals,
everyone, both inside and outside the court, approved.
Zǔsī alone said: 'Your Excellency, you have rectified the state with benevolence and magnanimity,
and upheld the duty of a trusted minister.
A gentleman loves others with virtue;
this is inappropriate.'
The Emperor heard this and disapproved, saying: 'Zǔsī, you are akin to Xún Lìng,
which is not what I expected.'
From then on, he was no longer given official appointments,
but was treated with great courtesy.
Yuán Chóngzǔ received a secret decree
to inquire among the court officials.
Yuán Hóng, Grand Master of Guanglu, said: 'I have received great kindness from the Sòng clan,

I dare not agree to advance,

Cuī Wénzhòng, General of Chángjūn, shared the same view as Chóngzǔ.
When the Emperor accepted the abdication,
Hóng retained his former爵,
while Wénzhòng and Chóngzǔ were both ennobled as marquises,

According to records, when the Sòng dynasty first discussed enfeoffing the Emperor as Duke of Liáng,

"The prophecy says: 'A golden knife, a sharp blade, will cut all equally.'
It is fitting now to use the name Qí,
which truly accords with the mandate of Heaven."
This was followed.
If so, how could Zǔsī have been completely loyal to Sòng?
Thus, this passage is deleted.
"I have finished writing the *Qí Shū*,
and the eulogy says: 'Yuān is from a prominent clan,
and Jiǎn is also a glory of the nation;
without relying on their maternal relatives,
how could they have cared for the state!'"
Diǎn was

Hé Shàngzhī served Sòng,

Jiǎn's mother was Princess Wǔkāng;

Therefore, Diǎn said this.
On the day of Jǐwèi in the 21st year,

Someone causing trouble rushed in and killed the King,

On the day of Xīnyǒu,

Zūnkǎo's younger brother, Sīkǎo,

On the day of Bǐngyín in the 22nd year,

and his late mother, Lady Chén, as Empress Xiào.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Nán Shǐ* places this event in the fourth month, on the day of Jiǎwǔ.
We follow the *Qí Shū* here.
On the day of Dīngmǎo in the 23rd year,
the imperial son Jūn was enfeoffed as King of Héngyáng.
The Emperor said to Yuán Chóngzǔ, Inspector of Yǎozhōu:

the Wèi were originally of the Suǒtóu tribe.
Suǒ is pronounced
with the "gè" sound reversed.)
"Without you, this barbarian cannot be controlled."
Thereupon, Chóngzǔ was transferred to be Inspector of Yùzhōu.
In the sixth month,
on the day of Bǐngzǐ,
Yaó Dáohé, General of Youji, was executed

This event is recorded in the previous volume, under the first year of Shēngmíng of Emperor Shùn of Sòng.
On the day of Jiǎzǐ,
Wáng Zé, the Crown Prince, was established as the Imperial Crown Prince;

On the day of Yǐyǒu,
Emperor Shùn of Sòng was buried at Suìníng Líng.
As the residents of Jiànkāng were mixed and numerous,
with many criminals and thieves,
the Emperor wished to establish a system of tallies and wards for mutual inspection.
Wáng Jiǎn, Right Grandee Secretary, remonstrated, saying:
"The capital region
is where people from all four directions converge.
If tallies must be held,
it will be troublesome for affairs and logically not spacious enough;
as Xiè Ān said, 'Otherwise, how could it be the capital?'"
Thereupon, the plan was abandoned.
Initially,
Lǐ Chángrén, Inspector of Jiāozhōu, died.
His younger cousin, Shūxiàn, took over the provincial affairs.
As his authority was not yet established,
he sent envoys to request an inspector from Sòng.
Sòng appointed Shěn Huàn, Administrator of Nánhǎi, as Inspector of Jiāozhōu,
and Shūxiàn as Huàn's Níngyuǎn Sīmǎ and Administrator of the two commanderies of Wǔpíng and Xīnchāng. (In the third year of Jiànhéng under Sūn Hào of Wú,
he attacked the Fúyán barbarians
and established Wǔpíng Commandery in their territory.
In the same year,
Xīnxīng Commandery was also established by dividing Jiāozhǐ.
In the third year of Tàikāng under Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it was renamed Xīnchāng.
Both belonged to Jiāozhōu.
Suí abolished Wǔpíng Commandery, making it Lóngpíng County,
and abolished Xīnchāng Commandery, making it Jiāníng County,
both belonging to Jiāozhǐ Commandery.
Táng changed Lóngpíng to Tàipíng,
still belonging to Jiāozhǐ,
and made Jiāníng County into Fēngzhōu.)
As the people submitted,
Shūxiàn dispatched troops to guard the passes
and did not admit Huàn.
Huàn stopped at Yùlín
and died of illness.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day of Dīngwèi,
an imperial edict stated:
"Jiāozhǐ and Bǐjǐng are isolated from our calendrical announcements." (This means they refused to obey the imperial mandate and did not accept the correct calendar.
In ancient times,
the Son of Heaven would always, in the last month of winter, issue the first day of each of the twelve months of the coming year to the feudal lords.
The feudal lords would receive and store them in their ancestral temples.
On the first day of each month, they would sacrifice a single sheep to the temple,
request permission, and then carry it out.)
"As they have gone astray and continued in that path,
it is proper to grant a special amnesty to Jiāozhōu,
and immediately appoint Shūxiàn as Inspector
to pacify and stabilize the southern lands."
Yáng Guǎngxiāng, the Lord of Jiālú Garrison of Wèi, requested to surrender.
On the day of Bǐngchén,
Guǎngxiāng was appointed Inspector of Shāzhōu.
According to geographical records,
this Shāzhōu should be located within the boundaries of Jǐnggǔ County, Lìzhōu, in the Táng dynasty.
In the eighth month,
on the day of Yǐhài,
the Wèi ruler went to Fāngshān. (Fāngshān is north of Píngchéng, above the Rúhún River.
The Wèi ruler and Empress Dowager Féng planned to build their tomb there,
so they frequently visited the area.)
On the day of Dīngchǒu,
they returned to the palace.
The Emperor heard that Wèi troops were about to invade.
In the ninth month,
on the day of Yǐsì,
Yí, King of Yùzhāng, was appointed Inspector of Jīng and Xiāng provinces,
with his overall command remaining as before. (In the first month of spring of this year,
Yí was appointed Inspector of Jīng Province
and Overseer of eight provinces.
Now he additionally inspects Xiāng Province.)
On the day of Bǐngwǔ,
Chǔ Yuān, Minister of Works, was appointed concurrently as Grand Secretary.
On the day of Rénzǐ,
Wèi appointed Pī, Attendant Counselor, Minister of the Masses, and King of Dōngyáng, as Grand Commandant.
Chén Jiàn, Attendant Counselor and Right Grandee Secretary, as Minister of the Masses.
Gǒu Tuí, Attendant Counselor, Grand Secretary, and a Dài native, as Minister of Works. (The *Wèi Shū*'s Monograph on Official Titles states: During Shényuán's time,
among the various tribes that entered the interior were those of the Ruògān clan,
who later changed their surname to Gǒu.)
On the day of Jǐwèi,
Chánglè, King Lì of Ānlè of Wèi, plotted rebellion and was granted death.
On the day of Gēngshēn,
Yuán Hè, King Xuān of Lǒngxī of Wèi, died.
In winter,
the tenth month,
38 On the *guǐwèi* day,
Wáng, the Great Queen Dowager of Rǔyīn, died.
She was Empress Wáng of Sòng Míngdì.
When Shùndì abdicated,
she was enfeoffed as the King of Rǔyīn.
The Great Queen Dowager was demoted to Great Queen.
39 Initially,
Lǐ Wūnú, a commoner from Jìnshòu, and Yáng Chéng, a Dī from Báishuǐ, along with others, plundered Liángzhōu.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: The Báishuǐ emerges from the northwest of Xīqīngshān, southeast of Táolín County.
Its water is white and turbid.
It flows southeast into the Yīnpíng region.
The Dī who live along this river are called the Báishuǐ Dī.
They attacked Yáng Chéng

When the affair of Shěn Yōuqī started,
see the previous volume, Sòng Shùndì, Shēngmíng first year.
He claimed to be coming to assist,
but in reality, he was observing the situation.
When the affair was settled,
the imperial court dispatched Wáng Xuánmiǎo to replace him.
An edict ordered Bǎinián to come down with Wūnú.
Wūnú advised Bǎinián not to accept the replacement.
While Bǎinián was still undecided,
Xuánmiǎo had already arrived.
Bǎinián then left Wūnú in Hànzhōng,
returned to Wèixīng,
and hesitated to advance.
Hú Xiézhī of Yùzhāng, the Left Guard Commander, once asked Bǎinián for a horse.
Bǎinián said:
"A horse is not a dog;
how can it fulfill endless demands!"
He treated the envoy very coldly.
When the envoy returned,
he told Xiézhī:
"Bǎinián said: 'What kind of dog is Hú Xiézhī!
His demands are insatiable!'"
Xiézhī resented this
and slandered him to the Emperor, saying:
"Bǎinián relies on the difficult terrain to gather people,
intending to exclusively control one province."
The Emperor ordered Wáng Chángmào of Nánjùn, the Prefect of Yōngzhōu, to lure Bǎinián
and appoint him as Chief Clerk of the governor's office.
When Bǎinián arrived in Xiāngyáng,
the Emperor wanted to forgive him,
but Xiézhī said:
"Having caught a tiger,
will you release it back into the mountains?"
*Gé*
means to capture,
and to fight.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Bǎinián was given death.
Lǐ Wūnú rebelled and joined the Dī,
relying on Yáng Wénhóng.
He led over a thousand Dī soldiers to raid Liángzhōu,
capturing Báimǎshù.
Báimǎshù is north of the Miǎnshǔi,
which is Yángpíngguān.
Wūnú attacked the provincial capital with light cavalry.
Xuánmiǎo ambushed and attacked them,
thoroughly defeating them.
Wūnú escaped alone and fled back to the Dī.
Initially,
Xuánmiǎo was the Prefect of Qīngzhōu.
At the beginning of Sòng Tàishǐ,
Xuánmiǎo occupied Pányáng to resist Wèi, and was consequently appointed Prefect of Qīngzhōu.
He was suspected by Sòng Tàizōng.
See volume 132, Tàishǐ sixth year.
He sent a letter to Xuánmiǎo to establish an alliance.
Fáng Shū'ān of Qīnghé, Xuánmiǎo's Chief Clerk, said:
"The General holds an important position in a major province.
If he abandons loyalty and filial piety without cause,
the men of Sānqí
would rather die by leaping into the East Sea.
Ever since Xiàngyǔ divided and established various kings,
the Qí territory was divided into three kingdoms,
thereafter the Qí region was called Sānqí,
just as Guānzhōng was called Sānqín.
Xuánmiǎo then did not reply to the letter to the Emperor.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Nánshǐ* states:
"He then sent Shū'ān with a memorial to the court to inform them.
The Emperor captured him on the way
and also demanded Xuánmiǎo's memorial.
Shū'ān said: 'General Wáng's memorial is addressed to the Son of Heaven,
not to the General.
Moreover, what I say
benefits the state, not the General,
so there is nothing to answer.'
Xún Bóyù advised the Emperor to kill him.
The Emperor said: 'Each serves his own lord;
there is nothing to blame him for.' "
Comment: At the time, Tàizǔ was a border general.
If he had captured Shū'ān
and not killed him,
he should not have remained a Sòng official.
The *Qíshū* has no record of this incident,
so we do not adopt it here.
When he arrived in Huái'yīn,
he marched straight through with a disciplined army.
Upon reaching Jiànkāng,
he informed Tàizōng
that the Emperor had different intentions.
When the Emperor became the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn),
after Cāngwú was assassinated,
the Emperor advanced to General of Agile Cavalry.
Xuánmiǎo was very afraid,
but the Emperor treated him as before.
After defeating Wūnú,
the Emperor said:
"Xuánmiǎo indeed did not betray my trust and treatment."
Shū'ān was the Prefect of Níngshǔ.
During the Sòng Yǒngchū period,
Guǎnghàn was divided to form Níngshǔ Commandery.
The Emperor wanted to use him for Liángzhōu,
but he died of illness.

on the *xīnhài* day,
Prince Péi was established as Crown Prince.
41 On the *guǐchǒu* day,
Wèi dispatched Jiǎjiāng Jūnshì Wáng Jiā, acting King of Liángjùn, to lead two generals out of Huái'yīn.
Gōng Chēn of Lǒngxī led three generals out of Guǎnglíng.
Xuē Hǔzi, Duke of Hédōng, led three generals out of Shòuyáng.
They escorted Dānyáng Wáng Liú Chǎng to invade.
At the beginning of Jǐnghé,
Chǎng fled to Wèi.
*Jiàng*,
pronounced *liàng*;
same below.
The clan had been enfeoffed in the south of the Yangtze River
and declared allegiance to Wèi.
To establish a state is called *zuò*,
also,
to guard the state is called *zuò*.
In the first year of Sòng Míng Tàiyù,
he surrendered to Wèi.
*Qiú*,
pronounced *cíyóu*.
Xiè Tiāngài, a commoner from Yìyáng, proclaimed himself Prefect of Sīzhōu,
intending to attach the province to Wèi.
Wéi Zhēn, the Garrison Commander of Lèlíng in Wèi, led his troops across the Huái River to meet him.
Wèi established Lèlíng Garrison in Bǐyáng,
now in the Tángzhōu region.
Wéi Zhēn plundered over seven thousand households and left.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The biography of Xiāo Jǐngxiān in *Qíshū* says:
"Tiāngài incited the barbarians.
Jǐngxiān reported to the Governor's office.
The King of Yùzhāng sent Huìlǎng to assist Jǐngxiān in suppressing Tiāngài's faction.
The barbarians soon dispatched the false Southern Commander of the Bureaucracy, Lèibá, to garrison Rǔnán,
and Fèng Shā, King of Chānglí and Prefect of Luòzhōu, to garrison Qīngqiū.
Jǐngxiān made strict preparations to await the enemy.
The barbarians retreated."
The biography of Wéi Zhēn in *Wèishū* says:
"Tiāngài appointed himself Prefect of Sīzhōu,
planning to submit internally.
The matter was exposed,
and he was besieged by Cuī Huìjǐng, a general under Dàochéng.
An edict ordered Zhēn to lead the troops and horses in his garrison across the Huái to support and receive him.
At that time, Dàochéng heard that Zhēn was approaching,
and sent his general Xún Yuánbīn to occupy the Huái River and resist Zhēn.
Zhēn attacked from front and rear,
defeating him.
Tiāngài was soon killed by his own men,
and surrendered to Huìjǐng.
Zhēn advanced triumphantly,
again defeating Huìjǐng,
and led over seven thousand surrendered households to resettle them inland,
memorializing to establish three commanderies: Chéngyáng, Gānglíng, and Yìyáng, to accommodate them."
Comment: Wèi generals Lèibá and Fèng Shā do not exist,
and Huìjǐng was also not the general who attacked Tiāngài.
It is likely that the historians of the two states at that time
each recorded hearsay,
with mutual errors.
We now generally adopt the main points from both histories.
He was the Emperor's cousin.
Wáng Jìngzé, the Prefect of Nányǎnzhōu, heard that Wèi generals were crossing the Huái,
abandoned his post and returned to Jiànkāng.
The soldiers and common people scattered in panic.
But then Wèi ultimately did not arrive.
The Emperor, considering him a meritorious official,
did not question him.
When the Emperor assisted Sòng,
he sent Wáng Hóngfàn, General of Agile Cavalry, as envoy to Ròurán,
agreeing to jointly attack Wèi.
Hóngfàn traveled from Shǔ through Tǔyùhún and the Western Regions to reach them.
By this time,
Ròurán, with over a hundred thousand cavalry, raided Wèi,
reached the frontier, and then returned.
42 In this year,
Wèi decreed that Gāo Yǔn, Supervisor of the Central Secretariat, should deliberate on drafting laws and regulations.
Although Yǔn was seriously old,
his ambition and intellect did not decline.
An edict stated that Yǔn's family was poor and his sustenance meager,
so ten musicians with strings and winds should visit Yǔn every five days to entertain him.
Meals were provided morning and evening.
Beef and wine were delivered on the first and fifteenth of each month.
Clothes, cotton, and silk were supplied monthly.
When he came for an audience, a small table and walking stick were prepared,
and he was consulted on governance.
43 The Qìdān Mòhéfú Wùgān 帥 led over ten thousand households of his tribe to pledge allegiance to Wèi,
settling east of Báilángshuǐ.
The Qìdān chieftain was called Mòhéfú.
The Suí Shū says: "The Qìdān and Kùmòxī are both descendants of the Dōnghú,

The Chū Xué Jì says: "The Lánghé flows northeast of Huánglóngchéng,
which is the Báilángshuǐ."
契,
pronounced qī qì;

帥,

The Jīngmán relied on the mountains and valleys,

Píngchāng Garrison Master Gǒu Yuánbīn defeated them.

Qín Yuǎn fled.
Wèi general Xuē Dàobiāo led his troops towards Shòuyáng.

Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Yuán Chóngzǔ gathered his civil and military officials to discuss the situation.

and dam the Féishuǐ to secure themselves.
All said:
"When Fó Lǐ invaded in the past,
see Volume 125, Sòng Wéndì, Yuánjiā twenty-seventh year.
治,
read as zhí zhī.
佛,
pronounced bì.
His numbers were several times greater than now,
yet we considered the outer city difficult to defend
and retreated to the inner city.
Moreover, the Féishuǐ has always been there,
but we have never dammed it.
We fear it will be laborious and useless."
Chóngzǔ said:
"If we abandon the outer city,
the barbarians will surely occupy it,
build watchtowers externally,
and construct a long siege wall internally,
then we will be easily captured.
Defending the outer city and building a dam
is my unassailable strategy."
He meant his strategy was already determined,
sufficient to control the enemy,
and not open to dissuasion.
According to the Shuǐ Jīng: "The Féishuǐ flows north from Lízāng Pavilion,
passing east of Shòuchūn city."
Erecting a dam here in the northwest
is because the northwest
is the direction of the barbarian attack;
furthermore, the upstream flow could be released to flood the barbarians.
Today, Ānfēng Military Prefecture has Xiǎoshǐdài,
which is where Chóngzǔ breached the dam.
He created a deep trench around it,
and had several thousand men guard it,
saying:
"When the barbarians see the small city,
they will think it can be taken in one go,
and will surely exert all their strength to attack it,
aiming to breach the dam;
I will then release the water to wash them away,
and they will all become floating corpses."
The Wèi people indeed swarmed and attacked the small city like ants.
Chóngzǔ donned a white gauze cap
and was carried in a shoulder palanquin onto the city wall.
In the late afternoon,
he breached the dam and released the water;
the Wèi forces attacking the city were swept and fell into the trench,
thousands of men and horses drowned.
The Wèi army retreated.
7 Xiè Tiāngài's troops killed Tiāngài and surrendered.
8 Since the Xiàojiàn reign of Sòng,
the political order had been lax and chaotic,
and the registers were erroneous.
The Emperor issued an edict to Huángménláng Yú Wánzhī (of Kuàijī) and others to re-inspect and verify them,
saying:
“The yellow registers [huángjí]
are the great record of the people,
and the foundation of the state's governance.
Dù Yòu said: The yellow registers [huángjí]
are the household registers.
會 (huì),
gōng wài fān.
治 (zhì),
zhí lì fān;
below, qiú zhì is the same.
How can they be reformed?”
Wánzhī submitted a memorial,
believing:
“In the Yuánjiā period,
the former Guānglù Dàfū Fù Lóng, though over seventy years old,
still personally handled the registers,
and diligently reviewed and corrected them himself.
隱 (yǐn) means
to sternly investigate the truth of the matter.
This must rely on diligent and clear-sighted magistrates.
Your foolish servant suggests that the registers from the twenty-seventh year of Yuánjiā should be taken as correct,
new clear regulations should be established,
and a single opportunity to confess and repent should be given;
those who remain deluded and do not return [to the truth]
shall be executed according to the regulations;
if there are any falsehoods or obscurities,
the prefectures and counties shall be subject to the same penalties.”
The Emperor followed his advice.
9 The Emperor, seeing that the Mán barbarians frequently rebelled,
divided Jīng and Yì to establish Bāzhōu to suppress them.
On the day Rénshēn,
Míng Huìzhāo, the Sānbā Xiàowèi, was appointed Cìshǐ of Bāzhōu,
and concurrently Tàishǒu of Bādōng.
In the second year of Tàishǐ of Sòng Míngdì,
due to the dangerous narrowness of the Sānxiá and the incursions of mountain barbarians,
there was a discussion to establish a Sānbā Xiàowèi to suppress them,
but it was soon abolished;
it was re-established in the second year of Shēngmíng of Shùndì.
校 (xiào),
hù jiāo fān.
Within the territory of Qí,
there were twenty-three zhōu,
three hundred ninety jùn,
and one thousand four hundred eighty-five xiàn.
The twenty-three zhōu were
Yáng, Nánxú, Yù, Nányù, Nányǎn, Běiyǎn, Běixú, Qīng, Jì, Jiāng, Guǎng, Jiāo, Yuè, Jīng, Bā, Yǐng, Sī, Yōng, Xiāng, Liáng, Qín, Yì, and Níng.
Among the three hundred ninety jùn,
some were temporarily administered,
some were newly established,
some were Lǐ jùn, Láo jùn, desolate jùn, Left jùn, or had no subordinate xiàn,
and some were desolate with no households.
Although many jùn and xiàn were established,
they existed in name only,
and the territory had shrunk since the Dàmíng period of Sòng.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
Cuī Wénzhòng dispatched his army commander Chén Jìng to capture Wèi’s Zhúyì,
killing the garrison commander Bái Zhòngdū;
Cuī Shúyán defeated Wèi’s Suīlíng,
killing Huáiyáng Tàishǒu Liáng È.
Zhúyì
was Zhú xiàn of Pèijùn in Hàn;
in the Later Hàn and Jìn dynasties, it was called Zhúyì,
and later abolished;
Wèi probably established a garrison in the old locality.
Xián said: The old city of Zhú is in modern-day Fúlǐ xiàn, Xúzhōu.
Suīlíng
was a Hàn xiàn,
subordinate to Línhuái;
in the Later Hàn and Jìn dynasties, it was subordinate to Xiàpī.
In the first year of Dàmíng of Sòng Xiàowǔ,
it was reclassified as subordinate to Jìyīn;
at that time, it was incorporated into Wèi,
which established Huáiyáng jùn.
10In the third month,
on Dīngyǒu shuò,
the Shìzhōng Xīchāng Hóu Luán was appointed Cìshǐ of Yǐngzhōu.
Luán was
the son of the Emperor's elder brother, Shǐ'ān Zhēnwáng Dàoshēng;
he became an orphan early
and was raised by the Emperor,
who favored him more than his own sons.
Later, Luán would usurp the throne and kill the Emperor's descendants, setting the stage.
11Wèi’s Liú Chǎng requested to withdraw his troops,
citing the imminent rain season, and the Wèi people granted his request;
on the day Bǐngwǔ,
Chējì Dàjiàngjūn Féng Xī was sent with troops to meet him.
12In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Xīnsì,
the Wèi ruler went to Báidēng Shān;
in the fifth month,
on Bǐngshēn shuò,
he went to Huǒshān;
Dù Yòu said: Yúnzhōu's seat was Yúnzhōng xiàn;
within the xiàn's boundaries were Báidēng Shān and Báidēng Tái.
The Shuǐjīngzhù says: South of Báidēng is Wǔzhōu Chuān;
southeast of the chuān is Huǒshān;
on the mountain are fire wells,
sixty-seven paces north-south,
a little less than a chi wide,
whose source is deep and bottomless;
the flames rise upwards,
constantly making a faint thunder-like sound;
if ignited with grass,
smoke billows and fire erupts.
On the day Rén'yín,
he returned to Píngchéng.
13Since the Jìn dynasty,
the outer wall of the Jiànkāng Palace had only a bamboo fence,
but it had six gates.
Someone then initiated the Bái Hǔ Zūn,
the Jìn Zhì says: On the first day of the New Year's grand assembly,
the Bái Hǔ Zūn was set up in the palace courtyard;
a white beast was placed on the lid of the zūn;
if anyone could offer frank words,
this zūn would be opened to drink wine.
According to rituals,
the Bái Shòu Zūn was an inherited style from Dù Jǔ;
the white beast lid was a later addition,
to show awe.
Bái Shòu
is Bái Hǔ;
the Jìn Shū changed it to Shòu to avoid the Táng taboo.
“The Bái Mén has three layers of gates,
the bamboo fence is never completely repaired.”
The Emperor was moved by these words,
and ordered the construction of a new city wall.
14Lǐ Wūnú frequently seized opportunities to raid Liángzhōu.
Yùzhāng Wáng Yí dispatched Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Wáng Túnán to lead Yìzhōu troops from Jiàngé to ambush him;
the Cìshǐ of Liáng and Nánqín, Cuī Huìjǐng, dispatched Liángzhōu troops to garrison Báimǎ,
and together with Túnán, attacked Wūnú from front and rear,
greatly defeating him,
and Wūnú fled to secure Wǔxīng.
Kǎoyì says: The Wèi Shū Dìjì:
“In the eighth month,
Huìjǐng raided Wǔxīng.”
Here, we follow the Huìjǐng Zhuàn.
He was a kinsman of Zǔ Sīzhī.
15In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Xīnhài,
the Wèi ruler went to Huǒshān.
16On the day Wǔwǔ,
the Imperial Crown Prince Mù Pèi Shì passed away.
After her death,
she was posthumously granted the title Mù.
17An edict ordered Nánjùn Wáng Chángmào to move his garrison to Xīzhōu.
18 The garrison commander of Jiǎochéng surrendered the city to Wèi.
For a note on Jiǎochéng, see next year.
Jiàng (降),
hú jiāng fān.
In the eighth month,
on the day Dīngyǒu,
Wèi dispatched Liángjùn Wáng Jiā (王嘉), the Inspector of Xúzhōu, to welcome him.
They also sent the General Who Pacifies the South, Láng Dàtán (郎大檀), and two other generals from Qúchéng.
Wèi Shōuzhì (魏收志) states: In Lángyá Qú Xiàn (琅邪胊縣) there is Qúchéng.
Qú (胊),
pronounced Qú.
Hǎixī (海西),
is the territory of Hàn Hǎixī Xiàn.
As Sòng Míngdì (宋明帝) lost the area north of the Huái River,
he provisionally established Qīngzhōu in Gànyú Xiàn.
In the seventh year of Tàishǐ,
Gànyú was partitioned to establish Yù Xiàn,
and Hǎixī Jùn was established.
Qí Míngdì (齊明帝) considered it Dōnghǎi Jùn.
In the seventh year of Wǔdìng of Dōngwèi,
Hǎixī Jùn was renamed.
Furthermore, Xiāngbì was divided to establish Hǎixī Xiàn.
Liánkǒu (連口),
is the mouth where the Liánshuǐ River flows into the Huái River.
At that time, it was within the borders of Xiāngbì Xiàn.
Suí renamed Xiāngbì Xiàn to Liánshuǐ Xiàn.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: There is Liánkǒu Ferry in Chǔzhōu Liánshuǐ Xiàn.
Yìng Shào (應劭) said:
Bì (賁),
pronounced Féi.
The General Who Guards the South, Hèluó (賀羅), emerged from Xiàcài.
According to Bānzhì (班志),
Xiàcài,
was the state of Zhōulái (州來) in the Spring and Autumn period,
which was destroyed by Chǔ.
Later, Wú conquered it.
Up to Fūchā (夫差),
he moved Cài Zhāohóu (蔡昭侯) here.
Four generations later, Hóu Qí (侯齊) was eventually destroyed by Chǔ,
hence it was called Xiàcài.
During the Hàn dynasty, it was a county,
belonging to Pèijùn,
but was later abolished.
In the sixth year of Wǔdìng of Dōngwèi,
the garrison of Liáng Huángchéng (梁黃城) was made Xiàcài Jùn.
During the Suí dynasty, it was a county,
belonging to Rǔyīn Jùn.
Judging from the relocation of Yuán Chóngzǔ (垣崇祖) to Xiàcài garrison,
this garrison was established west of the Huái River.
During the Five Dynasties period,
Zhōu Shìzōng (周世宗) moved the seat of Shòuchūn to Xiàcài,
which is this location.
19 On the day Jiǎchén,
the Wèi ruler went to Fāngshān.
On the day Wùshēn,
he visited the Stone Grotto Temple on Wǔzhōushān.
Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) states: The Wǔzhōu River flows southeast.
Beside the river are stone viharas and various cave chambers,
where bhikṣuṇīs resided.
The water then turns east, south of Língyán.
Stones were carved and mountains opened,
forming structures based on the cliffs.
The true forms are immense and magnificent,
rare in the world.
According to Dào Yuán (道元)'s words,
it is a place of grand splendor for the Buddhists.
On the day Gēngxū,
he returned to Píngchéng.
20 Cuī Huìjǐng (崔慧景) sent his Chief Clerk Péi Shúbǎo (裴叔保) to attack Lǐ Wūnú (李烏奴) at Wǔxīng.
He was defeated by the Dī king Yáng Wénhóng (楊文弘).
21 In the ninth month,
on the first day, Jiǎwǔ,
there was a solar eclipse.
22 On the day Bǐngwǔ,
Ròurán (柔然) sent envoys to offer tribute.
23 The Grand Administrator of Rǔnán, Cháng Yuánzhēn (常元真), and the General of Valiant Cavalry, Hú Qīnggǒu (胡青苟), surrendered to Wèi.
24 In the intercalary month,
on the day Xīnsì,
the Commander of the Guards, Lǐ Ānmín (李安mín), was dispatched to inspect the garrisons along the Qīng and Sì Rivers to guard against Wèi.
25 Wèi's Liángjùn Wáng Jiā (王嘉) led a force of 100,000 to besiege Qúshān.
The garrison commander of Qúshān, Xuán Yuándù (玄元度), held firm within the city.
Sūn Mǐn (孫愐) said: Xuán is a surname.
On the day Gēngyín,
Yuándù (元度) greatly defeated the Wèi army.
The imperial court dispatched army commanders such as Cuī Língjiàn (崔靈建) with over 10,000 men from the Huái River to the sea.
They arrived at night,
each raising two torches.
The Wèi army, seeing this,
fled.
26 In winter,
in the tenth month,
Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) repeatedly requested to be relieved of his selection duties,
which was granted.
Jiǎn was given the added title of Palace Attendant.
Hé Jí (何戢), the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince, was appointed to lead the selection.
The Emperor, considering Jí (戢)'s seniority,
wished to add the title of Regular Palace Attendant.
Chǔ Yuān (褚淵) said:
"The Emperor's frequent decree is that there should not be too many officials with the cicada-wing hat and a specific ornament.
Since I and Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) already have the left ornament,
if Jí (戢) is also added,
then there will be three officials with the sable ornament in the Eight Seats.
Since the Hàn dynasty,
the Palace Attendants and Regular Palace Attendants all wore the left sable ornament.
The Directors and Vice-Directors, along with the various department ministers, constituted the Eight Seats.
According to Jí (戢)'s biography: The Emperor was Commander of the Guards,
Jí (戢) was Chief Clerk of the Minister of Works,
they exchanged visits,
and often had joyful banquets.
Jí (戢) was an old acquaintance from the Emperor's time before ascension.
Fù (復),
fú yòu fān.
This would also not be few."
Shěn Yuē (沈約) said: The General of Valiant Cavalry and the General of Agile Cavalry
were both miscellaneous generals in the Hàn dynasty.
Wèi established them as Central Army generals.
By the Jìn dynasty,
the Commander, Protector, Left and Right Guards, Valiant, and Agile generals constituted the Six Armies.
"Not few"
means that the number of people chosen was already numerous.
Shǎo (少),
shī zhǎo fān.
He was given the added title of General of Valiant Cavalry.
27 On the day Jiǎchén,
Yáng Guǎngxīang (楊廣香), the Inspector of Shāzhōu, was made Inspector of Xīqínzhōu.
His son, Jìong (炅), was also made Grand Administrator of Wǔdū.
28 On the day Dīngwèi,
Wèi made Fény Xī (馮熙), King of Chānglí, the Chief Controller of the Western Route.
He, along with the General Who Conquers the South, Huán Dàn (桓誕), marched out of Yìyáng.
The General Who Guards the South, Hèluó (賀羅), marched out of Zhōnglí.
They jointly invaded.
29 The people of the four prefectures north of the Huái River were unhappy to be subject to Wèi.
The matter of the four prefectures entering Wèi can be found in Volume 133, Sòng Míngdì, Tàishǐ third year.
Lè (樂),
pronounced Luò.
The Emperor sent many spies to entice them.
Thereupon, Huán Biāozhī (桓標之), a civilian from Xúzhōu,
Kǎoyì (考異) states: Wèishū (魏書) says Huán Fù (桓富), a civilian from Lánlíng,
is probably Biāozhī.
We now follow Qíshū (齊書).
gathered a crowd and defended Wǔgù,
electing Sīmǎ Lángzhī (司馬朗之) as their leader.
Wèi dispatched Wèi Yuán (尉元), Prince of Huáiyáng, and the General Who Pacifies the South, Xuē Hǔzǐ (薛虎子), to suppress them.
30 In the eleventh month,
on the day Wùyín,
Wáng Sēngqián (王僧虔), the Administrator of Dānyáng, submitted a memorial:
"The prisons in prefectures and counties have a tradition of 'steaming' prisoners to death with hot water,
calling it 'saving the sick,'
but in reality, it is a cruel injustice.
When prisoners were sometimes afflicted with plague requiring sweating,
they would then be 'steamed' to death with hot water.
Shàng (上),
shí zhǎng fān.
And this hidden system controls the lower localities!
I humbly suggest that for a sick prisoner, one must first report to the prefecture,
Cì (刺) refers to the Inspector of the prefecture.
Jùn (郡) refers to the Grand Administrator.
Or it is said: to write down the names of the sick prisoners and report them to the prefecture is called cì.
Zhí sī (職司) refers to the officials in the prefecture who manage刑狱.
Only then should treatment be administered."
Chǔzhì (處治) refers to prescribing medicine and treating the illness.
Shěng (省),
xí jǐng fān.
Chǔ (處),
chāng lǚ fān.
Zhì (治),
zhí zhī fān.
31 On the day Wùzǐ,
Yáng Nándāng (楊難當)'s grandson, Hòuqǐ (後起), was made Inspector of Běiqínzhōu and King of Wǔdū,
garrisoned at Wǔxīng.
In the 32nd year, in the twelfth month,
on the day Wùxū,
Chǔ Yuān (褚淵), the Sīkōng, was made Sītú.
When Yuān entered court,
he used a waist fan to block the sun.
A waist fan
is worn at the waist;
today it is called a folding fan.
"朝" (cháo)
is pronounced 'zhí yáo fān';
the same below.
Someone said:
"To behave in such a manner,
ashamed to show one's face to others,
what good is a fan to block it!"
Yuān replied:
"A cold scholar (hánshì) is disrespectful!"
Xiáng (祥) said:
"If one cannot kill Yuán (袁) and Liú (劉),
how can one escape being a cold scholar!"
This refers to killing Yuán Càn (袁粲)
and Liú Bǐng (劉秉).
Liú Bǐng was Mùzhī's (穆之) grandson.
Xiáng (祥) was fond of literature,
but his character was rigid and blunt.
When he compiled the Sòng Shū (宋書),
he satirized and criticized the abdication of the throne.
Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) secretly reported this,
and he was exiled to Guǎngzhōu (廣州) where he died.
Liú Mùzhī (劉穆之) was a founding minister who aided the Sòng (宋) dynasty.
Xiáng (祥) thus offended Qí (齊),
which can be said to be not shaming his ancestor.
"好" (hǎo)
is pronounced 'hū dào fān'.
The Crown Prince hosted a banquet for court officials at Xuánpǔ (玄圃).
The Eastern Palace had a Xuánpǔ.
Wénjì (文季) angrily said:
"Yuān (淵) calls himself a loyal minister,
but on the day he dies, what face will he have to see Sòng Míngdì (宋明帝)!"
The Crown Prince smiled and said:
"Shěn (沈) is drunk."
The historians say that Chǔ Yuān (褚淵) lost his integrity,
and people could openly criticize him.
"率" (shuài)
is pronounced 'suǒ lǜ fān'.
On the 33rd day, Rénzǐ,
Yùzhāng Wáng Yí (豫章王嶷) was appointed Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監), Sīkōng (司空), and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (揚州刺史).
Línchuān Wáng Yìng (臨川王映) was appointed Dūdū Jīng‧Yōng děng Jiǔ Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì (都督荊‧雍等九州諸軍事)
and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史).
In this 34th year, Wèi (魏) Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Ruì (王叡) was promoted to the rank of Zhōngshān Wáng (中山王)
and given the additional title of Zhèndōng Dà Jiàngjūn (鎮東大將軍).
Twenty-two royal officials were appointed for him.
Zhèng Xī (鄭羲), a Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎), was made his Fù (傅).
All officials from Lángzhōng Lìng (郎中令) downwards were prominent figures of the time.
Furthermore, Ruì's (叡) wife, Lady Dīng (丁氏), was appointed [a title].
This matter was recorded in historical annals,
could it be an honor for Wáng Ruì (王叡)?
1. In spring,
the first month,
the imperial son Fēng (鋒) was enfeoffed as Jiāngxià Wáng (江夏王).
2. The Wèi (魏) people invaded Huáiyáng (淮陽)
and besieged army commander Chéng Mǎi (成買) at Yǒngchéng (甬城).
"甬城" (Yǒngchéng)
should be "角城" (Juéchéng).
The Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註) states: Juéchéng (角城) is in Xìapí Suīlíng Xiàn (下邳睢陵縣),
bordering the Huái River (淮水) to the south.
Its location is at the mouth where the Jì River (濟水) enters the Huái River.
Later, Liáng Wǔdì (梁武帝) established Huáiyáng Jùn (淮陽郡),
and Juéchéng (角城) became a county belonging to it.
Gāo Lǘ (高閭) said: Juéchéng (角城) is eighteen *lǐ* from Huáiyáng (淮陽).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Juéchéng (角城) was established during the Yìxī (義熙) reign of Jìn Āndì (晉安帝),
within the borders of Sùqiān Xiàn (宿遷縣);
the Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) writes it as
"甬城" (Yǒngchéng).
[They] rescued him with army commander Zhōu Pánlóng (周盤龍) and others.
The Wèi (魏) people plundered extensively along the Huái (淮),
and the people north of the Jiāng (江) all fled in terror across the river.
Chéng Mǎi (成買) fought bravely and died.
Pánlóng's (盤龍) son, Fèngshū (奉叔), with two hundred men, broke deep into the enemy lines.
The Wèi (魏) with over ten thousand cavalry spread their wings left and right to encircle him.
Someone reported to Pánlóng (盤龍),
saying,
"Fèngshū (奉叔) has fallen,"
Pánlóng (盤龍) galloped his horse, wielded his spear,
and charged straight into the Wèi (魏) formation,
sweeping all before him.
Fèngshū (奉叔) had already escaped,
but re-entered to look for Pánlóng (盤龍).
The father and son, on two horses, circled and harassed them;
the Wèi (魏) army of tens of thousands dared not confront them.
The Wèi (魏) army was subsequently defeated,
with tens of thousands killed and wounded.
The Wèi (魏) army retreated,
and Lǐ Ānmín (李安民) and others led troops to pursue them,
fighting at Sūnxī Zhǔ (孫溪渚),
and again defeating them.
Sūnxī Zhǔ (孫溪渚) is north of Huáiyáng (淮陽),
by the Clear River (Qīngshuǐ) bank.
3. On the day Jǐmǎo,
the Wèi (魏) ruler went on a southern tour,
Sīkōng Gǒu Tuí (苟頹) remained to guard.
On the day Dīnghài,
the Wèi (魏) ruler arrived at Zhōngshān (中山).
4. In the second month,
on Dīng
Mǎo, the first day of the month,

Wèi Shōu's (魏收) Zhì (志) states: Sìzhōu (肆州) was governed from Jiǔyuán (九原).
In Tiāncì (天賜) second year, it became a garrison.
In Zhēnjūn (真君) seventh year, Sìzhōu (肆州) was established,
administering the three commanderies of Yǒng'ān (永安), Xiùróng (秀容), and Yànmén (鴈門).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Wèi (魏) established Sìzhōu (肆州),
governing Xiùróng Chéng (秀容城).
Xiùróng (秀róng) was originally part of Hànyáng Qū Xiàn (漢陽曲縣) territory.
Zhōu Wǔdì (周武帝) moved Sìzhōu (肆州) to Yànmén (鴈門).
The Buddhist monk Fǎxiù (法秀) misled the masses with sorcery,
planning a rebellion in Píngchéng (平城).
Gǒu Tuí (苟頹) led the imperial guards to round them up,
capturing them all.
When the Wèi (魏) ruler returned to Píngchéng (平城),
the authorities imprisoned Fǎxiù (法秀),
putting a cage-head (lóngtóu) on him, but the iron lock spontaneously unbound itself.
The Wèi (魏) people pierced his neck bone,
praying:
"If there is truly a god,
let the piercing not enter the flesh."
Then they pierced it and paraded him,
and he died after three days.
Some commentators wished to kill all Buddhist monks.
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Qí Shū Wèi Lǔ Zhuàn (齊書魏虜傳) states:
"Xiányáng Wáng (咸陽王) wished to kill all Buddhist monks."
According to research, Xiányáng Wáng Xǐ (咸陽王禧) was still young at the time,
and was only enfeoffed in Tàihé (太和) ninth year,
so this is probably incorrect.
It then ceased.
7. When Yuán Chóngzǔ (垣崇祖) defeated the Wèi (魏) army,

Hearing of its relocation,

On the day Jǐyǒu,

killing and capturing thousands.
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Qí Shū (齊書) writes "丁卯" (Dīngmǎo).
According to the records, the first day of this month was Xīnmǎo (辛卯),
and there was no Dīngmǎo (丁卯).
We now follow the Qí Jì (齊紀).

and concurrently held the position of Commandant for the Southern Barbarians.
After Yí was dismissed,
Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng) Wáng Huàn was appointed to it.
Huàn firmly declined,

it is difficult to restore them from their ruin.

9 In the third month,
on Xīnyǒu, the first day of the month,

10 During Fǎ Xiù's rebellion in Wèi,
more than a hundred people, including Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ) Zhāng Qiú of the Lántái, were implicated,
all of whom were liable for clan extermination due to their rebellious actions.
Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū Lìng) Wáng Ruì requested that only the ringleaders be executed,
and the rest of the party be pardoned.
An imperial edict was then issued:
"Those who would have been executed with their five familial relationships [wǔzú],
shall be reduced to three familial relationships [sānzú];
those for whom three familial relationships [sānzú] would have been executed,
shall have their immediate family [ménzhū] executed;
those for whom immediate family [ménzhū] would have been executed,
shall only have themselves executed."
Over a thousand people were spared.
11 Summer,
fourth month,
on Jǐhài,
the Wèi ruler went to Fāngshān.
Empress Dowager Fēng enjoyed its mountains and rivers,
saying:
"One day I must be buried here,
it is not necessary to be interred with the imperial mausoleum."
So, a longevity tomb was built for the Empress Dowager,
and a Yonggù Stone Chamber (Yǒnggù Shíshì) was also built on the mountain,
intended to be a temple.
The *Commentary on the Water Classic* (Shuǐ Jīng Zhù) states: "On Fānglǐng is the tomb of Empress Wénmíng.
To the northeast of the tomb is the tomb of Gāozǔ.
To the south of the two tombs is the Yǒnggù Hall.
At the four corners of the hall, terraces, steps, railings, balustrades, as well as doors, windows, beams, walls, rafters, and tiles are arranged like pheasants,
all made of patterned stone.
The two pillars in front of the eaves
were made from the Eight Wind Valley (Bāfēnggǔ) stone of Luòyáng,
carved in high relief,
with clouds and pheasants inlaid with gold and silver,
resembling brocade.
On the four sides, both inside and outside the hall,
two stone canopies and green stone screens were erected,
edged with patterned stone,
all depicting loyal and filial figures in high relief,
and inscribed with names of chastity and obedience.
In front of the temple, stone tablets and stone beasts were carved.
The tablet stone was of the finest quality.
Cypress trees lined the left and right,
surrounding the area so densely that it obscured birds and the sun.
In the southern river, two stone pillars (què) stand tall.
Looking down from the imperial road,
the Spirit Spring (Língquán) palace pond
was clear as a painted mirror.
Huán Biāozhī and others had tens of thousands of troops.
They fortified themselves in dangerous terrain and sought assistance;
on Gēngzǐ,
an edict ordered Lǐ Ānmín to lead various generals to go and receive them.
He also sent Zhōushāntú, Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǎnzhōu, to enter Qīng from the Huái River,
doubling back to meet them.
Huán Lěi, a commoner north of the Huái River, defeated the Wèi army at Bàodúgù.
Lǐ Ānmín delayed in coming to their rescue,
and Biāozhī and his group were all wiped out by Wèi.
Several thousand families among the remaining troops managed to return south;
the Wèi people also plundered over thirty thousand people and brought them back to Píngchéng.
The *Kǎoyì* says: "The *Wèi Shū* states:
'The generals on the southern expedition defeated Xiāo Dàochéng's mobile general Huán Kāng at Huáiyáng.
Dàochéng's Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yùzhōu, Yuán Chóngzǔ, raided Xiàcài,
and Fēng Xī, King of Chānglí, defeated him.
Jiǎ Liángjùn, King Jiā, greatly defeated Dàochéng's general,
capturing over thirty thousand people and sending them to Píngchéng.'"
We now follow the *Qí Shū* and *Qí Jì*,
also consulting the *Wèi Shū*.
13 Wèi Rénchéng Kāngwáng Yún passed away.

on Rénxū,
King Xiàng Shū of Dèngzhì sent an envoy to pay tribute to Wèi.
Dèngzhì was

The *Běi Shǐ* says: "Dèngzhì was
the Báishuǐ Qiāng.

Their territory was from Jiētíng in the east,
Píngwǔ in the west,
Wènlǐng in the north,

Some say,
"Dèngzhì was

Dù Yòu says: "Dèngzhì is

'Shǐ' [使],

'Zhǒng' [種],

15 Sixth month,
on Rénzǐ,
a general amnesty was granted.
16 On Jiǎchén,
Wèi Zhōngshān Xuānwáng Wáng Ruì passed away.
While Ruì was ill,
the Grand Empress Dowager and the Wèi ruler frequently visited his home to check on his illness.
After his death,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor (Tàizǎi),
and a temple was erected for him south of Píngchéng.
Over a hundred literati composed mournful poems and eulogies for Ruì.
At his funeral,
over a thousand people, claiming to be relatives or old friends,

The Wèi ruler appointed Ruì's son, Middle Grand Master (Zhōngsàn Dàfū) Xí, to succeed Ruì as Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū Lìng),

18 Autumn,
seventh month,

19 The Emperor sent Staff Officer of the Rear Army (Hòujūn Cānjūn) Chē Sēnglǎng as an envoy to Wèi.
On Jiǎzǐ,
Sēnglǎng arrived in Píngchéng.
The Wèi ruler asked:
"The Qí assisted Sòng for a short time;

He replied:
"Yú and Xià ascended to power and became supreme rulers themselves.
Wèi and Jìn assisted and passed it down to their descendants.
These events are recorded in the annals of Hàn, Wèi, and Jìn."
20 On Xīnyǒu,
Tājī, a separate chieftain of the Ròurán, led his followers to surrender to Wèi.
21 Yáng Wénhóng sent an envoy to request surrender,

Previously,
Yáng Guǎngxiāng had died,

22 During the Shēngmíng (昇明) reign of Sòng (宋),

Upon hearing that the emperor had received the abdication,
Língdàn (靈誕) said to the Wèi (魏) Diǎnkè (典客):
"Diǎnkè (典客)
was an official title in Qín (秦),

During the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
there was also a Diǎnkè Lìng (典客令) as a subordinate official of the Dàhónglú (大鴻臚)."
"Sòng (宋) and Wèi (魏) have maintained good relations,

Now that Sòng (宋) is perishing,
if Wèi (魏) does not come to its aid,
what is the point of our harmonious kinship!"
When Liú Chǎng (劉昶) invaded,
Língdàn (靈誕) requested to be Chǎng's (昶) Sīmǎ (司馬),
but was refused.
In the ninth month,
on the day of Gēngwǔ (庚午),
Wèi (魏) reviewed its troops in the southern suburbs,
and then hosted a banquet for its officials.
Chē Sēnglǎng (車僧朗) was placed below Língdàn (靈誕).
Sēnglǎng (僧朗) refused to take his seat,
saying:
"Língdàn (靈誕) was formerly an envoy of Sòng (宋),
and is now a commoner of Qí (齊).
I beg the Wèi (魏) sovereign to treat him with due ceremony."
Língdàn (靈誕) then quarreled and reviled him.
Liú Chǎng (劉昶) bribed the surrendered Sòng (宋) man, Xiè Fèngjūn (解奉君), who assassinated Sēnglǎng (僧朗) at the gathering.
The Wèi (魏) people arrested Fèngjūn (奉君)
and executed him.
They gave a lavish funeral for Sēnglǎng (僧朗)
and allowed Língdàn (靈誕) and others to return south.
When Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
Zhāoxiān (昭先) fully reported Língdàn's (靈誕) words.
Língdàn (靈誕) was imprisoned and died.
Historians eventually recorded this event.
The character "下" (xià)

I carefully consider that the soldiers in the garrison

Their expenditures are without standard,
and before the replacements arrive,

Hǔzi (虎子) governed with benevolence and love,

At that time, Shào Ān (邵安), the Administrator of Pèijùn (沛郡), and Zhāng Pān (張攀), the Administrator of Xiàpī (下邳), were impeached by Hǔzi (虎子) for corruption.
Pèi (沛) and Xiàpī (下邳) were both under the jurisdiction of Xúzhōu (徐州).

An imperial edict ordered Ān (安) and Pān (攀) to be granted death,

25 The King of Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾), Shíyín (拾寅), died.

In winter,
the tenth month,
on the first day of Wùzǐ (戊子),
Dùyìhóu (度易侯) was appointed Inspector of Xīqín (西秦) and Hé (河) prefectures, and King of Hénán (河南王).
26 Wèi (魏) Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令) Gāo Lǘ (高閭) and others completed the revision of the new laws,
totaling 832 articles.

27 Initially,

The establishment of Gāochāng (高昌) as a kingdom with a king

That year,
his cousin Shǒuguī (首歸) killed Yìchéng (義成) and established himself.
The King of Gāochē (高車), Kězhìluó (可至羅), killed Shǒuguī (首歸) and his brothers.

He established Mǎrú (馬儒) as king.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day of Rénxū (壬戌),

and appointed Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令) Zhāng Xù (張緒) as Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (國子祭酒).
Emperor Wǔ (武) of Jìn (晉) first established the Guózǐ Xué (國子學)

on the day of Gēngshēn (庚申),

On the day of Rénxū (壬戌),
he died in the Línguāng Diàn (臨光殿).
He was fifty-six years old.
A general amnesty was granted.
Gāo Dì (高帝) was profound and magnanimous,
broadly learned and capable in writing.
He was naturally frugal and simple.
Among his personal effects, there was a jade scepter.
The "zhǔyī" (主衣)
was in charge of supplying imperial clothing.
There was a zhǔyī (主衣) treasury in the palace.
"Keeping this is precisely fostering the root of illness!"
He immediately ordered it to be smashed.
He then inspected and checked for any other unusual items,
and all were dealt with according to this example.
He often said:
"If I govern the world for ten years,

the fourth month,
on the day of Gēngyín (庚寅),

The Língqiū Road,

治 (zhì)

10. Lìbù Shàngshū Ji-yáng Jiāng Mì
was by nature obsequious and impetuous.
When Tàizǔ passed away,
Mì regretted not having been included in the dying instructions;
when the emperor ascended the throne,
Mì was again not promoted;
because of this, he harbored resentment and slandered.
Coincidentally, the emperor was unwell,
and Mì visited Yùzhāng Wáng Yí to request a private audience,
saying:
"His Majesty is not just suffering from an illness,
and the Eastern Palace also lacks talent.
What plan do you intend to make now?"
The emperor learned of this,
and ordered Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Shěn Chōng to present Mì's past and present crimes.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Mì was granted death.
When Shěn Yōu-zhī rebelled,
Jiāng Mì proposed the discussion of granting the *jiǎhuángyuè*,
and thereby attained prominence.
Since he had gained unmerited favor through obsequiousness and impetuosity,
it was fitting that he should also bring disaster upon himself through obsequiousness and impetuosity.
11. On the *guǐmǎo* day,
Nánkāng Wénjiǎn Gōng Chǔ Yuān died.
The heir, Shìzhōng Bēn, was ashamed of his father's loss of integrity;
after the mourning period,
he never again served in office,
yielding his noble title to his younger brother Zhēn,
and living in seclusion by his father's tomb for the rest of his life.
12. In the ninth month,
on the *dīngsì* day,
due to national mourning, the Guózǐxuě was abolished.
13. Dī King Yáng Wén-hóng died.
All his sons were young,
so he appointed his nephew Hòu-qǐ as his successor.
In the ninth month,
on the *xīnyǒu* day,
the Wèi made Hòu-qǐ the Prince of Wǔdū,
and Wén-hóng's son Jí-shǐ was made Grand Administrator of Báishuǐ.
The "Wǔ Dài Shǐ Zhì" states: Wǔdū Commandery, Jiànwēi County.
The Wèi established Báishuǐ Commandery.
In the early Zhēnguān era of the Táng,
Jiànwēi was abolished and merged into Jiānglì County.
Hòu-qǐ attacked and defeated them.
14. The Wèi, seeing the Bā and Dī peoples in Jīngzhōu causing unrest,
the Wèi Shìzǔ in the fifth year of Tàiyán established Jīngzhōu in Shàngluò,
administering commanderies such as Shàngluò, Shàngyōng, and Wèixīng.
The Bā and Dī are distinct groups.
Chóng
was the maternal cousin of Xiǎnzǔ.
When he was about to take up his post,
an imperial edict commanded that troops from Shǎn and Qín prefectures be dispatched to escort him.
Wèi Shōu's "Dìxíng Zhì" states: In the eleventh year of Tàihé,
Shǎn Prefecture was established.
This year (referring to the event being described)
was the seventh year of Tàihé,
which needs to be verified.
陝 (Shǎn)
is pronounced *shī rǎn fān*.
The border people lost harmony, originally resenting the Inspector.
Now I am sent by imperial edict to replace him,
and they will naturally be pacified;
only one imperial edict is needed,
there is no need to dispatch troops for self-defense
and cause them fear."
The Wèi court followed his advice.
Chóng then lightly led several tens of cavalry and swiftly arrived at Shàngluò,
proclaiming the edict and offering comfort,
and the populace and barbarians were completely appeased.
Chóng ordered the border garrisons to return all Qí people they had plundered,
and consequently, the Qí people also returned about two hundred of their captives,
and the two borders became harmonious,
with no more alarms of beacon fires.
After a long time,
he was transferred to become the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu.
Yǎn territory had previously been plagued by bandits,
so Chóng ordered each village to establish a watchtower,
and each tower to hang a drum.
When a robbery occurred,
they would beat it violently;
the neighboring villages, upon first hearing it,
would beat once as a signal,
then twice,
then thrice,
and in a moment,
the sound would spread for a hundred *lǐ*;
all would dispatch men to guard strategic points.
Consequently, when a robbery occurred,
no bandit failed to be captured.
Thereafter, all prefectures emulated this,
beginning with Chóng.
15. On the *xīnwèi* day,
Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn Wáng Sēng-qián was appointed Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and Shàngshū Yòu Púyè Wáng Huàn was appointed Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
16. Hóu Chāng-yǔ, Chief Clerk to Sòng's late Prince of Jiànpíng Jǐng-sù, and Wáng Chī, Secretary, along with Liú Jìn, a *xiùcái* recommended by them,
successively submitted memorials extolling Jǐng-sù's virtues and beauty,
and pleaded for justice on his behalf.
Jǐng-sù's death is mentioned in volume 134, fourth year of Sòng Cāngwǔ Wáng Yuán-huī.
為 (wèi)
is pronounced *yú wěi fān*.
In the tenth month,
on the *xīnchǒu* day,
an edict permitted him to be reburied in his old burial ground with the rites of a *shì*.
Jìn
was the younger brother of Huán.
17. In the eleventh month,
Wèi Gāozǔ intended to personally offer sacrifices at the Seven Ancestral Temples,
and ordered the officials concerned to prepare the rituals and regulations,
according to ancient customs, preparing sacrificial animals, utensils, attire, and musical scores;
from then on, all seasonal regular sacrifices were performed.
Shìzǔ Wǔ Huángdì Shàngzhīshàng
His personal name was Zé,
courtesy name Xuān-yuǎn, the eldest son of Gāo-dì.
Yǒngmíng First Year (*guǐhài*, 483 CE)
1. In spring,
in the first month,
on the *xīnhài* day,
the emperor offered sacrifice at the southern suburb,
granted a general amnesty,
and changed the reign title.
2. An edict stated that as the borders were peaceful and calm,
officials governing the people
would have their field income universally restored.
In the twenty-seventh year of Yuánjiā of Sòng Wéndì,
there were Wèi armies,
and due to military expenditures, the stipends of all officials were reduced.
Huáinán Tàishǒu Zhūgě Chǎn requested a reduction in salary,
comparing it to inner court officials,
whereupon all Cóngshì and Wèi officials in various prefectures, commanderies, and counties
also had their salaries reduced.
By the time of Míngdì,
military campaigns were ceaseless,
and the imperial treasury was empty,
so the stipends of all officials, both inside and outside the court,
were cut.
治 (zhì)
is pronounced *zhí zhī fān*;
the same applies below.
3. Tàiwèi Yùzhāng Wáng Yí was appointed concurrently as Tàizǐ Tàifù.
Yí did not participate in court affairs,
but often secretly offered strategies and plans,
and the emperor largely followed them.
4. On the *rénxū* day,
Imperial brother Ruì was established as Prince of Nánpíng,
Kēng as Prince of Yídū,
Imperial son Zǐ-míng as Prince of Wǔchāng,
and Zǐ-hǎn as Prince of Nánhǎi.
5. In the second month,
on the *xīnsì* day,
Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Yáng Jiǒng was appointed Inspector of Shāzhōu and Prince of Yīnpíng.
Jiǒng
was the son of Yáng Guǎng-xiāng.
炅 (Jiǒng)
is pronounced *gǔ jiǒng fān*,
and also *gǔ huì fān*.
6. On the *xīnchǒu* day,
Dàngchāng Wáng Liáng Mí-jī was appointed Inspector of Hé and Liáng prefectures,
and Dèngzhì Wáng Xiàng Shū was appointed Inspector of Xīliáng Prefecture.
7 In the late Sòng [Dynasty],
it was deemed that a six-year term for officials governing the people was too long.
Thus, a three-year term was set as the limit,
called xiǎomǎn (小滿).
However, transfers and changes of officials
could not always adhere to the three-year system.
In the third month,
on the Guǐchǒu day,
an edict stated:
"From now on, all shall be limited to the xiǎomǎn term."
8 The officials concerned requested a ritual of supplication, citing astrological anomalies.
The Emperor said,
"Responding to Heaven should be based on substance, not ceremony.
I strive to be self-disciplined and seek good governance,
hoping to promote benevolent policies.
If the calamities lie with me,
what good would supplication do!"
9 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the Rénwǔ day,
an edict proclaimed:
"Though Yuán Càn, Liú Bǐng, and Shěn Yōuzhī
did not end their lives well,
their initial sincerity is commendable."
All three were ordered to be reburied with proper rites.
The deaths of these three men are recorded in volume 134, under the third year of Shēngmíng, Emperor Shùn of Sòng.
10 When the Emperor was crown prince,
he considered himself to be of mature age,
having founded the great enterprise alongside Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ).
During the rebellion of Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn,
the Emperor also raised troops.
When Shěn Yōuzhī rebelled,
the Emperor held Pénchéng, acting as the commander for all armies.
In most cases, he made decisions independently
and often violated established rules.
He trusted his close attendants, Zhāng Jǐngzhēn.
Jǐngzhēn was arrogant and extravagant;
his clothing and possessions
presumptuously imitated those of the imperial carriage.
Those inside and outside the court feared him,
and none dared to speak out.
Sīkōng Zīyì Xún Bóyù,
who had always been highly favored by Grand Ancestor,
Zīyì
refers to Zīyì Cānjūn.
said, "What the Crown Prince does,
I, an official, cannot remain ignorant of.
How can I fear death
and cover my ears and eyes!
If I do not report it,
who will?"
When the Crown Prince went to pay respects at the imperial mausoleums—
these were the mausoleums of Yǒng'ān and Tài'ān,
both located in Wǔjìn—
Grand Ancestor became enraged
and ordered an inspection of the Eastern Palace.
When the Crown Prince returned from paying respects at the mausoleums,
he reached Fāngshān
late in the day
and was about to moor his boat.
To the northeast of Jiànkāng city, there was Fāngshān Dài,
which the Zhídú canal passed through.
According to the biography of Shěn Yǔ,
Fāngshān Dài was in Húshú Xiàn jiè.
Dù Yòu said: "From Eastern Jìn to Chén,
there was Shítóu Jīn to the west
and Fāngshān Jīn to the east.
Each had one Jīnzhǔ,
one Zéicáo, and five Zhíshuǐ to inspect prohibited goods."
Sòng Bái said: "The Dānyáng Jì records: Qín Shǐhuáng dug through Fāngshān in Jīnlíng,
creating a canal at the break.
