This means the current Huáishǔi flows through the city into the Dàjiāng,
which is called Qínhuái."
Fēiyàn
was the name of a famous horse.
The Crown Prince returned to the palace that night.
Grand Ancestor also waited for him, holding the palace keys.
The next day,
Grand Ancestor sent Nánjùn Wáng Chángmào and Wénxǐ Gōng Zǐliáng to deliver an imperial edict of reprimand,
and also showed them Zhāng Jǐngzhēn's crimes,
ordering them to arrest Jǐngzhēn under the Crown Prince's command
and execute him.
The Crown Prince, anxious and fearful,
feigned illness.
Over a month later,
Grand Ancestor's anger had not subsided.
While he was sleeping during the day in Tàiyáng Diàn,
Wáng Jìngzé entered directly,
prostrated himself, and reported to Grand Ancestor:
"Your Majesty has held the empire for only a short time.
The Crown Prince is being blamed without cause,
causing fear among the people.
I beg Your Majesty to go to the Eastern Palace to reconcile with him."
Grand Ancestor remained silent.
Jìngzé then loudly proclaimed an imperial order
to prepare for a trip to the Eastern Palace,
and also ordered the Tàiguān to prepare a feast,
calling for attendants to fetch a palanquin.
Grand Ancestor showed no intention of moving.
Jìngzé fetched clothes and dressed Grand Ancestor,
then forcefully helped him into the palanquin.
Grand Ancestor, having no choice, went to the Eastern Palace
and summoned the various princes for a banquet at Xuánpǔ.
Chángshā Wáng Huǎng held the huágài (ceremonial umbrella),
zhuō (捉) here also means zhí (執).
and a pheasant-tail fan,
made of pheasant feathers
to shield the imperial carriage.
Nánjùn Wáng Chángmào served wine.
The Crown Prince, Yùzhāng Wáng Yí, and Wáng Jìngzé personally served the wine and dishes.
They drank until evening
and returned only when thoroughly drunk.
Grand Ancestor praised Bóyù's loyalty,
trusting him even more.
Many confidential military and state affairs
were entrusted to him,
and his influence swayed the court.
When he mourned his mother's death,
his house, about two *lǐ* away,
was already besieged by carriages of officials.
Zuǒshuài Xiāo Jǐngxiān and Shìzhōng Wáng Yàn went together to condole with him.
From dawn until dusk,
they only just managed to advance.
By the time they left,
they were hungry and exhausted,
their breath faint,
and their indignation evident in their voices and expressions.
The next day,
they spoke to Grand Ancestor, saying:
"The gates of the two imperial palaces
that your humble servants have seen
could be set with a sparrow net compared to Xún Bóyù's residence."
"A sparrow net can be set outside the gate"
is a phrase from the Hànshū.
Shīgǔ's commentary says:
"It means it is so quiet that no one walks there."
He was a cousin of Jìnghóng.
Wáng Jìnghóng was employed during the Yuánjiā period.
Cóng (從)
is pronounced cái yòng (才用).
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Chén Yǐnshú
had also previously reported the faults of Jǐngzhēn and the Crown Prince,
but he told the Crown Prince that
"Bóyù reported it."
The Crown Prince thus deeply resented Bóyù.
Grand Ancestor secretly intended to replace the Crown Prince with Yùzhāng Wáng Yí.
However, Yí served the Crown Prince even more diligently,
so the Crown Prince's brotherly affection did not wane.
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Yuán Chóngzǔ did not align himself with the Crown Prince.
Coincidentally, Chóngzǔ defeated the Wèi army,
as recorded under the third year of Jiànyuán, Emperor Tàizǔ.
He secretly plotted with him.
The Crown Prince suspected this
and treated him with extra courtesy,
saying:
"I have cast aside the rumors in the world.
From now on, I entrust wealth and honor to you."
Chóngzǔ bowed in thanks.
Coincidentally, Grand Ancestor again sent Xún Bóyù
with orders concerning border affairs,
instructing him to depart that night after receiving the command
and not to bid farewell to the Eastern Palace.
The Crown Prince believed this showed a lack of sincerity
and resented him even more.
On his deathbed,
Grand Ancestor pointed to Bóyù, entrusting him to the Crown Prince.
After the Emperor ascended the throne,
Chóngzǔ was successively promoted to Wǔbīng Shàngshū,
and Bóyù to Sànqí Chángshì.
Bóyù harbored inner apprehension and fear.
The Emperor, knowing Bóyù was close to Chóngzǔ,
feared they might cause trouble
and paid extra attention to conciliating him.
On the Dīnghài day,
an edict falsely accused Chóngzǔ of colluding with the wild people north of the Jiāng river
and planning a rebellion with Bóyù.
Both were arrested and executed.
11 On the Gēngzǐ day,
the Wèi ruler went to Guōshān;
on the Rén Yín day,
he returned to the palace.
12 In the intercalary month,
on the Guǐchǒu day,
the Wèi ruler's concubine, Píngliáng Línshì,
gave birth to a son, Xún.
Later, Northern Wèi established Píngliáng Jùn by dividing Āndìng Jùn,
administering Qúnyīn and Yīnmì two counties.
Empress Dàhòu Wénmíng, believing Xún was destined to be Crown Prince,
ordered Línshì to commit suicide
and personally raised Xún.
13 In the fifth month,
on the Wùyín day (the first day of the month),
the Wèi ruler went to the Buddhist grotto temples on Wǔzhōushān.
14 Chēqí Jiāngjūn Zhāng Jìng'ér (車騎將軍 張敬兒) was fond of believing in dreams.
When he first became the Nányáng (南陽) Administrator,
his wife, Shàng Shì (尚氏), dreamt that one of her hands was hot like fire.
When he became the Yǒngzhōu (雍州) Governor,
she dreamt one of her shoulder blades was hot.
When he was granted the title of kāifǔ (開府),
she dreamt half her body was hot.
Jìng'ér (敬兒) harbored boundless ambitions,
and often told his intimates:
"My wife has dreamt again that her whole body is hot!"
He also claimed to have dreamt that the trees in his old village temple had grown as tall as the sky.
The Emperor heard of this and disliked it.
When Yuán Chóngzǔ (垣崇祖) died,
Jìng'ér (敬兒) became inwardly suspicious.
Coincidentally, someone reported that Jìng'ér (敬'ér) had sent people to the Southern Barbarian lands for trade.
Huòyì (貨易)
means tràdé (貿易),
to exchange what one possesses
for what one lacks.
Coincidentally, the Emperor was holding an Eight Precepts Fast (bāguānzhāi 八關齋) in the Huálín Yuán (華林園).
The Buddhist precepts are: 1.
Not to kill living beings;
Not to steal;
Not to engage in sexual misconduct;
Not to lie;
Not to drink alcohol or eat meat;
Not to wear flower garlands, necklaces,
or apply fragrant oils to the body, nor to purposefully watch or listen to singing, dancing, or entertainment;
Not to sit on high, wide, or large beds;
Not to eat after the noon fast.
The eight precepts listed above
are called the Eight Precepts.
The Zálù Míngyì (雜錄名義) states: "The Eight Precepts are
the precepts observed by lay devotees for one day and one night."
Referring to the eight precepts and one fast,
commonly called the Eight Precepts Fast,
clearly meaning a practice of prohibition and prevention.
Jìng'ér (敬'ér) was arrested at the gathering.
Jìng'ér (敬'ér) took off his cap and mink and threw them to the ground, saying:
"These things misled me!"
On the day of Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
Jìng'ér (敬'ér) was killed,
along with his four sons.
Jìng'ér's (敬兒) younger brother, Gōng'ér (恭兒),
always worried about being implicated by his elder brother's misfortunes.
He resided in Guānjùn (冠軍).
Guānjùn Xiàn (冠軍縣) had been part of Nányáng Jùn (南陽郡) since the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
In the Táng (唐) dynasty, it was Línkuān Xiàn (臨湍縣) of Dèngzhōu (鄧州).
In our dynasty, at the beginning of Jiànlóng (建隆), Línkuān (臨湍) was abolished and merged into Rǎnxìan (穰縣).
Guān (冠) is pronounced as gǔ wán (古玩) (old play/toy).
His village was deep and secluded,
with multiple layers of walls and fences.
Whenever Jìng'ér (敬'ér) sent a messenger,
Gōng'ér (恭兒) would immediately mount his horse and attach his quiver
before seeing them.
When news of Jìng'ér's (敬'ér) defeat arrived,
he quickly fled into the Southern Barbarian lands.
Later he came out on his own,
and the Emperor pardoned him.
Jìng'ér's (敬兒) daughter was the daughter-in-law of Xiè Chāozōng (謝超宗), Advisor to the Zhēngběi Cānjūn (征北諮議參軍).
Chāozōng (超宗) said to Dānyáng Yǐn (丹楊尹) Lǐ Ānmín (李安民):
" 'Last year Hàn Xìn (韓信) was killed,
this year Péng Yuè (彭越) was killed.'
What plan do you, Your Excellency, have?!"
This quotes Xuē Gōng's (薛公) words from the Hàn Shū (漢書),
meant to provoke Ānmín (安民)
into rebellion.
The Emperor had long disliked Chāozōng's (超宗) arrogance and disrespect,
so he ordered Yuán Tuàn (袁彖), concurrent Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞), to impeach Chāozōng (超宗).
On the day of Dīngsì (丁巳),
Chāozōng (超宗) was arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi (廷尉),
and exiled to Yuèxī (越嶲).
He was granted death on the way.
Because Tuàn's (彖) language was not sharp or precise,
the Emperor also ordered Zuǒchéng (左丞) Wáng Qūnzī (王逡之) to impeach Tuàn (彖) for his superficial and brief memorial,
which undermined the law and tolerated wrongdoing.
Tuàn (彖) was dismissed from office
and prohibited from holding office for ten years.
Chāozōng (超宗) was Lǐngyùn's (靈運) grandson;
Chāozōng (超宗) was the son of Lǐngyùn's (靈運) son Fèng (鳳).
He was also the disciple of Yǐ (顗).
Yuán Yǐ (袁顗) died during the calamity of Yìjiā (義嘉).
Yǐ (顗) is pronounced as yú qǐ (魚豈).
15 In autumn,
seventh month,
on the day of Dīngchǒu (丁丑),
the Wèi (魏) ruler and the Empress Dowager went to Shényuān Chí (神淵池).
In the first year of Tàihé (太和) of Wèi (魏),
the Yǒnglè Yóuguān Diàn (永樂遊觀殿) was built in the Northern Park,
and the Shényuān Chí (神淵池) was dug.
On the day of Jiǎshēn (甲申),
they went to Fāngshān (方山).
16 The Wèi (魏) envoy, acting Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍) Lǐ Biāo (李彪) from Dùnqīu (頓丘), came to offer tribute.
17 Shìzhōng (侍中), Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū (左光祿大夫), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司) Wáng Sēngqián (王僧虔) firmly declined the Kāifǔ (開府) position.
Last year,
Wáng Sēngqián (王僧虔) was appointed Kāifǔ (開府).
"You hold an important position in the court,
and your conduct has reached the level of the Sānsī (三司).
If I were to receive this appointment again,
it would mean that one family has two of the highest officials,
which I truly fear."
He declined it for several years,
until the Emperor finally allowed it.
On the day of Wùxū (戊戌),
Sēngqián (僧虔) was granted the special title of Tèjìn (特進).
Jiǎn (儉) built the Chángliáng Zhāi (長梁齋),
whose scale was slightly excessive.
Sēngqián (僧虔) looked at it,
was displeased,
and ultimately did not enter the door.
Jiǎn (儉) immediately demolished it that same day.
Originally,
Wáng Hóng (王弘) gathered with his brothers,
and allowed his grandsons to play freely.
Sēngdá (僧達) jumped to the ground like a tiger cub;
Sēngchuò (僧綽) sat properly,
arranging candle wax beads into a phoenix.
Sēngdá (僧達) snatched and broke it,
without any regret.
Sēngqián (僧虔) stacked twelve Go (bóqí 博棋) pieces,
neither letting them fall
nor restarting.
Hóng (弘) sighed:
"Sēngdá (僧達) is sharp and spirited,
and will be no less than others,
but I fear he will ultimately endanger our family.
Sēngdá's (僧達) death is recorded at the end of volume 128 in the third year of Shìzǔ Xiàojiàn (世祖孝建).
Sēngqián (僧虔) will surely become a venerable man,
rising to the rank of Gōngtái (公台)."
And indeed, all came true as he said.
18 In the eighth month,
on the day of Gēngshēn (庚申),
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (驍騎將軍) Wáng Hóngfàn (王洪範) returned from the Ròurán (柔然),
having traveled over thirty thousand li.
Jīngtú (經塗)
refers to the path traveled.
The mission of Wáng Hóngfàn (王洪範)
is mentioned in the second year of Gāodì Jiànyuán (高帝建元).
Huán (還) is pronounced as cōng xuān (從宣) (follow Xuān),
or as the character itself.
19 In winter,
tenth month,
on the day of Bǐngyín (丙寅),
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (驍騎將軍) Liú Zuǎn (劉纘) was sent to Wèi (魏) as an envoy.
Wèi Zhǔkèlìng (魏主客令) Lǐ Ānshì (李安世) presided over him.
Zhǔkèlìng (主客令) is the same as Diǎnkèlìng (典客令).
He had merchants sell his goods in the market.
Zuǎn (纘) said:
"Gold and jade are very cheap in Wèi (魏),
it must be due to the abundance from their mountains and rivers."
Ānshì (安世) said:
"The sacred dynasty does not value gold and jade,
hence they are as cheap as瓦礫 (wǎlì)."
Zuǎn (纘) initially intended to buy many,
but upon hearing his words,
he felt inwardly ashamed and stopped.
Zuǎn (纘) frequently served as an envoy to Wèi (魏),
and Empress Dowager Féng (馮) eventually took him as a private lover.
The historians say Empress Féng (馮) was licentious and unrestrained.
Shǐ (使) is pronounced as shū lì (疏吏) (sparse official);
the same below.
20 Twelfth month,
on the first day of Ěrsì (乙巳),
there was a solar eclipse.
21 On the day of Guǐchǒu (癸丑),
Wèi (魏) began to prohibit marriage between people of the same surname.
22 Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) was promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn (衞將軍),
and participated in overseeing selections.
23 In this year,
Bāzhōu (巴州) was abolished.
The establishment of Bāzhōu (巴州) is mentioned in the second year of Gāodì Jiànyuán (高帝建元).
24 Wèi Qínzhōu Cìshǐ (魏秦州刺史) Yú Luòhóu (于洛侯) was cruel by nature.
When punishing people, he would surely
sever their wrists,
pull out their tongues,
and hang their four limbs separately.
The entire prefecture was terrified,
and the prefectural citizens, Wáng Yuánshòu (王元壽) and others, all rebelled at once.
The authorities impeached him,
and the Wèi (魏) ruler sent an envoy to the prefecture.
At the usual place where Luòhóu (洛侯) executed people, he announced it to the officials and common people,
and then beheaded him.
Qízhōu Cìshǐ Hán Qílín
governed with leniency.
His Cóngshì, Liú Pǔqìng, said to Hán Qílín:
"You wield your authority across the land,
yet you have not executed anyone.
How can you demonstrate your might?"
Hán Qílín said:
"Punishment is for stopping evil.
A benevolent person uses it only as a last resort.
If the people do not violate the law,
why should I punish them?
If it is absolutely necessary to execute someone to establish authority,
I should use you for that purpose!"
Liú Pǔqìng, feeling ashamed and fearful, rose and left.
Niè Chóngqí punctuated, Wáng Chóngwǔ re-collated
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command
Later Learning Tiāntái
Shìzǔ Wǔ Huángdì, Volume Upper-Lower
Yǒngmíng Second Year (Jiǎzǐ, 484 CE)
1 Spring,
First month,
on the Yǐhài day,
Liǔ Shìlóng, formerly Hòujiāngjūn, was appointed Shàngshū Yòupúshè;
Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng was made Hùjūnjiāngjūn concurrently Sītú,
given command of troops and authorized to appoint assistants,
to guard Xīzhōu.
Zǐliáng was from a young age known for his purity and elegance,
and devoted himself to receiving guests.
Talented and outstanding scholars
all gathered at his gate.
He opened the West Mansion,
according to the biography of Zǐliáng;
the West Mansion was on Jīlóng Shān.
Jìshì Cānjūn Fàn Yún, Xiāo Chēn, Yuè'ān Rèn Fǎng, Fǎcáo Cānjūn Wáng Róng, and Wèijūn Dōnggékìjiǔ Xiāo Yǎn,
Jìshì Cānjūn,
managed secretarial affairs;
Fǎcáo Cānjūn,
managed criminal law.
These were all subordinates in Zǐliáng’s residence.
At that time, Wáng Jiǎn was Wèijiāngjūn,
and appointed Xiāo Yǎn as Dōnggéjìjiǔ.
Since the Jìn dynasty,
among the staff of ducal residences,
below the Chángshǐ, there were Dōnggé and Xīgé Jìjiǔ.
Chēn,
pronounced as chǒu lín.
Rèn,
pronounced as rén.
Fǎng,
pronounced as fú wǎng.
Bùbīng Xiàowèi Shěn Yuē, and the Xiùcai from Yángzhōu, Lù Chuí of Wú郡,
were all renowned for their literary talent,
and were especially favored and trusted,
known as the Eight Friends.
Fǎcáo Cānjūn Liǔ Yùn,
Tàixué Bóshì Wáng Sēngrú,
Jìn Wǔdì established Tàixué Bóshì, Tàicháng Bóshì, and Guózǐ Bóshì.
Gé,
was a Xiùcai recommended by Nánxúzhōu.
Jìyáng Jùn was at that time subordinate to Nánxúzhōu.
Jì,
pronounced as zǐ lǐ.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
among the various departments of the Shàngshū,
the Diànzhōng Láng was the head of all departments.
Zhěn,
pronounced as zhāng rěn.
Chēn,
was the paternal cousin of Huìkāi;
Xiāo Huìkāi is mentioned in Volume 131, Sòng Míngdì Tàishǐ First and Second Years.
Cóng,
pronounced as cái yòng;
same below.
the paternal grandnephew of Yuánjǐng;
Róng,
the grandson of Sēngdá;
Liǔ Yuánjǐng distinguished himself with military achievements during the reigns of Sòng Wén and Wǔ.
Wáng Sēngdá advanced due to his prestigious family background and talent.
the son of Shùnzhī;
Xiāo Shùnzhī,
was a clan cousin of Tàizǔ.
the grandson of Shù;
Yuē,
the son of Pú;
Sēngrú,
the great-grandson of Yǎ;
Xiè Shù is mentioned in Volume 123, Sòng Wéndì Yuánjiā Seventeenth Year.
Shěn Pú was meritorious in defending Xūyí;
in Yuánjiā Twenty-seventh Year,
at the beginning of Xiàowǔ Xiàojiàn,
he was executed for not welcoming the righteous army.
Wáng Yǎ is mentioned in Volume 107, Jìn Xiàowǔ Tàiyuán Fifteenth Year.
was the paternal cousin of Yún.
Zǐliáng was earnestly devoted to Buddhism,
attracting famous monks
to lecture and discuss Buddhist teachings.
The flourishing of both clergy and laity
was unprecedented in Jiāngzuǒ.
Sometimes, he personally served food and water to the monks,
which people at the time considered inappropriate for a Zǎixiàng.
Fàn Zhěn vehemently argued for the non-existence of Buddha.
Zǐliáng said:
"You do not believe in cause and effect."
Buddhism has the teaching of cause, condition, and karmic retribution.
Fàn Zhěn said:
"Human life is like tree blossoms blooming together,
scattered by the wind: some drift onto curtains and fall onto cushions,
while others hit fences and walls and fall into cesspits.
Those who fall onto cushions,
Your Highness is among them;
those who fall into cesspits,
your humble servant is among them.
Although nobility and humbleness follow different paths,
where then is cause and effect?"
Zǐliáng had no reply.
Fàn Zhěn also wrote the 'Discourse on the Extinction of the Spirit' (Shénmièlùn),
arguing:
"The body is the substance of the spirit,
and the spirit is the function of the body.
The spirit to the body
is like sharpness to a knife;
it has never been heard that a knife perishes and its sharpness remains,
how then can the body perish and the spirit endure?"
When this treatise came out,
the court and populace were in an uproar,
but ultimately could not refute him.
Wáng Yǎn of Tàiyuán wrote a treatise to ridicule Fàn Zhěn, saying:
"Alas, Master Fàn!
He doesn't even know where the spirits of his ancestors are!"
He intended to prevent Fàn Zhěn from responding further.
Fàn Zhěn replied:
"Alas, Master Wáng!
You know where the spirits of your ancestors are, yet you cannot sacrifice your life to follow them!"
Zǐliáng had Wáng Róng say to him:
"With your talent and virtue,
why fear not reaching the rank of Zhōngshū Láng?
Yet you deliberately create this perverse treatise."
Zhōngshū Láng,
refers to Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Là,
pronounced as lái gé.
"You should quickly destroy and discard it."
Fàn Zhěn laughed loudly and said:
"If Fàn Zhěn were to sell his treatise for an official position,
he would already be at the rank of Lìng and Pú."
Lìng and Pú,
refer to Shàngshū Lìng and the two Púshè.
Xiāo Yǎn was fond of strategy and calculation,
possessing both literary and military talent.
Wáng Jiǎn highly esteemed and regarded him as extraordinary,
saying:
"When Master Xiāo reaches thirty,
his nobility will be beyond words."
This marks the beginning of Xiāo Yǎn's affairs.
2 On the Rén Yín day,
Liǔ Shìlóng was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè,
and Lǐ Ānmín, the Dānyáng Yǐn, was appointed Yòupúshè.
Wáng Jiǎn concurrently held the post of Dānyáng Yǐn.
3 Summer,
Fourth month,
on the Jiǎ Yín day,
the Wèi ruler went to Fāngshān;
on the Wù Wǔ day,
he returned to the palace;
on the Gēng Shēn day,
he went to Hóngchí;
Hóngchí is Xuánhóngchí.
Shǔijīng Zhù: East of the mountain in Xuánhóng Xiàn, Liángchéng Jùn,
water accumulates to form a pond,
two lì from east to west,
four lì from north to south.
Also, in Tàizǔ Tiānxīng Second Year,
the Hóngyàn Chí was dug in Píngchéng.
on the Dīng Mǎo day
he returned to the palace.
4 Fifth month,
on the Jiǎ Shēn day,
Wèi dispatched Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì Lǐ Biāo and others to come for an envoy mission.
5. In the sixth month,
on the *rén yín* (壬寅) day,
Rú Fǎliàng (茹法亮) of Wúxīng (吳興), a Central Secretariat Drafter (*Zhōngshū Shèrén* 中書舍人), was enfeoffed as the Baron of Wàngcài (望蔡男).
Kāng (康) said: "Rú (茹)
is pronounced *rén zhū* (人諸)
and is a surname.
Wàngcài County (望蔡縣) belonged to Yùzhāng Commandery (豫章郡)."
Shěn Yuē (沈約) said: "During the *Zhōngpíng* (中平) era of Emperor Língdì (靈帝) of Hàn (漢),
the people of Shàngcài (上蔡) in Rǔnán (汝南) were moved and settled in this city, establishing a county
named Shàngcài (上蔡).
In the first year of *Tàikāng* (太康) of Emperor Wǔdì (武帝) of Jìn (晉),
it was renamed Wàngcài (望蔡)."
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: "Wàngcài County (望蔡縣) was originally Jiànchéng County (建成縣) in Hàn (漢).
Emperor Língdì (靈帝) divided it to establish Shàngcài County (上蔡縣).
Emperor Wǔdì (武帝) of Jìn (晉), considering that the people of Shàngcài (上蔡) missed their original homeland,
changed its name to Wàngcài (望蔡).
Today it is Gāo'ān County (高安縣),
the seat of Ruì Prefecture (瑞州)."
Each resided in a province [department],
and these were called
the "Four Households" (*Sìhù* 四戶).
Rú Fǎliàng (茹法亮) and Lǚ Wénxiǎn (呂文顯) from Línhǎi (臨海), among others, were appointed to them.
As they wielded great power,
their influence overshadowed the court.
Governors and magistrates were frequently transferred and replaced.
Annual tributes from all quarters
amounted to several million.
Fǎliàng (法亮) once told someone in public:
"Why bother seeking external emoluments!
From just one of these households,
a million can be acquired annually."
This was likely an understatement.
Later, due to an astrological anomaly,
Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) spoke strongly, saying:
"Wénxiǎn (文顯) and others monopolize power and act selfishly,
and heaven has shown this unusual sign; the calamity originates from the Four Households."
The emperor issued an imperial edict in reply,
but was unable to make changes.
6. The old Wei (魏) system stipulated that each household contributed two bolts of silk,
two *jīn* (斤) of floss,
one *jīn* (斤) of raw silk,
and twenty *hú* (斛) of grain.
Additionally, one bolt and two *zhàng* (丈) of silk were submitted
and entrusted to the state granaries,
to cover expenses beyond the regular levy.
The levies varied according to local produce.
On the *dīng mǎo* (丁卯) day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Establishing official posts and distributing salaries
is a long-standing practice.
Since the chaos in the Central Plains,
this system has been interrupted.
I, following the old regulations,
now begin to distribute official salaries.
Each household's levy will be increased by three bolts of silk
and two *hú* (斛) and nine *dǒu* (斗) of grain,
to serve as salaries for officials.
An additional two bolts of silk for other [extra-levy] purposes will be levied.
After salaries are implemented,
anyone whose corruption totals one bolt of silk shall die.
This reform and change in system
should be a new beginning,
therefore, there shall be a general amnesty throughout the realm."
7. In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the *jiǎ shēn* (甲申) day,
the imperial prince Zǐlún (子倫) was made Prince of Bālíng (巴陵王).
8. On the *yǐ wèi* (乙未) day,
the Wei (魏) emperor visited the grotto temple on Wǔzhōu Mountain (武州山).
9. In the ninth month,
a Wei (魏) edict announced that
the distribution of salaries would commence in the tenth month,
to be received quarterly.
Three months constituted one quarter.
For perverting justice for ten bolts of silk, or for unjust gains of twenty bolts of silk, the penalty was death.
By this time,
unjust gains of one bolt of silk,
or any amount of perverting justice,
all incurred the death penalty.
"Perverting justice" (*wǎngfǎ* 枉法)
refers to those who accepted bribes and twisted the law to acquit or convict people.
"Unjust gains" (*yìzāng* 義贓)
refers to private exchanges or gifts between individuals.
Even if not actively solicited,
the value received was still counted as illicit gain.
Inspectors tracked down corrupt governors and magistrates.
Lǐ Hóngzhī (李洪之) from Héngnóng (恆農), the Inspector of Qín (秦) and Yì (益) Prefectures, was prominent due to his imperial kinship.
Both Emperor Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖) and Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖) of Wei (魏) were descendants of the Lǐ (李) clan.
Wei (魏), to avoid Emperor Xiǎnzǔ's (顯祖) taboo name,
changed Hóngnóng (弘農) to Héngnóng (恆農).
After the implementation of salaries,
Hóngzhī (洪之) was the first to fall due to corruption.
The Wei (魏) emperor ordered him to be chained and brought to Píngchéng (平城),
gathered all officials, and personally interrogated him.
Still considering him a high-ranking minister,
he was allowed to commit suicide at home.
Over forty other governors and magistrates who were convicted of corruption and died.
Those who received salaries were all extremely cautious.
*Jú* (跼)
is pronounced *jú* (局).
*Jí* (蹐)
is pronounced *jí* (脊).
Bribery almost ceased.
However, for other crimes committed by officials and common people,
the Wei (魏) emperor generally showed leniency.
In cases of doubtful guilt, many were sentenced to reduction from death to exile to the border,
numbering in the thousands annually.
In the capital, those sentenced to capital punishment
did not exceed five or six people annually;
in the prefectures and garrisons, they were also few.
After a long time,
Wáng Tuó (王佗) of Huáinán (淮南)
submitted a memorial requesting the abolition of salaries, reverting to the old system.
Empress Dowager Wénmíng (文明太后) summoned her close ministers to discuss it.
Gāo Lǘ (高閭), the Central Secretariat Supervisor (*Zhōngshū Jiān* 中書監), believed:
"When hunger and cold afflict the body,
even a loving mother cannot protect her child.
Now, with salaries,
the upright are sufficient to avoid misconduct, and the greedy are encouraged to aspire to honesty.
Without salaries,
the greedy will be able to indulge their wickedness, and the upright will be unable to protect themselves.
Is the proposal of Huáinán (淮南) not mistaken?"
The imperial edict followed Lǘ's (閭) recommendation.
Lǘ (閭) also submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The northern barbarians are fierce and foolish,
like wild beasts.
Their strength lies in open battle,
their weakness in besieging cities.
The northern barbarians
refers to the Rúrú (蠕蠕).
Thus, even if numerous, they cannot cause trouble,
and even if they come, they cannot penetrate deeply.
Moreover,
the barbarians live scattered in wild marshes,
following water and grass.
When they fight, their families and property come with them;
when they flee, their livestock escape with them.
They do not carry provisions but are self-sufficient in food and drink,
which is why they have historically been a border threat.
The six garrisons are dispersed and divided,
and when outnumbered, they dare not fight.
This means if the enemy's strength is double,
the garrison people dare not fight.
It is difficult to control them.
I request that, following the precedents of Qín (秦) and Hàn (漢),
a Great Wall be built north of the six garrisons.
Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) of Wei (魏), after defeating the Rúrú (蠕蠕),
settled surrendered people south of the desert,
from Rúyuán (濡源) in the east
to Wǔyuán (五原) and Yīnshān (陰山) in the west,
extending three thousand *lǐ* (里).
This area was divided into six garrisons,
which are today Wǔchuān (武川), Fǔmíng (撫冥), Huáisuò (懷朔), Huáihuāng (懷荒), Róuxuán (柔玄), and Yùyí (禦夷).
It later says the six garrisons extend no more than a thousand *lǐ* (里 east to west,
so it should be from the northern border of the capital Dài (代) eastward to Rúyuán (濡源).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: 'The six garrisons of Later Wei (後魏) were all in the territories of Mǎyì (馬邑), Yúnzhōng (雲中), and Chányú (單于) Prefecture.'
Gates should be opened here and there,
with small fortresses built beside them,
and soldiers stationed to defend them.
Since the barbarians do not attack cities,
and their raids in the wilderness yield no plunder,
they will retreat when the grass is depleted,
and eventually they will be deterred.
The six garrisons extend no more than a thousand *lǐ* (里) east to west.
One man's labor for a month can build three paces of wall.
Combining strong and weak laborers,
no more than one hundred thousand people would be needed,
and it could be completed in one month.
Although there would be temporary toil,
it would bring perpetual peace.
The Great Wall has five benefits:
that is one;
the northern pastoralists will be free from raids,
that is two;
observing the enemy from the wall, awaiting the weary in leisure,
that is three;
it ends the need for constant readiness,
that is four;
annual provisions transport.
*Yóu* (遊)
means 'to transport'.
Transporting fodder and grain to stock the garrisons.
That is five."
The Wei (魏) emperor replied with a gracious edict.
In the 10th year, winter,
10th month,
on the dìngsì day,
Wáng Huǎng (長沙王晃), Prince of Chángshā and Governor of Nánxúzhōu, was appointed Grand Secretary of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān).
Initially,
when Tàizǔ (太祖) was on his deathbed,
he entrusted Huǎng to the Emperor,
instructing him to keep Huǎng close, either under the imperial carriage or in a nearby fiefdom,
and not to allow him to be sent far away.
He also said:
"If the Sòng (宋) clan does not engage in fratricide,
how can other clans exploit its weaknesses!
You must deeply admonish this!"
According to the old system, princes residing in the capital
were only allowed to have forty personal guards armed with swords (zhuōdāo).
Zhuōdāo
refers to those who hold swords to guard the左右.
When Nánxúzhōu was abolished,
Huǎng privately transported several hundred men and weapons back to Jiànkāng.
This was discovered by the Imperial Guard (Jìn Sī),
who threw them into the river.
Jìn Sī
was responsible for guarding against princes.
Hǎo (好),
pronounced hū dào;
similarly below.
The Emperor was furious
and intended to punish him according to the law,
but Wáng Ní (豫章王嶷), Prince of Yùzhāng, kowtowed and wept, saying:
"Huǎng’s crime is indeed inexcusable;
Your Majesty should remember the previous reign's concern for Huǎng."
The Emperor also shed tears,
and from then on, had no further ill intentions,
but neither was Huǎng favored or cherished.
Commentators believed the Emperor was superior to Wèi Wén (魏文)
but inferior to Hàn Míng (漢明).
Wèi Wén restricted and guarded the princes of Rèchéng (任城) and Chén (陳).
Hàn Míng showed fraternal love to the princes of Dōnghǎi (東海) and Dōngpíng (東平).
Ní (嶷),
pronounced yú lì.
Cháo (朝),
pronounced zhí yáo.
Bèi (被),
pronounced pí yì.
Wáng Yè (武陵王曅), Prince of Wǔlíng, was talented and artistic but careless and reckless,
and also not favored by the Emperor.
He once attended a banquet,
got drunk and collapsed on the ground,
so that his sable coat touched a meat platter.
The Emperor smiled and said:
"The meat will stain the sable."
Yè replied:
"Your Majesty cherishes feathers and furs but neglects flesh and blood."
The Emperor was displeased.
Yè was light-hearted with money and fond of giving,
hence he had no savings;
he named the rear hall mountain
"Shǒuyáng" (首陽),
likely resenting his poverty.
In the 11th year, King Lián (璉) of Gāolì (高麗) sent envoys to pay tribute to Wèi (魏),
and also to Qí (齊).
At that time, Gāolì was strong,
and Wèi had established diplomatic residences for various nations;
the Qí envoy's residence was ranked first,
with Gāolì's second.
In the 12th year, the Great Dù (大度) barbarians (liáo) of Yìzhōu, relying on the treacherous terrain, were arrogant and defiant.
The "Commentary on the Water Classic" (Shuǐjīng Zhù) states: Nán'ān (南安) County has the Méng (濛) Water,
which is the Great Dù Water,
flowing east into the Jiāng.
The "Comprehensive Gazetteer" (Huányǔ Jì) states: The Great Dù River originates from the Túbō (吐蕃) border, passes through various tribes in Yǎzhōu,
reaches the eastern border of Lízhōu,
and flows into the Tōngwàng (通望) region.
Liáo (獠),
pronounced lǔ hào.
When Chén Xiǎndá (陳顯達) became governor,
he sent envoys to demand their taxes and fines.
The barbarian chieftain said:
"Even the 'two-eyed governor' dared not subjugate us,
let alone a 'one-eyed' one!"
Thereupon, he killed the envoy.
Xiǎndá divided his generals and officials,
publicly stating he was going hunting.
At night,
he launched a surprise attack,
slaughtering all men and women, young and old.
Since the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
the governors of Yìzhōu had always been famous generals.
In the 11th month,
on the dìnghài day,
the Emperor for the first time appointed Wáng Jiàn (始興王鑑), Prince of Shǐxīng, as Commander of Military Affairs for Yì and Níng (益‧寧) and Governor of Yìzhōu,
and recalled Xiǎndá to be Central Protector of the Army (Zhōnghùjūn).
Previously,
the bandit leader Hán Wǔfāng (韓武方) had gathered over a thousand followers, blocking waterways and causing havoc,
and the commanderies and counties could not suppress them.
When Jiàn reached Shàngmíng (上明),
Wǔfāng surrendered.
His chief clerk Yú Cóng (虞悰) and others all requested that he be executed.
Jiàn said:
"Killing him would be a breach of trust, and would not encourage others to do good."
So he petitioned the court to pardon him,
and thereupon, all the Bāxī (巴西) barbarians who had been causing trouble submitted voluntarily.
Jiàn was fourteen years old at the time.
When he reached Xīnchéng (新城),
Xīnchéng
is modern-day Fángzhōu.
It was said
that "Chén Xiǎndá is extensively recruiting soldiers and horses,
and is unwilling to submit to the recall."
So Jiàn stopped at Xīnchéng
and sent his private secretary Zhāng Tánxī (張曇皙) to observe the situation.
Soon after, Xiǎndá sent an envoy to Jiàn.
Everyone advised Jiàn to arrest him.
Jiàn said:
"Xiǎndá has established his integrity in the imperial court;
he surely would not do such a thing."
Two days later,
Tánxī returned
and fully reported
that "Xiǎndá has already moved his family out of the city
and is eagerly awaiting Your Highness's arrival day and night."
Thereupon, Jiàn advanced.
Jiàn delighted in literature,
and his attire and implements were like those of a simple scholar,
which pleased the people of Shǔ (蜀).
On the yǐwèi day,
Lǐ Biāo (李彪) and others, who were Retainers at Large with Cavalry (Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì) from Wèi, came to offer greetings.
In this year, an imperial edict increased Wáng Ní's (豫章王嶷), Prince of Yùzhāng's, fiefdom to four thousand households.
During the Yuánjiā (元嘉) era of Sòng,
princes entering the inner chambers (zhāigé) were allowed to wear plain white clothes and a soft cap (qúnmào) when seeing the sovereign;
between the Sòng and Qí dynasties,
a system of high-crowned caps and draped skirts (xiàqún gài) was instituted.
Qún (帬),
pronounced qú yún.
Jiàn (見),
pronounced xián biàn.
They now had to wear court robes.
The Tàijí Hall (太極殿)
was the front hall,
with four wings.
The Emperor cherished Ní with fraternal love.
During private banquets in the palace,
Ní was permitted to follow the practices of the Yuánjiā era.
Ní humbly declined, not daring to do so.
Only when the imperial carriage arrived at his residence
would he wear plain white clothes and a black gauze cap to attend the banquet.
As for regulations on clothing and ceremonial objects,
he always petitioned the throne for every change,
never acting on his own authority,
and always sought to reduce and simplify.
The Emperor did not grant any of these requests.
Ní constantly worried about his excessive prosperity
and sought to resign from Yángzhōu,
entrusting it to Zǐliáng (竟陵王子良), Prince of Jìnglín.
The Emperor ultimately refused,
saying:
"Complete your life's tenure;
say no more."
Ní was seven feet eight inches tall,
skilled in maintaining a refined demeanor and ceremonial retinue,
and his propriety surpassed all officials.
Whenever he entered or exited the palace halls and departments,
those who looked upon him were invariably filled with solemn respect.
As for Lǐ Shūxiàn (李叔獻), Governor of Jiāozhōu, after receiving his appointment
(Shūxiàn was appointed Governor of Jiāozhōu,
see Volume 1, First Year of Tàizǔ's Jiàn Yuán reign),
the Emperor wanted to suppress him.
In the 1st year, spring,
1st month,
on the bǐngchén day,
Liú Kǎi (劉楷), Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng), was appointed Governor of Jiāozhōu,
and troops from Nánkāng, Lúlíng, and Shǐxīng were dispatched to suppress Shūxiàn.
Upon hearing this, Shūxiàn
sent an envoy to beg for an extension of a few more years,
offering twelve sets of pure silver helmets and peacock feathers;
the Emperor refused.
Fearing that Kǎi would launch a surprise attack, Shūxiàn
returned to court via a secret path from Xiāngzhōu.
He dared not take the route through Nánkāng and Shǐxīng,
to avoid Liú Kǎi's troops.
Jiān (間),
pronounced gǔ xiàn.
2 On the day of Wùyín,
Wèi issued an edict saying:
"The rise of prophecies and apocryphal texts
originated in the three decadent periods,
the decadent periods of the Three Dynasties.
讖 (chèn)
is pronounced chǔ zèn.
They are merely relied upon by evil spirits.
From now on, all prophecies, apocryphal texts, and esoteric works
shall be burned.
Those who keep them shall be judged with the death penalty!"
According to law,
anyone who is said to be "judged with" (以論)
faces the same penalty as the actual perpetrator.
辟 (bì)
is pronounced pí yì.
A straight road is called jiē,
a winding one is called xiàng.
委 (wěi)
means winding.
Zhèng Xuán said: wěixiàng
refers to what is done in the winding streets and neighborhoods.
覡 (xí)
is pronounced xíng dí.
3 Empress Dowager Féng of Wèi composed eighteen chapters of "Huáng Gào."
On the day of Guǐwèi,
she held a grand feast for all her ministers at Tàihuá Diàn,
and distributed the "Huáng Gào."
Wèi Gāozōng began constructing Tàihuá Diàn in the fourth year of Xīngguāng.
4 On the day of Xīnmǎo,
the Emperor performed sacrifices at the southern suburb,
and issued a general amnesty.
5 An edict reinstated the Guóxué;
the abolition of the Guóxué was mentioned in the previous volume under Gāodì's Jiàn Yuán fourth year.
Lǐ Yánshòu said: "During the early period of the Eastern Jìn,
there was no time to spare.
Up until the Sòng and Qí dynasties,
the Guóxué was sometimes established,
but encouragement and instruction were not widespread.
It could not be established for ten years,
probably just for appearances."
復 (fù)
is pronounced fú yòu.
6 In the second month,
on the day of Jǐhài,
Wèi decreed that imperial princes and grandsons with enfeoffments
should each have an annual stipend according to their rank.
7 On the day of Xīnchǒu,
the Emperor sacrificed at the northern suburb.
8 In the third month,
on the day of Bǐngshēn,
Wèi enfeoffed Imperial Brother Xī as King of Xiányáng,
Gàn as King of Hénán,
Yǔ as King of Guǎnglíng,
Yōng as King of Yǐngchuān,
Xié as King of Shǐpíng,
and Xiáng as King of Běihǎi.
All from Xī downwards were brothers of the Wèi ruler.
Tutors were selected to instruct the princes.
Among his brothers, Xié
was the most virtuous, intelligent, and fond of learning,
and skilled in writing.
The Wèi ruler especially admired and loved him.
9 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day of Guǐchǒu,
the Wèi ruler went to Fāngshān;
on the day of Jiǎyín,
he returned to the palace.
10 Initially,
Sòng Tàizōng established the Zǒngmíng Guān to gather scholars,
also called Dōngguān.
As the Guóxué had been established,
in the fifth month,
on the day of Yǐwèi,
the Emperor abolished the Zǒngmíng Guān.
At that time, Wáng Jiǎn held the position of Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
An edict ordered the establishment of a scholars' library at Jiǎn's residence,
stocked with the four divisions of books from Zǒngmíng Guān.
The books were divided into four categories: classics (jīng), histories (shǐ), philosophies (zǐ), and collected works (jí), corresponding to A, B, C, D.
Also, according to the Sòng Jì: Míngdì established the Zǒngmíng Guān in the sixth year of Tàishǐ,
summoning scholars to staff it;
twenty scholars were selected
and divided into five academic departments: Confucianism, Daoism, Literature, History, and Yīnyáng.
However, there were no practitioners for the Yīnyáng department.
If so, then these "four divisions of books"
might refer to books on Confucianism, Daoism, Literature, and History!
觀 (guān)
is pronounced gǔ wán.
Since Sòng Shìzǔ was fond of literature,
all officials and gentry prided themselves on their literary skills,
with none specializing in the study of classics as their profession.
Jiǎn, in his youth, was fond of ritual studies and the Spring and Autumn Annals.
In his discussions and actions, he always adhered to the Confucian way.
Because of this, the educated elite unanimously
changed their preference to Confucian arts.
Jiǎn compiled and arranged court ceremonies and national codes.
From the Jìn and Sòng dynasties onwards, there was no custom
that he did not know by heart.
憶 (yì)
means jì (to remember).
朝 (cháo)
is pronounced zhí yáo;
same below.
諳 (ān)
is pronounced wū hán.
His judgments were swift and clear.
Whenever he debated extensively and cited evidence,
the "eight seats," "censor," and "lang" officials could not contradict him.
"Eight seats," "censor," and "lang"
refer to officials from the eight high-ranking positions down to the left and right censors and various departmental lang officials.
斷 (duàn)
is pronounced dīng luàn.
坐 (zuò)
is pronounced cú wò.
His banquets were always full of guests.
Jiǎn handled and analyzed conversations,
with no delays at his side.
His spoken and written words
all possessed eloquence and elegance.
Every ten days, he would return to the Guóxué to supervise the students.
With his hat and scrolls in the courtyard,
and guards and clerks,
his bearing was very grand.
He wore his hair in a "loose topknot" (jiěsànjì).
According to the biography of Jiǎn in the Nán Shǐ, it says
"loose turban" (jiěsànzé).
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's Qí Shū says
"loose topknot,
with the hairpin inserted diagonally."
The court and the common people admired him
and imitated him.
Jiǎn often said to people:
"Among the elegant chancellors of the Eastern Jìn,
there was only Xiè Ān."
His intention was to compare himself to him.
The Emperor deeply trusted and relied on him.
In the selection and appointment of scholars,
none of his proposals were rejected.
11 In the sixth month,
on the day of Gēngxū,
Dù Yìhóu, King of Hénán, was promoted to Chējì Jiāngjūn.
Gěishìzhōng Qiū Guānxī of Wúxìng was dispatched as an envoy to Hénán,
also accompanying the Ròurán envoy.
12 On the day of Xīnhài,
the Wèi ruler went to Fāngshān;
on the day of Dīngsì,
he returned to the palace.
13 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day of Guǐwèi,
Wèi sent an envoy to confer upon Miéchéng, the nephew of Dàngchāng King Liáng Míji, the title of Dàngchāng King.
Initially,
when Míji died,
his son Míbó was enthroned.
He was pressed by the Tǔyùhún
and fled to Qiúchí.
吐 (tǔ)
is pronounced with the entering tone from tūn.
谷 (gǔ)
is pronounced yù.
Pitying their destruction,
(but) Míbó was violent and perverse,
and his subordinates disliked him.
Miéchéng was supported by the masses
and submitted a memorial requesting his reinstatement.
An edict granted it.
Liàng led thirty thousand cavalry to station at Lónghú.
Lónghú
is probably Lónghé,
located in the Gānsōng region.
The Yǔwén clan established the Lónghé garrison there.
During the Suí dynasty, it became Jiāchéng County of Fúzhōu,
and in the Táng dynasty, Sōngzhōu.
Dù Yòu said: Lónghé City
was the southern border of the Tǔyùhún,
over a thousand *lǐ* from Chéngdū.
In the early Tiānhé reign of Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu,
its king led his people to surrender,
and it was made Fúzhōu.
帥 (shuài)
is read shuài.
騎 (qí)
is pronounced qí jì.
He installed Miéchéng and then returned.
Liàng was the great-grandson of Chóngzhī.
Mù Chóng is mentioned in volume 111, Jìn Āndì, Lóng'ān third year.
On the 14th day, *wùzǐ*,
the Wei Emperor went to the Fish Pond.
In the fifth year of Wèi Tàizōng Yǒngdēng,
a fish pond was dug in the northern park of Píngchéng.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
he returned to the palace.
In the eighth month,
on the *jǐhài* day,
he went to Mízé.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
he ascended Niútóu Shān.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
he returned to the palace.
In the early days of the Wei dynasty,
many common people sought refuge and attached themselves to powerful families.
Those who sought refuge
attached themselves to powerful and influential families to seek protection.
These powerful families levied taxes at twice the rate of public taxation.
The Palace Attendant, Lǐ Ānshì, presented a memorial, saying:
“In years of famine, the people are displaced,
and their fields and properties are often seized by powerful magnates.
Although it is difficult to restore the *sāngjǐng* system—
*Sāngjǐng*
refers to the ancient well-field system,
where a five-mu plot of land
would have mulberry trees planted beneath its walls—
we should ensure that labor and property are commensurate.
Furthermore,
regarding disputed fields,
a time limit should be set for adjudication;
if a matter has been long-standing and is difficult to clarify,
it should all be returned to the current owner
to put an end to fraud and deception.”
The Wei Emperor approved of this,
and from then on, discussions about the Equal-Field System began.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the *dīngwèi* day,
an imperial edict was issued, dispatching envoys to tour the provinces and commanderies,
to, together with the provincial governors and commandery administrators, equalize and distribute land throughout the realm.
All male adults aged fifteen and above were to receive forty *mǔ* of *lùtián*,
and women twenty *mǔ*.
Dù Yòu’s *Tōngdiǎn* annotation states: Land where no trees are planted is called *lùtián*.
Capable adults,
meaning commoners who had reached adulthood,
received thirty *mǔ* of land.
The limit was four oxen.
For the land granted,
the rate was doubled for certain types;
for "three-change" land, it was doubled again;
to provide for cultivation and the increase or decrease of land to be returned or received.
The increase or decrease refers to the adjustment of land based on whether it is fallow or cultivated.
“Doubled” means
that if one should receive forty *mǔ*,
they are granted eighty *mǔ*.
This is for "one-change" land.
“Three-change” land
is cultivated for three years before reverting to its original state,
hence it is granted at twice the doubled amount.
The elderly were exempt [from returning the land];
upon their death, the land was returned.
Slaves, maidservants, and oxen were returned or received according to their presence or absence.
Those who initially received land,
male adults were given twenty *mǔ*,
and were required to plant fifty mulberry trees.
Mulberry fields were all hereditary property
and were not returned upon death.
When regularly counting the existing population,
those with a surplus neither received nor returned land;
those with insufficient land received crops according to the law;
those with a surplus could sell their surplus.
Officials who governed the people,
each received public land according to proximity, with varying amounts,
and transferred it to their successors upon change of office.
Those who sold it were punished according to the law.
On the 16th day, *xīnyǒu*,
Wèi Wèijùn Wáng Chén Jiàn died.
On the 17th day, Wèi Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì Lǐ Biāo and others came to establish diplomatic relations.
In the twelfth month,
on the *yǐmǎo* day,
the Wei dynasty appointed Shìzhōng Huáinán Wáng Tuó as Sītú.
The Ròurán violated the Wei frontier.
Wèi Rènchéng Wáng Chéng led his troops to resist them,
and the Ròurán fled.
Chéng
was the son of Yún.
Rènchéng Wáng Yún is mentioned in Volume 133, Sòng Míngdì Tàishǐ seventh year.
Rèn
is pronounced *rén*.
Shuài
is read as *shuài*.
An edict appointed Chéng as Dūdū Liáng-Yì-Jīng Sānzhōu Zhū Jūnshì and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ.
Wèi Gāozǔ initially established Liáng and Yì prefectures in Qiúchí.
He suppressed the rebellious and pacified the submissive,
and both the Dī and Qiāng peoples were pacified.
Initially,
Tàizǔ commanded Huángmén Láng Yú Wánzhī and others to inspect and verify the Yellow Registers.
See previous volume, Tàizǔ Jiàn yuán second year.
A separate office for examining registers was established,
with clerks appointed.
The number of fraudulent entries a person could achieve in a day was limited.
*Qiǎo*
refers to deception and fraud.
The people were anxious and discontent.
The Foreign Supervisor, Kuàijī Lǚ Wéndù,
The Foreign Supervisor
was subordinate to the Zhonglǐngjūn.
Yet his influence surpassed that of the Lǐngjūn.
Kuài
is pronounced *kuài*.
All those whose registration was rejected were sent to distant garrisons,
and many people fled to avoid punishment.
Táng Yǔzhī, a commoner from Fùyáng, consequently used sorcery to delude the masses and instigate rebellion,
capturing Fùyáng.
Fùyáng
is the former Fùchūn County of the Han dynasty,
originally belonging to Kuàijī,
later to Wú Jùn.
Because Jìn Jiǎnwén Zhèng Tàihòu’s taboo name was Chūn,
Xiàowǔ changed it to Fùyáng.
Yāo
is pronounced *yāo*.
His followers reached thirty thousand.
Wéndù, along with Rú Fǎliàng and Lǚ Wénxiǎn, were all favored by the emperor for their cunning flattery.
Wéndù, as Foreign Supervisor,
held exclusive control over military power,
while the Lǐngjūn held only a titular position.
Fǎliàng, as Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén,
wielded even greater power and influence.
Wáng Jiǎn often said:
“Although I hold a high position,
how can my authority compare to that of Duke Rú!”
In this year,
the Ròurán Buzhēn Kèhán died,
and his son Dòulún succeeded him.
Kè
is pronounced as *kè*.
Hán
is pronounced *hán*.
Lún
is pronounced *lún*.
Wèi Shōu said: His name was Fú Míngdūn,
which in Wei language means "constant."
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the *guǐhài* day, the new moon,
Wèi Gāozǔ held a court assembly,
and for the first time wore the *gǔnmiǎn* ceremonial robes.
Historians say that Emperor Xiàowén of Wei used Chinese customs to transform barbarian ones.
Cháo
is pronounced *cháo*.
2 On the *rénwǔ* day,
the Ròurán invaded the Wei border.
3 Táng Yǔzhī attacked and captured Qiántáng,
and many county magistrates in Wú Jùn abandoned their cities and fled.
Yǔzhī declared himself emperor in Qiántáng,
appointed a crown prince,
and established officials.
He dispatched his generals Gāo Dàodù and others to attack and capture Dōngyáng,
killing the Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng, Xiāo Chóngzhī.
Chóngzhī
was a cousin of Tàizǔ.
He also dispatched his general Sūn Hóng to raid Shānyīn,
reaching Pǔyáng Jiāng.
According to the *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù*,
Pǔyáng Jiāng
is today’s Cáonú Jiāng.
Its waters originate from Shàxī,
all flowing west,
then turning east at Cáonú Zhèn,
and flowing into the sea.
Jiá
is pronounced *jiá*.
He led several hundred horses
to attack Yǔzhī in the east.
When the imperial army reached Qiántáng,
Yǔzhī’s rabble,
fearing cavalry,
collapsed after a single battle,
and Yǔzhī was captured and executed.
The imperial army then pacified all the prefectures and counties.
The imperial army, riding on its victory,
engaged in considerable looting and pillaging.
Upon the army’s return,
the emperor, hearing of this,
had the army commander, former General Chén Tiānfú, executed in the marketplace.
Left General Liú Míngchè was dismissed from office, stripped of his title,
and handed over to Dōngyě.
Jiànkāng had two ironworks, east and west.
The present-day Yě Chéng is that location,
also known as Dōngyětíng.
Both were favored generals of the emperor,
but after their punishment,
everyone inside and outside the court was awestruck and solemn.
The emperor sent Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén, Liú Xìzōng of Dānyáng, with the army to offer comfort,
visiting all the prefectures and counties that had suffered from the rebels.
The common people who had been coerced [by the rebels] were all pardoned.
4th year, intercalary month.
On the guǐsì day,
Imperial Prince Zǐzhēn was appointed King of Shàolíng,
and Imperial Grandson Zhāowén was appointed Duke of Línrǔ.
5th year. The Dī King Yáng Hòuqǐ died.
On the dīngwèi day,
an imperial edict appointed Yáng Jíshǐ, the Administrator of Báishuǐ, as the Inspector of Běiqínzhōu and King of Wǔdū.
Jíshǐ
was the son of Wénhóng.
Hòuqǐ's younger brother, Hòumíng, became Administrator of Báishuǐ.
Wèi also appointed Jíshǐ as King of Wǔdū.
Jíshǐ entered the Wèi court to pay homage,
and Wèi appointed him Inspector of Nánqínzhōu.
6th year. On the xīnhài day,
the Emperor personally ploughed the ceremonial field.
7th year, 2nd month.
On the jǐwèi day,
Imperial Younger Brother Qiú was appointed King of Jìnxī,
and Xuàn was appointed King of Hédōng.
8th year. Wèi had no system ofxiang (鄉) or dang (黨) districts;
only宗主 Dūhù (宗主督護) were established.
Many commoners concealed themselves (from registration),
with thirty to fifty families counting as a single household.
Lǐ Chōng, the Director of the Inner Secretariat, submitted a memorial, saying:
The Secretariat (Mìshūshěng 祕書省) was located within the forbidden palace,
hence it was called Director of the Inner Secretariat (Nèi Mìshūlìng 內祕書令),
also known as Zhong Mi (中祕).
'上' (shàng),
read as 'shí zhǎng fān'.
"It is advisable to follow the ancient methods: establish a línzhǎng (鄰長) for every five families,
a lǐzhǎng (里長) for every five lín (鄰),
and a dǎngzhǎng (黨長) for every five lǐ (里),
selecting capable and diligent individuals from the local populace to serve.
A línzhǎng is exempt from one man's corvée,
a lǐzhǎng from two men's,
and a dǎngzhǎng from three men's.
If they serve for three years without fault,
they are promoted one rank.
As for the household tax (míndiào 民調),
for one man and one woman,
it is one bolt of silk
and two shi (石) of grain.
Generally, ten bolts of silk constitute the public tax (gōngdiào 公調),
two bolts are for miscellaneous expenses (diàowàifèi 調外費),
and three bolts are for the salaries of officials.
Besides these, there are other miscellaneous taxes.
For commoners aged eighty and above,
one son is permitted to be exempt from corvée.
The orphaned, solitary, infirm, elderly, seriously ill, and impoverished who cannot sustain themselves,
shall be cared for and fed alternately by the three zhǎng (長) within their jurisdiction."
After the memorial was presented,
an imperial edict ordered all officials to discuss it.
Zhèng Xī (鄭羲), the Director of the Central Secretariat, and others all deemed it unfeasible.
Tàiwèi Pī (太尉丕) said:
"Your servant believes that if this law is implemented,
it will benefit both the state and the people.
However, in a month with ongoing affairs,
reviewing and comparing households will surely cause hardship and resentment among the people.
I request that we wait until after this autumn,
and send envoys in winter;
that would be more appropriate for the matter."
Chōng said:
"'The people can be made to follow (it),
but they cannot be made to understand (it).'
These are the words of Kǒngzǐ in the Lúnyǔ.
During the tax assessment period,
the so-called month for assessing taxes and corvée,
if they do not yet see the benefits of equitable corvée and reduced levies,
resentment will surely arise in their hearts.
It is advisable to implement it during the month of tax assessment,
so they understand the fairness of the taxes and levies.
Once they understand the matter
and also gain from its benefits,
it will be easier to implement."
Many of the court officials (zhòu chén 㣥臣) said:
"The nine-grade tax differential
has been in place for a long time.
The nine grades,
high, middle, and low, each divided into three grades,
details can be found in volume 132, Sòng Míngdì's Tàishǐ 5th year.
We fear it will cause disorder."
Empress Dowager Wénmíng said:
"Establishing the 'three zhǎngs' will provide a fixed standard for taxes and corvée.
Households that conceal themselves can be uncovered,
and those who seek to evade (taxes) can be stopped.
Why would it be unfeasible!"
On the jiǎxū day,
the system of dǎng, lǐ, and lín (黨、里、鄰) 'three zhǎngs' was first established,
and the household registers were settled.
Initially, the people were all distressed and discontented,
especially the powerful and influential.
However, subsequently, the taxes and levies were reduced by more than ten times,
and both the higher and lower ranks found peace with it.
9th year, 3rd month.
On the bǐngshēn day,
the Ròurán sent an envoy, Móutí, to Wèi.
At that time, the Chìlè rebelled against the Ròurán,
and Ròurán Fúmíngdūn Kèhán (柔然伏名敦可汗) personally led an expedition to suppress them,
pursuing the fugitives to Xīmò.
Xīmò
is the western part of the Great Desert.
'將' (jiāng),
read as 'jí liàng fān'.
Gāo Lǘ (高閭), the Supervisor of the Central Secretariat, said:
"During the Qín and Hàn eras,
the whole country was unified,
thus it was possible to launch distant campaigns against the Xiōngnú.
Now, in the south, there are Wú bandits.
How can we abandon them and delve deep into barbarian territory!"
The Wèi ruler said:
"'Weapons are instruments of ill omen;
the sage uses them only when unavoidable.'
These are the words of Lǎozǐ.
This is because there are still un-subdued barbarians.
Now I inherit the legacy of peace;
how can I causelessly wage war!"
He treated their envoy with great courtesy and sent him back.
10th year, summer,
4th month.
On the xīnyǒu day, the first day of the month,
Wèi first established five ranks of official robes;
on the jiǎzǐ day,
for the first time, ceremonial robes and the imperial carriage were used for sacrifices in the southern suburb.
Official robes
were court attire;
the five ranks
were vermillion, purple, crimson, green, and blue.
Ceremonial robes
were the gǔnmiǎn (袞冕) robes worn for sacrificial ceremonies at the suburban altars and ancestral temples.
On the guǐyǒu day,
the Wèi ruler went to Língquán Pond;
Wèi built Língquángōng Palace south of Fāngshān,
drawing water from the Rúhún River to form Língquán Pond,
which was one hundred bù (步) from east to west
and two hundred bù (步) from north to south.
On the wùyín day
he returned to the palace.
12th year. The barbarians in Xiāngzhōu rebelled.
Lǚ Ānguó (呂安國), the Inspector, was ill and unable to suppress them.
On the dīnghài day,
Liǔ Shìlóng (柳世隆), the Left Chief Administrator of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Inspector of Xiāngzhōu
and suppressed them.
13th year, 6th month.
On the xīnyǒu day,
the Wèi ruler went to Fāngshān.
Kǎoyì says: The imperial annals of Wèi state
that on this day, he went to Fāngshān.
On the wùxū day of the 7th month, it also says he went to Fāngshān,
neither mentioning his return to the palace.
This is likely a textual omission.
14th year. On the jǐmǎo day,
Empress Dowager Wénmíng of Wèi bestowed a name upon Imperial Prince Xún (恂)
and issued a general amnesty.
15th year, autumn,
7th month.
On the wùxū day,
the Wèi ruler went to Fāngshān.
16th year, 8th month.
On the yǐhài day,
Wèi granted vermillion robes,
jade pendants,
and sashes (zǔshòu 組綬) of various sizes to officials of the five ranks and above in the Department of State Affairs.
Zǔshòu
refers to sashes formed by weaving.
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) said: Sashes are used to string jade pendants,
and are passed down.
The Hàn system stipulated:
seal sashes were first made by twisting single threads into one strand (xì 系),
four strands formed one fú (扶),
five fú formed one shǒu (首),
five shǒu formed one wén (文),
and a pure wén pattern formed one guī (圭).
Those with more shǒu had finer threads;
those with fewer had coarser threads,
all one chi (尺) six cùn (寸) wide.
read as 'gǔ fān'.
'綬' (shòu),
pronounced 'shòu'.
17th year, 9th month.
On the xīnmǎo day,
Wèi began constructing the Míngtáng (明堂) and Pìyōng (辟雍).
18th year, winter,
11th month.
Wèi discussed and decided that civilian officials' salaries would be based on the number of households they administered.
The amount of salary given varied according to the number of households they governed.
19th year, 12th month.
The Ròurán raided the Wèi border.
20 In this year,
Wèi changed the name of the Zhōngshū Xué (Central Secretariat School) to Guózǐ Xué (National Academy).
Wèi had previously established Zhōngshū Bóshì (Academicians of the Central Secretariat) and Zhōngshū Xuéshēng (Students of the Central Secretariat).
Now it changed its name to Guózǐ Xué,
following the Jìn system.
There were thirty-eight prefectures in total,
twenty-five in Hénán,
and thirteen in Hébĕi.
The twenty-five prefectures in Hénán were
Qīng, Nánqīng, Yǎn, Qí, Jì, Guāng, Yù,
Luò, Xú, Dōngxú, Yōng, Qín, Nánqín, Liáng, Yì, Jīng, Liáng, Hé, Shā.
At that time, Huá, Shǎn, Xià, Qí, Bān, Yǐng were also established,
making a total of twenty-five.
The thirteen prefectures in Hébĕi were
Sī, Bīng, Sì, Dìng, Xiàng, Jì, Yōu, Yān, Yíng, Píng, Ān.
At that time, Yíng, Fén were also established,
making a total of thirteen.

Xiāo Zǐxiǎn said: Yōng, Liáng, Qín, Shā, Jīng, Huá, Qí, Hé, Xīhuá, Níng, Shǎn, Luò, Jīng, Yǐng, Běiyù, Dōngjīng, Nányù, Xīyǎn, Dōngyǎn, Nánxú, Dōngxú, Qīng, Qí, Jì, Guāng—these twenty-five prefectures were in Hénán.
Xiàng, Fén, Huái, Dōngyōng, Sì, Dìng, Yíng, Shuò, Bīng, Jì, Yōu, Píng, Sī and other thirteen prefectures were in Hébĕi.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Dīnghài (the first day of the month),
the Wèi ruler issued an edict to standardize musical compositions,
removing any that were not elegant.
2 On the day Wùzǐ,
Xiāo Yì, Prince of Yùzhāng, was appointed Dàsīmǎ (Grand Marshal);
Xiāo Zǐliáng, Prince of Jìnglíng, was appointed Sītú (Minister of Education);

Xiāo Yìng, Prince of Línchuān, Wèi Jiāngjūn Wáng Jiǎn, and Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn Wáng Jìngzè were all granted the rank of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Open Palace with the Privileges of the Three Ducal Ministers).
Zǐliáng proposed that his secretary Fàn Yún be appointed to a commandery.
The Emperor said:
"I hear he often sells himself out.
I will not pursue the law against him again,
but will pardon him by sending him far away."
Zǐliáng said:
"That is not true.
Yún always advised and exhorted me,
and his remonstrance memorials are all preserved."
Thereupon, he took them and presented them,
totaling over a hundred pages,
all with frank and direct language.
The Emperor sighed,
and said to Zǐliáng:
"I did not expect Yún to be capable of this;
I intend to have him assist you,
how can he be sent out to govern a commandery!"
Wénhuì Tàizǐ (Crown Prince Wénhuì) once went to the Eastern Field to observe the harvest.
At that time, the Crown Prince had established the Eastern Field to the east of the Eastern Palace,
stretching far and wide,
magnificent and boundless.
The Qí Jì also states: The Crown Prince built a tower and lodge at the foot of Zhōngshān mountain,
named the Eastern Field.
"Harvesting this is also truly a sight to behold."
Everyone said:
"Yes, yes."
Yún alone said:
"The tasks of the three seasons
are indeed a long and arduous labor.
The tasks of the three seasons refer to spring plowing, summer weeding, and autumn harvesting.
One should not indulge in a single day's leisure and ease!"
3 Huán Tiānshēng, a barbarian who claimed to be a descendant of Huán Xuán,
incited the barbarians of Yōng and Sī prefectures,
occupied the old city of Nányáng,
requested troops from Wèi,
and was about to invade.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
an edict was issued to grant Xiāo Jǐngxiān, Dānyáng Yǐn, a staff of authority,
to command all infantry and cavalry,
and march directly to Yìyáng.
All the armies in Sī prefecture were to obey his orders.
Furthermore, Hùjūn Jiāngjūn Chén Xiǎndá was granted a staff of authority,
to lead Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Dài Sēngjìng and other naval forces towards Wǎn and Yè.
All the armies in Yōng and Sī prefectures were to obey Xiǎndá's orders,
to suppress them.
4 Gāo Yǔn, Wèi Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Splendid Happiness) and Xiányáng Wéngōng (Duke Wén of Xiányáng),
served five emperors: Tàiwǔ, Jǐngmù, Wénchéng, Xiànwén, and Gāozǔ were the five emperors.
He served in three departments:
Shàngshū Shěng, Zhōngshū Shěng, and Mìshū Shěng.
He was never censured;
Empress Dowager Féng and the Wèi ruler held him in high regard,
often ordering Zhōnghuángmén Sū Xìngshòu to assist him.
Yǔn was benevolent, lenient, simple, and calm.
Although he held a position of great importance,
his sentiments were like those of a humble scholar;
he held books and recited them, day and night, never letting them leave his hands;
he taught people good things,
earnestly and tirelessly.
Yáng Zhōnglì said: Xúxún means wholeheartedly sincere.
Zhū Yuánhuì said: Xúxún describes a sincere and trustworthy appearance.
He neglected no one.
Xiǎnzǔ pacified Qīng and Xú,
and moved all their prominent families to Dài.
This event is recorded in volume 132, year 5 of Tàishǐ era of Sòng Míngdì.
They were displaced and suffered from hunger and cold;
Yǔn emptied his household to provide relief,
and all found their proper places.
He also recommended them to the court according to their talents and conduct.
Many critics questioned them as newly surrendered,
but Yǔn said:
"In employing the worthy and capable,
what difference does 'new' or 'old' make!
If they are truly useful,
how can they be suppressed on this account!"
Yǔn was originally free from illness,
but at this time he felt a slight discomfort.
Yet, his daily life was as usual.
He died a few days later,
at the age of ninety-eight.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) and Sīkōng (Minister of Works),
and received generous funeral gifts.
Cloth and silk are called fù;
clothes and quilts are called suì.
Fù
is pronounced fù.
Suì
is pronounced suì.
Both the living and the dead received his beneficence,
none were left out.
5 Huán Tiānshēng led over ten thousand Wèi troops to Bǐyáng.
In the Hàn dynasty, Bǐyáng county belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Yīng Shào said: It is where the Bǐ river originates.
During the Tàihé era of Wèi, Dōngjīng prefecture was established in the old city of Bǐyáng.
Sòng Bái said: The present Bǐyáng county in Tángzhōu is the old city of the prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Bǐyáng county is seventy-five lǐ northeast of Tángzhōu.
Dài Sēngjìng's biography states that Shēnqiáo is forty lǐ from Bǐyáng.
Bǐ
is pronounced bǐ.
Tens of thousands were killed or captured.
Tiānshēng retreated to secure Bǐyáng.
Sēngjìng besieged it,
but failed to conquer it and returned.
Hú Qiūshēng, a barbarian, raised an army in Xuánhù to support Qí.
The Wèi people defeated him,
and Qiūshēng came over to surrender.
Tiānshēng again led Wèi troops to invade Wǔyīn.
Yīn Gōngmǐn, the commander of Wǔyīn garrison, resisted and attacked them,
defeating them,
killing their deputy Zhāng Qílín.
Tiānshēng was wounded and fled.
In the third month,
on the day Dīngwèi,
Chén Xiǎndá was appointed Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yōng prefecture).
Xiǎndá advanced and occupied Wǔyáng city.
6 In summer,
the fifth month,
on the day Rénchén,
the Wèi ruler went to Língquánchí.
7 On the day Guǐsì,
Wèi Nánpíng Wáng Hún passed away.
8 On the day Jiǎwǔ,
the Wèi ruler returned to Píngchéng.
An edict was issued to exempt the descendants of the seven ancestral temples and maternal relatives wearing sí má mourning clothes or higher
from corvée labor and taxes.
9 Gōngsūn Suì, Wèi Nánbù Shàngshū, and Zhāng Shū, Gōng of Shànggǔ, led their troops with Huán Tiānshēng to again invade Wǔyīn.
Yīn Gōngmǐn attacked and defeated them;
Tiānshēng retreated and hid in the wilderness.
Suì
was the grandson of Biǎo.
Gōngsūn Biǎo served as a general under Wèi Míngyuán.
In the spring and summer,
Wèi suffered a great drought,
especially severe in the Dàidì region.
In addition, there was a cattle plague, and many people starved to death.
In the sixth month,
on the guǐwèi day,
an edict ordered all internal and external officials to speak plainly without concealment.
Hán Qílín (韓麒麟), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Qízhōu (齊州), submitted a memorial, saying:
"The wise kings of ancient times
accumulated reserves for nine consecutive years (九稔).
In ancient times,
after three years of farming,
there was one year's surplus food;
after nine years of farming,
there were three years' surplus food.
If the national expenditure was managed based on a thirty-year average,
there should be nine years of reserves.
A state without nine years of reserves is said to be insufficient;
without six years of reserves, it is said to be in urgent need;
without three years of reserves, it is said that the state is not truly a state.
When there is a good harvest (稔),
the granaries are overturned.
This industry was also promoted;
those who offered grain received the same rank as those who defeated enemies,
and diligent farmers received the same rewards as those who displayed filial piety and brotherly submission.
The Hàn dynasty allowed common people to obtain official ranks by offering grain.
There were also categories for filial piety and diligent farming.
Many do not farm;
those who wander and live off others' food
make up two-thirds of the population.
Since peace has lasted for a long time,
with many years of abundant harvests,
people have competed to show off,
leading to an extravagant custom.
In wealthy households,
even child servants wear fine clothes;
among merchants and artisans,
retainers eat luxurious food.
Zhāng Yàn (張晏) said: 'Yùshí (玉食)
means rare delicacies.'
Yet silkworm farmers lack even simple garments.
Thus, the number of cultivators decreases daily,
and fields lie fallow;
grain and silk are depleted from the state treasuries,
while treasures and valuable goods abound in the markets;
food and clothing are scarce in homes,
but beautiful clothes overflow on the roads.
The root cause of hunger and cold
truly lies in this.
I humbly suggest that all rare and exotic items
should be prohibited;
rites for auspicious and inauspicious occasions
should be uniformly standardized;
and agriculture and sericulture should be encouraged and supervised,
with strict rewards and punishments.
Within a few years,
there will certainly be sufficiency.
In past years, when household registers were checked,
Máo Huǎng (毛晃) said: 'Guàn (貫)
refers to the village register.'
The Qízhōu (齊州) under my administration
yielded just enough grain rent to pay salaries,
with virtually none entering the granaries.
Although this benefits the people, it cannot last long.
Should there be military campaigns
or natural disasters,
I fear there would be no means
of supply and relief.
The taxes on silk and cloth can be reduced,
and grain rent increased.
When the year is abundant, more should be stored;
when the year is lean, it should be distributed as relief.
'Jǐan (儉)' (lean) refers to a year with low income.
'Zhèn (賑)'
is pronounced zhěn;
same below.
If stored in official hands,
and officials have long-term reserves,
then the people will not suffer from barren years."
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the jǐchǒu day,
an edict ordered officials to open granaries for relief and loans,
and allowed people to leave the passes to seek food.
The Wèi capital was Píngchéng (平城).
Outside the imperial domain,
passes were set up at strategic roads for inspection and taxation.
Those who left or stayed were dispatched in groups;
they were given grain at every place they passed,
and were supported by the sānzhǎng (三長) upon arrival.
The Rouran Fúmíngdūn Kèhán (柔然伏名敦可汗) was cruel,
Kè (可)
is pronounced from kān.
Hán (汗)
is pronounced hán.
and had been advised to make peace with Wèi.
Fúmíngdūn (伏名敦) was enraged
and executed him and his clan.
Due to this, his tribesmen became disaffected.
In the eighth month,
the Rouran raided the Wèi border.
Wèi appointed Shàngshū (尚書) Lù Ruì (陸叡) as Dūdū (都督),
attacked the Rouran,
and decisively defeated them.
Ruì (叡)
was the son of Lì (麗).
Lù Lì (陸麗)
was the son of Lù Sī (陸俟),
and died during the chaos caused by Yǐ Hún (乙渾).
Earlier,
Àfúzhìluó (阿伏至羅) of Gāochē (高車) had over a hundred thousand tribesmen
subjugated by the Rouran.
When Fúmíngdūn (伏名敦) invaded Wèi,
Àfúzhìluó (阿伏至羅) remonstrated,
but was not heeded.
Àfúzhìluó (阿伏至羅) was angered,
and with his younger cousin Qióngqí (窮奇), led his tribesmen west,
reaching the northwest of the former部,
and established himself as king.
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The Gāochē biography in the Wèishū (魏書) says this was in the eleventh year of Tàihé (太和),
while the Rúrú (蠕蠕) was in the sixteenth year.
We now follow the Gāochē biography.
Note that the character '傳' (biography)
should
be under Rúrú (蠕蠕).
He titled himself 'Hòulóufúllè' (候婁匐勒),
which means 'Son of Heaven' in Xiàyán (夏言);
Qióngqí (窮奇) was titled
'Hòubèi' (候倍),
which means 'Crown Prince' in Xiàyán (夏言).
Xiàyán (夏言)
refers to the language of the central plains.
Xià (夏)
is pronounced hùyǎ fān (戶雅翻).
They divided their tribes and established their own rule.
Àfúzhìluó (阿伏至羅) settled in the north,
Qióngqí (窮奇) in the south.
Fúmíngdūn (伏名敦) pursued and attacked them,
but was repeatedly defeated by Àfúzhìluó (阿伏至羅),
and so led his forces to move east.
History says the Rouran gradually declined.
Bài (敗)
is pronounced bǔmài fān (補邁翻).
In the ninth month,
on the xīnwèi day,
Wèi issued an edict to abolish useless construction projects by the Qǐbù (起部).
The Qǐbù (起部) managed all kinds of craftsmanship.
The Shūjīng (書經) says: "The hundred crafts rise!"
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the dīngwèi day,
another edict abolished the production of brocades, embroideries, damasks, and gauze by the Shàngfāng (尚方);
if the four classes of people wished to produce them,
they were allowed without prohibition.
The four classes of people
are scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants.
Wèi had long been peaceful,
and its treasuries were full.

An edict ordered that eight-tenths of the clothes and treasures from the imperial household, miscellaneous utensils from the Tàiguān (太官), riding gear from the Tàipú (太僕), and bows, arrows, swords, and quivers from the imperial armory
(內庫); and the greater part of the clothes, silk, cloth, and raw silk
from the outer treasuries that were not for national use,
be distributed to all government departments,
down to artisans, merchants, and common laborers,
and extending to the six garrisons and border outposts,
as well as the widowed, solitary, orphaned, childless, poor, and infirm within the imperial domain,
all according to their respective categories.
Liú Xī's (劉熙) Shìmíng (釋名) says: 'A man without a wife is called guān (鰥);
worried and unable to sleep,
his eyes are always open like a fish (guānguān rán).
The character is formed with the 'fish' radical,
as fish eyes are always open.
A woman without a husband is called guǎ (寡);
guǎ (寡),
means 'bare' (luǒ),
solitary and alone (luǒrán).
A child without a father is called gū (孤);
gū (孤),
means 'looking around' (gù),
looking around with no one to rely on (wú suǒ zhān jiàn).
A person without children is called dú (獨);
dú (獨),
means 'deer' (lù),
wandering aimlessly with no one to depend on (lùlù wú suǒ yī).
Without wealth is called pín (貧).
Fatigued and ill is called lóng (癃).'
Wèi Mìshū Lìng (祕書令) Gāo Yòu (高祐) and Chéng (丞) Lǐ Biāo (李彪) submitted a memorial requesting to change the national history's annual chronology into biographies, treatises, tables, and monographs;
the Wèi ruler agreed.
Yòu (祐) was Yǔn's (允) cousin.
In the twelfth month,
an edict ordered Biāo (彪) and Zuòzhù Láng (著作郎) Cuī Guāng (崔光) to revise and compile the national history.
Guāng (光) was Dàogù's (道固) cousin's grandson.
The ruler of Wèi asked Gāo Yòu,
"How can one stop banditry?"
He replied,
"In the past, Sòng Jūn established virtue,
and fierce tigers crossed the river;
Zhuó Mào practiced moral transformation,
and locusts did not enter his territory.
Sòng Jūn's affair is found in volume forty-five, in the seventh year of Yǒngpíng of Emperor Míng of Hàn.
Zhuó Mào served as the magistrate of Mì,
and his moral transformation was widely implemented.
During the reign of Emperor Píng of Hàn,
there was a great locust plague throughout the land,
but it alone did not enter the borders of Mì Prefecture.
So,
if the local administrators (shǒuzǎi) are the right people,
and their governance (zhìhuà) has a method,
stopping it will be easy."
Yòu also submitted a memorial, stating:
"Current elections
do not consider the merits and demerits of governing ability,
but solely simplify based on the length of service.
This is not what is meant by 'exhausting talent'.
It is appropriate to stop these shallow practices,
discard that decaying service,
and only promote based on talent;
then officialdom will be serene.
Fāng
means 'way'.
Mù
means 'harmony',
and 'clarity'.
Although diligence over years may be commendable, if a person lacks the talent to govern the people,
they may be granted titles and rewards,
but should not be entrusted with substantive appointments (fāngrèn).
This is what is meant by 'a king may give private individuals wealth,
but not give private individuals official positions'."
"A king does not give private individuals official positions" is a phrase from the eulogy in the biography of favored courtiers (Nìngxìng Zhuàn) in the Former Hàn History.
Yòu was sent out to be the Inspector of Xīyǎnyì Zhōu,
stationed at Huátái.
Believing that although commanderies and kingdoms had schools,
prefectures and districts should also have them,
he then ordered prefectures to establish lecture halls (jiǎngxué)
and districts to establish elementary schools (xiǎoxué).
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the Yǐwèi day,
Wèi issued an edict:
"For those who have committed capital crimes,
if their parents or paternal grandparents are old
and have no other adult sons or grandsons,
and have no qīqīn (mourning relatives of one-year mourning period) among their collateral relatives,
a full report should be submitted for consideration."
Qīqīn
refers to those for whom one wears mourning clothes for one year.
2 Initially,
Prince Zǐxiǎng, the Right Guard General, was adopted by Prince Yùzhāng Yí;
later, Yí had a son of his own,
and memorialized to keep him as his heir.
Each time Zǐxiǎng entered court,
seeing his carriages and attire were different from the other princes,
he repeatedly punched the carriage walls.
The Emperor heard of this
and issued an edict for his carriages and attire to be the same as the Imperial Princes.
Thereupon, the relevant officials proposed that Zǐxiǎng should return to his original family.
In the third month,
on the Jǐhài day,
Zǐxiǎng was enfeoffed as Prince Bādōng.
3 Zhāng Pú, the garrison commander of Juéchéng,
took advantage of a heavy fog to travel by boat into Qīngzhōng to collect firewood.
Qīngzhōng
refers to the middle of the Qīng River.
Jiāng,
is pronounced as liàng.
The garrison chief Huángfǔ Zhòngxián became aware of this,
led his troops to resist and fight at the gate,
and barely managed to repel them.
Over three thousand Wèi infantry and cavalry had already reached outside the moat,
but Wáng Sēngqìng, the military commander of Huáinīn, and others led troops to rescue them,
and the Wèi forces then retreated.
4 In summer,
the fourth month,
Huán Tiānshēng again led Wèi troops out to occupy Gécchéng.
An edict ordered the Palace Grandee (Yóujī Jiāngjūn) Cáo Hǔ of Xiàpí to oversee the various armies and attack him.
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Zhū Gōngēn led troops to set up an ambush (táfú),
encountered Huán Tiānshēng's raiding party,
fought them,
defeated them,
and then advanced to besiege Gécchéng.
Huán Tiānshēng led over ten thousand Wèi infantry and cavalry to fight,
but Cáo Hǔ fought valiantly,
greatly defeating them,
capturing and beheading over two thousand people.
The next day,
they attacked and captured Gécchéng,
beheaded Bó Wūzhù, the Administrator of Xiāngchéng,
and again captured and beheaded over two thousand people.
Huán Tiānshēng abandoned Píngshì City and fled.
Píngshì
was a Hàn county,
belonging to Nányáng Commandery,
and in the Jìn and Sòng dynasties, it belonged to Yìyáng Commandery.
To the southwest of the county is Tóngbǎi Mountain,
where the Huái River originates.
The Wǔdài Annals state: Píngshì County of Huái'ān Commandery,
established by Wèi as Hànguǎng Commandery.
During Our Dynasty (Sòng), in the fifth year of Kāibǎo, Píngshì County was abolished as a town
and merged into Bìyáng County of Tángzhōu.
5 Chén Xiǎndá invaded Wèi;
on the Jiǎyín day,
Wèi dispatched Tàbá Jīn, the Inspector of Yùzhōu, to lead troops to resist him.
6 On the Jiǎzǐ day,
Wèi issued a general amnesty.
7 On the Yǐchǒu day,
the ruler of Wèi went to Língquán Pond;
on the Dīngmǎo day,
he went to Fāngshān;
on the Jǐsì day,
he returned to the palace.
8 Wèi built a city at Lǐyáng.
Lǐyáng was probably north of the Lǐ River.
The "Commentary on the Water Classic" states: The Lǐ River originates from Tóngbǎi Mountain,
