sharing the same source as the Huái but flowing separately,
flowing westward,

The grand imperial procession of Wèi

3 On the Rénxū day,
Sòng Yìng, Prince Xiàn of Línchuān, died.
4 Originally,
when the Emperor was Chief Clerk to the General of the West,
the chief clerk Wáng Yàn was favored by him due to his obsequiousness and flattery.
In the fourth year of Yuánhuī of Sòng Cāngwúwáng,
the Emperor was Chief Clerk to the General of the West
and acting governor of Yǐngzhōu,
and appointed Wáng Yàn as chief clerk.
When the Emperor was Crown Prince,
Wáng Yàn was Zhōngshùzǐ.
When the Emperor offended Tàizǔ,
the details can be found in the first year of the previous volume.
Upon his accession,
Wáng Yàn was appointed Governor of Dānyáng,
and the Emperor's trust in him was as before;
he was seen once in the morning and evening,
and court affairs were discussed;
even Prince Yùzhāng Xiāo Yí and Wáng Jiǎn all treated him with deference.
In the second month,
on the Rén Yín day,
Wáng Yàn was sent out to be Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
but Wáng Yàn did not wish to leave the capital,
so he was kept and reappointed as Minister of Personnel.
5 In the third month,
on the Jiǎ Yín day,

Zǐjùn as Prince of Guǎnghàn,
Zǐlín as Prince of Xuānchéng,
and Zǐmín as Prince of Yì'ān.
6 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Dīngchǒu day,
the Wèi Emperor issued an edict saying:
"Ascending towers and scattering goods to bestow upon the common people
has resulted in people and horses trampling each other,
causing many injuries and damages;
this practice should now be stopped.
The funds originally spent on these items
should be given to the elderly, the sick, the poor, and the solitary."
7 On the Dīnghài day,
the Wèi Emperor went to Língquán Chí,
then went to Fāng Shān;
on the Jǐchǒu day,

8 The Emperor treated Wáng Jiǎn, Duke Wénxiàn of Nánchāng, with exceptional courtesy,
decreeing that he should return to court only once every three days,
and that clerks from the Department of State Affairs should go out to consult him on matters.
The Emperor still considered the comings and goings too frequent,
so he again decreed that Wáng Jiǎn should return to the Lower Department of State Affairs,
and was allowed to be out of the office for ten days each month.
Wáng Jiǎn firmly requested to be relieved from personnel selection duties.
An edict changed his title to Director of the Central Secretariat,
and he participated in managing selection affairs.
In the fifth month,
on the Yǐsì day,
Wáng Jiǎn died.
As Wáng Yàn was already in charge of selection and
his authority extended throughout the imperial chancellery,
he was quite resentful towards Wáng Jiǎn.
The ritual officials wished to follow the precedent of Wáng Dǎo
and grant Wáng Jiǎn the posthumous title Wénxiàn.
Wáng Yàn reported to the Emperor, saying:
"Only Wáng Dǎo received this posthumous title;
but since the Sòng dynasty,
it has not been conferred upon those of different surnames."
He went out
and said to his close associates:
"The 'Píngtóu Xiàn'
matter has been carried out."
Píngtóu
refers to the character 'Wáng'.
Posthumous title.
Regarding the death of Xú Zhànzhī,
Xú Zhànzhī's death can be found in Volume 137, in the thirtieth year of Yuánjiā of Sòng Wéndì.
At eight years old,
Xú Xiàosì inherited the title Duke of Zhījiāng County
and married Princess Kānglè of Sòng.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Xú Xiàosì was Imperial Censor,
dignified and modest in manner.
Wáng Jiǎn said to others:
"Xú Xiàosì will certainly become a chancellor in the future."
The Emperor once asked Wáng Jiǎn:
"Who can succeed you?"
Wáng Jiǎn replied:
"When I am in Dōngdū (the Eastern Capital),
perhaps it will be Xú Xiàosì!"
This referred to the Duke of Zhōu, who, having settled Luòyáng,
invited Míngnóng.
The Zhōu capital was Fēng and Hào,
and Luòyáng was designated as the Eastern Capital.
Xú Xiàosì was then Administrator of Wúxīng,
and was summoned to be Minister of Five Armies.
9 On the Gēngxū day,
the Wèi Emperor performed sacrifice at Fāngzé.
Fāngzé refers to
a square mound built in a marsh for sacrificing to the Earth God.
10The Emperor wished to employ Wáng Huàn, General of the Army, as Grand Minister of State,
and consulted Wáng Yàn about it.
Wáng Yàn and Wáng Huàn were not on good terms.
He replied:

On the Jiǎzǐ day,
Liǔ Shìlóng, Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Grand Minister of State,

the Six Towns rebelled.

Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Wèi’s capital was Píngchéng (平城).
Huáishuò Town was established over three hundred *lǐ* (里) north of Mǎyì (馬邑) Commandery.
After the move to Luò (洛),
Shuòzhōu was established.
Jiàng (將),
is pronounced *liàng* (亮);
the same below.
All were liable to death for embezzlement.
Empress Dowager Féng (馮) and the Wèi ruler presided at the Huángxìntáng (皇信堂).
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* (水經註) says: The south of the Tàijí Diàn (太極殿) faces the Chéngxián Mén (承賢門).
South of the gate is the Huángxìntáng.
The Wèi Book, Imperial Annals says: In the tenth month of the seventh year of Tàihé (太和),
the Huángxìntáng was completed.
In the sixteenth year,
the Ānchāng Diàn (安昌殿) was made the inner bedchamber,
and the Huángxìntáng the central bedchamber.
The Empress Dowager issued an order saying:
"Do you, gentlemen, believe we should preserve relatives and destroy the law,
or destroy relatives to uphold the law?"
The ministers all said:
"The two kings
are the sons of Jǐngmù Huángdì (景穆皇帝).
Jǐngmù Huángdì,
son of Shìzǔ (世祖),
died,
and was posthumously titled Jǐngmù Huángdì,
but did not assume the imperial throne.
The two kings are great-uncles to Gāozǔ (高祖)."
The Empress Dowager did not agree.
The Wèi ruler then issued an edict,
stating:
"The crimes committed by the two kings are unforgivable.
However, the Grand Empress Dowager recalls the profound fraternal affection of Gāozōng (高宗);
the two kings were brothers to Wénchéng Dì (文成帝).
The *Shī* (詩) says: Brothers have profound affection.
Wéi (惟),
means 'to think'.
It is known throughout the realm,
and they are specially exempted from death,

Originally,
the Wèi court heard of Zhēn's (楨) greed and cruelty,
and sent Zhōngsàn (中散) Lǘ Wénzǔ (閭文祖) to Cháng'ān (長安) to investigate him.
Zhōngsàn,
is Zhōngsàn Dàfū (中散大夫).
Sàn (散),
is pronounced *xīdàn* (悉亶).
He concealed it for him;
when the matter came to light,
Wénzǔ also suffered punishment.
Empress Dowager Féng said to the ministers:
"Wénzǔ previously claimed to be incorruptible,
but now he has actually violated the law.
From this,
human hearts are indeed unknowable."
The Wèi ruler said:
"In ancient times, there were ministers who awaited dismissal.
The *Chūnqiū Gōngyáng Zhuàn* (春秋公羊傳) says: Jìn (晉) dismissed its minister Xū Jiǎfù (胥甲父) to Wèi (衞).
What does 'dismissed' mean?
It means 'do not leave'.
But then what does the expression mean?
It means 'close to upright'.
How is this 'close to upright'?
In ancient times,
once a minister had left, he waited three years for dismissal.
For the ruler to dismiss him was wrong;
for a minister to await dismissal was upright.
This means
allowing them to resign their positions
and return to their residences."
Zǎiguān (宰官) and Zhōngsàn Mùróng Qì (慕容契) came forward and said:
Qì (契) likely held the title of Zǎiguān while also being Zhōngsàn Dàfū.
"The hearts of small men are inconstant, but the laws of emperors and kings are constant;

I beg to be allowed to retire and be dismissed."
The Wèi ruler said:
"Qì knows that the heart cannot be constant,

Why must he seek to retire?"
He was promoted to Zǎiguān Lìng (宰官令).
Qì
was a disciple of Báiyào (白曜).
Mùróng Báiyào (慕容白曜) had the achievement of pacifying Qí (齊).
13 In autumn,
seventh month,
on the *bǐngyín* (丙寅) day,
the Wèi ruler visited the Língquán Chí (靈泉池).
14 The Wèi ruler had his ministers discuss,

What do you think?"
Shàngshū (尚書) Yóu Mínggēn (游明根) said:

Now to send envoys again,

The Wèi ruler followed his advice.
Eighth month,
on the *yǐhài* (乙亥) day,
he dispatched concurrently Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍) Xíng Chǎn (邢產) and others to come and establish relations.

Wèi released palace women

The Northern Towns
were the Six Towns.
One was Huáishuò Town,
directly north of Píngchéng.
16 In winter, eleventh month,
on the *jǐwèi* (己未) day,
Wèi’s Ānfēng Kuāng Wáng (安豐匡王) Měng (猛) suddenly died.
17 Twelfth month,
on the *bǐngzǐ* (丙子) day,
Wèi’s Hédōng Wáng (河東王) Gǒu Tuí (苟頹) died.
18 Píngnán Cānjūn (平南參軍) Yán Yòumíng (顏幼明) and others went as envoys to Wèi.
19 Wèi appointed Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Wèi Yuán (尉元) as Sītú Zuǒ Púyè (司徒左僕射),
and Mù Liàng (穆亮) as Sīkōng (司空).
20 Yùzhāng Wáng (豫章王) Yì (嶷), considering his position too important,
deeply desired a life of retirement.
In this year,
he petitioned to return to his residence;
the Emperor ordered his heir, Zǐlián (子廉), to take his place as the commander of the Eastern Commandery.
21 Tàizǐ Zhānshì (太子詹事) Zhāng Xù (張緒) concurrently served as Yángzhōu Zhōngzhèng (揚州中正).
Chángshā Wáng (長沙王) Huǎng (晃) wanted to appoint Wúxīng (吳興) Wén Rén Yōng (聞人邕) as the province's Yìcáo (議曹).
Xù did not permit it.
Huǎng sent a scribe to insist,
Xù sternly said:
"This is my family's native province and village;
how can Your Highness coerce me?"
From Wèi and Jìn (晉) times onwards,
the Zhōngzhèng (中正) typically employed respected local people from their own province.
22 Shìzhōng (侍中) Jiāng Xiào (江斅) was appointed Dūguān Shàngshū (都官尚書).
Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人) Jì Sēngzhēn (紀僧真) enjoyed the Emperor's favor.
His appearance and demeanor had the bearing of a scholar.
He petitioned the Emperor, saying:
"I am from a military family in my home county.
I have encountered a fortunate era.
"Yāo" (邀)
in *Nán Shǐ Jiāng Xiào Zhuàn* (南史江斅傳) is written as
"Jiǎo" (憿).
The *Shuōwén* (說文) says: It means 'luck'.
The *Jíyùn* (集韻) says: Jiǎo (憿), Jiǎo (僥), Jiǎo (徼) are interchangeable,
pronounced *jiānyáo* (堅堯).
As a child, I married Xún Zhāoguāng's (荀昭光) daughter.
Immediately, I had nothing else I needed.
I only ask Your Majesty to make me a scholar-official."
The Emperor said:
"This is up to Jiāng Xiào and Xiè Yuè (謝瀹).

You may go to them yourself."
Sēngzhēn, following the order, went to Xiào.
After he sat down on the couch,
Xiào looked at his attendants and ordered:

Sēngzhēn, disheartened, retreated,

Xiào
was the grandson of Zhàn (湛);
Yuè

The two families conducted themselves with integrity and reputation,

Fěi (朏),

Therefore, *xiá* is *dì*.

Wáng Sù further states: ‘Both the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords perform the *dì* sacrifice at the ancestral temple,

hence called *xiá*;
it is a *dì* sacrifice performed with careful examination,
hence called *dì*.
They are not names for two different sacrifices.
“A *xiá* once every three years,
a *dì* once every five years”—
these are comprehensive and mutually illustrative terms.
Therefore, it is referred to as 'twice grand sacrifices in five years,'

are generally as stated.

is a great sacrifice.’

Lǔ performed the ceremonies of the Son of Heaven,

One season means
that sacrifices should not be too frequent,
and three *dì* sacrifices in a year would be excessive.”
The edict stated:
“Mínggēn, Lǘ, and others have elaborated thoroughly on the *dì* and *xiá* sacrifices
based on the interpretations of the two schools;
however, as for adopting a compromising approach to the matter,
it is still not entirely satisfactory.
Lǘ considers *dì* and *xiá* to be names
whose meaning is the same as Wáng [Sù]'s view,
and the *dì* sacrifice at the Round Mound
is consistent with Zhèng [Xuán]'s view on the matter,
without any discrepancy.
Mínggēn considers Zhèng [Xuán]'s view as two names and two sacrifices,
both existing and both used concurrently,
but this reasoning is not entirely coherent.
To claim to follow both interpretations,
performing *dì* and *xiá* in one season and omitting the *dì* of the other two seasons,
is a matter difficult to accept.
The former kings established the rites,
internally based on the feelings of children towards their parents,
and externally in accordance with the order of hierarchy.
Thus, the Son of Heaven had seven temples;
when the number was exhausted, they were destroyed,
and the spirit tablets were stored in the Grand Ancestor's temple,
where a *xiá* sacrifice was performed every three years.
When a generation was exhausted, the temple was destroyed,
to demonstrate the principle of an end;
the *xiá* every three years
was to express the sentiment of revering the distant ancestors.
Since *dì* and *xiá* are already one sacrifice,
to divide them into two
has no basis.
Destroying a temple and performing a *xiá* every three years,
and furthermore not covering all four seasons,
is a deficiency in the rites.
The seven temples have regular sacrifices in all four seasons,
while the *xiá* is performed once every three years,
and again does not cover all four seasons,
which is too simple in terms of sentiment.
Wáng [Sù]'s view that *xiá* is one sacrifice
is superior in principle.
Zhèng [Xuán]'s view that the *dì* at the Round Mound is the same as the great sacrifice at the ancestral temple
is also appropriate in name and meaning.
Now, we shall adopt a compromise between Zhèng [Xuán]'s and Wáng [Sù]'s interpretations:
the *dì* and *xiá* sacrifices shall be combined into one,
following Wáng [Sù];
*dì* is the name for the great sacrifice at the Round Mound,
used by all ranks,
following Zhèng [Xuán].
If it is considered excessive to be frequent,
then a *dì* sacrifice once every five years,
changing *xiá* to follow *dì*.
With a *dì* sacrifice once every five years,
then all four seasons will have *dì* sacrifices,
to accord with current sentiments.
Then, the rite of "touring Heaven" (*lǚtiān*)
and the ritual texts,
which prioritize *dì* before seasonal sacrifices,
shall be immediately implemented,
stipulated in the ordinances,
and made a perpetual law for generations.”

On Dīngmǎo,
wearing the ceremonial robe and cap,
he bade farewell to the Tàihé Miào,
and led the hundred officials to move the spirit tablets to the new temple.
The newly built Tàimiào was completed,
so the spirit tablets were moved to the new temple.
Shuài
is pronounced as 'shuài'.
19 Yǐhài,
Wèi greatly reformed official ranks.
Wùxū,
all regional governors and prefects were evaluated.
20 Wèi sent Lǐ Biāo and others, acting as Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, to offer tribute.
21 According to the old Wèi system,
all ministers paid respects in the last month of winter,
performing their duties in trousers and jackets.
This was called Xiǎosuì [Minor New Year].
On Bǐngxū,
an edict abolished it.
22 In the twelfth month,
on Rénchén,
Wèi moved the altar of the land to the west of the inner city.
23 Wèi appointed Āndìng Wáng Xiū as Tàifù,
and Qíjùn Wáng Jiǎn as Tàibǎo.
24 Gāolì Wáng Lián died,
aged over a hundred sui.
The Wèi Zhǔ had a plain wěimào [cap] and a plain cloth deep garment made for him,
and expressed grief in the eastern suburbs;
he dispatched the Yèzhě Púyè Lǐ Ānshàng to confer upon him posthumously the title of Tàifù,
and the posthumous name Kāng.
His grandson Yún then succeeded him.
25 Yǐyǒu,
the Wèi Zhǔ first welcomed spring in the eastern suburbs.
From then on, he personally welcomed the qi of all four seasons.
26 Originally,
when Wèi Shìzǔ conquered Tǒngwàn and Gūzāng,
he obtained court music instruments, ceremonial attire, and artisans.
In the fourth year of Yuánjiā of Sòng Wéndì,
Wèi conquered Tǒngwàn;
in the sixteenth year,
it conquered Gūzāng.
During the chaos of Yǒngjiā of Jìn,
many imperial music artisans fled to Héxī;
the Xià conquered Cháng'ān,
obtaining Qín court music.
Thus, both states possessed these instruments, attire, and artisans.
Subsequently, through several reigns, no one paid attention to them.
Cháo
is pronounced 'zhí yáo fān' [straight distant turn].
Many of the musical sounds and systems were lost.
Gāozǔ first ordered the relevant officials to seek out those knowledgeable in music theory among the people to deliberate and establish court music.
At that time, no one was truly capable of doing so.
However, the adornments of metal, stone, feathers, and yak tails
gradually became more magnificent than in earlier times.
On Xīnhài,
an edict was issued to select and appoint music officials,
to have them fulfill their duties;
it also ordered the Zhōngshū Jiān Gāo Lǘ to participate in its determination.
At first,
Zhāng Fěi and Dù Yù of the Jìn dynasty jointly annotated the thirty volumes of the Lǜ (laws),
which had been in use since the Tàishǐ era.
This refers to the Tàishǐ era of Jìn.
Sometimes, within a single chapter,
the interpretations of the two families
differed vastly on matters of life and death,
leading to ad hoc deliberation,
which allowed officials to commit malpractice.
The Emperor paid close attention to laws and regulations,
and issued an edict to the judicial officials to thoroughly review and correct the old annotations.
In the seventh year,
Wáng Zhí, the Shān Dìng Láng of the Shàngshū, compiled and finalized the two annotations,
and presented them in a memorial.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
the various departments of the Shàngshū had no Shān Dìng Láng.
This position was likely established for editing and revising the Lǜ and their annotations.
Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng oversaw the entire project;
for matters where the various opinions differed and could not be unified,
the imperial decree provided the final arbitration.
In this year,
the book was completed.
Kǒng Zhìguī of Shānyīn, the Tíngwèi, submitted a memorial,
arguing:
"Although the legal text is finalized,
if its application is unjust,
then the law books will merely be bright within their cases.
'Zhì'
is the same as 'zhì'.
I humbly observe that among the famous scholars of antiquity,
many were learned in law;
but among the scholars of today,
none are willing to make it their profession.
Even if there are those who study it,
they are looked down upon by public opinion.
I fear that this book will forever fall into the hands of mere clerks.
If we now establish law assistant instructors,
following the example of the Five Classics,
and if any Guózǐshēng wish to study it,
they can be tested and those with high grades
will be promoted and employed
to fill internal and external official positions.
Perhaps then, the scholarly class will be encouraged and inspired."
The Emperor assented to his request,
but the matter was ultimately not implemented.
At first,
Fàn Yángmài, the King of Línyì,
whose lineage had passed down through generations—
Fàn Yángmài is mentioned in Volume 124, during Yuánjiā 23rd year of Sòng Wéndì—
sent envoys to offer golden mats and other items.
An imperial edict appointed Dāng Gēnchún as Dūdū Yuánhǎi Zhū Jūnfǎ, King of Línyì.
This laid the groundwork for Xià Fàn Zhūnóng to attack Dāng Gēnchún.
'Shǐ'
is pronounced 'shū lì'.
Xián Yángwáng Xǐ, the Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu in Wèi, entered the court.
The relevant authorities submitted a memorial stating:
"Three thousand people of Jìzhōu praise Xǐ for his clear and benevolent governance,
and request that Jìzhōu be his hereditary fief."
The Wèi Emperor decreed:
"While 'Lì Jiàn' (establishing a fief) is ancient,
it may not be appropriate now;
the Yì Jīng says: 'Lì Jiàn Hóu.'
It is not a matter for subjects to request."
The Zhōu Lǐ states: "Only the King establishes states,
distinguishes directions and sets positions, embodying the state and managing the fields."
Zhèng Xuán's annotation states: "Jīng
refers to setting out the measurements."
At first,
Wèi Wénmíng Tàihòu favored and entrusted the eunuch Lüèyáng Fú Chéngzǔ,
who rose to the position of Shìzhōng,
overseeing Dūcáo affairs.
This refers to overseeing the Dūcáo affairs of the Shàngshū.
When the Empress Dowager passed away,
Chéngzǔ was implicated in corruption and deserved death,
but the Wèi Emperor pardoned him,
stripping him of his office and confining him to his home.
He was then appointed Bèiyì Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as Nìngzhuó Zǐ,
but died a month later.
While Chéngzǔ was in power, his relatives competed to curry favor and seek benefits.
His maternal aunt, Yáng Shì, married into the Yáo family.
'Cóngmǔ'
means 'maternal aunt'.
'Cóng'
is pronounced 'cái yòng'.
She often said to Chéngzǔ's mother:
"Although you have temporary glory,
it is not as good as your sister's joy of having no worries."
Her sister gave her clothes,
but she often refused them;
if forced to accept,
she would say:
"My husband's family has always been poor,
beautiful clothes make people uneasy."
Out of necessity,
she would sometimes accept them and bury them.
When given servants,
she would say:
"My family has no food,
we cannot feed them."
She always wore worn-out clothes
and personally performed arduous labor.
Chéngzǔ sent a carriage to fetch her,
but she refused to get up;
when people forcibly carried her into the carriage,
she cried loudly, saying:
"You want to kill me!"
Because of this, among Fú's relatives,
she was called
"the foolish aunt."
When Chéngzǔ fell,
the authorities arrested his two maternal aunts and brought them to the imperial court.
One of them was executed.
The Emperor saw that the Yáo family's aunt was poor and simple,
and specially pardoned her.
When Lǐ Huì was executed,
the event is recorded in Volume 134, during Shēngmíng 2nd year of Sòng Shùndì.
Wèi Xiàowén posthumously honored his mother, Lǐ Guìrén, as Empress Sī.
Chánglè was executed for disloyalty.
This event is recorded in Volume 135, during Jiànyuán 1st year of Gāo Dì.
'Cóng'
is pronounced 'cái yòng'.
'Lè'
is pronounced 'luò'.
Fèngzǐ Ānzǔ and four others escaped and went into hiding,
and emerged only after an amnesty.
Later, the Wèi Emperor inquired about his maternal relatives who were still alive,
found Ānzǔ and others,
and enfeoffed them all as marquises,
and bestowed upon them general titles.
Later, he granted them an audience
and said:
"Your ancestors
twice committed offenses against the state.
'Xiānshì'
refers to Huì and Fèng.
'Jiàn'
is pronounced 'xián biàn'.
To be promoted based on being an imperial relative
is a practice of the late generations.
Since you have no special abilities,
you may return home.
From now on, any imperial relatives without ability should be viewed this way."
Later, by imperial decree, their peerage was generally reduced to earls,
and their military titles were removed.
'Jūnhào'
refers to the title of general.
'Qù'
is pronounced 'qiāng lǚ'.
He treated the Lǐ family too poorly;
Gāo Lǘ of Tàicháng once spoke about it,
but the Emperor did not listen.
When Shìzōng later honored and favored his maternal relatives,
he appointed Ānzǔ's younger brother Xīngzǔ as Zhōngshān Tàishǒu,
and posthumously granted Lǐ Huì the titles of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Zhōngshān Gōng,
with the posthumous name Zhuāng.
In spring,
the first month,
on the day of Wùwǔ,
the Wèi Emperor held a court banquet for his officials at Tàihuá Diàn,
but hung without joy.
On the day of Jǐwèi,
the Wèi Emperor offered sacrifices to Xiǎnzǔ in the Míngtáng, associating him with the Supreme Deity,
then ascended the Língtái to observe celestial phenomena,
and descended to Qīngyáng Zuǒgè
to administer state affairs.
Zhèng Shì said: "Qīngyáng Zuǒgè is the northern side of the east hall of the great sleeping quarters."
Sànqí Chángshì Yǔ Bì and others were envoys to Wèi.
The Wèi Emperor ordered Shìláng Chéng Yān to lead Bì and others south of the guest hall,
to look up and perform the rituals.
These were the rituals of sacrificing at the Míngtáng and ascending the Língtái.
On the day of Xīnyǒu, the Wèi dynasty began to associate Tàizǔ with the Southern Suburbs in sacrifices.
3 The Emperor of Wèi ordered his ministers to deliberate on the dynastic sequence.
This was the sequence of the Five Phases.
They considered:
"Emperors and kings without exception take the Zhōngyuán as the legitimate succession,
and do not base the granting or taking away (of legitimacy) on the number of generations,
nor right or wrong on good or evil.
Therefore, although Jié and Zhòu were extremely tyrannical,
the calendars of Xià and Shāng were not abolished;
and though Lì and Huì were extremely muddled,
this did not harm the records of Zhōu and Jìn.
Jìn succeeded Wèi as Metal,
Zhào succeeded Jìn as Water,
Yàn succeeded Zhào as Wood,
and Qín succeeded Yàn as Fire.
After Qín had perished,
Wèi then claimed imperial authority over Xuánshuò (the North);
moreover, the Wèi clan's surname
originated from Xuānyuán.
The Wèi Shū states: 'The ancestors of Wèi came from the Huángdì Xuānyuán Shì.'
Huángdì's son Chāngyì was enfeoffed in the northern country,
where there was the Dà Xiānbēi Shān,
and they thus took it as their designation.
According to the Shǐ Jì,
the Xiōngnú were considered descendants of the Xiàhòu Shì;
probably there is such a principle.
According to the Imperial Annals of the Wèi Shū: In the first year of Tiānxīng under Emperor Dàowǔ,
the ministers memorialized that 'Our state, succeeding Huángdì,
should be Earth virtue.'
Gāo Lǘ probably merely reiterated the previous proposal."
They also considered:
"Emperor Shényuán and Emperor Wǔ of Jìn maintained friendly relations;
and up to Emperor Huán and Emperor Mù,
they aimed to assist the Jìn dynasty.
These events are all recorded in the Jìn Jì.
Emperor Shényuán was Lìwēi;
Emperor Huán was Yītuō;
Emperor Mù was Yīlú.
Hénán Commandery, Hénán County,
was the Royal City of Zhōu,
which is Jiárǔ.
Formerly, when Qín unified the realm,
Hàn still compared it to Gònggōng,
and eventually succeeded Zhōu as Fire virtue;
the Treatise on Pitch-pipes and the Calendar in the Hàn Lǜ Lì Zhì states: the sacrificial canons say: 'The Gònggōng Shì dominated the nine regions.'
This means that although it had Water virtue,
it was between Fire and Wood,
which was not its proper sequence;
it relied on cunning and punishment to gain power,
and thus dominated but did not rule as a true king.
Qín, with Water virtue, was between Zhōu (Wood) and Hàn (Fire),
the Zhōu people changed its sequence of phases,
therefore it is not recorded in the Yì (Book of Changes).
With its narrow territory and short duration,
Wèi inherited its defects,
how can it abandon Jìn and become Earth virtue?"
Sīkōng Mù Liàng and others all requested to follow the proposal of Biāo and others.
On the *rénxū* day,
an imperial edict proclaimed that Wèi would succeed Jìn as Water virtue,
worshipping *shēn* and performing the *là* sacrifice on *chén*.
The Examination of Differences states: The Treatise on Rites says:
"In the first month of the fifteenth year of Tàihé,
Mù Liàng and others said" and so on.
According to the Imperial Annals:
"On the *rénxū* day of the first month of the sixteenth year,
an imperial edict settled the dynastic sequence,
taking Water to succeed Metal."
Probably the Treatise mistakenly took
"six"
for
"five."
4 On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Wèi abolished rent and taxes.
"Rent and taxes" (租課),
Lǐ Yánshòu's Annals of Wèi writes
"stripped naked" (袒裸).
5 There were many of the Wèi imperial clan and descendants of meritorious ministers who were enfeoffed as kings.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Except for the descendants of Emperor Lièzǔ,
all other kings shall be demoted to dukes,
and dukes demoted to marquises,
but their rank shall remain as before."
The Barbarian King Huán Dàn was also demoted to duke;
only Zhǎngsūn Guān, King of Shàngdǎng,
was specially not demoted
because his ancestor had performed great meritorious service.
Zhǎngsūn Dàoshēng was enfeoffed as King of Shàngdǎng for his merits.
The title King of Sòng was granted.
6 According to the old Wèi system,
sacrifices at the ancestral temple in all four seasons were held in the middle period (of the season).
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
an imperial edict proclaimed that they would begin to use the first month of each season,
selecting a day for the sacrifice.
Since the Hàn dynasty,
the ancestral temple had five annual sacrifices: those in the first month of each of the four seasons and the *là* sacrifice.
Wèi initially used the middle period,
which was a barbarian rite.
7 Xiāo Zǐliáng, Prince of Jìnglíng, was concurrently appointed Director of the Department of State Affairs.
8 The Emperor of Wèi demolished Tàihuá Palace to build Tàijí Palace.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
he moved his residence to Yǒnglè Palace.
He appointed Minister Lǐ Chōng to concurrently hold the post of Grand Architect,
to jointly supervise its construction with Sīkōng Mù Liàng.
9 On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Wèi abolished the Hánshí festival feast.
The old tradition states that Hánshí is one hundred and five days after the Winter Solstice.
The Chūxué Jì says: Zhōu Jǔ's communication, Emperor Wǔ of Wèi's order on clear punishments, and Lù Huì's Records of Yè
all state that the fire ban during Hánshí originated from Jiè Zǐtuī.
However, the Rites of Zhōu states that the Officer in charge of Fire, in mid-spring,
would use a wooden-tongued bell to proclaim a fire ban throughout the capital.
The commentary says: this was because new fire was about to be produced in mid-spring.
Today, Hánshí, according to the solar terms, is at the end of mid-spring,
and Qīngmíng is at the beginning of the third month;
thus the fire ban is also a Zhōu institution.
Wèi previously offered sacrifices to ancestors during Hánshí;
now, considering it improper,
it was abolished.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
the Emperor of Wèi first sacrificed to the morning sun in the eastern suburb.
From then on, he personally performed both the morning sun and evening moon sacrifices.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
an imperial edict commanded sacrifices to Yáo in Píngyáng,
Shùn in Guǎngníng,
Yǔ in Ānyì,
and the Duke of Zhōu in Luòyáng,
all based on their former capitals.
Huángfǔ Mì said: "Where Shùn had his capital is sometimes said to be Púbǎn,
sometimes Pān."
Pān
is today's Shànggǔ.
Guǎngníng County originally belonged to Shànggǔ.
Also, according to the Commentary on the Classic of Waterways,
"Pān"
should be written as
"Fèn."
The temple to Xuānní (Confucius)
was sacrificed at in the Zhōngshū Shěng.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
the posthumous title of Xuānní was changed to Wénshèng Nífù (Cultured Saint, Ni Father),
and the Emperor personally performed the bowing and sacrifice.
Heaven was sacrificed to every year in the western suburb.
The Emperor of Wèi, accompanied by dukes and ministers and more than two thousand cavalry,
would circle the altar in military attire;
this was called *tà tán* (stepping on the altar).
The next day,
they would again ascend the altar in military attire to offer sacrifices,
and then again circle the altar;
this was called *rào tiān* (circling Heaven).
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn said: "Circling the altar in military attire,
the Wèi Emperor made one circuit,
and the dukes and ministers seven circuits;
this was called *tà tán*.
The next day,
they would again ascend the altar in military attire to sacrifice to Heaven,
the Wèi Emperor making three circuits, and the dukes and ministers seven circuits; this was called *rào tiān*."
On the *guǐyǒu* day,
an imperial edict completely abolished these practices.
10 On the *xīnsì* day, Wèi appointed Yún, King of Gāolì, as Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Liáohǎi, Duke of Liáodōng, and King of Gāogōulí,
and ordered Yún to send his heir apparent to court.
Yún declined due to illness,
and sent his paternal cousin-uncle Shēnggān to accompany the envoy to Píngchéng.
11 Summer,
fourth month.
On the *dīnghài* day, the first day of the month,
Wèi promulgated new laws and ordinances,
and issued a great amnesty.
12th day, Xīnchǒu.
Yùzhāng Wénxiàn Wáng Yí died.
He was posthumously granted the titles of acting General-in-Chief with Yellow Axe, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs inside and outside the imperial domain, and Chancellor.
His funeral rites were all conducted according to the precedents set for Hàn Dōngpíng Xiàn Wáng.
Yí was by nature benevolent, cautious, honest, and frugal.
He did not concern himself with wealth or bribes.
When the zhāi treasury caught fire,
zhāi treasury refers to
the treasury inside his zhāi (fasting chamber/residence).
In the second year of Gāozǔ's Jiànyuán era,
Yí returned from Jīngzhōu to become Governor of Yángzhōu.
Píngzhí means
to assess the value of his possessions.
When his illness became critical,
he left a dying instruction to his sons, saying:
“Talents have their superior and inferior,
positions have their opening and closing,
fortune has its rich and poor;
these are the principles of nature.
There is no reason to look down upon or insult one another.”
This was likely his wish that his sons would not oppress each other based on their positions or power.
Sè (塞)
is pronounced with the tone of zé.
After a long time,
when Yí was mentioned,
the Emperor would still sigh and shed tears.
On the day Yí died,
his mansion’s treasury had no ready cash.
The Emperor ordered a monthly allowance of one million coins for Yí’s mansion;
this was only discontinued at the end of the Emperor’s reign.
13th day, fifth month.
Jǐsì.
Jìnglíng Wáng Ziliáng was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu.
14th day, during the mourning period for Wèi Wénmíng Tàihòu,
an envoy was sent to inform the Tǔyùhún.
Tǔyùhún Wáng Fúliánchóu received the imperial decree disrespectfully.
Tǔ (吐)
is pronounced like tūn, entering tone.
Yù (谷)
is pronounced like yù (浴).
The Wèi Emperor refused to grant his request.
He also requested the return of his tribute gifts.
The Emperor said:
“Tribute gifts are the proper rites for a subject.
If we do not accept them now,
it means we are abandoning and severing ties with them.
Even if they wish to reform themselves,
there will be no way for them to do so.”
Consequently, he ordered the return of the captives from Táoyáng and Níhé.
These were captives taken by Zhǎngsūn Bǎinián last year.
Autumn,
seventh month.
Gēngshēn.
The Tǔyùhún sent their heir apparent Hèlǔtóu to pay homage to Wèi.
An imperial edict appointed Fúliánchóu as Grand Administrator of Military Affairs for the Western Frontier, Duke of Xīhǎi, and King of Tǔyùhún.
Zhāng Lǐ, who held the concurrent title of Member of the Secretariat and Palace Aide with the rank of Cavalier Attendant, was dispatched as envoy to Tǔyùhún.
Fúliánchóu said to Lǐ:
“Previously, the Dàngchāng always referred to themselves by name and were addressed as Great Kings.
Now, they suddenly refer to themselves as 'I' (仆), and they also detained our envoy.
Should I send a detached force to question them?
What do you think?”
Lǐ replied:
“Both you and the Dàngchāng are vassals of Wèi.
Your repeated attacks against them
greatly violate the duties of a subject.
On the day I left the capital,
the high officials said
that if you can acknowledge your faults,
then your vassal state can be preserved;
if you do not mend your ways,
disaster will surely befall you.”
Fúliánchóu fell silent.
15th day, Jiǎxū.
Wèi sent Sòng Biàn of Guǎngpíng, who held the concurrent title of Member of the Secretariat and Palace Aide with the rank of Cavalier Attendant, and others to pay a visit.
When they returned,
the Wèi Emperor asked Biàn:
“How is Jiāngnán?”
Biàn replied:
“The Xiāo clan, father and son, have no great accomplishments in the world.
Having seized power through rebellion,
they are unable to govern with virtue.
Their decrees are harsh and fragmented,
their taxes and corvée are heavy.
There are no trusted ministers in the court,
and the populace in the countryside is full of grief and resentment.
It would be fortunate for them to merely die a natural death;
it is not the way to establish a lasting legacy for their descendants.”
16th day, eighth month.
Yǐwèi.
Wèi appointed Yángpíng Wáng Yí, the General of Huáishuò Garrison, and Lù Ruì, the Grand General who Awesthe North, as Grand Administrators,
to command twelve generals,
with one hundred thousand infantry and cavalry,
divided into three routes to attack the Rouran:
the central route departed from Hēishān,
the eastern route headed towards Shìlú Hé,
and the western route headed towards Hóuyán Hé.
The army crossed the Great Desert
and decisively defeated the Rouran before returning.
17th day, in the beginning,
Rouran Fúmíngdūn Kèhán.
Kè (可)
is pronounced like kān, entering tone.
Hán (汗)
is pronounced like hán.
Fúmíngdūn had been repeatedly defeated,
while Nàgài had achieved repeated victories.
The people of the kingdom believed that Nàgài had received divine assistance,
so they killed Fúmíngdūn and enthroned Nàgài,
who was titled Hòuqífúdàikùzhě Kèhán.
Wèi Shōu said: In Wèi language, this means "joy and happiness."
Ān.
18th day, Wèi Sītú Wèi Yuán and Dàhónglú Qīng Yóu Mínggēn repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement due to old age.
The Wèi Emperor granted their requests.
He granted them an audience,
bestowing Yuán with a dark cap and plain clothing.
The Shíqú Lùn states: "Dark cap and court attire."
Dài Shèng said: "Dark cap
is wěimào (ceremonial cap)."
Here, the dark cap and wěimào are distinct forms.
He also bestowed them with various garments and other items before sending them off.
The Wèi Emperor personally honored the Sānlǎo (Three Elders) and Wǔgēng (Five Mentors) in the Míngtáng.
Jǐyǒu.
An imperial edict appointed Yuán as Sānlǎo
and Mínggēn as Wǔgēng. The Emperor bowed twice to the Sānlǎo,
personally bared his arm to slaughter a sacrificial animal,
held the goblet, and offered it to them.
He performed a solemn bow to the Wǔgēng.
The Zhōu Lǐ lists nine types of bows,
the ninth being a solemn bow (sùbài).
Zhèng Sīnóng said: "Sùbài
is merely bowing and lowering the hands,
which is the present-day yì (撎)."
Lù Démíng said: "Yì (撎),
pronounced like yì,
is the present-day yī (揖, a bow with hands clasped)."
Gēng (更)
is pronounced like gēng (工衡翻).
Yuán and Mínggēn exhorted the Emperor to transform the people through filial piety and brotherly affection.
He also honored common elders and state elders below the steps.
After the ceremony,
Yuán and Mínggēn were each bestowed with a hand-pulled cart and clothing.
A hand-pulled cart
does not use oxen or horses,
but is pulled by people on foot.
Wǔgēng with Yuánqīng.
Yuánqīng
is equivalent to Shàngqīng (Senior Minister).
19th day, ninth month.
Jiǎyín.
The Wèi Emperor arranged the ancestral tablets in order of generation in the Míngtáng
and offered sacrifices to Wénmíng Tàihòu in the Xuánshì (Dark Chamber).
“Xuánshì”
is written as
“Xuántáng” (Dark Hall) in the Běishǐ.
Zhèng Xuán said: "Xuántáng is the north hall."
Xīnwèi.
After one year of mourning for Wénmíng Tàihòu, the Wèi Emperor
wept beside the Yǒnggù Mausoleum,
crying without ceasing throughout the day,
and did not eat for two days in total.
Jiǎxū.
He took leave of the mausoleum
and returned to Yǒnglè Gōng (Eternal Joy Palace).
20th day, Yáng Jíshǐ, the Dī King of Wǔxīng,
attacked Hànzhōng,
reaching Báimǎ.
Yīn Zhìbó, the Governor of Liángzhōu, dispatched Army Commander Huán Lúnú
and Yīn Chōngchāng
to defeat them,
capturing and beheading several thousand people.
Jíshǐ fled back to Wǔxīng
and requested to surrender to Wèi.
Xīnsì.
He paid homage to Wèi.
Wèi appointed Jíshǐ as Governor of Nánqínzhōu, Marquis of Hànzhōng Commandery, and King of Wǔxīng.
21st day, winter,
tenth month.
Jiǎwǔ.
The Emperor performed the Yīnjì (Grand Sacrifice) at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
Yīnjì means a grand sacrifice.
22nd day, Gēngxū.
Wèi appointed Āndìng Wáng Xiū as Grand Marshal
and Tèjìn FÉNG Dàn as Sītú.
Dàn was
the son of Xī.
See Féng Xī in Volume 132, Shēngmíng first year of Sòng Shùndì.
Xī was
the brother of Empress Wénmíng.
23rd day, the Wèi Tàijí Diàn (Supreme Ultimate Hall) was completed.
In the twelfth month of the 24th year,
Sītú Cānjūn Xiāo Chēn and Fàn Yún were sent as envoys to Wèi.
The Wèi sovereign greatly esteemed the Qí people
and personally conversed with them.
He turned to his attendant ministers and said,
"Jiāngnán has many excellent officials."
The attendant minister Lǐ Yuánkǎi replied,
"Jiāngnán has many excellent officials,
but they change their lord once a year;
Jiāngběi has no excellent officials,
but they change their lord once a century."
The Wèi sovereign was greatly ashamed.
On the 25th, the Emperor ordered Crown Prince Household Registrar Shěn Yuē to compile the *Sòng Shū*.
Shěn Yuē was unsure whether to include a biography for Yuán Càn,
and sought the Emperor's counsel.
The Emperor said,
"Yuán Càn was indeed a loyal minister of the Sòng dynasty."
This shows the impartiality of his heart,
for right and wrong cannot be obscured.
The Emperor said,
"The deeds of Xiàowǔ cannot be entirely omitted.
I once served Míng Dì;
you should consider the principle of concealing evil."
According to the principle of the *Chūnqiū*,
one conceals for the respected.
In this same year,
Zhū Nóng, grandson of Lín Yì King Fàn Yángmài,
led his people to attack Fàn Dānggēnchún
and regained his kingdom.
The seizure of the Lín Yì kingdom by Fàn Dānggēnchún
is recorded in the previous year.
帥 (shuài)
is read as 率 (shuài).
種 (zhǒng)
is pronounced zhāng-yǒng.
復 (fù)
is pronounced fú-yòu.
Wèi Nányáng Gōng Zhèng Xī formed a marriage alliance with Lǐ Chōng.
Lǐ Chōng then appointed him Zhōngshū Lìng.
He was later appointed Western Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
Western Yǎnzhōu at that time was administered from Huátái.
Empress Dowager Wénmíng had his daughter taken as a consort for the Wèi sovereign,
and he was summoned to serve as Mìshū Jiān.
When he died,
the Shàngshū proposed the posthumous title Xuān.
An imperial edict stated:
"To determine a posthumous title upon closing the coffin
is to praise the good and condemn the bad.
Thus, although Hé Céng was filial,
good historians recorded his flaws and ugliness.
(This is recorded in volume 80, Jìn Wǔdì Xiánníng 4th year.)
Upright scholars called him Huāng Gōng.
(This is recorded in volume 81, Jìn Wǔdì Tàikāng 3rd year.)
The posthumous title law states: 'Confused and disorderly in conduct is called huāng.'
Yet his governance lacked integrity and clarity.
How can the Shàngshū's sentiment go against ultimate impartiality,
and err against the clear code?
According to the posthumous title law: 'Extensively learned and widely seen is called wén;
achieving fame without diligence is called líng.'
He may be granted his original office,
and given the posthumous title Wénlíng."
Punctuation by Niè Chóngqí, collated by Wáng Chóngwǔ.
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by imperial command.
Hòu Xué Tiān Tái
Shìzǔ Wǔ Huángdì Xià
Yǒngmíng 11th year (Guǐyǒu, 493)
1. In spring,
first month,
Pìqí Dàjiàngjūn Wáng Jìngzé was appointed Sīkōng,
and Zhènqūn Dàjiàngjūn Chén Xiǎndá was appointed Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Xiǎndá, considering his humble family background and high position,
(Chén Xiǎndá, a native of Southern Péngchéng,
rose from the ranks of soldiers.)
often showed an expression of shame and fear,
warning his sons not to oppress others with their wealth and status;
but many of his sons were extravagant and wasteful.
When Xiǎndá heard of this,
he was displeased.
(Although Chén Xiǎndá, while enjoying favor, remained apprehensive,
he ultimately could not escape suspicion and violence in that court.
That he resorted to rebellion and died,
was it not due to the times he encountered?)
He passed through Jiǔjiāng.
(From Jiànkāng to Yǐngfǔ,
one first passes Jiǔjiāng.)
"Whisk tails and fly swatters
are objects of the Wáng and Xiè families.
You must not hold these!"
(Meaning one should not try to distinguish oneself with refined elegance.)
捉 (zhuō)
means 執 (zhí).
He burned them in front of them.
2. Initially,
the Emperor constructed three thousand open carts at Shítou,
intending to march to Péngchéng.
The Wèi people learned of this.
Liú Chǎng repeatedly wept and appealed to the Wèi sovereign,
begging to be stationed at the border,
to gather remnants of the people,
and to avenge his personal humiliation.
(This was because the Xiāo clan usurped the Sòng and exterminated the Liú clan.)
數 (shù)
is pronounced suǒ-jiǎo.
處 (chǔ)
is pronounced chāng-lǚ.
(*Wèi Shū*, Emperor's Annals: In Tàihé 12th year,
the Jīngwǔ Hall was built.)
A large amount of fodder for horses was accumulated between the Huái and Sì rivers.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he appointed Yòuwèi Jiàngjūn Cuī Huìjǐng as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ to guard against them.
(This laid the groundwork for the Wèi invasion below.)
3. Wèi dispatched Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng Xíng Luán and others to make an alliance.
Luán
was the grandson of Yǐng.
(Yǐng
was a descendant of the Cáo Wèi Tàicháng Xíng Zhēn.)
(Xíng Yǐng is mentioned in volume 122, Sòng Wéndì Yuánjiā 8th year.)
4. On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Wénhuì Tàizǐ Chángmào died.
The Crown Prince had a very gentle demeanor.
In his later years, the Emperor enjoyed excursions and banquets,
and the affairs of the Shàngshū were divided and sent to the Crown Prince's palace for review,
which consequently gave him authority both within and outside the court.
The Crown Prince was extravagant and luxurious by nature.
The construction of his halls, palaces, and gardens exceeded those of the imperial palace,
costing tens of millions.
Fearing the Emperor might see them,
he planted tall bamboo beside the gate.
All his garments and ornaments
were mostly excessive and luxurious.
He petitioned to build a small park in Dōngtián,
ordering the Eastern Palace officials and soldiers to take turns constructing it.
The constructions enveloped the city lanes,
extending far and wide in their magnificence.
(Meaning they were extremely magnificent
and extended far.)
He placed many informants,
so no one dared to report the Crown Prince's actions.
The Emperor once visited the Crown Prince's Dōngtián,
saw its grandeur,
and was greatly enraged,
ordering the arrest of the chief supervisors of the work.
The Crown Prince hid them all,
for which he received severe reprimands.
He also ordered his favored retainer Xú Wénjǐng to build palanquins and imperial chariots and accoutrements.
The Emperor once visited the Eastern Palace in haste,
so there was no time to hide the palanquins.
(怱怱 [cōngcōng]
means in a hurry.)
So the Emperor was not suspicious.
Wénjǐng's father, Táo Rén, said to Wénjǐng,
"I should just sweep the tomb and await the mourning!"
(Sweeping the tomb
means cleaning the grave site.)
Later, Wénjǐng was indeed granted death,
and Táo Rén consequently did not weep.
When the Crown Prince died,
the Emperor walked through the Eastern Palace
and saw his garments and ornaments.
Greatly enraged,
he commanded the officials concerned to destroy them without exception.
As Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng was close to the Crown Prince
but did not report his actions,
he was also blamed.
The Crown Prince had always disliked Xīchāng Hóu Luán.
He once said to Zǐliáng,
"I really don't like this person.
I don't understand why,
it must be because he has little fortune."
Zǐliáng tried to defend him.
When Luán gained power,
none of the Crown Prince's descendants were spared.
(The matter of Xīchāng Hóu exterminating the Crown Prince's descendants is recorded later.)
(According to the record, Luán eliminated the sons of Gāo and Wǔ and the Crown Prince's descendants to accomplish his usurpation.
Even if Wénhuì had not disliked him,
his descendants would still not have been spared.)
(Observing the events of the Lóngchāng and Jiànwǔ eras,
gentlemen say Wénhuì knew well whom to dislike.)
5. In the second month,
the Wèi sovereign first ploughed the ceremonial field south of Píngchéng.
(Wèi originated from the northern wilderness
and had never practiced the ancient ritual of the Son of Heaven personally ploughing.
Now Xiàowén began to perform it.)
藉 (jiè)
is pronounced zài-yì.
6 The Inspector of Yōngzhōu, Wáng Huàn, disliked Liú Xīngzǔ, the Commander of the Pacifying Man,
so he arrested and imprisoned him.
He falsely accused him of inciting the mountain Man people
to rebel.
An imperial edict ordered Xīngzǔ to be sent down to Jiànkāng;
from Xiāngyáng, one travels downstream east to Jiànkāng,
hence the term "down."
He falsely claimed to have hanged himself.
The Emperor was greatly enraged.
He dispatched the Grand Secretary of the Central Secretariat, Lǚ Wénxiǎn, and the General of the Imperial Guard, Cáo Dàogāng, leading five hundred elite guards to arrest Huàn.
"Zhāizhàng" refers to
elite weaponry from the imperial armory supplied to the brave and strong imperial guards.
Jiàng
is pronounced like liàng.
Huàn's son, Biāo,
was always ferocious and treacherous,
and Huàn could not control him.
The Chief Clerk, Yīn Ruì,
who was Huàn's son-in-law,
said to Huàn:
"When Cáo and Lǚ arrive,
and if they do not show a genuine imperial edict,
I fear it might be a deceitful plot.
It is proper to apprehend them."
Lù means
to seize,
or to capture.
Huàn adopted his advice.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Nánshǐ* says:
"Huàn's son, Biāo, proposed closing the gates and resisting the order.
Ruì admonished him, saying: 'If we open the gates now and receive the imperial envoys in plain clothes,
at most it will mean losing office and titles.'
Biāo stubbornly disagreed.
Ruì further requested to send a clerk with a secret message to transmit a memorial,
and Huàn assented.
The clerk left the city
but was seized by Wénxiǎn.
Ruì said: 'The loyal do not betray their country,
and the brave do not flee death.'
He urged Huàn to take poison.
Ruì and Biāo were executed together."
We now follow the *Qíshū*.
Huàn opened the armory and distributed weapons,
came out of the South Hall,
arrayed his troops,
and closed the gates to defend.
Huàn's retainer, Zhèng Yǔ, kowtowed and entreated Huàn,
begging to leave the city to welcome the imperial envoys.
Huàn said:
"I am not a rebel.
I intended to send a memorial first to explain myself.
I just fear that petty people like Cáo and Lǚ will insult and trample upon us."
Líng means
to insult and rise above;
jiè means
to step on and push down.
Jiè
is pronounced like cíyè.
Biāo then went out
and fought with the Tiger Army.
His troops were defeated,
and he fled back.
In the third month,
on the day Yǐhài,
the Sīmǎ, Huáng Yáoqǐ, and the Commander of the Pacifying Man, Péi Shūyè of Hédōng, raised troops within the city,
attacked Huàn,
and beheaded him.
This sets the stage for Huàn's son, Sù, to eat Yáoqǐ's flesh later.
All were executed.
Biāo's elder brothers, Róng and Chēn, died in Jiànkāng.
Chēn's younger brother, the Secretary-Compiler, Sù, alone managed to escape
and fled to Wèi.
This sets the stage for Wáng Sù repeatedly leading Wèi troops to invade.
Chēn
is pronounced like chǒulín.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Nánshǐ* says:
"Huàn's younger brother, Fèn, personally surrendered to ask for punishment,
and the Emperor pardoned him.
When Sù repeatedly led Wèi people to the border,
the Emperor said to Fèn: 'Have there been any recent reports from the north?'
Fèn replied: 'Sù recently forgot his ancestral graves;
how could he remember having a subject (like me) far away!'"
According to our research, Huàn died in the third month,
and the Emperor passed away in the seventh month.
That winter,
Sù first met the Wèi ruler in Yè.
The *Nánshǐ* is mistaken.
The *Qíshū* does not contain this statement.
7 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Jiǎwǔ,
Wáng Zhāoyè of Nánjùn was established as the Imperial Grandson.
All civil and military officials of the Eastern Palace were changed to officials of the Imperial Grandson.
The Eastern Palace officials:

For civil posts, there were Grand Tutor, Junior Tutor, Chamberlain for the Palace Grandson, Director of the Palace Attendants, Steward, Household Provisioner, Palace Grandee, Palace Attendant, Attendant to the Grandson, Secretary to the Grandson, Gentleman-in-Waiting to the Grandson, and Gentleman-in-Waiting;

for military posts, there were Right and Left Commanders of the Guards, Commanders of the Yi Army, Infantry, and Garrison Cavalry, Palace Gentlemen of the Valiant Guards, Right and Left Generals of Crossbowmen, Generals of the Palace, Supernumerary Generals of the Palace, and Supervisors of the Imperial Guards.
The wife of the King of Nánjùn was established as the Imperial Grandson Consort.
She was the daughter of Hé Jí.
For Hé Jí, see Volume 135, First Year of Jiànyuán of Gāodì.
Jí
is pronounced like zélì,
and also like jílì.
8 The Grand Chancellor of Wèi, Pī, and others requested the establishment of an Empress.
On the day Wùxū,
Empress Féng was established.
The Empress
was the daughter of Xī.
This sets the stage for Empress Féng later being deposed due to slander.
Emperor Zhāng of Hàn gathered scholars at the White Tiger Hall
to discuss the similarities and differences of the Five Classics,
resulting in the *Báihǔ Tōng*.
"Kings do not treat the parents of their wives as subjects."
An imperial edict ordered the Grand Tutor to not refer to himself as a subject in memorials
and not to bow when entering court.
Xī firmly declined.
9 The commander of the Guāngchéng Man, General Conquering the Captive, Tián Yìzōng, leading over four thousand households from his tribe, rebelled
and surrendered to Wèi.
Shěn Yuē said: Guāngchéng Commandery
was probably established during the Dàmíng era by dividing Yìyáng.
The *Wǔdàishǐ Zhì* says: Guāngshān County of Guāngzhōu
was formerly Guāngchéng Commandery.
Mán shuài is pronounced like suǒlèi;
Zōng shuài
is read as lǜ.
Jiàng
is pronounced like hùjiāng.
10 In the fifth month,
on the day Rénxū,
the Wèi ruler hosted a banquet for the descendants of the four ancestral temples in Xuānwéntáng,
personally sitting among them by age,
using family rites.
The descendants of the four ancestral temples
refer to the descendants of Shìzǔ, Gōngzōng, Gāozōng, and Xiǎnzǔ.
In the twelfth year of Tàihé,
Xuānwéntáng and Jīngwǔdiàn were built.
"Using family rites" means
setting aside the respect due to a sovereign and arranging by seniority.
11 On the day Jiǎzǐ,
the Wèi ruler presided over the imperial court
and invited dukes and ministers and below to resolve doubtful political matters
and review prisoners.
The Emperor said to the Minister of Works, Mù Liàng:
"From now on, for court affairs,
before noon,
you gentlemen will first discuss among yourselves;
after noon,
I will decide with you gentlemen."
12 On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Wáng Kēng of Yídū was appointed Inspector of Nányùzhōu.
Previously, Zǐqīng, the son of the King of Lúlíng, was Inspector of Nányùzhōu.
When he was heading to his post,
he playfully arranged his troops as a navy on the way.
The Emperor heard of this
and was greatly enraged,
killing his clerk;
Kēng was appointed to replace him.
Zǐqīng returned to his residence,
and the Emperor never saw him again throughout his life.
13 The Man chieftain of Xiāngyáng, Léi Pósi, and others, leading over a thousand households, sought to relocate inland to Wèi.
The Wèi people settled them north of the Miǎn River.
At this time, the land north of the Miǎn River was still within Qí territory.
Léi Pósi and the others probably lived south of the Miǎn,
and relocating to north of the Miǎn
would bring them closer to Wèi territory.
Qiú
is pronounced like cíyóu.
Shuài
is read as lǜ.
Chǔ
is pronounced like chānglǚ.
14. The Wèi zhǔ, believing that Píngchéng was too cold a place,
with snow falling in the sixth month,
an extremely Yin region,
where snow fell even in high summer.
雨 (yǔ),
read Wáng Yù fan;
from above downwards is called 雨 (rain).
Wind and sand,
meaning strong winds raising sand.
Fearing that his retainers would not follow him,
he proposed a major expedition to attack Qí,
intending to coerce the multitude.
He purified himself in the left chamber of the Míngtáng.
Zhèng Xuán said: "The left chamber of the Míngtáng
is the eastern side of the south hall of the main sleeping quarters."
个 (gè),
read Gǔ Hè fan.
When he encountered the Guǎ (Hexagram 49, Revolution),
the Emperor said:
" 'Tāng and Wǔ brought about revolution (gémìng),
responding to Heaven and according with humanity.'
This is the judgment text (tuàn cí) of the Guǎ hexagram."
諶 (chén),
read Shì Rén fan.
His retainers dared not speak.
The Shàngshū, Rènchéng Wáng Chéng, said:
"Your Majesty's lineage shines brightly through generations,
and the empire possesses the Central Plains.
Now, to dispatch an army to conquer the unsubdued,
and to receive the omen of Tāng and Wǔ's revolution,
is not entirely auspicious."
The Emperor said in a stern voice:
"The oracle says: 'The great man changes like a tiger,'
why do you say it's inauspicious!"
Chéng replied:
"Your Majesty's Dragon Ascendance has long been established;
how can you now be 'changing like a tiger'!"
The Emperor's countenance changed, and he said:
"The altars of soil and grain (shèjì) are my altars of soil and grain!
Does Rènchéng wish to discourage the multitude!"
Chéng replied:
"Although the altars of soil and grain belong to Your Majesty,
I, your minister, am a minister of the altars of soil and grain.
How can I know of danger and not speak!"
After a long pause, the Emperor relented,
saying:
"Let each speak his mind;
what harm is there in that!"
When he returned to the palace,
he returned to the palace from the left chamber of the Míngtáng.
He privately said to him:
"Regarding the Guǎ hexagram earlier,
we should discuss it further now, my dear.
My anger in the Míngtáng was because I feared everyone would compete to speak,
frustrating my great plan.
Therefore, I used my voice and expression to intimidate the civil and military officials.
I trust you understand my intention."
Then, dismissing others, he said to Chéng:
"Today's undertaking
is truly not easy.
However, the state originated in the northern lands,
and then moved to Píngchéng.
This is a place for military endeavors,
not suitable for civil governance.
Now, I intend to change customs and transform habits.
This path is truly difficult.
I wish to take this opportunity to relocate the capital to the Central Plains.
What do you think, my dear?"
The Wèi zhǔ first confided his feelings to Rènchéng Wáng Chéng.
"Your Majesty wishes to choose a new capital in the Central Plains to administer and govern the four seas.
This is how the Zhōu and Hàn dynasties achieved their prosperity."
Comparing him to King Chéng and King Kāng of Zhōu,
and Emperor Guāng and Emperor Míng of Hàn.
"The northern people are accustomed to their traditions and are attached to the old ways;
they will certainly be alarmed and disturbed.
What then?"
Later, Mù Tài and others' conspiracy
ultimately turned out as the Emperor had feared.
"Extraordinary matters
are therefore beyond the grasp of ordinary people.
Your Majesty decides with your sagely heart;
what can they possibly do!"
The Emperor said:
"Rènchéng,
you are my Zǐfáng!"
Zhāng Liáng advised Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn to move the capital to Cháng'ān,
hence the comparison.
In the sixth month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
an order was given to build a bridge over the Hé (Yellow River),
intending to transport the army.
The Mìshūjiān, Lú Yuān, submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"Previous rulers of peaceful reigns
never personally led the six armies
to decide victory or defeat amidst the battle lines.
Was it not because victory was not enough to enhance their martial prestige,
and defeat would diminish their authority and reputation!
In the past, Wèi Wǔ, with ten thousand exhausted troops, defeated Yuán Shào."
This event is recorded in Volume 62, in the fifth year of Jiàn'ān of Emperor Xiàndì of Hàn.
This event is recorded in Volume 105, in the eighth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn.
"Victory is decided in an instant,
not by the size of the forces."
The imperial reply stated:
"The reason why rulers of peaceful reigns
do not personally engage in military affairs
is either because they have no enemies within their unified realm,
or because they are cowardly and seek ease.
To call it a unified realm now would not be accurate."
When the world is unified,
then carriages have the same track width,
and writings use the same characters.
"If it were truly the case that a king should not personally lead the army,
then why did the ancient kings establish the 'gélù' (leather chariot)?
What purpose would it serve?"
The Zhōu system had five types of chariots;
the 'gélù'
had dragon-head reins (lónglèlei),
five tiers of tassels (yīng wǔ jiù),
and raised the great white banner to go into battle.
Zhèng's commentary states: "The 'gélù'
was covered with leather and lacquered,
without other decorations."
條 (tiáo),
read as tāo.
"Victory comes from relying on righteousness;
Fú Shì's defeat
also came from losing political control.
How could the few necessarily overcome the many,
or the weak necessarily control the strong!"
On the day Dīngwèi,
the Wèi zhǔ conducted a military review,
ordering the Shàngshū, Lǐ Chōng, to oversee the selection of military personnel.
At this time, wanting to deploy troops,
he ordered Chōng to oversee the military selection,
to choose talented and brave officers.
選 (xuǎn),
read Xū Juàn fan.
15. In Jiànkāng, the monk Fǎzhì and the Xúzhōu commoner Zhōu Pánlóng and others rebelled.
This is another Zhōu Pánlóng,
not the father of Zhōu Fèngshú.
They attacked the city of Xúzhōu
and entered it.
The Cìshǐ, Wáng Xuánmiǎo, attacked and executed them.
Xúzhōu city is the same as Zhōnglí city.
16. In autumn,
seventh month,
on the day Guǐchǒu,
Wèi established the imperial son Xún as Crown Prince.
This laid the groundwork for the Wèi zhǔ later deposing Xún.
17. On the day Wùzǐ,
Wèi issued general warnings both inside and outside the capital,
issued proclamations and official letters,
stating their intention to campaign south.
Military operations should generally be kept secret.
The Wèi zhǔ now publicly announced the matter to the four directions,
hence it is also called a "lùbù";
the "yíshū"
were official letters sent to the Qí border.
They widely set up recruitment stations to prepare for it.
The Zhōngshūláng, Wáng Róng,
relied on his personal talent and family background.
Wáng Róng had outstanding talent,
hence he prided himself on his personal ability;
and as a great-grandson of Wáng Hóng,
he prided himself on his family background.
Once, when on night duty in the imperial secretariat,
he patted the desk and sighed:
"To be so quiet and still!"
爾 (ěr),
means "like this."
寂寂 (jìjì),
means cold and desolate.
Dèng Yǔ was Sītú of Hàn at twenty-four;
Róng was already past that age,
hence he said this.
"The crowded and narrow passage prevents advancement.
The Zhūquè Héng was at the Zhūquè Gate of Jiànkāng,
crossing the Qínhuái River north and south banks for pedestrians,
a major thoroughfare.
When the movable bridge (héng) was opened, travelers would be packed.
湫 (qiū),
read Zǐ Xiǎo fan,
meaning narrow.
Jīngdiǎn Shìwén says: "湫 (qiū),
Xú's pronunciation is qiū,
also Zài Jiǔ fan."

If I were to speak from my heart,

it would only be half right."

each holding their fortresses and walls to await Qí's rescue.

Yǒu and others advanced towards Cháng'ān.

Mù Liàng from Guānyòu.

Fèngshú (奉叔) asked the emperor for a marquisate of a thousand households;

Fèngshú (奉叔) was furious,

After Fèngshú (奉叔) had taken his leave,

Luán (鸞) and Xiāo Chén (蕭諶), claiming to act on imperial decree,

the *zhōu* and *zhèn* shall list the performance of their subordinate officials.
After two evaluations,
promotions and demotions shall be carried out.'
For the fifteen years past, all capital officials have been evaluated and ranked into three grades.
'Fifteen years past'
still refers to the fifteenth year of Tàihé.
Your servant proposes to apply the method of evaluating external officials
to determine the performance of capital officials."
He wished to use the method of evaluating subordinate officials of *zhōu* and *zhèn* to evaluate capital officials.
載 (*zài*),
pronounced *zǐ hài fān*.
行 (*xíng*),
pronounced *xià mèng fān*.
"The matter of performance evaluation is serious
and should concern My personal hearing;
it cannot be lightly initiated.
We shall wait until autumn."
The historians say that Wèi Xiàowén understood the essence of being a ruler
and did not allow power to rest with his ministers.
18. In the intercalary month,
on the day *dīngmǎo*,
Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn Luán was restored to his original title
and appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
His original title
was Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn.
19th day, Wùchén cyclical day:
Xīn'ān Wáng Zhāowén was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu.
20th day, 5th month:
Jiǎxū cyclical day, the first day of the month:
There was a solar eclipse.
The "Investigation of Discrepancies" states: The imperial annals in both the Qí Shū and Wèi Shū make no mention of this eclipse.
This record is based on the Treatise of the Qí Shū and the Annals of the Nán Shǐ.
21st day, 6th month:
Jǐsì cyclical day:
Wèi dispatched Lú Chǎng, who concurrently held the posts of Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì, and Wáng Qīngshí, who concurrently held the post of Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng, to come on a diplomatic mission.
Chǎng
was the son of Dùshì.
Lú Dùshì avoided the disaster caused by Cuī Hào.
Later, he emerged from hiding,
and Wèi Tàiwǔ favored and trusted him.
Sàn
is pronounced like "xī dǎn."
Qí
is pronounced like "qí jì."
Chǎng
is pronounced like "chǒu liǎng."
The Wèi emperor said to Qīngshí:
"You should not feel self-conscious about being a southerner.
When they (the southern court officials) have knowledge, they will show it,
if they wish to be seen, they will be seen,
and if they wish to speak, they will speak.
In general, for an envoy, harmony is paramount.
Do not boast or brag to each other,
showing it in your words or expressions,
which would be contrary to the deportment of one bearing a mandate."
Jiāng
means "to bear" or "to receive."
To act upon receiving a mandate
is called jiāngmìng.
22nd day, Autumn,
7th month:
Yǐhài cyclical day:
Wèi appointed Sòng Wáng Liú Chǎng as Shǐ Chíjié, Dūdú Wú‧Yuè‧Chǔ Zhū Jūnshì, and Dà Jiāngjūn,
to garrison Péngchéng.
The region south of the Yangtze River comprised the territories of the three states of Wú, Yuè, and Chǔ during the Spring and Autumn period.
Wáng Sù was appointed Chǎng's Fǔ Chángshǐ.
When Chǎng arrived at the garrison,
he was unable to maintain good relations with his former allies and subordinates.
In the time of Sòng Cāngwú Wáng Chū,
Chǎng was garrisoned at Péngchéng
and abandoned the garrison to defect to Wèi,
hence the presence of his former allies and subordinates there.
23rd day, Rénwǔ cyclical day:
Wèi Āndìng Jìng Wáng Xiū died.
From his death to his embalmment,
the Wèi emperor visited his residence three times.
He was buried with the same rites as Wèi Yuán,
and the emperor escorted him out of the city,
weeping sorrowfully before returning.
24th day, Rénxū cyclical day:
The Wèi emperor made a northern tour.
25th day: After Xīchāng Hóu Luán had executed Xú Lóngjù and Zhōu Fèngshú,
nuns who came in from outside
began to spread various rumors.
The Zhōngshū Lìng Hé Yìn,
being the empress's cousin,
was close to the emperor
and was made to serve in the Zhídiàn Shěng.
The emperor conspired with Yìn to eliminate Luán,
ordering Yìn to take charge;
Yìn dared not accept,
and equivocated in his advice,
so the emperor's intention halted.
They then planned to send Luán out to Xīzhōu,
and imperial decrees were issued to direct affairs
without consulting Luán anymore.
At this time,
Xiāo Chén and Xiāo Tǎnzhī held military power,
and the Zuǒ Púshè Wáng Yàn presided over the affairs of the Shàngshū.
Chén secretly summoned the various princely secretaries (diǎnqiān),
instructed and warned them,
forbidding the princes from interacting with people outside.
Yuēyǔ zhě
means to restrain and speak to them.
Yǔ
is pronounced like "niú jù."
Everyone feared and obeyed him.
Luán informed Wáng Yàn of his plan,
and Yàn, hearing it,
responded in agreement.
He also informed the Dānyáng Yǐn Xú Xiàosì,
who also concurred.
Lè Yù of Nányáng, the Piàojì Lùshì, said to Xiàosì:
"Rumors are widely spread,
suggesting an affair like that of Yī and Zhōu.
You, Sir, received extraordinary favor from Emperor Wǔ,
and bear the heavy trust placed in you.
Xú Xiàosì was recommended by Wáng Jiǎn,
and Emperor Wǔ promoted and employed him,
entrusting him with all the affairs of the Shàngshū in his dying edict.
Piào
is pronounced like "pǐ miào."
Qí
is pronounced like "qí jì."
Hè
is pronounced like "xià kě."
People laugh at Chǔ Gōng,
and their teeth still ache from the chill."
This refers to Chǔ Yuān.
Laughter reveals the teeth,
hence the saying "teeth ache from the chill."
The emperor said to Xiāo Tǎnzhī:
"People say that the Zhènjūn, Wáng Yàn, and Xiāo Chén intend to depose me together.
Luán at that time held the title of Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn,
hence he is referred to.
What have you heard?"
Tǎnzhī replied:
"How could such a thing exist in the world?
Who would willingly depose the Son of Heaven without reason?
The court nobles would not make such an argument.
It must be the words of those nuns and old women;
how can they be believed?
If Your Majesty were to remove these three
men without cause,
who would dare to feel secure?"
Zhíhé Jiāngjūn Cáo Dàogāng suspected external irregularities
and had made secret arrangements,
but his plan could not be launched.
This refers to Cáo Dàogāng's secret plot against Luán and others, which he could not launch.
Chù
is pronounced like "chāng lǚ."
Fèn
is pronounced like "fú wèn."
At that time, Shǐxīng Nèishǐ Xiāo Jìchǎng and Nányáng Tàishǒu Xiāo Yǐngjī were both being transferred back to the capital.
Chén wanted to wait for the two to arrive,
to use their power to launch the affair.
Because the two were returning from outer commanderies,
each having military forces escorting them,
their power could be utilized.
He told Tǎnzhī this,
and Tǎnzhī hurried to Chén and said:
"Deposing the Son of Heaven is
a major event from ancient times.
Recently, I heard that Cáo Dàogāng, Zhū Lóngzhī, and others have become increasingly suspicious.
If the Wèiwèi does not act tomorrow,
it will be too late.
You have a mother of a hundred years;
how can you idly await disaster?
You should make other plans!"
Chén, in panic, agreed.
On the 31st day of the ninth month,
on the *Rénshēn* day,
the Wèi court issued an edict saying:
“Evaluating performance over three years,
and promoting or demoting after three evaluations;
this was the system of Táng and Yú.
Three evaluations result in promotions or demotions.
Three evaluations mean nine years.
載 (*zài*)
is pronounced *zǐ-hài* (子亥).
Those who could be promoted are greatly delayed.
Now, I will conduct an evaluation every three years,
and immediately implement promotions and demotions,
wishing to prevent the ignorant and stagnated from hindering the worthy,
and to ensure that talent is not confined to lower positions.
Let each department assess the superior and inferior qualities into three grades,
and the upper and lower two grades should still be further divided into three.
The upper grade and the lower grade are each again divided into three grades.
The Shàngshū will re-examine;
for officials of the fifth rank and above,
I will personally discuss their merits and demerits with the Gōngqīng.
The best of the best will be promoted,
the worst of the worst will be demoted,
and those in the middle will retain their original posts. ”
When the Wèi ruler went on his northern tour,
he left Rènchéng Wáng Chéng to select and appoint old officials.
From Gōnghóu downwards,
officials numbered in the tens of thousands.
Chéng graded their superior and inferior qualities and abilities into three classes,
and no one harbored resentment.
History states that Rènchéng Wáng Chéng was fair and just.
On the *Rénwǔ* day,
the Wèi ruler presided over the court,
promoting and demoting numerous officials,
and said to the various Shàngshū:
“The Shàngshū
hold positions of pivotal importance;
they are not merely to manage all affairs
and handle documents;
my successes and failures
are entirely dependent on this.
You, gentlemen, have held office
for nearly two terms,
yet you have never offered acceptable suggestions or rejected improper ones,
nor have you promoted a worthy person or demoted an unworthy one.
This is the greatest of crimes. ”
He then said to Lù Shàngshūshì Guǎnglíng Wáng Yǔ:
“You are my brother,
holding a position of strategic importance to the right,
yet you have no reputation for diligence and integrity,
but rather traces of factionalism.
Now I demote you from Lù Shàngshū and Tíngwèi,
and you shall only be Tèjìn and Tàizǐ Tàibǎo. ”
He then said to Shàngshūlìng Lù Ruì:
“Shūfān, when you first arrived at the province,
you had an excellent reputation;
but recently you have been biased and negligent,
because you were unable to guide him with righteousness.
Although there is no major fault,
a minor punishment is appropriate;
I now confiscate your salary for one term. ”
He then said to Zuǒ Púyè Tuòbá Zàn:
“Shūfān was demoted,
and you should face capital punishment;
but since the fault is attributed to one person,
I will not punish you again;
I now dismiss you from Shàoshī,
and cut your salary for one term. ”
He then said to Zuǒ Chéng Gōngsūn Liáng and Yòu Chéng Qǐfú Yìshòu:
“Your crimes also warrant capital punishment;
you may retain your original posts as commoners,
but your caps, robes, and salaries for the support of relatives
— Wèi officials,
besides their basic salary,
also had a separate allowance for supporting relatives —
will be suspended. If you achieve something in three years,
you will be restored to your original posts;
if not,
you will forever return to farming. ”
He then said to Shàngshū Rènchéng Wáng Chéng:
“Shūshén is arrogant,
so he may be dismissed from Shàobǎo. ”
Chéng was the uncle of the Wèi ruler.
“You are not diligent in your duties,
and repeatedly cite illness as an excuse;
you may be dismissed from Chángjiān,
and your salary cut for one term. ”
As for the other Shàngshū, Wèiyǔ, Lú Yuān, and others,
all were deemed incompetent,
and either dismissed from their posts,
or demoted,
or had their salaries confiscated;
their faults were enumerated to their faces before the punishments were carried out.
Yuān
was Chǎng's brother.
The Emperor also said to Lù Ruì:
“Northerners often say,
‘Northern customs are rustic and unrefined,
how can they understand books!’
When I heard this,
I was deeply saddened!
Now, many know books,
but are they all sages!
It simply depends on whether one studies or not.
I rectify the hundred officials,
and promote rites and music;
my ambition is indeed to change customs.
As the Son of Heaven,
why must I reside in the Central Plains!
I simply want your descendants to gradually be influenced by beautiful customs,
and to broaden their knowledge and horizons;
if they were to permanently reside in the constant north,
and again encounter a ruler who dislikes culture,
they would inevitably be like facing a wall. ”
The *Shū* says: If one does not study,
one is like facing a wall.
It means standing directly facing a wall,
seeing nothing.
“Indeed, as the sage said.
If Jīn Rìdī had not entered service in the Hàn court,
how could his family have been renowned for seven generations. ”
The account of Jīn Rìdī can be found in Volume 71, Hàn Wǔdì, Hòuyuán first year.
“Renowned for seven generations”
refers to serving as inner attendants for seven generations.
磾 (*dī*)
is pronounced *dīng-xī*.
朝 (*cháo*)
is pronounced *zhí-yáo*.
32When Yùlín Wáng was deposed,
Póyáng Wáng Qiāng initially knew nothing of the plot.
As Xuānchéng Gōng Luán's power and influence grew,
everyone inside and outside the court knew he harbored disloyal ambitions.
Whenever Qiāng visited Luán,
Luán would always go barefoot to the rear of the carriage to welcome him;
it means he was so eager to welcome him that he didn't have time to put on his shoes properly.
He spoke with tears flowing,
and Qiāng believed him because of this.
Everyone within the palace and administration

屬 (*zhǔ*)
is pronounced *zhī-yù*.
Zhìjújìan Xiè Càn persuaded Qiāng and Suí Wáng Zǐlóng, saying:
“The two princes only need to ride an oiled-wall carriage into the palace

度 (*dù*)

He was very hesitant.
Mǎ Duìzhǔ Liú Jù,

Qiāng ordered his carriage, about to enter,

The Diǎnqiān knew of his plan

On the *Guǐyǒu* day,

At that time, among Tàizǔ's sons,

should be
“Shìzǔ”.
The Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, Prince Zǐmào of Jìn'ān, heard that the Princes of Póyáng and Suí were dead,

He said to his personal guard, Lù Chāozhī of Wújun,

If it fails, I will still be a righteous ghost."
The princes appointed personal guards,
using brave and resourceful men,
to defend their residences and offices.
Dù Yòu's Tōngdiǎn states: "Under the Táng system: princely establishments were all provided with personal guards (fánggé), servants (shùpú), and 'white-collar' guards (báizhí).

"Although this prefecture is small,
Sòng Xiàowǔ often used it."
This refers to Emperor Sòng Xiàowǔ raising an army from Jiāngzhōu to execute the arch-villain Shào.
"Who can stop us!"
Zǐmào's mother, Lady Ruǎn, was in Jiànkāng.
He secretly sent a letter to summon her.
Lady Ruǎn advised her full brother, Yú Yáozhī, to devise a plan.
Yáozhī galloped to inform Duke Xuānchéng, Luán.
On the yǐhài day,
Luán was granted the huángyuè (imperial battle-axe),

"yǐwèi".

"kuǐyǒu",

That is all.
Troops were also dispatched under Military Commander Péi Shúyè and Yú Yáozhī to first attack Xúnyáng,
claiming to be the Sīmǎ (adjutant) of the Yǐng prefecture.
Zǐmào knew this,

Shúyè sailed upstream directly.
At night,
he launched a surprise attack on Pénchéng.
The City Affairs Supervisor Lè Bēn opened the gates and let them in.
Inspectors of various prefectures each had a City Affairs Supervisor,
responsible for repairs, dredging, and defense.
(They) led the prefectural troops to hold the city and defend themselves.

"Yǒng" (勇),
should be

Yōng (雍),
pronounced "yū yòng" (於用翻).
Yú Yáozhī was sent to persuade Zǐmào, saying:

Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the Central Army) Yú Línzhī,

Línzhī, with two hundred men,

Zǐmào cursed, saying:

Wáng Xuánmiǎo seized Dǒng Sēnghuì,

Zǐmào's son, Zhāojī,

Yú Línzhī advised Lù Chāozhī to flee.

The story of Tián Héng's retainers is found in Volume 11, under Emperor Gāo's fifth year of Hàn.
Chāozhī held fast to death,
hence he used these words to shame Línzhī.
Chāozhī sat upright, awaiting his fate.
Chāozhī's disciple, thinking that killing Chāozhī would earn a reward,

His head fell, but his body did not stiffen.
Xuánmiǎo gave him a lavish burial.

The historian speaks of the righteous bravery of Dǒng Sēnghuì and Lù Chāozhī.
Zhé (折),
pronounced "ér shè" (而設翻).
Luán dispatched General Píngxī, Wáng Guǎngzhī, to attack the Inspector of Nányánzhōu, Prince Zǐjìng of Ānlù.

Prince Zhāoxiù of Línhǎi was the Inspector of Jīngzhōu.

Xuánqìng arrived at Jiānglíng,

In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the dīngyǒu day,

King Xuānchéng planned to succeed to the imperial throne,

The Attendant Counselor Xiè Fěi was unwilling in his heart,
