Chén Guāng 曰: I, your minister, heard
that “those who wear others’ clothes harbor others’ worries;
those who eat others’ food die for others’ affairs.”
History records this as Huáin Yīn Hóu’s reply to Kuǎi Chè’s words.
衣人之衣 (yī rén zhī yī)
is pronounced *yú jì fān*.
To stand shoulder to shoulder with the noble and powerful,
enjoying honor and emoluments,
yet oblivious to impending danger—
can a minister like this
be called loyal?
Many in the world achieve fame despite being like this.
Although Xuānchéng Wáng monopolized state power,
public sentiment had not yet submitted.
The King had a red mole on his shoulder.
Piàojì Zīyì Cānjūn Kǎochéng Jiāng Shí urged the King to display it to the people.
The King showed it to Jìnshòu Tàishǒu Wáng Hóngfàn, saying:
“People say this is a sun-moon symbol;
please do not disclose it!”
Hóngfàn replied:
“Your Highness has the sun and moon on your body;
how can it be hidden?
You should spread the word!”
Wáng Hóngfàn was
an old minister of the imperial guard.
Luán tested him with this,
and his words were thus.
Luán became even more unrestrained.
相 (xiàng)
is pronounced *xī liàng fān*.
It was the paternal aunt of Shí.
On the *wùxū* day,
Guìyáng Wáng Shuò, Héngyáng Wáng Jūn, Jiāngxià Wáng Fēng, Jiàn’ān Wáng Zǐzhēn, and Bālíng Wáng Zǐlún were killed.
Shuò and Póyáng Wáng Qiāng were equally famous.
Qiāng was fond of literature,
while Shuò enjoyed *mínglǐ* (discussions on names and principles).
People at the time called them "Pó and Guì."
After Qiāng died,
Shuò felt uneasy.
He went to Dōngfǔ to see Xuānchéng Wáng.
Upon returning,
he said to his attendants:
“Just now, Lù Gōng received me with such warmth,
(Luán was Tàifù Lù Shàngshū Shì;
Tàifù was a senior ducal office,
hence referred to as Lù Gōng.)
with an air of reluctance to part.
This surely means he intends to kill me.”
That very evening,
he was murdered.
Whenever Xuānchéng Wáng killed princes,
he would usually send soldiers at night to surround their residences,
break down gates and scale walls,
shouting and rushing in.
All household property would be sealed and inventoried.
Jiāngxià Wáng Fēng
possessed talent and integrity.
Xuānchéng Wáng once spoke with him:
“Yáoguāng’s talent and ability are trustworthy.”
Fēng replied:
“Yáoguāng is to Your Highness
what Your Highness is to Gāo Huáng;
safeguarding the ancestral temples
and stabilizing the state
indeed has a purpose.”
During Dōnghūn Hóu’s reign,
Yáoguāng’s actions ultimately bore out Fēng’s words.
When the princes were being killed,
Fēng sent a letter to Xuānchéng Wáng,
reproaching him.
Xuānchéng Wáng greatly feared him
and dared not seize Fēng at his residence.
Instead, he made Fēng concurrently serve as a sacrificial official at the Tàimiào.
(Sacrificial officials
are those who perform sacrificial duties.)
Then he sent soldiers to seize him in the temple.
As Fēng exited
and boarded his carriage,
the soldiers wanted to get onto the carriage.
Fēng, being strong,
struck several soldiers with his hands, knocking them all to the ground,
before he died.
Xuānchéng Wáng sent Diǎnqiān Kē Lìngsūn to kill Jiàn’ān Wáng Zǐzhēn.
(According to the *Xìngpǔ* (Genealogy Record): Kē
is a surname,
descended from Kē Lú, a son of the King of Wú.)
Lìngsūn personally dragged him out.
Zǐzhēn kowtowed, begging to become a slave,
but was not allowed and died.
He also sent Zhōngshū Shèrén Rú Fǎliàng to kill Bālíng Wáng Zǐlún.
Zǐlún was brave and resolute by nature.
At the time, he was Nánlánlíng Tàishǒu,
garrisoned at Lángyá,
where the city had defending soldiers.
(The Jìn dynasty established Nánlánlíng Jùn in Púzhōu, Jiāngchéng;
Qí moved its administration to Báixià,
which bordered the riverbank to the north.
Hence, it had defending soldiers.)
Xuānchéng Wáng consulted Diǎnqiān Huà Bómào about this.
Bómào said:
“If Your Highness takes him by force,
I fear it cannot be accomplished immediately.
If you entrust it to Bómào,
it will be the effort of just one man.”
So Bómào personally brought a cup of poisoned wine and forced Zǐlún to drink it.
Zǐlún straightened his clothes and cap,
came out to receive the edict,
and said to Fǎliàng:
“The former court, in the past, destroyed the Liú clan.
(See volume 135, *Jiànyuán* first year of Gāozǔ.)
朝 (cháo)
is pronounced *zhí yáo fān*.
This was surely according to the laws of fate.
You are an old retainer of this family.
(Rú Fǎliàng served Shìzǔ,
holding significant power.)
This must be something unavoidable given the circumstances.
This wine is not a toast of camaraderie.”
He then drank it and died,
aged sixteen.
Fǎliàng and his attendants all shed tears.
Initially,
when the princes were sent out to garrison,
Diǎnqiān were always appointed.
These Diǎnqiān were in charge of all matters in their respective regions,
which were entirely entrusted to them.
They would come to the capital to report on affairs
several times a year.
The current ruler would always converse with them,
inquiring about the affairs of the prefecture.
The good or bad reputation of the *cǐshǐ* (inspecting censor) depended entirely on their words.
From the *cǐshǐ* downwards, none failed to humble themselves and serve them,
constantly fearing they might fall short.
Thus, their authority extended throughout the prefectural divisions.
(Prefectural divisions
refers to the internal departments of a prefecture.)
When Wǔlíng Wáng Yè was in Jiāngzhōu,
his nature was fierce and upright,
and he could not be swayed.
Diǎnqiān Zhào Wòzhī said to people:
“Now it’s easy to go to the capital and replace a *cǐshǐ*!”
When he met Shìzǔ,
he vehemently slandered Yè.
Yè was subsequently dismissed and returned home.
Nánhǎi Wáng Zǐhǎn was stationed in Lángyá.
He wanted to visit the East Hall briefly,
but Diǎnqiān Jiāng Xiù would not permit it.
Zǐhǎn returned
and tearfully told his mother:
“Your son cannot even move five steps;
how is this different from being a prisoner!”
Shàolíng Wáng Zǐzhēn once requested bear fat.
(The *Běncǎo Tújīng* says: Bears resemble large pigs
but are agile and strong,
fond of climbing tall trees.
When they see people, they fall head over heels to the ground.
In winter, they often enter caves to hibernate,
emerging in early spring.
Their fat is called *xióngbái* (bear white),
taken in the eleventh month,
specifically the fat from their back.
Lù Diàn’s *Píyǎ* says: Bears have white fat like jade in their chest,
which tastes very good,
commonly called *xióngbái*.)
Jiāng Xiù dared not grant it.
During the Yǒngmíng era,
Bādōng Wáng Zǐxiǎng killed Liú Yín and others.
(The incident is found in volume 138, Yǒngmíng eighth year.)
Shìzǔ said to his close ministers:
“Zǐxiǎng has rebelled!”
Dài Sēngjìng loudly declared:
“All the princes should rebel,
not just Bādōng!”
The Emperor asked him why.
He replied:
“The heavenly princes are innocent,
yet they are all imprisoned.
To get a piece of lotus root or a cup of juice,
they must all consult the *qiānshuài* (Diǎnqiān commander).
If the *qiānshuài* is absent,
they endure thirst all day.
In all the prefectures, only the *qiānshuài* is heard of,
not the *cǐshǐ*.
How can they not rebel?!”
Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng once asked the assembled people:
“Why do scholar-officials visit the *qiānshuài*?”
Cānjūn Fàn Yún replied:
“Visiting the *chángshǐ* (chief clerk) and below is useless,
but visiting the *qiānshuài* immediately yields double the original value.”
(This means that whatever was presented to the *qiānshuài*
would result in a return double its original value.)
Zǐliáng showed a look of shame.
When Xuānchéngwáng executed the various princes,
he ordered his diǎnqiān to kill them all.
None were able to resist.
Kǒng Guī heard of this
and wept, saying:
“The princes of Héngyáng and Jiāngxià of Qí were most well-intentioned,
saying they intended to assist and support the imperial house.
If diǎnqiān generals had not been appointed,
this would surely not have happened.”
This section recounts the abuses of the diǎnqiān.
Then an edict was issued:
“From now on, if any prefecture has urgent matters,
they should be secretly reported to the throne;
do not send diǎnqiān to the capital again.”
From then on, the office of diǎnqiān gradually diminished in importance.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn commented: The sons of emperors and kings,
raised in wealth and luxury,
leaving the palace in the morning
and governing distant regions in the evening,
preventing arrogance and curtailing excess,
has been a constant practice for generations.
Therefore, assistant chancellors (fǔ) and above
were chosen by the emperor's heart;
veteran attendants
were appointed as chief commanders,
and their every move, whether eating, drinking, or rising,
was to be reported and approved.
Though their position was weighty,
they had no agency in their conduct.
Their authority was not their own,
and their benevolence did not reach below.
When difficulties suddenly arose,
expecting them to relinquish their positions to save the endangered,
how could it be possible!
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says: The feudal lords relinquished their positions to assist the royal house.
Dù Yù's commentary says: Jiān
is like yǔ (to participate).
They left their positions and participated in the governance of the king's affairs.
By the Qí dynasty, this system became particularly corrupt.
The practice of appointing diǎnqiān for the various princes began in the Sòng dynasty,
hence the statement.
On the day of Guǐmǎo in the 36th year,
Xiāo Yáoxīn was appointed Inspector of Yùzhōu as General of Níngshuò;
Xiāo Yáochāng was appointed Inspector of Yǐngzhōu as Palace Attendant;
Xiāo Dàn was appointed Inspector of Sīzhōu as General of Fǔguó.
Yáochāng
was Yáoxīn’s younger brother;
Dàn
was Chén’s elder brother.
The historian states that Xuānchéngwáng used his close relatives and partisans to take control of various regions.
Chén is pronounced shìmrén fān.
On the day of Jiǎchén in the 37th year,
Wèi appointed Pī, Prince Dōngyáng, as Grand Tutor and Director of the Department of State Affairs,
to remain and guard Píngchéng.
On the day of Wùshēn,
the Wèi Emperor personally announced to the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
sending Gāoyángwáng Yǒng and Yú Liè to escort the spirit tablets to Luòyáng.
On Xīnhài,
they departed from Píngchéng.
When Hǎilíngwáng was on the throne,
his daily life and diet
all required consultation with Xuānchéngwáng before proceeding.
He once craved steamed fish and vegetables,
but the director of the imperial kitchens replied that there was no recorded order from the duke,
and so he was not given it.
On the day of Xīnhài,
the Empress Dowager issued an order saying:
“The successor to the throne is young and immature,
and ignorant of many state affairs;
furthermore, he contracted a debilitating illness early.
Yīng (嬰)
means to entangle.
Wāng (尫)
is pronounced wūhuáng fān,
meaning weak.
Dù Yù said: it means a wasting illness.
The Grand Tutor Xuānchéngwáng
is a descendant of Xuānhuáng
and greatly beloved by Tàizǔ.
Xiāo Chéngzhī was posthumously honored as Emperor Xuān (Xuānhuángdì),
the father of Tàizǔ and grandfather of Luán.
Tàizǔ also always loved Luán,
hence the statement.
The Emperor may be demoted and enfeoffed as Hǎilíngwáng,
and I shall retire to a separate palace.”
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's Qí Shū
places this passage in the biography of Hǎilíngwáng.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's Qí Shū
places this statement in the biography of Míngdì.
On Guǐhài,
Gāozōng ascended the imperial throne,
granted a general amnesty,
and changed the era name.
At this time, the era name was changed to Jiànwǔ.
Sīkōng Chén Xiǎndá was appointed Grand Tutor,
Shàngshūlìng Wáng Yàn was given the additional title of General-in-chief of Agile Cavalry,
Zuǒ Púshè Xú Xiàosì was given the additional title of General-in-chief of the Central Army,
and Zhōnglǐngjūn Xiāo Chén was appointed General of the Palace Guard.
Dùzhī Shàngshū Yú Cóng claimed illness and did not attend the enthronement ceremony.
The Emperor, considering Cóng an old acquaintance, wished to appoint him to assist in governance.
He sent Wáng Yàn to show Cóng the documents concerning the deposition and enthronement.
Cóng said:
“The Emperor is sagacious and enlightened,
and the dukes and ministers are working together.
Why would you need a decrepit old man like me to aid in the renewal?
The Shī says: Its mandate is new.”
He then wept bitterly.
The historian states that Yú Cóng was gentle yet upright,
far surpassing Xiè Yà's brothers.
Xú Xiàosì said:
“This is also a remnant of ancient integrity.”
So the matter was dropped.
The Emperor held a banquet with his close ministers,
and ordered meritorious officials to offer wine.
Wáng Yàn and others rose from their seats,
but Xiè Yà alone did not rise,
saying:
“Your Majesty received the mandate,
responding to Heaven and conforming to the people;
Wáng Yàn presumptuously claims heavenly merit as his own achievement!”
The Emperor laughed heartily
and appeased him.
After the banquet,
Yàn called Yà to return together in a carriage to the Dapartment of State Affairs (lìngshěng).
Yà sternly said:
“Where is your lair (nèst)?”
Yàn greatly feared him.
On the day of Dīngmǎo in the 39th year,
an edict stated:
“Regarding local officials (fānmù shǒuzǎi)
who offer tributes,
if the items are not indigenous to their land,
meaning not like the Yǔ Gòng where tributes are made according to the products of the land.
On the day of Jǐsì in the 40th year,
the Wèi Emperor went to Xìndū.
On the day of Gēngwǔ,
an edict stated:
“Recently, I have heard that the barbarians along the border
frequently plunder the southern lands,
causing fathers and sons to be separated
and families to be torn apart.
I am now unifying the realm
and nurturing the myriad people.
If this continues,
how will the southerners know the virtue of the court?
It means the people of Jiāngnán will not know the virtue of the Wèi court.
Cháo (朝)
is pronounced zhíyáo fān.
The barbarian people must be prohibited and restrained
from any aggression or violence.”
Wèi initially established Jīngzhōu at Shàngluò.
During the Tàihé reign,
it was moved to Rángchéng.
Yǐngzhōu was established at Zhēnyáng.
Zhēnyáng
was Shènyáng County of Rǔnán Commandery in the Hàn dynasty.
Dōngjīngzhōu was established at Bǐyáng.
In the eleventh month,
on the day of Guǐyǒu,
Shǐ'ānwáng Yáoguāng was appointed Inspector of Yángzhōu.
On the day of Dīngchǒu in the 42nd year,
the Wèi Emperor went to Yè.
On the day of Gēngchén in the 43rd year,
Imperial Prince Bǎoyì was enfeoffed as Prince Jìn'ān,
Bǎoxuán as Prince Jiāngxià,
Bǎoyuán as Prince Lúlíng,
Bǎoyín as Prince Jiàn'ān,
Bǎoróng as Prince Suíjùn,
and Bǎoyōu as Prince Nánpíng.
On the day of Jiǎshēn in the 44th year,
an edict stated:
“The salaries of county magistrates are meager,
but even if tributes are always made according to the products of the land,
from now on, all such practices are abolished.”
From this,
it appears that in the government of the Jiāngzuǒ,
counties and townships, independent of prefectures, were also permitted to offer tributes directly to the imperial court (tiāntái).
On the day of Yǐyǒu in the 45th year,
the deceased Shǐ'ānzhēnwáng was posthumously honored as Emperor Jǐng,
and his wife as Empress Yì.
On the day of Bǐngxū in the 46th year,
Wénxǐgōng Yáoxīn was appointed Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
and Fēngchénggōng Yáochāng as Inspector of Yùzhōu.
At that time, the Emperor's eldest son, Jìn'ānwáng Bǎoyì, suffered from a chronic illness.
Gùjí (痼疾) meaning a chronic, incurable illness, hence unusable as a 'fèijí' (廢疾) or debilitating illness.
Cháng (長)
is pronounced zhīliǎng fān.
Therefore, Yáoguāng was placed in the central position,
“placed in the central position” refers to being appointed Inspector of Yángzhōu.
On the day of Wùzǐ in the 47th year,
Imperial Prince Bǎojuàn was established as Crown Prince.
48 The Wèi sovereign arrived in Luòyáng.
Wishing to clarify the grades of officials,
he appointed Shàngshū Cuī Liàng as acting Lìbù Láng.
Liàng
was the elder brother's grandson of Dàogù.
At the beginning of the Tàishǐ era of Sòng,
Cuī Dàogù surrendered to Wèi.
49 The Wèi sovereign commanded Hòujūn Jiāngjūn Yǔwén Fú to inspect pastureland.
Fú reported that from Shíjì westward,
and Hénèi eastward,
the area adjacent to the Yellow River was ten lǐ wide.
The Wèi sovereign moved various livestock from Dài and placed them in that area,
making Fú responsible for them;
as the animals suffered no loss,
he was made Sīwèi Jiān.
Initially,
Shìzǔ pacified Tǒngwàn, Qín, and Liáng.
In the fourth year of Yuánjiā of Sòng Wéndì,
Wèi pacified Tǒngwàn.
In the eighth year,
Hèlián Dìng destroyed Qín;
Dìng soon fled westward
and was captured by Tǔyùhún,
and all the Qín territory fell to Wèi.
In the sixteenth year,
Wèi pacified Liángzhōu.
These areas were used as pastureland,
and the livestock multiplied greatly,
with horses reaching over two million,
camels half that number,
and countless cattle and sheep.
When Gāozǔ later established pastures in Héyáng,
he consistently kept one hundred thousand warhorses there.
The Héyáng pasture
was the pastureland designed by Yǔwén Fú.
The livestock
were pronounced xù (許六翻).
Gradually moved southward again,
intending for them to gradually adapt to the local climate and soil,
to avoid deaths and injuries,
and the pastures west of the Yellow River became even more prolific.
However, after Zhèngguāng,
all were plundered by bandits,
leaving none remaining.
In the first year of Pǔtōng of Liáng Wǔdì,
Wèi changed its era name to Zhèngguāng.
The historian recounts Wèi's horse administration.
50 During the Yǒngmíng era,
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Shěn Yuān memorialized,
that all officials aged seventy
should be ordered to retire,
applying the ancient saying that one retires at seventy.
On the day of Gēngzǐ,
an edict ordered that the old system of selection and appointment be followed.
The princes executed by the regent
were all restored to their registers,
and their sons were enfeoffed as hóu.
51 The sovereign falsely claimed that Hǎilíng Gōngwáng was ill,
repeatedly sending imperial physicians to examine him,
and consequently caused his death.
The funeral rites all followed the precedent of Hàn Dōnghǎi Gōngwáng.
Hàn Dōnghǎi Wáng Qiáng had yielded the throne,
and his funeral was given special rites.
52 Wèi Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ Wéi Zhēn.
Wéi Zhēn had previously served as Lèlíng Zhènjiàng, stationed with Dōngjīngzhōu Cìshǐ Huán Dàn in Bǐyáng,
and later became Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ.
The Wèi sovereign bestowed upon him fine horses, grain, and silk.
Zhēn gathered the orphans and the poor in his jurisdiction,
distributed everything to them,
saying to them:
"The Son of Heaven grants me grain and silk because he trusts I can pacify and comfort you,
how dare I keep it for myself!"
53 The Wèi sovereign, learning that the current sovereign had deposed Hǎilíng Wáng and established himself,
planned a major invasion.
Coincidentally, border generals reported
that Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Xiàpī Cáo Hǔ had sent an envoy to request surrender to Wèi.
In the eleventh
month,
on the day Xīnchǒu of the new moon,
Wèi dispatched Xíng Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn Xuē Zhēndù to lead four generals toward Xiāngyáng,
Dàjiāngjūn Liú Chǎng and Píngnán Jiāngjūn Wáng Sù toward Yìyáng,
Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Tuòbá Yǎn toward Zhōnglí,
and Píngnán Jiāngjūn Guǎngpíng Liú Zǎo toward Nánzhèng.
Zhēndù
was the cousin's younger brother of Āndū.
Shàngshū Púyè
Lú Yuān was appointed Ānnán Jiāngjūn,
to oversee the vanguard forces heading to Xiāngyáng.
Yuān declined, citing his unfamiliarity with military campaigns,
but was not allowed.
Yuān said:
"I only fear that Cáo Hǔ might be a Zhōu Fáng."
The incident involving Zhōu Fáng is found in volume seventy-one,
in the second year of Tàihé of Wèi Míngdì.
Fáng
is pronounced fāng (符方翻).
54 The Wèi sovereign wished to change old customs.
On the day Rén'yín,
an edict prohibited officials and commoners from wearing Hú (barbarian) attire.
Many of the common people were displeased.
"Common people" refers to
descendants of those who arose in the northern wilderness, along with Wèi.
Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì Liú Fāng,
a cousin of Zànzhī.
Liú Zàn had served Qí and frequently visited Wèi,
both he and Fāng were from Péngchéng,
likely descendants of Chǔ Yuánwáng.
Both were favored by the emperor for their literary talents and treated with respect,
often invited to discuss and secretly deliberate on state affairs;
the great ministers and imperial relatives all felt estranged by this,
showing signs of displeasure.
The emperor had Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng Lù Kǎi privately admonish them, saying:
"His Majesty merely wishes to broaden his knowledge of ancient matters
and inquire about the precedents of former generations;
he will never favor them and alienate you."
The public sentiment then gradually eased.
Kǎi
was the son of Bó.
Lù Bó is mentioned in volume one hundred thirty-three, in the seventh year of Tàishǐ of Sòng Míngdì.
Bó
is pronounced bó (蒲撥翻).
55 The Wèi sovereign wished to personally lead an invasion.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
a general alert was sounded throughout the capital and provinces.
On the day Wùshēn,
an edict granted a three-year exemption from rent and taxes to the people of Dài who had moved to Luòyáng.
Xiàngzhōu Cìshǐ Gāo Lǘ
memorialized, stating:
"Luòyáng is newly established.
Cáo Hǔ has not sent hostages,
so he surely lacks sincerity.
It is not appropriate to act rashly."
The Wèi sovereign did not heed him.
After a long time,
Hǔ's envoys stopped coming.
The Wèi Emperor summoned the high ministers to discuss whether to proceed or halt.
Some high ministers thought it advisable to halt,
others thought it advisable to proceed.
The Emperor said:
"Everyone is confused,
and no one knows what to follow.
If we are to fully assess the advantages of proceeding or halting,
there should be a guest and a host,
to mutually provoke discussion.
Rènchéng and Zhènnán will argue for halting.
'Zhènnán'
should be
'Zhèn Jūn'.
Rèn,
pronounced 'rén'.
The various dukes will listen to the merits and demerits,
and the elder's view will be followed."
Everyone said:
"Yes."
Zhèn Jūn
General Lǐ Chōng said:
"We, your servants, believe that since the capital has just been moved and a new beginning is being made,
people desire a period of stability;
those who would act as internal collaborators have not been thoroughly assessed,
so it is not advisable to act rashly."
The Emperor said:
"Whether their surrender is genuine or feigned,
it is indeed impossible to know.
If it is feigned,
I will tour and pacify the Huái region,
and inquire into the sufferings of the people,
letting them know where the sovereign's virtue lies,
and thus inspire a desire to turn north;
if it is genuine,
and we do not respond in time now,
we will lose the opportunity to act at the right moment,
abandon the sincerity of those who seek righteousness,
and spoil my grand strategy."
Gū,
means to fail or neglect.
Bài,
pronounced 'bǔ mài'.
"Hǔ offers no security or hostage,
and his envoy has not returned,
so his deceit is evident.
The people who have recently relocated from the former capital,
all harbor a longing for their original homes.
Supporting the old and leading the young,
they have just settled in Luòyì,
with no dwelling of even a single rafter,
and no store of even a dān-shí of grain.
Yīng Shào says: The people of Qí call a small jar dān;
a dān holds two shí.
Dān,
pronounced 'dū làn'.
Spring plowing is about to begin,
this is the time for 'a hundred walls to rise'
and 'to commence working the southern fields'.
'A hundred walls to rise'

and Qí soldiers arrived in great numbers,
their warships blocking the river.
Yáng Bō formed a battle array on the south bank to resist them,
allowing all the armies to cross.
Qí soldiers converged from all sides, surrounding Yáng Bō,
who formed a circular array to defend,
personally engaging in combat,
killing a great many.
They resisted for two nights,
by which time the army had run out of food,
and the encircling forces became more pressing.
The Wèi zhǔ watched from the north bank,
unable to rescue them due to the high water.
After a while, the water level gradually receded.
Yáng Bō led three hundred elite cavalry past the Qí warships, shouting loudly:
"I intend to cross now! Those who dare to fight, come!"
He then led his troops across.
Yáng Bō
was the elder brother of Yáng Chūn.
Yáng Chūn is mentioned in Volume 137, during Wǔdì's Yǒngmíng eighth year.
After the Wèi army had retreated,
there were ten thousand remaining soldiers on Shàoyáng Zhōu,
who requested to surrender five hundred horses
and be granted passage to return.
Cuī Huìjǐng wished to cut off their path and attack them,
but Zhāng Xīntài said:
"Do not obstruct an army returning home;
the ancients feared this.
The art of war says: do not obstruct a retreating army,
and do not pursue a desperate foe.
They should not be taken lightly.
To defeat them now would not demonstrate valor,
and to fail would merely negate our previous achievements;
it is better to agree to their request."
Cuī Huìjǐng followed his advice.
Xiāo Tǎnzhī returned
and reported to the emperor:
"There were ten thousand desperate bandits on Shàoyáng Zhōu,
but Huìjǐng and Xīntài let them go instead of capturing them."
For this reason, neither was rewarded.
On the day of Jiǎshēn,
the alert was lifted.
The Wèi forces had already retreated,
hence the lifting of the alert.
Originally,
when the emperor heard that the Wèi zhǔ intended to water his horses in the Jiāng,
he was afraid,
and ordered Xiāo Yǐngzhòu, the Grand Administrator of Guǎnglíng and acting Governor of Nányān Zhōu, to move residents into the city.
The people were alarmed and terrified,
wanting to pack everything and cross south.
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu, considering the Wèi invaders still far away,
did not immediately implement the order,
and the Wèi troops ultimately did not arrive.
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu
was a cousin of Tàizǔ.
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu
was the son of Tàizǔ's cousin Chìfǔ.

The emperor sent Shàngshū Zuǒ
Púyè Shěn Wénjì to assist Fēngchéng Gōng Yáo Chāng in defending Shòuyáng.
In the first month of spring that year,
Shěn Wénjì was dispatched to supervise the armies of Yùzhōu.
Yùzhōu's seat was Shòuyáng.
He halted the roving troops and did not allow them to go out,
kept the city gates wide open,
and strengthened the defenses.
The Wèi troops soon retreated.
When Wèi invaded,
Lú Chǎng and others were still in Jiànkāng.
After the King of Hǎilíng ascended the throne,

Lú Chǎng arrived in Jiànkāng after the emperor had already been enthroned.
He was fed steamed beans.
Lú Chǎng was terrified,
and as he ate them,
tears and sweat streamed down his face.
The usher, Zhāng Sīníng, with unyielding speech and demeanor,
died at the legation.
Upon his return,
the Wèi zhǔ reprimanded Lú Chǎng, saying:
"Who does not die?
Why did you degrade yourself to the level of cattle and horses,
bending your body and disgracing the nation!
Even if you do not aspire to Sū Wǔ—
Sū Wǔ was an envoy to the Xiōngnú,
and for nineteen years he did not bend his principles."
He was then demoted to a commoner.
On the day of Wùzǐ,
Wèi Tàishī Jīngzhào Wǔ Gōng Féng Xī died in Píngchéng.
On the day of Yǐwèi,
the Wèi zhǔ went to Xiàpéi;
in summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day of Gēngzǐ,

on the day of Xīnchǒu,

Pī and Ruì were then left in charge of Píngchéng.
"[Since the beginning of] creation,

"Their commanders are contemptible;

So, he led his troops to swiftly attack one camp,
capturing it.
The four camps all collapsed.
Liáng Jìyú was captured alive,
over 3,000 heads were severed,

Capitalizing on the victory, they pressed forward relentlessly,
advancing to besiege Nánzhèng.
Yì also sent his general Jiāng Xiū to attack Yīng,

As he was about to return,
a separate army under Yì arrived.
The officers and soldiers were already exhausted,
and not expecting their arrival,
they were greatly frightened
and wanted to flee.
Yīng deliberately slackened his reins and rode slowly,
his demeanor calm and composed.
He climbed high to observe the enemy,
gesticulating east and west,
as if giving orders,
and then he arrayed his troops and advanced.
Yì's army suspected an ambush,
hesitated and retreated.
Yīng pursued and attacked them,
defeating them,
and then besieged Nánzhèng.
He forbade his officers and soldiers from plundering and abusing,
and people near and far were pleased and attached themselves to him,
vying to supply taxes and provisions.
Yì fortified the city and defended himself.
Fàn Jié, a military commander, had previously led over 3,000 men outside the city.
When he returned to relieve Nánzhèng,
Yīng ambushed and attacked him,
capturing them all.
The city was besieged for several tens of days,
and there was fear and agitation within the city.
Yǔ Yù of Xīnyě, the Registrar and Staff Officer, sealed dozens of empty granaries,
pointed them out to the officers and soldiers, and said:
"The grain in these is all full,
enough to last for two years.
Just exert yourselves and hold fast!"
The morale of the troops then stabilized.
Coincidentally, the Wei ruler recalled his troops.
Yīng sent the old and weak ahead first,
and personally led the elite troops as the rearguard.
Diànjūn (rearguard) means to be at the rear of the army to resist pursuing troops.
Yì thought it was a trick;
Yīng had been gone for one day,
but Yì still did not open the gates.
On the second day,
he then sent a general to pursue him.
Yīng dismounted and fought hand-to-hand with his soldiers.
Yì's soldiers dared not press forward.
After marching for four days and four nights,
Yì's soldiers finally returned.
Yīng entered Xié Gǔ,
where it happened to rain heavily.
The soldiers cut bamboo to store rice,
and cooked it on horseback with torches.
Earlier,
Yì had sent people to entice and persuade the various Dī tribes in Chóuchí
to raise troops and cut off Yīng's supply routes and return path.
Yīng commanded his troops to fight bravely,
fighting and advancing simultaneously.
An arrow struck Yīng's cheek,
but he ultimately returned with his entire army to Chóuchí.
Yīng, pressing on his victory, advanced deep into enemy territory,
but without subsequent reinforcements,
though he barely managed to return with his entire army,
he was also in great peril.

13 On the day of wùwǔ,
Wei changed to using longer rulers and larger measures,
their regulations being based on the Hànzhì.
The Hàn Lǜlì Zhì (Treatise on Musical Tubes and the Calendar) measured one guǎng (width) of a medium-sized black millet grain (zǐgǔ jùshǔ),
making it one ninetieth of the length of a huángzhōng tube.
One such unit was one fēn,
ten fēn made one cùn,
and ten cùn made one chǐ.
Furthermore, taking one thousand two hundred medium-sized black millet grains (zǐgǔ jùshǔ), they filled a yuè.
Ten yuè made one hé,
ten hé made one shēng,
and ten shēng made one dǒu.

Hence Guō Zuò cited this.
Lè (樂),
pronounced yú-jiāo.
The Emperor said:
“Wèi Míngdì erred through extravagance in the past;
how can I emulate him now!”
The Emperor loved to read,
never letting a scroll leave his hand.
Whether in a carriage or on horseback,
he never forgot to discuss the Dao.
He was skilled at writing,
often composing orally while on horseback.
Once completed,
he would not change a single character.
From Tàihé year ten onwards,
he personally drafted all imperial edicts and decrees.
He loved the worthy and delighted in goodness,
with an eagerness like hunger and thirst.
With those he associated and befriended,
he often shared sincere intentions,
such as Lǐ Chōng, Lǐ Biāo, Gāo Lǘ, Wáng Sù, Guō Zuò, Sòng Biàn, Liú Fāng, Cuī Guāng, Xíng Luán and others,
all of whom were cherished for their literary elegance,
and were appointed to high and influential positions.
He instituted rites and composed music,
presenting a flourishing and admirable sight,
embodying the spirit of great peace.
Historians say that Gāozǔ of Wei was capable of governing with culture.
The Grand Inquisitor, Shì Yùshǐ (治書侍御史), Xuē Cōng (薛聰),
was the great-grandson of Xuē Biàn (薛辯).
Xuē Biàn (薛辯) is mentioned in volume 124, in the twenty-first year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) of Emperor Wén (文帝) of Sòng (宋).
治 (Zhì)
is pronounced zhí.
If the Emperor (帝) sometimes wished to be lenient,
Cōng (聰) would invariably argue against it.
The Emperor (帝) often said:
"When I see Xuē Cōng (薛聰),
I cannot help but be in awe of him,
let alone others!"
From then on, the powerful relatives restrained themselves.
He was successively promoted to Zhí Gé Jiāngjūn (直閤將軍),
concurrently serving as Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng (給事黃門侍郎) and Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
The Emperor (帝) treated him externally with moral uprightness and respect,
and internally entrusted him with his innermost thoughts and plans.
The imperial guards and forbidden troops
were all under Cōng's (聰) command.
Thus, throughout the entire Tàihé (太和) era,
he constantly held the position of Zhí Gé Jiāngjūn (直閤將軍).
After the multitude of officials retired from court,
Cōng (聰) would always attend the Emperor (帝) in his private chambers,
speaking day and night.
Regarding the successes and failures of contemporary politics,
he would promptly offer remonstrances,
and his advice was often heeded.
Yet, he was profound, steady, and secretive,
so no one outside could fathom his depths.
The Emperor (帝) wished to advance him to higher positions and titles,
but he consistently declined them with great humility.
The Emperor (帝) also greatly understood and appreciated him,
saying to him:
"Your heavenly rank is naturally exalted,
indeed, it cannot be honored by a human rank."
Mèngzǐ (孟子) said: "Gōng (公), Qīng (卿), Dàfū (大夫),
these are human ranks;
benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and trustworthiness,
these are heavenly ranks."
In the 9th month, 21st day,
on the Gēngwǔ (庚午) day,
Wèi's (魏) six palaces, civil, and military officials all moved to Luòyáng (洛陽).
"Six palaces" refers to
the Empress, consorts,嫔御 (pínyù).
"Civil and military" refers to
all the civil and military officials, both inside and outside the court.
On the Bǐngxū (丙戌) day, 22nd day,
the Wèi (魏) Emperor (主) went to Yè (鄴),
and repeatedly visited the residence of Gāo Lǘ (高閭), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Xiāngzhōu (相州).
"Guǎn" (館)
refers to the Cìshǐ's (刺史) official residence.
相 (Xiāng)
is pronounced xì liàng.
He was generously rewarded.
Lǘ (閭) repeatedly requested to return to his home province,
and an imperial edict stated:
"Lǘ (閭), in his old age (literally, "the year of hanging up the carriage"),
still seeks to 'return home in brocade robes.'
When Xuē Guǎnghàn (薛廣漢) of Hàn (漢) retired from office,
he hung up his comfortable carriage to show his descendants.
The ancients had a saying,
'To be rich and honored and not return to one's hometown
is like wearing brocade robes and walking at night.'
衣 (Yī)
is pronounced yū jì.
This contains a flaw in humble virtue;
he may be demoted in title to Píng Běi Jiāngjūn (平北將軍).
As an elder statesman of the court,
he should be granted his wish,
and be transferred and appointed as Cìshǐ (刺史) of Yōuzhōu (幽州).
Gāo Lǘ (高閭) was a native of Yōngnú (雍奴), Yúyáng (漁陽),
which is within the jurisdiction of Yōuzhōu (幽zhou).
朝 (Cháo)
is pronounced zhí yáo.
Both grace and law are applied."
His request was granted to encourage goodness and show favor,
while his title was demoted to uphold the law.
The Emperor (帝) admonished him, saying:
"To serve as a regional governor is both easy and difficult: 'If one's person is upright,
orders are followed without being given,'
this is why it is easy;
'If one's person is not upright,
orders are not obeyed even if given,'
this is why it is difficult."
He used Kǒngzǐ's (孔子) words to elaborate on the ease and difficulty.
易 (Yì)
is pronounced yǐ chǐ.
On the Jǐchǒu (己丑) day, 23rd day,
Prince Bǎo Yōu (寶攸) of Nánpíng (南平) was transferred to become Prince of Shàolíng (邵陵);
Prince Zǐwén (子文) of Shǔjùn (蜀郡) was transferred to become Prince of Xīyáng (西陽);
Prince Zǐjùn (子峻) of Guǎnghàn (廣漢) was transferred to become Prince of Héngyáng (衡陽);
Prince Zhāoxiù (昭秀) of Línhǎi (臨海) was transferred to become Prince of Bālíng (巴陵);
Prince Zhāocàn (昭粲) of Yǒngjiā (永嘉) was transferred to become Prince of Guìyáng (桂陽).
Bǎo Yōu (寶攸) was the Emperor's son;
the others were all descendants of Gāo (高) and Wǔ (武).
On the Yǐwèi (乙未) day, 24th day,
the Wèi (魏) Emperor (主) returned from Yè (鄴);
he returned to Luòyáng (洛陽).
In the 10th month,
on the Bǐngchén (丙辰) day,
he arrived in Luòyáng (洛陽).
On the Rénxū (壬戌) day, 25th day,
the Wèi (魏) imperial edict stated:
"The outstanding officials in all provinces
shall be assessed in three grades according to their successes and failures and reported."
Another edict stated:
"The six provinces of Xú (徐), Yǎn (兗), Guāng (光), Nán Qīng (南青), Jīng (荊), and Luò (洛)
shall strictly organize their military preparations,
and be ready to gather."
Wèi's (魏) Xúzhōu (徐州) governed Píngchéng (彭城), Nányángpíng (南陽平), Pèi (沛), Lánlíng (蘭陵), Běi Jìyīn (北濟陰) and other commanderies.
Yǎnzhōu (兗州) governed Tàishān (泰山), Lǔ (魯), Gāopíng (高平), Rènchéng (任城), Dōngpíng (東平), Dōngyángpíng (東陽平) and other commanderies.
Guāngzhōu (光州) was administered from Yèchéng (掖城),
established in the fourth year of Huángxīng (皇興) by dividing Qīngzhōu (青州),
and governed Dōnglái (東萊), Chángguǎng (長廣), Dōngmóu (東牟) and other commanderies.
Nán Qīngzhōu (南青州) was formerly Dōng Xúzhōu (東徐州),
renamed by the Wèi (魏) Emperor (主),
and governed Dōng'ān (東安) and Dōngguǎn (東莞) commanderies.
Wèi (魏) initially established Jīngzhōu (荊州) at Shàngluò (上洛),
governing Shàngluò (上洛), Shàngyōng (上庸), Wèixīng (魏興) and other commanderies.
In the eleventh year of Tàihé (太和),
it was renamed Luòzhōu (洛州),
and Jīngzhōu (荊zhou) was established at Rǎngchéng (穰城),
governing Nányáng (南陽), Shùnyáng (順陽), Xīnyě (新野), Xiāngchéng (襄城) and other commanderies.
The edict to prepare military forces
indicates a plan to resume the southern campaign.
In the 11th month,
on the Dīngmǎo (丁卯) day,
an edict abolished Shìzōng's (世宗) Eastern Field,
and demolished Xīngguāng Lóu (興光樓).
The Eastern Field is mentioned in the annals of Emperor Wǔ (武帝).
Xīngguāng Lóu (興光樓)
was probably also built by Crown Prince Wénhuì (文惠太子).
On the Jǐmǎo (己卯) day, 27th day,
Crown Prince Chǔ Shì (褚氏) was taken in as consort,
and a general amnesty was declared.
She was the daughter of Chǔ Chéng (褚澄).
Chǔ Chéng (褚澄) is mentioned in volume 133,
in the second year of Yuánhuī (元徽) of King Cāngwú (蒼梧王) of Sòng (宋).
On the Gēngwǔ (庚午) day, 28th day,
the Wèi (魏) Emperor (主) went to Wěisù Shān (委粟山)
to establish the Yuánqiū (圜丘) altar.
On the Jǐmǎo (己卯) day,
the Emperor (帝) summoned various scholars to discuss the rites for the Yuánqiū (圜丘) altar.
The Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat, Lǐ Biāo (李彪), suggested:
"When the people of Lǔ (魯) were about to perform sacrifices to the Lord on High (上帝),
they would first perform sacrifices at the Pàngōng (泮宮) college."
This is from the "Lǐqì" (禮器) chapter of the "Lǐ Jì" (禮記).
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) noted: "Pàngōng (泮宮)
is a suburban school."
This was followed.
On the Jiǎshēn (甲申) day,
the Wèi (魏) Emperor (主) offered sacrifices at the Yuánqiū (圜丘) altar;
a general
amnesty was declared.
In the 12th month,
on the Yǐwèi (乙未) day (which was the first day of the month),
the Wèi (魏) Emperor (主) met with his multitude of officials in Guāngjí Táng (光極堂),
and announced the "Lower-Grade Officials Ordinance,"
which marked the beginning of a major selection process.
Yú Lì (于烈)'s son Dēng (登), who was Guānglùxūn (光祿勳), cited precedents to request promotion.
Lì (烈) submitted a memorial, stating:
"In this present enlightened reign,
uprightness and humility should be the norm,
yet my son Dēng (登) cites others to seek advancement;
'citing others'
refers to citing examples of other people.
朝 (Cháo)
is pronounced zhí yáo.
I beg that he be dismissed!"
"Dismissed" refers to dismissal from office and removal from position.
"These are the words of a man of insight;
I would not have thought Lì (烈) capable of such a thing!"
Thereupon, he granted an audience to Dēng (登),
and said to him:
"I intend to spread transformation throughout the world,
and because your father possesses the virtue of humility and the character of an upright scholar,
I therefore promote you to Tàizǐ Yìjūn Xiàowèi (太子翊軍校尉)."
He also added Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) to Lì's (烈) titles
and enfeoffed him as the Viscount of Liáochéng Xiàn (聊城縣).
The Wèi (魏) Emperor (主) said to his multitude of officials:
"There has always been one regrettable matter in our state: that officials are unwilling to publicly speak about successes and failures.
The ruler fears not being able to accept remonstrance,
and the official fears not being able to fully express loyalty.
From now on, if I appoint someone,
and there is anything unsuitable,
you all must speak directly of their faults;
if there is someone with talent whom I do not recognize,
you all should also recommend them.
If this is done,
those who recommend suitable persons will be rewarded,
and those who fail to speak will be punished.
You all must understand this."
Despite Wèi Xiàowén (魏孝文)'s such efforts to seek remonstrance and talent,
the officials of that time still could not meet the Emperor's expectations.
Could it be that in court deliberations,
the Emperor (帝) was keen to display his eloquence and impose it,
leading to those who harbored thoughts but dared not fully express them?
30 Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
an imperial edict was issued to repair the imperial tombs of the Jìn (晉) emperors,
and increase their guards.
These imperial tombs of the Jìn (晉) emperors
refer to those in Jiāngnán (江南).
31 Jiǎzǐ (甲子),
the Wèi (魏) ruler granted an audience to his attendant officials in Guāngjí Táng (光極堂),
and bestowed caps and robes.
Caps and robes were bestowed to replace the Hú (胡) attire.
32 Previously, the Wèi (魏) people had never used money.
The Wèi (魏) ruler now ordered the casting of Tàihé Wǔzhū (太和五銖) coins.
This year,
the minting was largely ready,
and an edict commanded their use by both public and private sectors.
33 The Wèi (魏) appointed Tián Yìguāng (田益光), the Mán (蠻) chieftain of Guāngchéng (光城),
as the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Nánsī Zhōu (南司州),

Later, Dōngyù Zhōu (東豫州) was established in Xīncài (新蔡),
and Yìguāng (益光) was made its Cìshǐ (刺史).
According to the Běishǐ (北史),
"Yìguāng" (益光)
should be
"Yìzōng" (益宗).
Since Yìzōng (益宗) had crossed north of the Huái (淮) River,
the Wèi (魏) considered that he could not remain Cìshǐ (刺史) of Sī Zhōu (司州),
so they established Dōngyù Zhōu (東豫州) in Xīncài (新蔡).
Also, according to the Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) and Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註),
"Xīncài" (新蔡)
should be
"Xīnxī" (新息).
34 The Dī (氐) king Yáng Jiǒng (楊炅) died.

2 The Wèi (魏) ruler issued an edict,
stating:
"Northern people call earth 'Tuò' (拓),
and empress 'Bá' (跋).
The ancestors of Wèi (魏) originated from Huángdì (黃帝),
and ruled by the virtue of earth,
hence they were the Tuòbá (拓跋) clan.
Now, earth
is the color of yellow in the center,
and the origin of all things;
it is fitting to change the surname to Yuán (元).
All meritorious officials and old clans who came from Dài (代),
whose surnames are duplicated,
shall all change them."
Thereupon, the Bábá (拔拔) clan was changed to Chángsūn (長孫),
Dálā (達奚) to Xī (奚),
Yǐzhān (乙旃) to Shūsūn (叔孫),
Qiūmùlíng (丘穆陵) to Mù (穆),
Bùliùgū (步六孤) to Lù (陸),
Hèlài (賀賴) to Hè (賀),
Dúgū (獨孤) to Liú (劉),
Hèlóu (賀樓) to Lóu (樓),
Wùniǔyú (勿忸于) to Yú (于),
Wèichí (尉遲) to Wèi (尉);
the other changes
are too numerous to record.
For individuals like Chángsūn Sōng (長孫嵩), Xī Jīn (奚斤), Shūsūn Jiàn (叔孫建), Mù Chóng (穆崇), and Yú Lìdī (于栗磾),
histories often use their later changed surnames,
for simplicity and convenience in writing,
not their original ones.
As for other northern surnames,
which were changed to later surnames,
notes have already briefly appeared earlier.
This is because some of their changed surnames
clashed with existing surnames of the Huá (華) people.
Niǔ (忸),
is read nǐu (女九翻) and also liù (女六翻).
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: Meritorious officials in the early Wèi (魏) had surnames that were all duplicated, complex, and unusual.
During the Tàihé (太和) era of Xiàowén (孝文),
the Hú (胡) customs were transformed,
and surnames were first changed.
Wèi Shōu (魏收), in compiling the Wèishū (魏書),
already fully used the new surnames,
not the old ones.
What is referred to in the Sòngshū Suǒlǔ Zhuàn (宋書索虜傳) and Nánqíshū Wèilǔ Zhuàn (南齊書魏虜傳)
were probably their old surnames.
We now follow the Wèishū (魏書) for simplicity.
The Wèi (魏) ruler highly valued clan status.
Considering the four clans of Fànyáng Lú Mǐn (范陽盧敏), Qīnghé Cuī Zōngbó (清河崔宗伯), Xíngyáng Zhèng Xī (滎陽鄭羲), and Tàiyuán Wáng Qióng (太原王瓊)
to be highly esteemed by the gentry,
he took their daughters into his harem.
Lǒngxī Lǐ Chōng (隴西李沖), known for his talent and insight,
was highly regarded at court.
His marital connections
were all with distinguished families;
the emperor also took his daughter as a Fūrén (夫人).
An edict ordered Huángmén Láng (黃門郎) and Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ (司徒左長史) Sòng Biàn (宋弁)
to assess the gentry of various provinces,
leading to many promotions and demotions.
Another edict stated:
"The people of Dài (代) previously had no surnames or clans.
Even the descendants of meritorious and virtuous individuals
were no different from the common folk;
thus, those who achieved official success reached the highest positions of Gōngqīng (公卿),
while their relatives by 'gōng' (功) and 'shuāi' (衰) mourning grades remained in humble posts.
'Gōng' (功) and 'shuāi' (衰)
refer to mourning grades from Xiǎogōng (小功) and Dàgōng (大功) up to Qíshuāi (齊衰).
Wěi (猥)
means lowly.
Shuāi (衰)
is pronounced cuī (倉回翻).
Wěi (猥)
is pronounced huì (烏賄翻),

However, according to the Wèishū Guānshì Zhì (魏書官氏志),

Wèi (尉),
is pronounced yù (紆勿翻).
Those whose achievements were eminent in their time,
and whose positions reached the pinnacle of kings and dukes,
clearly discernible,
shall be reported to the Sī Zhōu (司州) and Lìbù (吏部),
and not be assigned to humble offices,
being treated the same as the Four Clans.
The Four Clans
are Lú (盧), Cuī (崔), Zhèng (鄭), and Wáng (王).
Xià (下),
is pronounced jià (戶嫁翻).
Those who should be ranked among the scholar-gentry
will be decided by a subsequent special edict.
As for those who were previously tribal chieftains,
and whose officials from Huángshǐ (皇始) onward for three generations were Gěishì (給事) or higher, or whose ranks reached kings and dukes, they shall be given surnames.
If they were not originally chieftains,
but their officials from Huángshǐ (皇始) onward for three generations were Shàngshū (尚書) or higher, or whose ranks reached kings and dukes, they shall also be given surnames.
Descendants of chieftains whose official positions were not prominent shall be considered a clan.
If they were not originally chieftains but their official positions were prominent, they shall also be considered a clan.
All such surnames and clans
must be carefully verified,
and no false claims allowed.
Let Sīkōng (司空) Mù Liàng (穆亮) and Shàngshū (尚書) Lù Xiù (陸琇) and others make the detailed decisions,
striving for fairness."
Xiù (琇)
was the son of Bó (馛).
When Wèi Xiàowén (魏孝文) received the abdication,
Lù Bó (陸馛) served as his tutor,
hence all his sons achieved prominence.
Xiù (琇),
is pronounced xiù (秀).
Bó (馛),
is pronounced bó (蒲撥翻).
The old system of the Wèi Dynasty stipulated that all princes' chamberlains should marry into the Eight Clans or other families of pure descent.
Wángguó shèrén (princes' chamberlains):
Shè (chamberlains),

Bāzú (Eight Clans):
refers to the eight surnames that came from Dài previously.
Lìhù (servile households):

When Wèi established its clan system,
it was indeed unable to fully satisfy public opinion;
to now issue an edict for the princes to change their wives
is a great transgression against human relations.
Husband and wife are equals;
once they are united as equals,
this should not change throughout their lives.
Even common gentry feel ashamed
when they replace their wives due to wealth,
how much more so for the emperor's brothers!
Once this edict is issued,
what will the world think!

At the beginning of Tàishǐ of the Sòng Dynasty,
Zhèng Xī followed Tuòbá Shí to pacify Rǔ and Yǐng.
At that time, the various Lǐ families of Zhàojùn
had many eminent figures,
each upholding their family traditions,
hence, those of the world who spoke of high nobility
considered the Five Surnames as preeminent.
The Lú, Cuī, Zhèng, Wáng, and Lǐ families constituted the Five Surnames.
The various Lǐ families of Zhàojùn,
northerners called them Zhào Lǐ;
Lǐ Líng, Lǐ Shùn, Lǐ Xiàobó, and their nephews
were all Zhào Lǐ.
Public opinion regarded the Xuē clan as a prominent family of Hédōng.
The Emperor said:
"The Xuē clan
is from Shǔ,
how can they be included among the 'county surnames'!"
Zhíhé Xuē Zōngqǐ, holding a halberd below the殿 (hall),
stepped forward and replied:
"My ancestors

Ruì had not yet departed.

secretly gathering Zhèn Běi Dàjiāngjūn Lèlíng Wáng Sīyù, Ānlè Hóu Lóng, Fúmíng Zhènjiāng Lǔjùn Hóu Yè, Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Chāo, and others,
together endorsing Shuòzhōu Cǐshǐ Yángpíng Wáng Yí as their leader.
Sīyù was the son of Tiāncì;
Rǔyīn Wáng Tiāncì,
son of Jǐngmù Tàizǐ,
was the Wèi zhǔ's grand-uncle.
Lè,
pronounced *luò*.
Jiāng,
pronounced *jí liàng fān*.
Xiāo,
pronounced *jiān yáo fān*.
Qí,
pronounced *qí jì fān*.
He was the younger brother of Pī;
Lóng and Chāo
were both sons of Pī.
Ruì believed that Luòyáng was peaceful and enlightened.
*Zuǒ Zhuàn*: The Chu Zǐ attacked the Lùhún Róng,
then reached Luò,
displaying his troops on the borders of Zhōu.
King Dìng sent Wángsūn Mǎn to comfort the Chu Zǐ;
the Chu Zǐ inquired about the size and weight of the tripods.
Wángsūn Mǎn said:
"If virtue is peaceful and enlightened,
though small,
it is heavy;
if it is treacherous, perverse, chaotic,
though large,
it is light.
Heaven bestows its favor on bright virtue,
and there is a limit to its end.
Though Zhōu's virtue is in decline,
Heaven's mandate has not changed,
so the lightness or heaviness of the tripods
cannot be inquired about."
Tài therefore did not act.
Yí falsely promised Tài and others to reassure them,
but secretly reported the situation.
Acting Minister of Personnel Rènchéng Wáng Chéng was ill.
"Acting Minister of Personnel" means
acting as Minister of Personnel,
not yet a full appointment.
Rèn,
pronounced *rén*.
He said to him:
"Mù Tài is plotting rebellion,
inciting the imperial clan.
If it truly happens,
the capital has only just been moved.
The northern people are nostalgic for the old ways,
and if there is turmoil between north and south,
my Luòyáng will not be established.
This is a major affair of the state,
and only you can handle it.
Although you are ill,
force yourself to travel north for me
and carefully observe the situation.
If their strength is weak,
go directly and capture them;
if they are already strong,
you may act under imperial authority to mobilize the troops of Bìng and Sì to attack them."
He replied:
"Tài and the others are foolish and deluded,
precisely because they are nostalgic for the old ways,
which is why they made this plan;
they have no deep strategy or foresight.
Although I am humble and timid,
I am sufficient to control them.
I beg Your Majesty not to worry.
Though I have the illness of a dog or horse (a humble term for illness),
how can I refuse!"
The emperor smiled and said:
"If Rènchéng is willing to go,
what more do I have to worry about!"
Thereupon, he bestowed upon Chéng a *jié*, bronze tiger tallies, bamboo tallies, and imperial guards,
in the second year of Hàn Wéndì,
copper tiger tallies and bamboo tallies were first given to commandery governors.
Yīng Shào said: Copper tiger tallies,
from first to fifth,
when the state wished to dispatch troops or send envoys,
they would go to the commandery to match the tallies;
only if they matched would they be obeyed.
Bamboo tallies,
all made of five bamboo arrows,
five inches long,
carved with seal script,
from first to fifth.
From Wèi and Jìn onwards,
bamboo tallies were from first to tenth.
"Yùzhàng Zuǒyòu" (imperial guards)
refers to those who carried imperial weapons by the emperor's side,
bestowed upon Chéng to serve as his escort.
Shǐ,
pronounced *shū lì fān*.
They marched to Yànmén,
where the Grand Administrator of Yànmén reported that night:
“Tài has already led his troops west to Yángpíng.”
Yángpíng Wáng Yí (王頤) was the Inspector of Shuòzhōu,
located west of Píngchéng.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Shuòzhōu is two hundred sixty *lǐ* northeast of Píngchéng.
The Right Vice-Minister Mèng Bīn (孟斌) said:
“The situation is not yet ascertainable.
It is advisable to follow the imperial edict and summon the troops from Bìng (幷) and Sì (肆),
and then advance slowly.”
Chéng (澄) said:
“Since Tài (泰) is plotting rebellion,
he should occupy a strong city;
yet he instead went to meet Yángpíng (陽平).
Judging by his actions,
it appears his position is weak.
Since Tài does not resist us,
there is no reason to dispatch troops.
That would not be advisable.
We should just quickly go and pacify the area,
and the people's hearts will naturally settle.”
So, they doubled their pace and marched day and night.
He first sent the Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ (治書侍御史) Lǐ Huàn (李煥) with a single horseman into Dài (代).
Emperor Xuān of Hàn (漢宣帝) visited the Xuānshì (宣室),
residing in seclusion while making decisions,
and ordered two Shìyùshǐ (侍御史) to manage documents by his side.
Later, a separate office was established,
called Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ.
The Wèi (魏) called Píngchéng (平城) the Dàidū (代都).
治 (zhì),
read as *zhí zhī fān*.
騎 (qí),
read as *qí jì fān*.
He made known to Tài's (泰) faction,
showing them the consequences of fortune and misfortune,
but none of them served him.
Tài had no recourse.
He led several hundred of his subordinates to attack Huàn (煥),
but failed,
and fled out of the city to the west.
They pursued and captured him.
Chéng (澄) also arrived soon after.
尋 (xún),
means to follow.
He arrested Lù Ruì (陸叡) and over a hundred others,
all of whom were imprisoned.
The common people were pacified.
Chéng (澄) submitted a detailed report.
The Emperor was pleased,
and summoned the *gōngqīng* (公卿),
showing them the report and saying:
“Rènchéng (任城) can truly be called a minister of the state.
Observing his judicial decisions,
how could Gāotáo (皋陶) have surpassed them!”
He looked at Xiányáng Wáng Xī (咸陽王禧) and others and said:
“If you were in this situation,
you would not have been able to handle it.”
23 The Wèi (魏) ruler planned to invade.
He granted an audience to his *gōngqīng* in the Qīnghuī Táng (清徽堂),
saying:
“I have established my capital in the center of the land,
and the main threads of governance are roughly in place.
The *Shū* (書) says in the ‘Yuè Mìng’ (說命): 'If the net is on the main rope,
there will be order and no confusion.'
見 (xiàn),
read as *xián biàn fān*.
粗 (cū),
read as *zuò wǔ fān*.
How can I imitate the emperors of recent times who secluded themselves behind screens in their deep palaces!
My southern expedition is now decided,
but I do not yet know the exact timing.
Recently, all the diviners have said that
if we go now, we will surely conquer.
This is a great matter for the state.
It is proper for the ruler and ministers to each express their views,
without being swayed by my initial words and equivocating now,
only to differ later.”
Lǐ Chōng (李沖) replied:
“In all military operations,
it is advisable to first consider human affairs,
and then observe the ways of Heaven.
Although the divination is auspicious, human affairs are not yet ready.
The relocation of the capital is still new,
and the autumn grains have not ripened well.
It is not suitable to raise an army now.
In my humble opinion,
it is advisable to wait until next autumn.”
The Emperor said:
“Seventeen years ago,
I had an army of two hundred thousand.
This was the eleventh year of Yǒngmíng (永明) under Qí Shìzǔ (齊世祖),
and the seventeenth year of Tàihé (太和) under Wèi Gāozǔ (魏高祖).
The Wèi (魏) decided to move the capital to Luò (洛) and ceased the southern expedition,
only invading last year, which was nineteen years later.
‘Nineteen years’ refers to the period between the cessation of the southern expedition and the invasion last year.
‘Two hundred thousand’
should also be
‘three hundred thousand’.
These matters are all recorded in the previous year.
去 (qù),
means 'last'.
Also, at that time, the common report was three hundred thousand,
but in reality, it was only two hundred thousand.
However, the timing was unfavorable.
Now that the celestial timing is auspicious,
you again say that human affairs are not yet ready;
if we follow your words, *Púshè* (僕射),
then there will never be a time for conquest.
The enemy is at our doorstep,
and in the future, this will become a worry for the state.
How dare I feel at ease!
If the autumn expedition is not victorious,
all of you gentlemen shall be handed over to the Sīkòu (司寇).
You must not hold back your thoughts.”
Since the Wèi (魏) had moved its capital to Luò (洛),
it was close to the Huái (淮) and Hàn (漢) rivers,
hence the urgency for a southern expedition to push back the encroaching territories.
24 The Wèi (魏) ruler, seeing that many of those exiled to the border for crimes escaped,
then decreed that if one person escaped,
the entire household would be conscripted into service.
Cuī Tǐng (崔挺) of Bólíng (博陵), the Inspector of Guāngzhōu (光州), submitted a memorial advising against it, saying:
“In the world, good people are few,
and evil people are many.
If one person commits a crime,
and it extends to the entire household,
then Sīmǎ Niú (司馬牛) would suffer the punishment of Huán Tuí (桓魋),
and Liǔxià Huì (柳下惠) would be subjected to the execution of Dào Zhí (盜跖).
Sīmǎ Niú (司馬牛) and Huán Tuí (桓魋),
and Liǔxià Huì (柳下惠) and Dào Zhí (盜跖),
were all brothers.
The worthy and the unworthy are indeed far apart,
and brothers are not held accountable for each other's crimes;
this is ancient law.”
魋 (tuí),
read as *tú huí fān*.
跖 (zhí),
read as *zhī shí fān*.
The Emperor approved of it,
and consequently abolished the decree.
