Gāozōng Míng Huángdì (高宗明皇帝), Part II
Jiànwǔ (建武) Fourth Year (Dīngchǒu, 497 CE)
1 Spring,
First Month,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Qí Dì Jì* (齊帝紀) says:
“On the day *gēngwǔ* (庚午),
a general amnesty was proclaimed.”
According to the *Chánglì* (長曆),
the *jǐchǒu* (己丑) day was the first day of this month,
and there was no *gēngwǔ* day,
hence the date is not specified.
2 On the day *bǐngshēn* (丙申),
the Wèi (魏) established Imperial Prince Kè (恪) as crown prince.
The Wèi (魏) ruler hosted a banquet in the Qīnghuī Táng (清徽堂).
When the conversation turned to Crown Prince Xún (恂),
Lǐ Chōng (李沖) apologized, saying:
“I am unworthy of the title of tutor,
and have been unable to guide him.”
The Emperor said:
“I myself cannot change his wickedness,
why should the tutors apologize!”
3 On the day *yǐsì* (乙巳),
the Wèi (魏) ruler made a northern tour.
4 Initially,
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Yàn
was favored and trusted by Shìzǔ.
Details can be found in volume 136, Shìzǔ Yǒngmíng 7th year.
Yàn then gladly offered his support.
Details can be found in volume 139, Yuánnián.
The Emperor hosted a banquet for Yàn at Dōngfǔ,
and when the conversation turned to current affairs,
Yàn slapped his palm and said:
"Your Majesty often said I was timid;
how do I seem now?"
After the Emperor ascended the throne,
Yàn considered himself a meritorious official who helped establish the new dynasty,
and often disparaged Shìzǔ's old practices.
Having taken his place at court,
the position of Shàngshū Lìng was superior to all other court officials.
Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo.
He filled key internal and external positions
with his own trusted associates,
often disputing with the Emperor over appointments.
Although the Emperor needed Yàn due to the circumstances,
Shìjì
refers to the juncture of undertaking affairs;
Xū
means relying on him for use.
The Emperor once sorted through Shìzǔ's internal decrees
and found over three hundred personal letters between Shìzǔ and Yàn,
all discussing state affairs.
He also found Yàn's memorial advising Shìzǔ on the matter of the Emperor's leadership in selections,
as seen in volume 137, Yǒngmíng 8th year.
Xuǎn,
pronounced xū juàn.
Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng advised the Emperor to execute Yàn,
but the Emperor said:
"Yàn has rendered service to me;
moreover, he has not yet committed any crime."
Yáoguāng said:
"If Yàn couldn't serve Wǔdì,
how can he serve Your Majesty?"
The Emperor remained silent.
The Emperor sent his trusted confidants Chén
Shìfàn and others to patrol the streets and alleys,
listening for unusual remarks.
Yàn, being careless and unguarded,
hoped to be appointed Kāifǔ,
and frequently called in physiognomists to examine him,
who said he would achieve great nobility.
When speaking with guests,
he liked to dismiss others for private conversations.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he suspected Yàn intended to rebel,
and thus harbored the intention to execute Yàn.
Fèngcháoqǐng Xiānyú Wéncàn secretly probed the Emperor's intentions
and reported that Yàn had rebellious ambitions.
Shìfàn further reported to the Emperor, saying:
"Yàn plans to use the Southern Sacrifice in the fourth year
to conspire with Shìzǔ's former commanders to launch an attack along the road."
It so happened that a tiger trespassed near the sacrificial altar,
which made the Emperor even more fearful.
The day before the sacrifice,
an imperial edict was issued to suspend it,
first informing Yàn and Xú Xiàosì.
Xiàosì followed the decree,
but Yàn argued,
"The suburban sacrifice is a grand affair;
it must be carried out with utmost effort."
The Emperor became even more convinced by Shìfàn's words.
On the day Bǐngchén,
Yàn was summoned to Huálín Shěng
and executed.
Shěng was located in Huálínyuán,
hence the name.
Kǎoyì states: Yàn's biography says:
"After the New Year's assembly concluded,
Yàn was summoned and executed."
The Basic Annals state:
"On Bǐngchén,
Yàn was executed."
Bǐngchén
was the twenty-eighth day of the first month.
According to the sacrificial rites, the suburban sacrifice must be in the first month.
Since it says an edict suspended the sacrifice one day before,
Yàn's execution certainly could not have been on the day of the New Year's assembly.
The biography likely means after the New Year's assembly rituals.
Míngdá
was probably a commander during Shìzǔ's time.
An imperial edict stated:
"Yàn, along with Yì and Míngdá, plotted to enthrone Hédōng Wáng Xuán, knowing his abilities were weak,
and make him a puppet ruler."
Yàn's younger brother Xǔ, the Governor of Guǎngzhōu,
was attacked and killed by the Emperor's envoy, Nán Zhōngláng Sīmǎ Xiāo Jìchǎng.
Jìchǎng was
the Emperor's cousin (son of paternal grandfather's brother).
Xiāo Yì was extravagant and fond of archery and horsemanship,
which made him feared by the Emperor,
so he was framed for this incident.
Yì
was Gāodì's cousin,
and the son of Xīnwú Hóu Jǐngxiān.
Hǎo,
pronounced hū dào.
He was not yet killed by the Emperor.
When Xuán had an audience with the Emperor,
he always bowed deeply and hunched,
not daring to walk straight or look directly.
By this time,
he had grown somewhat older,
and consequently was dismissed from office due to Yàn's affair
and forbidden from communicating with outsiders.
When Yùlín Wáng was about to be deposed,
Yàn's cousin (son of paternal uncle) Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Sīyuǎn said to Yàn:
"Brother, you received great kindness from Shìzǔ,
yet now you suddenly support someone in such an affair.
He may need you temporarily for strategic reasons,
but I don't know how you will sustain yourself in the future!
If you were to make a decisive break now,
you could still preserve your family's integrity
and maintain your reputation."
This meant he wanted him to die during Yùlín's crisis.
"I am currently eating porridge,
I don't have time for this matter."
When he was appointed Piàojì Jiāngjūn,
after the Emperor first ascended the throne, Yàn was promoted to Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn.
Dàn,
pronounced tú làn,
also tú lǎn.
Piào,
pronounced pǐ miào.
Qí,
pronounced qí jì.
He said to Sīyuǎn's elder brother, Sīzhēng,
"At the end of Lóngchāng,
Āróng advised me to take my own life;
if I had followed his words,
how could I have achieved what I have today!"
Sīyuǎn quickly replied:
"Regardless of Āróng's view,
it is not too late now."
Among people in the Jìn and Sòng eras,
it was common to refer to one's cousin (son of paternal uncle) as Āróng;
this continued into the Táng dynasty.
For example, Dù Fǔ's poem on staying up late at his cousin Dù Wèi's home says
"staying up late at Āróng's home,"
which is an example.
Taking an opportune moment, he said to Yàn:
"Current affairs are becoming somewhat different,
Brother, do you not perceive it?
People are generally clumsy at planning for themselves but clever at planning for others."
Yàn did not respond.
After Sīyuǎn withdrew,
Yàn sighed and said:
"There are actually people in the world who advise others to die!"
Ten days later, Yàn was ruined.
The Emperor heard Sīyuǎn's words,
and therefore did not punish him,
instead promoting him to Shìzhōng.
Yàn's maternal cousin, Wèishì Ruǎn Xiàoxù, also knew that Yàn would surely fail.
Wèishì County
belonged to Chénliú in the Hàn dynasty;
during the Eastern Jìn, it was temporarily established in the area of present-day Liùhé County,
belonging to Qínjùn.
The Ruǎn clan was originally from Wèishì,
but at this time they might not have resided in Qínjùn.
Wàidì
refers to a wife's younger brother.
He went into hiding and was not seen.
He once ate some delicious sauce
and, learning it came from Yàn's household,
he spat it out and overturned the rest.
He spat out what he had eaten,
and also overturned what was left.
People were fearful for him,
but Xiàoxù said:
"Being related but not partisan,
what is there to fear?"
He ultimately escaped punishment.
5 In the second month,
on Rénxū,
the Wèi ruler arrived at Tàiyuán.
6 On Jiǎzǐ,
Zuǒ Púshè Xú Xiàosì was appointed Shàngshū Lìng,
replacing Wáng Yàn.
Replacing Yàn's younger brother, Xǔ.
7 On the day Guǐyǒu,
the Wèi ruler arrived at Píngchéng.
He summoned Mù Tài and Lù Ruì's faction for questioning.
Not a single person claimed to have been wronged.
At the time, everyone admired Rènchéng Wáng Chéng's sagacity.
Mù Tài and his close associates were all executed.
Lù Ruì was granted death in prison,
his wife and children were pardoned,
and exiled to Liáoxī as commoners.
Kǎoyì states: Qíshū, Wèilǔ Zhuàn says:
"The false Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn, Héngzhōu Cìshǐ, Jùlùgū Hèlùhún guarded Sānggān.
Hóng's paternal uncle, Píngyáng Wáng Ānshòu, garrisoned Huáizhà,
northwest of Sānggān.
Hún, not being a Chinese official appointed by Hóng,
conspired with the false Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ, Féngyì Gōng Zìlín, and Ānlè Gōngzhǔ Tuòbá Āgānr to establish Ānshòu
and jointly occupy Héběi.
The plan was long delayed and did not succeed.
Ānshòu became afraid
and reported it to Hóng.
Hún and several hundred others were killed,
and Ānshòu was retained as before."
This differs entirely from the names in Wèishū.
Now we follow Wèishū.
Initially,
when the Wèi ruler moved the capital
and changed old customs,
Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ Xīnxīng Gōng Pī was displeased by everything.
The emperor, considering him an elder of the imperial clan,
did not compel him,
but merely guided him with profound principles,
so that he would not have differing views.
He only showed him the general principles of affairs,
and did not repeatedly instruct him.
Yǒu (誘)
is pronounced Yǒu.
While crimson-robed officials filled the seats,
Pī alone wore Hú attire among them.
Later, he gradually adopted caps and sashes,
but was unable to refine his appearance and demeanor.
The emperor also did not force him.
When Crown Prince Xún was about to move from Píngchéng to Luòyáng,
Yuán Lóng and Mù Tài and others secretly conspired to detain Xún,
then raise an army to block the passes,
planning to occupy Xíngběi.
Xíngběi
is the land of Héngzhōu and Shuòzhōu.
The passes
are the two passes, Dōngxíng and Xīxíng, of Yànmén.
Duàn (斷)
is pronounced Dīngguǎn.
Xíng (陘)
is pronounced Xíng.
Lóng and others informed Pī of their plan.
Pī, externally fearing failure,
verbally raised objections,
but inwardly rather approved of it.
When the matter was discovered,
Pī followed the emperor to Píngchéng.
The emperor frequently interrogated Tài and others,
always letting Pī sit and observe.
Officials memorialized that Yuán Yè, Yuán Lóng, and Yuán Chāo's crimes deserved extermination of their clan,
and Pī should be implicated.
The emperor, remembering that Pī had previously received an edict promising him immunity from death,
allowed him to be spared death and become a commoner,
keeping his second wife and two sons
to reside with him in Tàiyuán.
Lóng, Chāo, and their full brother Yǐshēng were killed.
Tóngchǎn (同產)
means brothers by the same mother.
Initially,
Pī and Ruì, along with Púyè Lǐ Chōng and Lǐngjūn Yú Liè, had all received edicts promising immunity from death.
After Ruì was executed,
the emperor sent an edict to Chōng and Liè, saying:
"Ruì's rebellious intentions
were known only to the netherworld;
his violation of the oath was on his part,
and does not concern me.
Since the rebellion is different,
even if I wished to be lenient regarding his other offenses,
how could it be possible?
Nevertheless, I did not forget my previous words,
allowing him to die in a separate residence,
not being granted death at the Héngzhōu Cìshǐ's mansion but dying in prison,
hence called 'separate residence'.
His Nálù were spared.
The Shūgān Shì says: 'I will Nálù you.'
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary says: Ná (拏)
means son.
To spare his Nálù
means Ruì's wife and children were spared death and exiled to Liáoxī.
Ná (拏)
is pronounced Nú.
As the primary instigator of the rebellion,
he deserved death by implication,
but was specifically pardoned to be a commoner.
I originally intended a lifelong relationship, but he abandoned it himself,
going against my wishes and intentions.
How utterly regrettable!
Therefore, I am explaining this separately,
hoping you will not find it strange.
Besides the conspiracy to rebel,
everything is clear as day."
Chōng and Liè both submitted memorials expressing their gratitude.
Sūn Guāng said: The power to establish or abolish ranks and emoluments,
and to grant or deny life and death,
is the great prerogative by which a ruler controls his ministers.
This is what the Zhōulǐ calls the "eight levers" for controlling all ministers.
Yǔ (予)
is read as Yǔ.
Even if one has kin, old friends, talent, ability, merit, nobility, diligence, or is a guest,
if they commit a crime,
they are not directly pardoned;
judgment must be deliberated under the huáihuang and jízhōng (court),
which is what the Zhōulǐ calls the "eight deliberations."
Huáijí (槐棘)
refers to the positions of the Duke and Ministers.
Wángzhì says: When a judgment is reached,
the Grand Minister of Crime hears it under the date tree.
If pardonable, then pardon;
if punishable, then punish;
if deserving death, then execute.
The severity depends on the circumstances,
and leniency or harshness varies with the times.
Thus, the ruler can bestow favor without losing his authority,
and the ministers can be absolved of guilt without becoming overconfident.
However, in Wèi, it was not so.
Meritorious and noble ministers
were often promised immunity from death in advance;
when they became arrogant and committed crimes,
they were then executed.
This is to entice them into death by unreliable decrees.
Among the failures of criminal administration,
none is greater than this!
8 At this time,
many old families from the Dài region
were involved in the conspiracy with Tài and others.
Only Yú Liè
was untainted,
and the emperor therefore valued him even more.
The emperor, considering that the northern chiefs and hostage princes feared the summer heat,
allowed them to pay court in Luòyáng in autumn
and return to their tribes in spring.
People at the time called them
"Yànchén" (Goose Ministers).
This is because geese fly south to avoid the cold
and return north when it becomes warm.
Cháo (朝)
is pronounced Zhíyáo.
9 In the third month,
on the day Jǐyǒu,
the Wèi ruler traveled south to Líshí.
Líshí
was a Hàn county,
part of Xīhé Jùn.
In the Suí dynasty, it became Líshí Jùn;
in the Táng dynasty, it was Shízhōu.
An edict granted pardon.
In summer,
fourth month,
on the day Gēngshēn,
he arrived at Lóngmén and sent envoys to sacrifice to Xià Yǔ.
Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The upper mouth of Lóngmén is in Qū Xiàn, northeast of the Hàn River,
what is called Mèngmén.
The lower mouth of Lóngmén is northwest of Píshì Xiàn in Hédōng,
carved by Dà Yǔ,
hence the sacrifice here.
On the day Guǐhài,
he arrived at Púbǎn and sacrificed to Yú Shùn.
Huángfǔ Mì said: Shùn made Púbǎn his capital,
hence the sacrifice here.
Bǎn (坂)
is pronounced Fǎn.
On the day Xīnwèi,
he arrived at Cháng'ān.
10 After Wèi Crown Prince Xún was deposed,
he somewhat repented his misdeeds.
Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi Lǐ Biāo secretly memorialized that Xún was again conspiring rebellion with his attendants.
The Wèi ruler sent Zhōngshū Shìláng Xíng Luán and Xiányáng Wáng Xǐ with an edict and pepper wine to Héyáng
to grant Xún death,
Pepper has a pungent,
very hot,
and poisonous taste,
especially those with closed mouths.
In the debate concerning Hàn Huánsī Hòu,
Lǐ Xián carried pounded pepper with him.
The emperor boiled two hú of pepper
to kill the descendants of Gāo and Wǔ;
all were this substance.
He was buried at Héyáng.
11 On the day Guǐwèi,
Wèi Dàjiāngjūn Sòng Míng Wáng Liú Chǎng died at Péngchéng
and was buried with exceptional rites.
Shìfǎ says: "Thoughtful and far-sighted is called Míng."
This refers to Chǎng's foresight,
and his resolute defiance of hardship to return to Wèi.
12th day of the fifth month,
on the day of Jǐchǒu,
the Wèi ruler returned east,
floating down the Wèi River into the Yellow River.
On the day of Rénchén,
he sent envoys to sacrifice to King Wén of Zhōu at Fēng and
King Wǔ at Hào.
They were also sacrificed to at the old capital.
Fēng and Hào of Zhōu,
during the Hàn dynasty, were entirely within the Shànglín Park.
使 (shǐ),
read shū lì.
On the day of Gēngshēn,
he returned to Luòyáng.
13th day of the ninth month,
Wèi dispatched 200,000 soldiers from five prefectures: Jì, Dìng, Yíng, Xiāng, and Jì.
In the 8th year of Tàicháng of Wèi Tàizōng,
Jì Prefecture was established at Què'áo City in Jìběi,
governing the commanderies of Jìběi, Píngyuán, Dōngpíng, and Nánqīnghé.
相 (xiàng),
read xī liàng.
濟 (jǐ),
read zǐ lǐ.
14When Mù Tài of Wèi rebelled,
Mù Pí, the Wèi County Duke and Central Secretariat Supervisor, conspired with him.
After the amnesty, the matter came to light,
and his official title and noble rank were stripped, reducing him to a commoner.
Mù Pí's younger brother, Sīkōng Liàng, entrusted the affairs of the directorate to Sīmǎ Mùróng Qì,
and submitted a memorial impeaching himself.
The Wèi ruler issued a gracious edict denying his request;
Liàng persisted in his repeated pleas.
On the day of Guǐhài,
Liàng was permitted to resign his position.
15On the day of Dīngmǎo,
Wèi divided its six armies to determine who would march and who would remain.
16Autumn,
seventh month,
Wèi established Consort Fēng Zhāoyí as Empress.
The Empress wished to raise Crown Prince Kè as her own son;
Kè's mother, Lady Gāo, traveled from Dài to Luòyáng,
but died suddenly in Gòng County.
Consort Fēng Zhāoyí had already slandered and deposed her sister,
and then secretly killed the Crown Prince's mother.
Her heart was indeed like that of an owl or a jackal.
With the Wèi ruler's sagacity,
yet allowing her to occupy the principal position in the inner court,
it would be fortunate if he did not die at her hands another day.
Gòng County,
since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Hénèi Commandery.
During the Jìn and Later Wèi, it belonged to Jí Commandery.
In the Táng dynasty, it was Wèi Prefecture.
Gòngchéng County is its location.
共 (gòng),
sound gōng.
17On the day of Wùchén,
Wèi appointed Mù Liàng as General-in-chief Who Conquers the North, Opener of the Palace with the Rank of the Three Dukes, and Inspector of Jì Prefecture.
18Eighth month,
on the day of Bǐngchén,
Wèi issued an edict to the court and provinces to prepare for war.
They were about to march south.
19On the day of Rénxū,
Wèi enfeoffed Imperial Prince Yú as Prince of Jīngzhào,
Yì as Prince of Qīnghé,
and Huái as Prince of Guǎngpíng.
20They posthumously honored Lady Wáng, the mother of Emperor Jǐng, as Empress Dowager Gōng.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he honored Zhēn, Prince of Shǐ'ān, as Emperor Jǐng.
Using "Emperor" (Huáng) but not "Di" (帝),
followed the Hàn system.
21On the day of Jiǎxū,
Wèi held a military exercise in Huálín Park;
on the day of Gēngchén,
the army departed from Luòyáng.
He appointed Rènchéng Prince Chéng, the Minister of Personnel, to remain and guard the capital;
Rènchéng Prince Chéng only now truly became Minister of Personnel.
守 (shǒu),
read shì yòu.
"Zhōngchéng"
should be written
"Zhōngwèi".
【Chapter: The twelve-line edition correctly writes
"Zhōngwèi";
the Kǒng edition is the same;
Zhāng's collation is the same.】度 (dù),
read tú luò.
He provisionally appointed Péngchéng Prince Xié as General of the Central Army.
Xié declined, saying:
"Using both close and distant relatives is the ancient way.
Who am I alone,
to be repeatedly honored with such appointments!
In the past, Chénsī sought it but was not granted.
During the reign of Emperor Wén of Cáo Wèi,
Chénsī Prince Zhí submitted a memorial requesting to prove himself by attacking Wú and Shǔ,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
How far apart are misfortune and prosperity!
When heaven and earth interact, it is called prosperity (tài);
when heaven and earth do not interact, it is called misfortune (pǐ).
For Chénsī with Emperor Wén of Wèi,
the sentiments of superior and subordinate were not communicated,
hence it was called misfortune.
For Xié, the sentiments between ruler and minister, and between brothers, were without gap,
hence it was called prosperity.
否 (pǐ),
read pí bǐ.
He took Xié's hand and said:
"The two Cáos were jealous of each other's talent and fame.
The two Cáos,
refer to Emperor Wén of Wèi and Chénsī Prince Zhí.
22The Emperor sent Army Commander and Chamber Guard General Hú Sōng to assist Chéng Gōngqī, the Administrator of North Xiāngchéng, in guarding Zhěyáng.
Army Commander Bào Jǔ assisted Huáng Yáoqǐ, the Administrators of West Rǔnán and North Yìyáng Commanderies, in guarding Wǔyīn.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's Qí Zhì states: West Rǔnán belonged to Yōng Prefecture,
North Yìyáng belonged to Yōng Prefecture's Níngmán Directorate.
Since the end of the Sòng dynasty, there were no administrators of "double-headed" commanderies;
they usually governed from one location.
Wǔyīn County,
since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Nányáng Commandery,
and served as the seat of government for the two commanderies of West Rǔnán and North Yìyáng.
23Wèi appointed the Dī chieftain Yáng Língzhēn as Inspector of Nánliáng Prefecture.
Língzhēn brought his entire prefecture to surrender.
Wèi established Liáng Prefecture at Qiúchí,
and Nánliáng Prefecture at Wǔxīng.
帥 (shuài),
read suǒ lèi.
降 (jiàng),
read hù jiāng;
the same below.
He sent his younger brother Póluō Àbúzhēn to lead over 10,000 infantry and cavalry to attack Wèi's Prince Yáng Jíshǐ of Wǔxīng,
killing his two younger brothers Jítóng and Jízhòng.
Jíshǐ, in distress and urgency,
requested to surrender.
Ninth month,
on the day of Dīngyǒu,
the Wèi ruler appointed Lǐ Chóng, the Administrator of Hénán, as Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs in Lǒngyòu,
leading tens of thousands of soldiers to suppress them.
24 Initially,
when Wèi moved to Luòyáng,
Xuē Zhēndù, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, advised the Wèi emperor to first capture Fán and Dèng.
At this time, Wèi's Jīngzhōu administration was still in Lǔyáng.
Fán and Dèng were close to Luòyáng,
so he wished to capture them first to expand the territory.
Prefect Fáng Bóyù defeated them.
This refers to the defeat at Shā'è last year.
擊敗 (jībài, defeated),
read bù mài.
As Nányáng was a small commandery,
(the Wèi emperor's) ambition was surely to annihilate it.
He then led his troops towards Xiāngyáng;
Pénchéng Wáng Xié and other thirty-six armies followed one after another,
with a declared force of a million,
their whistles boiling the earth.
"Whistling lips" (chuīchún) means
biting one's lip with teeth and blowing air,
the sound is like that of an eagle or a hawk.
Those of lesser skill pinch their lips with fingers and blow,
then there is a sound,
called "whistling fingers" (xiàozhǐ).
On the day Xīnchǒu,
the Wèi emperor left his generals to attack Zhěyáng,
and personally led his troops south;
on the day Guǐmǎo,
he reached Wǎn,
and attacked its outer wall by night,
capturing it.
Fáng Bóyù barricaded himself inside the inner city and held out.
The Wèi emperor sent the Palace Secretary Sūn Yánjǐng
(A textual variant states: the Qí Shū writes
"Gōngsūn Yún",
now following the Wèi Shū.)
(who said): "I am now sweeping and uniting the entire realm.
It is not like the former times when we came in winter and left in spring.
Unless something is conquered,
I will ultimately not return north.
Your city stands at the head of my six dragons.
The Yì Jīng says: 'At times riding six dragons to drive across the sky.'
This is the image of a sovereign.
The longest term is one year,
the shortest is one month.
Being enfeoffed or having your head severed,
the matter is within a moment's decision.
You should plan well!
Moreover, you have three crimes,
which I now make known to you: You first served Emperor Wǔ,
and received extraordinary favor,
yet you failed to demonstrate loyalty unto death and fulfill your duty to his enemy.
This is your first crime.
(Emperor Míng exterminated the descendants of Emperor Wǔ,
hence he is called the enemy.)
You harmed my detached force.
This is your second crime.
Now the imperial carriage has personally arrived,
yet you do not bind yourself and surrender to my command.
This is your third crime."
Bóyù sent his army deputy Lè Zhìróu to reply:
"I understand you wish to besiege us,
and are determined to conquer.
As a humble common man,
to be able to resist such great might,
can truly be called finding a place to die!
Your humble subject was chosen by Emperor Wǔ,
how could I forget his kindness!
However, the successor emperor lost virtue,
and the current sovereign grandly inherited the main lineage.
(This means the emperor, from a minor lineage, became the third son of Emperor Gāo,
to inherit the main lineage.)
He also embodies the last decree of Emperor Wǔ.
Therefore, this humble one devotes himself,
not daring to fail.
In the past, when the northern army advanced deeply,
raiding and disturbing the border populace,
I merely urged my officers and soldiers to perform their professional duties.
Judging by this,
I should not be blamed."
At the southeast corner of Wǎnchéng, there was a bridge over a ditch.
The Wèi emperor led his troops across it.
Bóyù sent several brave warriors,
dressed in spotted clothes,
wearing tiger-head hats,
to hide beneath a culvert.
They suddenly rushed out and attacked,
startling both the Wèi emperor and his horse;
he summoned the skilled archer Yuán Língdù to shoot them.
They fell at the sound of the bowstring,
and he was thus saved.
25 Lǐ Chóng cut through the mountains, dividing his forces,
appearing where the Dī did not expect,
attacking them from both inside and out;
all the Dī abandoned Yáng Língzhēn and scattered,
Língzhēn's forces were reduced by more than half.
Chóng advanced and occupied Chìtǔ.
(Wèi Shōu's records state that
Nán Qínzhōu's Wǔjiē Commandery had Chìtǔ County.
The Five Dynasties' records state: Wǔdū Commandery's Fùjīn County,
Later Wèi established Wǔjiē Commandery.)
(Yáng Língzhēn) stationed at Lóngmén,
and personally led a crack force of ten thousand to station at Jiùxiá;
(According to Wèi Shōu's records,
Dōng Yìzhōu's Wǔxìng Commandery had Shímén County.
The Five Dynasties' records state: Wǔdū Jiānglì County,
formerly called Shímén.
Also,
below Qíuchí Mountain, there is Fēilóng Xiá,
named after the Dī chief Yáng Fēilóng who occupied Qíuchí.
Also,
today, twenty lǐ east of Lóngzhōu's Jiāngyóu County, there is Lóngmén Mountain;
also,
one hundred lǐ east of Jiāngyóu County, there is Shímén Garrison.
Wǔxìng
is now Xīngzhōu;
Lóngzhōu is very far from Xīngzhōu,
so the Lóngmén where Yáng Jiàn was stationed must not be that of Jiāngyóu.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù states: northeast of Qíuchí there is Lóngmén Garrison,
this might be it!
Jiùxiá should be southwest of Lóngmén.)
從 (cóng, followed),
read cái yòng.
帥 (shuài, led),
read shuài;
same below.
鷲 (jiù, griffin),
sound jiù.
He felled trees to block the roads;
at the mouth of Jiùxiá,
he gathered rolling stones,
and dropped them from the cliff,
to resist the Wèi troops.
Chóng ordered Supervising General Mùróng Jù to lead five thousand men to enter by another path,
and at night,
attacked Lóngmén,
defeating it.
Chóng himself attacked Jiùxiá;
Língzhēn was repeatedly defeated in battle and fled.
(Chóng) captured his wife and children,
and then conquered Wǔxìng.
Yīn Guǎngzōng, Inspector of Liángzhōu, and Zhèng Yóu, a staff officer, etc., led troops to rescue Língzhēn;
Chóng advanced and attacked,
greatly defeating them,
beheading Yáng Póluó Ābúzhēn,
and capturing Yóu and others alive.
Língzhēn fled back to Hànzhōng.
When the Wèi emperor heard of this,
he rejoiced, saying:
"The one who frees me from worries about the west
is Lǐ Chóng."
He appointed Chóng as Supervisor of All Military Affairs of Liáng and Qín Two Prefectures, and Inspector of Liángzhōu,
to pacify and settle the region.
On the *dìngwèi* day
, the Wèi Lord departed Nányáng
, leaving Grand Commandant Xiányáng-wáng Xǐ and others to attack it.
On the *jǐyǒu* day
, the Wèi Lord arrived at Xīnyě
. The Administrator of Xīnyě, Liú Sījì, refused to surrender and held out.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the *dìngsì* day
, the Wèi army attacked it but could not overcome it.
They built a long siege wall to surround and guard it
, and sent someone to tell those in the city:
"Fáng Bóyù has already surrendered.
Why do you alone wish to be crushed to pieces!"
Sījì sent someone to reply:
"The city still has plenty of soldiers and provisions
, we do not have time to speak with you petty barbarians!"
Hán Xiǎnzōng, the Chief Clerk of the Wèi Right Army Prefecture, led a separate army to garrison Zhěyáng.
The Right Army Prefecture
refers to the Right Army General's Prefecture.
*Jiàng*
is pronounced *liàng*
; the same applies below.
Hú Sōng was assisting in the defense of Zhěyáng at that time.
They defeated them
and beheaded their deputy general Gāo Fǎyuán.
When Xiǎnzōng arrived at Xīnyě
, the Wèi Lord said to him:
"You have defeated the bandits and beheaded a general
, greatly boosting the army's morale.
I am now attacking a strong city
, why do you not prepare a *lùbù*?"
The *History of the Five Dynasties* (Wǔdài Shǐ Zhì) states: whenever the Later Wèi achieved victory in battle
, wishing the world to know
, they would write on silk and erect it on a pole
, naming it *lùbù*.
The Wèi Lord meant that if Xiǎnzōng were to report the *lùbù* to the imperial encampment
, it would enhance the Wèi army's momentum of victory
, and could shake the resolve of those holding out in the city.
"Recently I heard that Zhennán General Wáng Sù captured two or three bandits
and several donkeys and horses
, and all were made into *lùbù*;
when I was at Dōngguān
, I privately often ridiculed it.
Hán Xiǎnzōng, having answered policy questions with a *jiǎ* grade
, was appointed Director of the Imperial Library (Zhùzuò Láng),
hence the mention of being at Dōngguān.
*Guān*
is pronounced *gǔwán*.
*Shěn*
is pronounced *shǐyǐn*;
to smile without altering one's countenance is called *shěn*.
I managed to crush the despicable barbarians,
but with few soldiers and limited strength
, not many were captured or beheaded.
If I were to again boastfully display long pieces of silk
, fabricating achievements
, and emulating such behavior
, my sin would be even greater."
The *Zuo Zhuan* (Zuǒ Zhuàn) says: "To emulate such behavior,
the sin is even greater."
*Yóu*
means to blame,
to err,
a word to emphasize.
*Fù*
is pronounced *fúyòu*.
This merely explains the above.
The Wèi Lord admired his wisdom even more.
The Emperor issued an edict to Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Péi Shúyè to lead troops to relieve Yōngzhōu.
Shúyè reported, saying:
"The northerners do not like long journeys
, they only enjoy looting.
If we invade the barbarian territory
, then the raiders in Sī and Yōng will naturally be divided."
The Emperor followed his advice.
Shúyè led troops to attack Hóngchéng
. This was the Hóng County city of Pèijùn in the Hàn dynasty.
Shīgǔ says: *Hóng*
is pronounced *gòng*.
When Northern and Southern armies contended
, its territory was on the border of Xiàqiū County in Xíapī;
the Táng dynasty re-established it as Hóng County
, belonging to Sìzhōu.
*Hóng*
is now read as *jiàng*.
On the *jiǎxū* day
, the Emperor sent太子中庶子 Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ Xiāo Yǎn and Right Army Sīmǎ Zhāng Jì to relieve Yōngzhōu.
In the eleventh month,
on the *jiǎwǔ* day
, Former Army General Hán Xiùfāng and fifteen other generals surrendered to Wèi.
On the *dìngyǒu* day
, Wèi defeated the Qí army north of the Miǎn River
, and General Wáng Fúbǎo and others were captured by Wèi.
, Yáng Língzhēn was appointed North Qínzhōu Cìshǐ.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The Qí Dī Biography writes
"North Liángzhōu"
, now following the *Qí Shū*.
In the twelfth month,
on the *gēngshēn* day
, the Wèi people attacked and captured it.
Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Cái Hǔ was not on good terms with Fáng Bóyù
, and therefore slowly provided relief,
stationing his army at Fánchéng.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The Qí Wèi Lǔ Biography says
"Jūnkǒu"
, now following Hǔ's Biography.
I believe that Cáo Hǔ's stationing his army at Fánchéng
was not only due to his disagreement with Fáng Bóyù
, but also because he feared the strength of the Wèi army and dared not advance.
On the *dīngchǒu* day
, an imperial edict was issued to send Dùzhī Shàngshū Cuī Huìjǐng to relieve Yōngzhōu
. Cuī Huìjǐng was granted a *jié* (imperial insignia)
, and led a host of twenty thousand men and a thousand cavalry towards Xiāngyáng
, with all the armies of Yōngzhōu placed under his command.
On the *gēngwǔ* day
, the Wèi Lord went south to the Miǎn River;
on the *wùyín* day
, he returned to Xīnyě.
General Wáng Tánfēn
led over ten thousand men to attack the Wèi’s Nánqīngzhōu Huángguō Garrison.
The Wèi records state: In the 7th year of Wǔdìng (549 CE) of Emperor Xiàojìng of Eastern Wèi, Yìtáng Jùn was established,
with its seat at Huángguō Chéng.
Furthermore, according to the Five Dynasties Gazetteer: Haizhōu Huáirén Xiàn,
Liáng established the Northern and Southern Qīng Zhōu.
Eastern Wèi abolished the zhōu [provinces],
and established Yìtáng Jùn and Huáirén Xiàn.
Tán,
pronounced tú hán.
The entire army was annihilated.
Generals Lǔ Kāngzuò and Zhào Gōngzhèng led ten thousand soldiers to invade Wèi’s Tàicāngkǒu.
According to Fù Yǒng’s biography: Tàicāngkǒu was in the territory of Wèi’s Yù Zhōu.
At this time, Wèi established Yù Zhōu in Guǎnglíng Chéng of Rǔnán Xīnxī Xiàn,
facing Qí’s Yìyáng across the Huái River,
so Tàicāngkǒu must have been on the northern bank of the Huái River,
and it got its name because the Wèi people stored grain there.
Kāngzuò and others’ army was south of the Huái River,
Yǒng’s army was north of the Huái River,
separated by over ten lǐ.
Yǒng said:
“Southerners are fond of raiding camps at night,
they will surely place fires at the crossing points of the Huái River to mark the shallows.”
So he divided his troops into two divisions at night,
lying in ambush outside the camp.
He also filled gourds with fire,
and secretly sent men across to the southern bank of the Huái River,
placing them in deep water,
cautioning them:
“When you see fires rising,
light yours also.”
Rán,
same as rán (燃).
Kāngzuò and others indeed led their troops to raid Yǒng’s camp,
and the ambushers attacked them from both sides.
Kāngzuò and others fled towards the Huái River.
Since fires had sprung up everywhere,
they did not know which way to go,
and several thousand were drowned or decapitated.
Gōngzhèng was captured alive,
and Kāngzuò’s body was brought back.
The Inspector of Yù Zhōu, Péi Shūyè, invaded Wèi’s Chǔwáng Garrison.
Péi Shūyè was probably transferred to Yù Zhōu from Xú Zhōu.
Shuǐjīng Zhù (Commentary on the Classic of Waters) states: Tóngyáng Xiàn has Gélíng Chéng,
northeast of the city is the tomb of King Wǔ of Chǔ,
which the people call Chǔwáng Sè Chéng.
Wèi probably established a garrison here,
and thus called it Chǔwáng Garrison.
Yǒng sent one of his trusted aides to Chǔwáng Garrison,
ordering him to fill the outer moat,
and to ambush a thousand warriors outside the city at night.
At dawn, Shūyè and others arrived at the eastern part of the city,
intending to set up a long siege.
Yǒng’s ambushers attacked their rear guard,
defeating them.
Shūyè left his generals and aides to guard the camp,
and personally led several thousand elite troops to rescue them.
Yǒng climbed the gate tower,
and seeing Shūyè heading south for several lǐ,
immediately opened the gates and fiercely attacked,
thoroughly defeating them,
capturing Shūyè’s umbrella, fans, drums, tents, armor, and weapons, over ten thousand items.
Shūyè lost his ground and
fled.
His attendants wanted to pursue him,
Yǒng said:
“My weak troops are less than three thousand,
their elite armor is still strong;
they were not defeated by lack of strength,
but fell into my trap.
Since they cannot ascertain my true strength,
it is enough to make them lose heart.
Capturing these is sufficient,
why pursue them further!”
The Wèi sovereign sent an imperial emissary to appoint Yǒng as Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Rǔnán Tàishǒu,
and enfeoffed him as the Earl of Bèiqiū Xiàn.
Yǒng was brave and strong,
fond of learning and skilled in writing.
The Wèi sovereign often sighed and said:
“Able to defeat rebels on horseback,
able to draft documents off horseback,
only Fù Xiūqī!”
Meaning Yǒng possessed both military prowess
and literary talent.
Fù Yǒng,
courtesy name Xiūqī.
29 Qújiāng Gōng Yáo Xīn was fond of military matters.
The Emperor, as his sons were still young,
relied on Yáo Xīn and his brothers among his close relatives,
and among his outer relatives, he relied on his Empress’s younger brother Xīzhōngláng Chángshǐ Liú Xuān of Péngchéng, and his Inner Consort’s younger brother Tàizǐ Zhānshì Jiāng Shí.
The Emperor’s mother was Empress Jǐng,
who was Shí’s aunt,
hence he is called ‘Inner Consort’s younger brother’.

Jiāng Shí's [Jiāng Shí] mind wavered,
and he asked Xiāo Tǎn Zhī [Xiāo Tǎn Zhī].
Tǎn Zhī [Tǎn Zhī] was then observing mourning for his mother,
but was recalled to serve as Commander of the Imperial Guards.
"Recalled to serve" means
being recalled from amidst the mourning hut and earth-pillow,
and restored to one's position.
(Tǎn Zhī [Tǎn Zhī] said:) "When Emperor Míng [Míng] ascended,
it was already out of sequence,
and the empire has never submitted to this day.
If we do this again,
I fear the four quarters will disintegrate.
I, for my part, dare not speak."
He then returned home to observe mourning.
Xiāo Tǎn Zhī [Xiāo Tǎn Zhī] was steeped in glory and power;
how could he have intended to complete the mourning period!
He merely felt that deposing and establishing an emperor was a major matter,
and he did not want to be involved in its calamity,
so he used this as an excuse to withdraw.
Jiāng Shí [Jiāng Shí] and Jiāng Sì [Jiāng Sì] secretly said to the Minister of Personnel, Xiè Tiǎo [Xiè Tiǎo]:
"The King of Jiāngxià [Jiāngxià] is young.
If by chance he is unable to bear the burden,
how can we afford to depose and establish again!
The King of Shǐ'ān [Shǐ'ān] is older,
and his ascension to the throne would not go against public expectation.
It is not that we seek wealth and honor by this,
it is truly for the security of the state."
政 (zhèng) is the same as 正 (zhèng).
They wanted to draw him in as a partisan,
but Tiǎo [Tiǎo] did not answer.
Shortly after,
Yáo Guāng [Yáo Guāng] appointed Tiǎo [Tiǎo] to concurrently manage the affairs of the Grand Master of Ceremonies.
Tiǎo [Tiǎo] was afraid.
As a minister concurrently holding the post of a high official, the matter itself was not cause for fear;
what he feared was
that he would be seen as having been put in place by Yáo Guāng [Yáo Guāng],
and would suffer his calamity.
His burgeoning courage dared not manifest.
Tiǎo [Tiǎo] also persuaded Liú Xuān [Liú Xuān], saying:
"If Shǐ'ān [Shǐ'ān] suddenly faces south (becomes emperor),
then Liú Fēng [Liú Fēng] and Liú Yàn [Liú Yàn] will occupy your current position,
and they will simply consider you a fickle person."
Yàn [Yàn] was
Yáo Guāng's [Yáo Guāng] Staff Officer for Urban Affairs.
Xuān [Xuān] feigned surprise,
and rushed to inform Yáo Guāng [Yáo Guāng] and Jiāng Shí [Jiāng Shí].
Yáo Guāng [Yáo Guāng] wanted to send Tiǎo [Tiǎo] out as the Administrator of Dōngyáng [Dōngyáng] Commandery.
Tiǎo [Tiǎo] had always looked down on Jiāng Shí [Jiāng Shí].
Xiè Tiǎo [Xiè Tiǎo] slighted Jiāng Shí [Jiāng Shí] due to his family's prestige.
Yáo Guāng [Yáo Guāng] then arrested Tiǎo [Tiǎo] and handed him over to the Grand Judge,
and together with Xiāo Xiàosì [Xiāo Xiàosì], Jiāng Shí [Jiāng Shí], Liú Xuān [Liú Xuān], and others, jointly submitted a memorial
stating: "Tiǎo [Tiǎo] stirred up trouble inside and outside,
falsely slandered the imperial carriage,
secretly discussed palace taboos,
sowed discord among close and worthy officials,
and spoke lightly of court officials."
Tiǎo [Tiǎo] consequently died in prison.
Xuān [Xuān], realizing that if Yáo Guāng [Yáo Guāng] were to be established,
he would lose the尊 (zūn) of being the emperor's maternal uncle,
refused to agree with Jiāng Shí's [Jiāng Shí] proposal.
Therefore, Jiāng Shí [Jiāng Shí] hesitated for a long time and could not decide.
Yáo Guāng [Yáo Guāng] was greatly angered,
and sent his attendant Huáng Tánqìng [Huáng Tánqìng] to assassinate Xuān [Xuān] at Qīngxī [Qīngxī] Bridge.
Tánqìng [Tánqìng], seeing Xuān's [Xuān] numerous retinue,
dared not make a move.
Xuān [Xuān] became aware of this,
and then revealed Jiāng Shí's [Jiāng Shí] plot.
The emperor ordered the arrest of Jiāng Shí [Jiāng Shí] and his brothers.
At that time, Jiāng Sì [Jiāng Sì] was on duty in the inner palace.
Suspecting something amiss,
he sent a messenger to inform Jiāng Shí [Jiāng Shí], saying:
"Liú Xuān [Liú Xuān] seems to have a different plot.
What plan should we make now?"
Jiāng Shí [Jiāng Shí] said:
"We should simply keep quiet and calm the situation."
Soon after, an imperial edict summoned Jiāng Shí [Jiāng Shí] for an audience,
and he was detained in the Central Secretariat.
Previously,
Yuán Wénkuàng [Yuán Wénkuàng] was due to be enfeoffed for his achievement in executing Wáng Jìngzé [Wáng Jìngzé].
The execution of Wáng Jìngzé [Wáng Jìngzé] is mentioned in the previous volume, in the first year of the Yǒngtài [Yǒngtài] era of Emperor Míng [Míng].
At that time, Cuī Gōngzǔ [Cuī Gōngzǔ], for having stabbed and crippled Jìngzé [Jìngzé],
contended with Wénkuàng [Wénkuàng] for the credit.
Jiāng Shí [Jiāng Shí] refused to grant it to him,
which was probably why.
"To take" means
"to kill".
(Wénkuàng [Wénkuàng] said to Jiāng Shí [Jiāng Shí] before killing him:) "Can you still deprive me of my enfeoffment?!"
He and his younger brother Jiāng Sì [Jiāng Sì] both died.
Liú Xuān [Liú Xuān], hearing of Jiāng Shí's [Jiāng Shí] death,
was greatly startled in his sleep,
and stumbled out of his door,
asking his attendants:
"Have the arrests reached us yet?"
After a long while,
his mind settled,
he returned to his seat,
and said with great sorrow:
"If I don't think of Jiāng Shí [Jiāng Shí],
I will only hurt myself!"
Xuān [Xuān] knew that calamity would soon befall him.
From then on, the emperor had no scruples,
became even more unrestrained,
and day and night, with his close attendants, he would beat drums and shout in the rear hall
while playing with horses.
He often went to bed at the fifth watch (around 4 am),
and did not rise until late afternoon.
Officials attending court on fixed days and on the first day of the month for audience:
"朔" (shuò) refers to the first day of each month.
In addition to attending court on the first day of the month, there were also designated days for court attendance within the month,
which were then called "節" (jié).
Sometimes they were dismissed in the dark.
(Because) they appeared at court after bu (late afternoon),
and the emperor again did not come out,
thus they were dismissed in the dark.
He would respond to memorials only after several tens of days in a month,
or sometimes his whereabouts were unknown.
Eunuchs would wrap fish and meat to take home,
along with official documents from the five departments.
Since the Wèi [Wèi] and Jìn [Jìn] dynasties,
there were Six Boards of Ministers.
South of the Yangtze River, there were five boards: Civil Appointments, Rites, Military, Household, and Finance.
Each formed a department,
called the Five Departments of the Ministry of Personnel.
"案" (àn) refers to
official documents;
they were stored as records.
The ministers used yellow slips of paper,
hence they were called "yellow documents."
"致" (zhì) means
"extreme";
(it also means) "to reach the point of happiness."
(The emperor said:) "Jiāng Shí [Jiāng Shí] always forbade me from riding horses.
If that boy were still here,
how could I enjoy this!"
He then asked:
"Who else remains among Jiāng Shí's [Jiāng Shí] relatives?"
The reply was:
"Jiāng Xiáng [Jiāng Xiáng] is now in the ironworks (as a convict)."
The emperor had executed Jiāng Shí [Jiāng Shí] and his brothers;
only Jiāng Xiáng [Jiāng Xiáng] was spared death and assigned to the Eastern Ironworks.
The emperor bestowed death upon Jiāng Xiáng [Jiāng Xiáng].
Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng (始安王遙光) had long harbored ambitions.
He secretly conspired with his younger brother, Jīngzhōu (荊州) Cìshǐ (刺史) Yáoxīn (遙欣), to raise an army and seize the Eastern Palace (東府).
He intended for Yáoxīn (遙欣) to lead his troops swiftly down from Jiānglíng (江陵).
They set a date for the uprising,
but Yáoxīn (遙欣) died of illness.
When Jiāng Shí (江祏) was executed,
the Emperor summoned Yáoguāng (遙光) into the palace hall
and informed him of Shí's (祏) crimes.
Yáoguāng (遙光) was afraid,
fearing that disaster would befall him as well.
"Shěng (省)" here refers to the Zhōngshū Shěng (中書省).
Yáoguāng (遙光) was then the Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令).
So he claimed illness and no longer entered the imperial secretariat (臺).
Returning to the Eastern Palace (東府),
he then claimed illness and no longer entered the imperial city (臺城).
"Hào (號)"
is pronounced hù gāo fān (戶高翻).
Yáoguāng's (遙光) younger brother, Yùzhōu (豫州) Cìshǐ (刺史) Yáochāng (遙昌), died,
and all his retainers (部曲) went over to Yáoguāng (遙光).
When Yáoxīn's (遙欣) coffin was returned
and stopped at the sandbar in front of the Eastern Palace (東府),
a great multitude of people from Jīngzhōu (荊州) came to escort it.
"Qiánzhǔ (前渚)"
is the Qínhuái (秦淮) sandbar.
The Eastern Palace (東府) faced the Qínhuái (秦淮) river.
Fearing Yáoguāng (遙光) felt uneasy,
it was proposed to promote him to Sītú (司徒)
and allow him to return to his residence.
He would be promoted to Sītú (司徒) to elevate his position and prestige,
and then sent back to his residence to recuperate from his illness.
Yáoguāng (遙光) feared he would be killed.
On the *yǐmǎo* (乙卯) day, in the late afternoon,
he gathered the retainers (部曲) from the two prefectures at the east gate of the Eastern Palace (東府).
The "retainers (部曲) from the two prefectures"
refers to those who came from Jīngzhōu (荊州) and Yùzhōu (豫州).
He used "punishing Liú Xuān (劉暄)" as a pretext.
That night,
he sent several hundred men to break into the Eastern Armory (東冶),
release prisoners,
and take weapons (仗) from the Imperial Armory (尚方).
"Zhàng (仗)"
refers to weapons (兵仗).
Yuán Lìshēng (垣歷生) arrived with Xìn (信).
Xiāo Tǎnzhī's (蕭坦之) residence was east of the Eastern Palace (東府) city.
Yáoguāng (遙光) sent men to seize him.
Tǎnzhī (坦之), bare-chested, scaled the wall and fled.
"Lù (露)" means
bare-headed;
"tǎn (袒)" means
bare-chested.
He ran towards the imperial secretariat (臺),
intending to report the matter.
A patrol leader (遊邏主)
was a commander of soldiers patrolling outside the imperial city (臺城).
"Luó (邏)"
is pronounced láng zuǒ fān (郎佐翻).
Seeing Tǎnzhī (坦之) running, bare-headed and bare-chested,
he suspected him of having committed a crime and escaping.
So he arrested him.
Tǎnzhī (坦之) stated that Yáoguāng (遙光) was in revolt,
but the patrol leader did not believe him.
He went to investigate personally,
and knowing it to be true,
he then gave Tǎnzhī (坦之) a horse,
and they went into the imperial secretariat (臺) together.
Yáoguāng (遙光) also tried to seize Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (尚書左僕射) Shěn Wénjì (沈文季) at his residence,
intending to make him Dūdū (都督),
but Wénjì (文季) had already entered the imperial secretariat (臺).
Yuán Lìshēng (垣歷生) persuaded Yáoguāng (遙光) to lead the city's troops to attack the imperial secretariat (臺) that night.
He suggested carting reeds to burn the city gates,
saying,
"Your Grace need only ride in your carriage behind them."
"Yú (轝)" is the same as "yú (輿)."
Yáoguāng (遙光) was hesitant and dared not go out.
As dawn approached,
Yáoguāng (遙光), in military attire, came out to the audience hall (聽事).
He ordered his guards to ascend the wall and bestow rewards.
Lìshēng (歷生) again urged him to send out troops,
but Yáoguāng (遙光) refused,
hoping for a change to occur within the imperial secretariat (臺) itself.
When the sun rose,
the imperial troops (臺軍) gradually arrived.
When the disturbance was first heard in the imperial secretariat (臺),
the populace was in a panic.
Towards dawn,
an edict summoned Xú Xiàosì (徐孝嗣).
When Xiàosì (孝嗣) entered,
the people's hearts were finally settled.
Zuǒ Jiāngjūn (左將軍) Shěn Yuē (沈約) heard of the disturbance.
According to the biography of Shěn Yuē (沈約) in the *Liáng Shū* (梁書),
Yuē (約) was then Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn (左衞將軍).
This omits
the character "wèi (衞)."
Some advised him to wear military attire.
Yuē (約) said,
"The imperial secretariat (臺) is in chaos.
If they see me in military attire,
some might think I am in league with Yáoguāng (遙光)."
So he entered in a scarlet robe.
On the *bǐngchén* (丙辰) day,
an edict granted a partial amnesty for Jiànkāng (建康),
and a general alert was issued both inside and outside the capital.
Xú Xiàosì (徐孝嗣) and others were stationed to guard the palace city.
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) led the imperial troops (臺軍) to attack Yáoguāng (遙光).
Xiàosì (孝嗣) was inwardly apprehensive and fearful.
He sat with Shěn Wénjì (沈文季), both in military attire, atop the Southern Yèmén Gate (南掖門),
wishing to discuss current affairs with him.
Wénjì (文季) always diverted the conversation with other topics,
and thus he never managed to bring it up.
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) was encamped at Xiānggōng Sì (湘宮寺).
Xiānggōng Sì (湘gōng Sì)
was built by Sòng Míngdì (宋明帝).
The six gates of the outer wall of the imperial city (臺城) were merely brushwood gates,
without outer ramparts.
The Eastern Palace (東府) was east of the imperial city (臺城),
so Xīngshèng (興盛) was ordered to encamp at the Eastern Brushwood Gate (東籬門) to attack Yáoguāng (遙光).
According to the biography of Cáo Hǔ (曹虎): the Great Bridge (大橋)
was the bridge over Qīngxī (青溪).
Three sides of the Sītú Fǔ (司徒府) were set on fire.
During the Yuánjiā (元嘉) reign of the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng (彭城王義康) served as Sītú (司徒).
He moved his residence to the Eastern Palace (東府),
and a Sītú Fǔ (司徒府) was built next to the Eastern Palace (東府).
The imperial troops (臺軍) suffered repeated defeats,
and their military commander Sāng Tiān'ài (桑天愛) was killed.
When Yáoguāng (遙光) raised his army,
he consulted his Cānzhì Yì Cānjūn (諮議參軍) Xiāo Chàng (蕭暢).
Chàng (暢) sternly refused to comply.
On the *wùwǔ* (戊午) day,
Chàng (暢) and Fǔjūn Chángshǐ (撫軍長史) Shěn Zhāolüè (沈昭略) secretly exited through the South Gate,
went to the imperial secretariat (臺) and surrendered,
which greatly disheartened the morale
of the Eastern Palace (東府) troops.
"Jǔ (沮)"
is pronounced zài lǚ fān (在呂翻).
Chàng (暢) was the younger brother of Yǎnzhī (衍之);
Zhāolüè (昭略)
was the nephew of Wénjì (文季).
On the *jǐwèi* (己未) day,
Yuán Lìshēng (垣歷生) sallied forth from the South Gate to fight,
then abandoned his spear and surrendered to Cáo Hǔ (曹虎).
Hǔ (虎) ordered him to be beheaded.
Yáoguāng (遙光) was greatly enraged,
leaping up from his bed.
He ordered Lìshēng's (歷生) son to be killed.
That evening,
the imperial troops (臺軍) used fire arrows to burn the northeast corner tower.
By night,
the city wall collapsed. Yáoguāng (遙光) returned to his small study tent,
dressed in robes and a cap, and sat,
holding a candle to illuminate himself.
He ordered his men to resist,
but the study's doors were all heavily bolted,
and his左右 (aides) all scattered, climbing over the roof.
The imperial military commanders (臺軍主) Liú Guóbǎo (劉國寶) and others were the first to enter.
Yáoguāng (遙光) heard the outside troops approaching,
extinguished the candle, and crawled under the bed.
The soldiers forced open the doors and entered,
dragged him out in the darkness,
and beheaded him.
The imperial troops (臺軍) entered the city,
burning almost all the houses.
Liú Fēng (劉渢) fled back home
and was killed by someone.
Pān Shào (潘紹), a general from Jīngzhōu (荊州), heard of Yáoguāng's (遙光) rebellion
and plotted to join him.
He intended to respond from Jiānglíng (江陵).
"Jiàng (將)"
is pronounced jí liàng fān (即亮翻).
At that time, Nánkāng Wáng Bǎoróng (南康王寶融), as Xī Zhōngláng Jiāng (西中郎將), was garrisoned in Jiānglíng (江陵),
with Xiàhóu Xiáng (夏侯詳) as Sīmǎ (司馬).
"Xià (夏)"
is pronounced hù yǎ fān (戶雅翻).
So Pān Shào (潘紹) was beheaded,
and the prefecture and commandery were pacified.
"Zhōu (州)" refers to Jīngzhōu (荊州);
"fǔ (府)" refers to the Xī Zhōngláng Fǔ (西中郎府).
On the *jǐsì* (己巳) day,
Xú Xiàosì (徐孝嗣) was made Sīkōng (司空);
Shěn Wénjì (沈文季) was given the title Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn (鎮軍將軍),
while his positions of Shìzhōng (侍中) and Púyè (僕射) remained as before.
Shěn Wénjì (沈文季) was given the title of Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn (鎮軍將軍),
and his original official positions remained unchanged.
His position as Yòu Jiāngjūn (右將軍) remained as before.
At the beginning of the Emperor's reign,
Tǎnzhī (坦之) was Yòu Jiāngjūn (右將軍).
After Yáoguāng (遙光) was suppressed,
he was made Yòu Púyè (右僕射) and Dānyáng Yǐn (丹楊尹),
but his military title of Yòu Jiāngjūn (右將軍) remained the same.
Cáo Hǔ (曹虎) was made Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) and Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn (右衞將軍).
All were rewarded for their meritorious service in suppressing Shǐ'ān (始安).
18. Shěn Líng (沈陵), the Inspector of Southern Xúzhōu (徐州) under the Northern Wèi (魏), surrendered.
Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖) of Wèi (魏) established Southern Xúzhōu (徐州) at Sùyù (宿豫).
Upon his surrender,
his household registered in Jiāngfān (江翻).
He was a cousin of Wénjì (文季).
Shěn Wénxiù (沈文秀) served the Sòng (宋) as the Administrator of Dōngyáng (東陽),
and in the fifth year of Tàishǐ (泰始) of Emperor Míng (明), he perished under Wèi (魏).
Wénxiù (文秀)
was a close cousin of Wénjì (文季);
Líng's (陵) entry into Wèi (魏)
must have been around this time.
All matters of the government were decided by the Chief Clerk Lú Yuān (盧淵).
Yuān (淵) knew that Líng (陵) was about to rebel,
and ordered the various cities to secretly prepare for it;
敕 (chì)
means to warn or instruct.
The Wèi (魏) court did not listen.
Líng (陵) then killed his generals and subordinates,
and led the populace of Sùyù (宿豫) to defect.
The various garrisons along the Huái (淮) River were saved because of their preparations.
Líng (陵) had been on the frontier for years,
secretly forming connections with the local gentry of the border prefectures.
After Líng (陵) rebelled,
many commanderies and counties captured and sent in Líng's (陵) partisans,
but Yuān (淵) consoled and pardoned them all,
only assigning guilt to Líng (陵) himself,
whereupon the people's hearts were set at ease.
If guilt were to extend to relatives and associates,
then the gentry along the border would fear punishment,
and would certainly lead each other to flee south.
Therefore, all were pardoned to reassure those with wavering loyalties.
19. In the intercalary month,
on the day of Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
Jiānglíng Gōng (江陵公) Bǎolǎn (寶覽) was enfeoffed as Shǐ'ān Wáng (始安王),
to continue the line of Jìng Wáng (靖王).
This was because Yáoguāng (遙光) had been executed, and Jìng Wáng (靖王) had no heir.
Shǐ'ān Zhēn Wáng (始安貞王) Dàoshēng's (道生) eldest son Fèng (鳳) had died during the Sòng (宋) era.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ (建武) of Emperor Míng (明),
he was posthumously honored as Shǐ'ān Jìng Wáng (始安靖王).
Yáoguāng (遙光)
was the son of Jìng Wáng (靖王).
20. Shěn Líng (沈陵) was appointed Inspector of Northern Xúzhōu (徐州).
The Southern Xúzhōu (徐州) of Qí (齊) was administered from Jīngkǒu (京口),
and Northern Xúzhōu (徐州) from Zhōnglí (鍾離).
Now Shěn Líng (沈陵) had surrendered from Wèi's (魏) Southern Xúzhōu (徐州),
and using his existing position,
it was renamed Northern Xú (徐).
21. After Jiāng Shí (江祏) and others were defeated,
the emperor's close attendants, the "sword-bearers" and "order-receivers,"
all wielded power arbitrarily.
People at the time called them
"Dāochì" (刀敕), or "Sword and Edict."
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) was stubborn and domineering,
and the emperor's favorites feared and detested him.
More than twenty days after Yáoguāng's (遙光) death,
the emperor dispatched Yánmíng (延明) Commander Huáng Wénjì (黃文濟) with troops to surround Tǎnzhī's (坦之) residence
and kill him.
Yánmíng Zhǔshuài (延明主帥)
likely refers to the Commander of Yánmíng (延明) Palace.
狠 (hěn)
is pronounced hù kěn fān.
嬖 (bì)
is pronounced bēi yì fān,
also bó jì fān.
帥 (shuài)
is pronounced suǒ lèi fān.
將 (jiàng)
is pronounced jí liàng fān;
the same below.
Tǎnzhī's (坦之) paternal cousin Yìzōng (翼宗) was the Administrator of Hǎilíng (海陵).
Shěn Yuē's (沈約) *Jìnshū* (晉書) states: Emperor Ān (安) of Jìn (晉) divided Guǎnglíng (廣陵) to establish Hǎilíng (海陵) Commandery.
Present-day Tàizhōu (泰州) is that area.
從 (cóng)
is pronounced cái yòng fān.
守 (shǒu)
is pronounced shì yòu fān.
He had received the appointment for Hǎilíng (海陵) but had not yet departed.

The Grand Administrator of Wèixìng, Péi Shīrén, and the Grand Administrator of Qíxìng, Yán Sēngdōu, both refused Yǎn's command,
and raised troops to attack Xiāngyáng.
Wěi and Dàn dispatched troops to intercept them at Shǐpíng,
and decisively defeated them.
The eastern boundary of Wèixìng Jùn, Yúnhxiāng and Xī counties, were detached to form Qíxìng Jùn.
Shěn Yuē says: On the left bank of the Jiāng, Shǐpíng Jùn was temporarily established,
with its seat at Wǔdāng.
The Wǔdài Zhì says: Wǔdāng Xiàn in Xīyáng Jùn
originally had Shǐpíng Jùn temporarily established there,
and Qíxìng Jùn was also established there.
Thus, both commanderies were established within the present-day Jūnghōu territory.
Sòng Bái says: In the seventh year of Yǒngmíng of Qí, Qíxìng Jùn was established in Yúnhxiāng Xiàn, Jūnghōu.
Shǒu,
read as Shì Yòu.
3 Wèi Xiányáng Wáng Xī was appointed Shàngxiàng.
Xī, as Tàiwèi, assisted in governance,
holding a position above all other officials,
hence called Shàngxiàng.
He was arrogant, extravagant, greedy, and licentious,
committing many illegal acts,
which the Wèi ruler greatly disliked.
Xī sent a servant to Yu Liè, the Commander of the Imperial Guards, to request the former imperial guards and tiger-guards
to carry weapons when entering and exiting.
The character "舊" (jiù, old)
is superfluous.
"Carrying weapons when entering and exiting" means
he wished them to carry weapons and guard him every time he entered or exited.
Bēn,
pronounced as Bēn.
"The Son of Heaven is in mourning,
so affairs are entrusted to the prime ministers.
The Commander of the Imperial Guards is only responsible for managing the palace guards;
without an imperial edict, I dare not act against principles for private reasons."
Xī's servant returned dejectedly.
Wǎngrán means
looking dispirited.
Wǎng,
pronounced as Wǎng.
"I am
the emperor's
uncle,
serving as the chief minister.
If I have any needs,"
"needs" means what one desires.
Liè said with a stern expression:
"I am not unaware of the Prince's nobility,
but how can a private servant demand the Son of Heaven's imperial guards!
My head can be taken,
but the imperial guards cannot!"
Xī was enraged,
and appointed Liè as Héngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Liè did not wish to leave the capital,
and firmly declined, but his request was not granted;
he then feigned illness and did not go out.
He stayed in his private residence and did not go out.
Liè's son, Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng Zhōng, commanded the Zhíhé guards.
In Northern Qí, the Left and Right Guards had Zhíhé,
with subordinate officials like Zhūyī Zhíhé, Zhíhé Jiāngjūn, Zhíqǐn, Zhízhāi, Zhíhòu, etc.
Liè had Zhōng speak to the Wèi ruler, saying:
"The various princes are self-indulgent;
their intentions are unpredictable.
It is advisable to dismiss them early
and seize the reins of power yourself."
Běihǎi Wáng Xiáng also secretly reported Xī's faults to the Emperor,
and further stated that Péngchéng Wáng Xié had gained great popular support,
and should not be allowed to assist in governance for long.
The Emperor agreed.
At this time, a Yuè sacrifice was about to be held.
Among the sacrifices to the ancestral temple,
the spring sacrifice is called Yuè.
Yuè,
read as Yú Ruò,
meaning meager.
As spring plants are just beginning to grow,
the sacrifice is still meager.
The Emperor secretly sent Yú Zhōng to tell Liè at night:
"Come in to see me tomorrow morning;
there will be arrangements."
At dawn,
Liè arrived.
The Emperor ordered Liè to lead over sixty Zhíhé guards,
to convey an imperial decree summoning Xī, Xié, and Xiáng,
and escort them to the Emperor's presence.
Xī and others entered to see him at Guāngjí Diàn.
Guāngjí Diàn
was built by Wèi Xiàowén Dì in the nineteenth year of Tàihé
for receiving all officials.
Jiàn,
read as Xián Biàn.
"Although Kè is ignorant,
I unworthily inherited the imperial succession.
Recently, I have been afflicted by illness,
(the Wèi ruler's name was Kè,
he referred to himself by his personal name before his uncles,
showing humility.)
Bǐ,
read as Pí Zhì,
means recently.
Wāng,
read as Wū Guāng,
means weak.
Chèn,
read as Chǒu Rèn,
means illness.
Barely prolonging my life,
three years have passed swiftly.
My uncles have dutifully retired;
I shall now personally manage all affairs.
You may return to your respective government offices;
there will be separate arrangements."
"Return to your government offices" means
to return to the places where they performed their duties in their respective public offices.
"Lately, affairs in the north and south have been pressing,
making it impossible to fully realize my humble aspirations."
"Affairs in the north and south have been pressing" refers to
sending Xié to garrison Zhōngshān in the north,
and to capture Shòuyáng in the south
and then defend it.
Chōng,
means humble,
empty;
Chōngcāo,
means humble aspirations.
"Yet I dared to long violate the former edict."
"Former edict" refers to the dying edict of Gāozǔ,
seen in volume 142, Dōnghūn Hóu, Yǒngyuán first year.
Xié apologized, saying:
"Your Majesty is filial and respectful,
reverently following the former imperial edict,
achieving the virtue of sagacity above,
and fulfilling the aspirations of your humble minister below.
Reflecting on the past and present,
joy and sorrow intermingle deeply."
Wéi,
means to think.
On Gēngxū,
an edict ordered Xié to return to his residence as a prince;
Xī was promoted to Tàibǎo;
his rank was advanced, but his power was taken away.
This laid the groundwork for Xiáng to be charged with the crime of self-indulgence.
He fled
out of Luòyáng city,
and was impeached by the Imperial Censor-in-chief, Zhēn Chēn of Zhōngshān.
An imperial edict severely reprimanded him.
Yú Liè was again appointed Língjūn,
and additionally made Chējì Dàjiāngjūn.
From then on, he served continuously within the Forbidden City,
and was able to participate in all major military and state affairs.
The Wèi zhǔ was then sixteen years old,
unable to personally manage all affairs,
and entrusted them to his attendants.
Thereupon, the favored ministers Rú Hào,
Zhào Jùn wáng Zhòngxìng, Shànggǔ Kòu Měng, Zhào Jùn Zhào Xiū, Nányáng Zhào Yōng, and the maternal relative Gāo Zhào, among others, began to wield power,
and Wèi politics gradually declined.
Zhào Xiū was especially favored,
and within a month,
he was repeatedly promoted to Guānglù Qīng;
each time he was promoted,
the emperor personally went to his residence to host a banquet,
and all the princes, dukes, and officials followed.
This laid the groundwork for the later execution of Zhào Xiū.
The character "從" (cóng)
is read as "cái yòng".
On the day Xīnhài,
the Dōnghūn Hóu performed a sacrifice at the southern suburb
and issued a general amnesty.
On the day Dīngsì,
the Wèi zhǔ received his officials at the Tàijí Qián Diàn,
informing them of his intention to govern personally.
On the day Rénxū,
Xiányáng Wáng Xǐ was appointed to lead the Tàiwèi,
and Guǎnglíng Wáng Yǔ was made Sītú.
The Wèi zhǔ led Yǔ into the inner chambers
and personally conferred the appointment upon him.
Yǔ firmly declined, saying:
"Yànhé was originally unwilling,
but Your Majesty forcibly gave it to him.
Péngchéng Wáng Xié,
whose courtesy name is Yànhé,
his deeds are recorded in the previous volume, last year.
The character "強" (qiáng)
is read as "qí liǎng".
This will surely invite public criticism."
So, he was appointed Sīkōng instead.
In the second month,
on the day Yǐchǒu,
Nánkāng Wáng appointed Guānjūn Zhǎngshǐ Wáng Mào as Jīangzhōu Cìshǐ,
Jìnglín Tàishǒu Cáo Jǐngzōng as Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Shàolíng Wáng Bǎoyōu as Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Jiǎxū,
Wèi issued a great amnesty.
On the day Rénwǔ,
the Dōnghūn Hóu dispatched the Yǔlín troops to attack Yōngzhōu,
and the central and outer armies were put on alert.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
Xiāo Yǎn arrived at Jìnglín,
ordering Wáng Mào and Cáo Jǐngzōng to be the vanguard,
and assigning Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Zhāng Fǎ'ān to guard Jìnglín city.
When Mào and others reached Hànkǒu,
the generals discussed uniting their forces to besiege Yǐng,
and dividing their troops to attack Xīyáng and Wǔchāng.
Yǎn said:
"Hànkǒu is not even a li wide,
the arrow paths crisscross,
meaning that when ships come down from mid-stream,
the enemy shoots them from both banks,
their arrows crisscross.
it serves as a pincer with Yǐngchéng;
if we advance with all our forces,
Sēng Jì will surely cut off our rear,
and it will be too late for regrets.
It is better to send Wáng and Cáo's armies to cross the river,
to merge with the Jīngzhōu army,
to press on Yǐngchéng;
I will personally besiege Lǔshān to open up the Miǎn and Hàn rivers.
Miǎn is Hàn,
one river with two names.
Ānlù was
the state of Yúnzǐ in the Spring and Autumn period,
hence it was called Yúnchéng.
The character "鄖" (yún)
is pronounced "yún".
Dù Yù said: Southeast of Yúndù County in Jiāngxià, there is Yúnchéng.
Liú Xù said: Chángshòu County in Yǐngzhōu
was ancient Jìnglín.
The character "方" (fāng)
means "fú".
The character "舟" (zhōu)
means "boat".
The Shī Jīng says: 'When it is deep,
use rafts and boats.'
The character "泭" (fú)
is pronounced "fú".
With abundant soldiers and sufficient provisions,
why worry that the two cities will not be captured!
The affairs of the world
can be taken while reclining."
"Taken while reclining" means it does not require strenuous battle.
They halted at Jiǔlǐ.
That place was nine li from Yǐngchéng,
hence it was named as such.
The character "帥" (shuài)
is read as "shuài".
Mào and others defeated him,
Guāng Jìng died,
and Chōng held the city.
Jǐngzōng then occupied Shíqiáo Pǔ,
with continuous armies,
reaching down to Jiāhú.
Jiāhú is within the borders of Shèyáng County in Jiāngxià,
its waters flow from north to south into the river,
thirty li from Yǐngchéng.
Jīngzhōu dispatched Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Dèng Yuánqǐ, Jūnzhǔ Wáng Shìxīng, and Tián Ānzhī with several thousand men to rendezvous with the Yōngzhōu troops at Xiàshǒu.
Yǎn built Hànkǒu City to guard Lǔshān,
and ordered Shuǐjūn Zhǔyì Yáng Zhāng Huìshào and others to patrol and block the river,
cutting off communication between Yǐng and Lǔ cities.
Yáng Gōngzé led the forces of Xiāngzhōu to rendezvous at Xiàkǒu.
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu ordered all Jīngzhōu armies to follow Gōngzé's command,
even Xiāo Yǐngdá was subordinate to him.
The Fǔcháo discussed sending someone to manage the affairs of Xiāngzhōu but found it difficult to find the right person.
Nánkāng Wáng opened the Xiàngguó fǔ,
hence it was called Fǔcháo.
The character "朝" (cháo)
is read as "zhí yáo".
"The people of Xiāng soil
are easily stirred and hard to trust;
if military men are used, they will plunder the common people,
if civil officials are used, their authority will not be strong;
if one truly wishes to pacify the entire province
and ensure sufficient food for the army and people,
none is better than this old man."
So Tǎn was appointed Fǔguó Zhǎngshǐ and Chángshā Tàishǒu,
to manage the affairs of Xiāngzhōu.
Tǎn had previously been in Xiāngzhōu,
having many old favors,
and those who came to greet him filled the roads.
According to the biography of Liú Tǎn: he had previously been in Xiāngzhōu.
This was probably during a sojourn.
The character "屬" (zhǔ)
is read as "zhī yù".
Capable officials were selected and dispatched to the ten commanderies.
Xiāngzhōu administered the ten commanderies of Chángshā, Guìyáng, Línglíng, Héngyáng, Yíngyáng, Xiāngdōng, Shàolíng, Shǐxīng, Línhè, and Shǐ'ān.
As a result, provisions were not lacking.
In the third month,
Xiāo Yǎn ordered Dèng Yuánqǐ to advance and occupy Nántáng Xīzhǔ.
Nántáng was south of Yǐngchéng,
blocking the shooting range to the north,
and close to the river islet to the west.
Wáng Shìxīng halted at Qūshuǐ Gùchéng.
Qūshuǐ Gùchéng
was probably the place where officials of the Yǐngfǔ performed lustration rituals,
located east of the city.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
Zhāng Chōng died of illness.
Xiāojì Jiāngjūn Xuē Yuánsì, along with Chōng's son Zī and Zhēnglǔ Zhǎngshǐ, Jiāngxià Nèishǐ Chéng Mào, jointly defended Yǐngchéng.
Zhāng Chōng was promoted from Fǔguó Jiāngjūn to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
with Chéng Mào as Zhǎngshǐ.
The character "驍" (xiāo)
is read as "jiān yáo".
The character "騎" (qí)
is read as "qí jì".
On the *yǐsì* day,
King Nánkāng (南康) ascended the imperial throne in Jiānglíng (江陵).
*Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The Chronicle of Dōnghūn (東昏) says:
"On the *dīngwèi* day,
King Nánkāng, whose personal name was [蕭寶融] (Xiāo Bǎoróng), ascended the imperial throne."
This was probably the day when Jiànkāng (建康) first heard of it.
Now, we follow the Chronicle of Emperor Hé (和帝) and the Chronicle of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng (梁武帝).
A general amnesty was declared,
and the reign era was changed to Zhōngxīng Yuánnián (中興元年).
The city gates of the prefectures and commanderies were all modeled after the Jiànkāng Palace.
Five departments of the Department of State Affairs were established.
The Grand Administrator of Nánjùn (南郡) was appointed as Yin (尹).
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu (蕭穎冑) was appointed as Shàngshūlìng (尚書令).
Xiāo Yǎn (蕭衍) was appointed as Zuǒpúyè (左僕射).
King Jìn'ān (晉安) Bǎoyì (寶義) was appointed as Sīkōng (司空).
King Lúlíng (廬陵) Bǎoyuán (寶源) was appointed as Chējì Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
King Jiàn'ān (建安) Bǎoyín (寶寅) was appointed as Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (徐州刺史).
Bǎoyì, Bǎoyuán, and Bǎoyín were all in Jiànkāng,
and these appointments were merely honorary.
Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍) Xiāo Wěi (蕭偉) was appointed as Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ (雍州刺史).
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
an imperial edict enfeoffed the commoner Bǎojuàn (寶卷) as King Fúlíng (涪陵).
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Shàngshūlìng Xiāo Yǐngzhòu was appointed acting Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史).
Xiāo Yǎn was given the added title of Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn (征東大將軍) and Dūdū Zhēngtǎo Zhūjūnsì (都督征討諸軍事),
and granted the yellow *yuè* (axe).
At this time, Yǎn was stationed at Yángkǒu (楊口).
Emperor Hé dispatched Yùshǐzhōngchéng (御史中丞) Zōng Jué (宗夬) to comfort the army.
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) Yǔ Yù (庾域) of Xīnyě (新野) hinted to Jué, saying:
"The yellow *yuè* has not yet been conferred,
so he cannot command the marquises and counts."
When King Wǔ (武) attacked Zhòu (紂),
all the feudal lords gathered.
Upon reaching Mùyě (牧野),
the king held the yellow *yuè* in his left hand,
and a white *máo* (banner) in his right hand to signal.
In later generations, from Wèi Wǔ (魏武) downwards,
the yellow *yuè* was typically conferred.
Kǒng Ānguó (孔安國) said: The yellow *yuè*
is an axe adorned with gold.
*Shuài* (帥),
is read as *lǜ* (率);
the same applies below.
Jiānglíng was in the west,
hence it was called Xītái (西臺).
Xuē Yuánsì (薛元嗣) sent his army commander Shěn Nándāng (沈難當) to lead several thousand light boats, crossing the current to engage in battle.
Zhāng Huìshào (張惠紹) and others attacked and captured them.
To cross a river by cutting across the current is called *luàn* (亂).
The *Shī* (詩) says: "Crossing the Wèi (渭) makes *luàn*."
pronounced *gē*.
On the *guǐchǒu* day,
the Dōnghūn Hóu (東昏侯) appointed Chén Bózhī (陳伯之), the Cìshǐ of Yùzhōu (豫州), as Cìshǐ of Jiāngzhōu (江州), granted him *jié* (節), and made him Dūdū Qiánfēng Zhūjūnsì (都督前鋒諸軍事),
to attack Jīng (荊) and Yōng (雍) in the west.
In the summer,
in the fourth month,
Xiāo Yǎn advanced from Miǎn (沔).
He ordered Wáng Mào (王茂), Xiāo Yǐngdá (蕭穎達), and others to advance and press upon Yǐngchéng (郢城);
Xuē Yuánsì did not dare to sally forth.
He dared not go out to battle.
Yǎn did not permit it (the attack).
Yǎn wanted to prolong the engagement to exhaust the strength of Yǐng (郢) and Lǔ (魯) cities.
The Wèi (魏) King Huì (惠) of Guǎnglíng (廣陵), Yǔ (羽), had an affair with the wife of Yuánwàiláng (員外郎) Féng Jùnxìng (馮俊興).
He went there at night, was attacked by Jùnxìng, and hid it.
In the fifth month,
on the *rénzǐ* day,
he died.
When the Wèi ruler (魏主) began to personally manage state affairs,
his favorites and cronies usurped power.
Dukes and princes rarely gained an audience.
Qí (齊)
Marshal Liú Xiǎogǒu (劉小苟) repeatedly told Xǐ (禧) that
he heard people close to the Son of Heaven say they wanted to execute Xǐ.
Xǐ became even more afraid.
So, he plotted rebellion with his elder brother, Jǐshì Huángménshìláng (給事黃門侍郎) Lǐ Bóshàng (李伯尚), and the Di (氐) kings Yáng Jíshǐ (楊集始), Yáng Língyòu (楊靈祐), Qǐfú Mǎjū (乞伏馬居), and others.
It happened that the emperor went hunting in Běimáng (北邙).
Xǐ and his associates gathered in a small house west of the city,
intending to raise troops and attack the emperor.
He sent his eldest son, Tōng (通), to secretly enter Hénèi (河內) and raise troops in coordination.
Qǐfú Mǎjū persuaded Xǐ:
"Return to Luòchéng (洛城),
muster the troops, close the gates, and the Son of Heaven will surely flee north to Sānggān (桑乾)
— meaning to return north to Píngchéng (平城).
Píngchéng was the former capital of Wèi.
*Gān* (乾)
is pronounced *gān*.
You will be the Son of Heaven of Hénán (河南)."
The mood of the crowd was indecisive and not unified.
Xǐ's heart softened further.
From dawn until dusk,
he hesitated and could not make a decision,
so they agreed not to reveal their plans and dispersed.
After Yáng Jíshǐ left,
he immediately galloped to Běimáng and reported it.
Zhíqǐn (直寢) Fú Chéngzǔ (苻承祖) and Xuē Wéisūn (薛魏孫) were involved in Xǐ's plot.
At this time,
the eunuch Fú Chéngzǔ, favored by Empress Dowager Féng (馮), was already dead;
this was another Fú Chéngzǔ.
In the ninth year of Tàihé (太和) of Emperor Xiàowén (孝文) of Later Wèi,
the Zhíqǐn of the Hòuzhāi (後齋) was first established.
The emperor was sleeping in the shade of a stupa.
Wéisūn intended to assassinate the emperor.
Chéngzǔ said:
"I have heard that those who kill the Son of Heaven will suffer from leprosy."
Wéisūn then stopped.
Soon after, the emperor awoke,
and Jíshǐ also arrived.
All of the emperor's attendants had gone out to hunt,
and there were few guards.
In the emergency, he did not know what to do.
Zuǒzhōnglángjiāng (左中郎將) Yú Zhōng (于忠) said:
"My father, the Commander of the Army, remains to guard the capital city.
I expect that defenses are prepared,
and there is no need to worry."
The emperor sent Zhōng to ride quickly and observe.
Yú Liè (于烈) had already dispatched troops and was on strict alert.
He had Zhōng return and report, saying:
"Although I am old,
my heart and strength can still be used.
These reckless people
are not worth worrying about.
I wish Your Majesty would clear the imperial road and return slowly,
to pacify the public's expectations."
The emperor was very pleased,
and returned to the palace from Huálínyuán (華林園).
Huálínyuán was the Fānglínyuán (芳林園) built by Emperor Míng of Wèi.
Later, to avoid the taboo of King Fāng (芳) of Qí (齊),
it was renamed Huálínyuán.
*Huán* (還),
is pronounced *xuán* (宣),
and also as written.
"You indeed satisfy one's expectations!"
Xǐ did not know the matter had been exposed.
He stayed with his concubines and attendants at Hóngchí Biéshù.
Hóngchí was the Hóngchí of the Hàn dynasty,
located twenty *lǐ* east of Luòyáng.
A field-dwelling was called a *shù* (別墅),
which people today call a *biéyè* (別業).
Since the Jìn dynasty,
it was common to build ponds and pavilions
and enjoy excursions within them.
*Shù*,
read as Chéng Yǔ Fān.
It is said that he was inspecting the harvest.
Xiǎogǒu reached Běimáng
and had already encountered soldiers.
Surprised by Xiǎogǒu’s red clothing,
they wanted to kill him.
Trapped and pressed, Xiǎogǒu
said he wanted to report a rebellion.
They then let him go. Someone said to Xǐ:
“Your Highness has gathered a multitude to plan affairs,
but then stopped when your intentions were revealed.”
This means that his intentions had already been discovered, and he stopped.
*Jiàn* (見),
read as Xián Biàn Fān.
“How can you be so relaxed tonight!”
Xǐ said:
“I have this body,
and I should know to cherish it myself;
why wait for others to tell me!”
Someone else said:
“Your Highness’s eldest son has already crossed the river.
Neither of you knows of the other’s situation;
isn’t this concerning!”
Xǐ said:
“I have already sent someone to pursue him,
and he should be returning by now, I reckon.”
At that time, Tōng had already entered Hénèi,
arrayed weapons,
and released prisoners.
Yú Liè sent the Director of the Palace Gate, Shúsūn Hóu, with three hundred imperial guards to apprehend Xǐ.
When Xǐ heard of this,
he fled southeast from Hóngchí.
With only a few servants,
he crossed the Luò River
and reached Bǎigǔwù.
The pursuing soldiers arrived,
captured him,
and sent him to Huálín Dūtíng.
Huálín Dūtíng was likely outside the gate of Huálín Yuán.
On the *rénxū* day,
he was granted death at his private residence.
More than ten co-conspirators were executed.
All his sons were removed from the household register,
and were barely given assets and slaves.
The rest of the family property was entirely distributed to the families of Gāo Zhào and Zhào Xiū.
The remainder was bestowed upon inner and outer officials,
extending even to those outside the official ranks.
