is read as "shuài" (率).
General of Auxiliary State Huī garrisoned Pòdūn,
and his younger cousin, General of Ning朔 Jǐng, garrisoned Guǎnglíng.
Jǐng's original name was Bǐng (昺).
Lǐ Yánshòu, when writing the Nán Shǐ,
to avoid the taboos of the Táng imperial family,
changed Bǐng (昺) to Jǐng (景).
The Tōngjiàn followed this.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Bǐngshēn,
Wèi appointed Grand General of Agile Cavalry Mù Liàng as Sīkōng.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
Prince Běihǎi Xiáng was appointed Tàifù,
and concurrently held the position of Sītú.
Initially,
Xiáng wanted to seize the Sītú position from Prince Péngchéng Xié,
so he slandered and demoted him.
Afterward, fearing public criticism,
he only held the position of Grand General.
It was not until this point that he assumed the office.
Xiáng was noble and prosperous, very prominent.
Grand Craftsman Wáng Yù often acceded to Xiáng's wishes,
privately supplying him with government property.
Lǐ Yánshòu said: Wáng Yù was originally from Fēngyì, Lǐ Rùnzhèn Qiāng.
His ancestors were a powerful clan among the Qiāng.
They called themselves Wáng,
later changing to the Qián'ěr clan.
During the reign of Wèi Xuānwǔ,
they changed back to Wáng.
He was castrated for an offense,
and gradually promoted to Minister of Personnel,
ennobled as Duke of Dàngchāng.
"Your Highness,"
[he said,] "is the Duke of Zhōu for the state,
acting as Āhéng to the royal house.
Āhéng
refers to being like Yī Yǐn.
Zhèng Xuán said: 'Ā' (阿)
means 'to rely on';
'Héng' (衡)
means 'to balance'.
Yī Yǐn was relied upon by Tāng to achieve balance,
hence it became an official title.
You should naturally observe the imperial will.
'Guān zhǐ' (關旨)
means to observe the imperial will.
You are harming the public for private gain!"
Wáng Yù was already apprehensive,
and Xiáng also felt ashamed and apologized.
Zhōng was often resented by Xiáng for his straightforward honesty.
Xiáng once cursed Zhōng, saying:
"I worry that I will see you die first,
I don't worry about you seeing me die!"
Zhōng replied:
"Life in this world
has its own predetermined fate.
If I am destined to die by Your Highness's hand,
avoiding it will not save me.
If not,
Your Highness cannot kill me!"
For his achievement in quelling Prince Xiányáng Xǐ, Zhōng
was enfeoffed as Duke of Wèijùn,
promoted to Palace Attendant,
and concurrently General of the Palace Guard.
Taking advantage of Zhōng's memorial to decline the honor, Xiáng
secretly advised the Wèi ruler to appoint Zhōng as a high-ranking minister,
to remove him from his positions as Palace Attendant and General of the Palace Guard,
which kept him by the emperor's side.
The Palace Attendant and General of the Palace Guard were positions always at the emperor's side.
Thereupon, an edict was issued to revoke his enfeoffment,
and he was honorably promoted to Minister of the Grand Treasury.
Xiáng was able to use this stratagem to distance Zhōng,
but he did not know that Gāo Zhào had already gained control behind his back.
Bādōng Xiànwǔ Gōng Xiāo Yǐngzhòu, seeing that Xiāo Guī and Cài Dàogōng were deadlocked,
became distressed and fell ill.
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu, seeing that Xiāo Yǎn's eastern campaign was
victorious wherever it went,
while he himself was assisting Nánkāng in Jiānglíng,
was unable to control Xiāo Guī nearby.
With no means to subdue the ambitions of the cunning heroes externally, and with an internal enemy at his side,
this was why he became distressed and fell ill.
"Guī" (璝)
is pronounced as "gǔ huí fān" (古回翻).
On the day Rénwǔ,
he died.
Xiàhóu Xiáng kept it a secret,
had someone imitate his handwriting to forge commands,
and secretly reported to Xiāo Yǎn.
Yǎn also kept it a secret.
Xiáng conscripted troops from Yōngzhōu,
and Xiāo Wěi dispatched Xiāo Dàn to lead troops to assist him.
Guī and others, hearing that Jiànkāng was in danger,
became fearful and dispersed.
Guī and Lǔ Xiūliè both surrendered.
Then Yǐngzhòu's death was announced,
and he was posthumously granted Attendant, Chancellor.
Thereupon, all hopes turned to Yǎn.
Xiàhóu Xiáng requested to participate in military and state affairs with Xiāo Dàn.
An edict appointed Xiáng as Attendant, Right Executive Assistant of the Department of State Affairs,
and soon after, he was made Bearer of Credentials, General Fǔjūn, and Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Xiáng firmly yielded the position to Dàn.
So Dàn was made Acting Governor of Jīngzhōu and military administrator of the province.
Wèi rebuilt the Round Mound (圜丘) on the south bank of the Yī River.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ (495) of Qí Míngdì,
Wèi Xiàowén had established the Round Mound on Wěisù Mountain.
Now it was changed.
The Shuǐ Jīng says: The Yī River originates from Xúnqú Mountain in the west of Nányáng County,
flows northeast past Lùhún Xīnchéng County,
then northeast past Yīquè,
and then northeast to the south of Luòyáng County, turning north to flow into the Luò River.
Wèi evidently established the Round Mound to the south of Luòyáng,
and to the north of the Yī River.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
sacrifices were first offered there.
Wèi General Zhennán Yuán Yīng submitted a memorial, saying:
"Xiāo Bǎojuǎn is becoming increasingly wild and unrestrained,
harming the innocent.
His Governor of Yōngzhōu, Xiāo Yǎn, is campaigning eastward to Mòlíng,
sweeping the land and raising an army,
advancing downstream.
There is only an isolated city left,
with no further strong defenses.
This refers to Xiāngyáng being empty.
This is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.
If we do not seize this,
what shall we wait for?
I beg to personally lead 30,000 infantry and cavalry,
heading directly to Miǎnyīn.
Xiāngyáng is south of the Miǎn River.
South of the water is 'yīn'.
'Shuài' (帥)
is read as 'shuài' (率).
We will cut off the path of the Black Water.
The dim-witted and tyrannical ruler and his ministers are devouring each other.
We are in the upper reaches,
our prestige shaking near and far.
[We can] drive south,
advancing to capture Jiānglíng,
then the land of the Three Chǔs can be taken in one morning.
Grand Historian said: There are three Chǔs: the customs from Huái, Pèi, Chén, Rǔnán, Nánjùn,
this is Western Chǔ;
east of Péngchéng,
Dōnghǎi, Wú, Guǎnglíng,
this is Eastern Chǔ;
Héngshān, Jiǔjiāng, Jiāngnán, Yùzhāng, Chángshā,
this is Southern Chǔ.
If we take Jīng and Xiāng,
then the route from Mín and Shǔ to Jiànkāng will also be cut off.
Wèi Yángzhōu governed Shòuyáng,
Xúzhōu governed Péngchéng.
The fish are swimming in the cauldron,
allowing us to unify the writing and vehicles and bring great harmony,
blending heaven and earth into one.
I humbly request Your Majesty to make a decisive decision,
without allowing any doubts or debates.
If this opportunity is missed,
'shuǎng' (爽)
means 'missed'.
The matter will be put aside and not reported."
Chēqí Dàjiàngjūn Yuán Huái (源懷) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Xiāo Yǎn (蕭衍) is committing internal aggression,
Bǎo Juàn (寶卷) is isolated and in peril.
The garrisons at Guǎnglíng (廣陵), Huáinán (淮陰), and other places are all watching to see who wins and loses.
This is truly a divinely revealed opportunity,
a time for annexation.
It is advisable to strike simultaneously from east and west,
to achieve a sweeping victory.
If Xiāo Yǎn (蕭衍) succeeds,
and everyone is united,
not only will future plans be difficult,
but Yángzhōu (揚州) will also be in danger.
Why so?
Shòuchūn (壽春) is only seven hundred *lǐ* (里) from Jiànkāng (建康).
Wèi (魏) established Yángzhōu (揚州) in Shòuchūn (壽春),
as seen in the previous volume, previous year.
All of this is familiar to them.
If they have no internal or external worries,
and their ruler-subject relationship is settled,
they can embark on boats and use the water,
arriving suddenly and swiftly,
which would not be easy to resist.
Now Bǎo Juàn's (寶卷) capital is on the brink of collapse,
and the border cities have no hope of reinforcement.
To clear the Jiāngbiǎo (江表) region [south of the Yangtze],
now is precisely the day."
The Wèi (魏) ruler then appointed Rènchéng Wáng Chéng (任城王澄) as Dūdū Huáinán Zhū Jūnshì (都督淮南諸軍事), Zhènnán Dàjiàngjūn (鎮南大將軍), Kāifǔ Yītóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (揚州刺史),
and tasked him with planning the strategy;
but in the end, it was not carried out.
If Wèi (魏) had followed the advice of these two officials,
making the Yangtze their border,
the chaos of Hóu Jǐng (侯景) would not have had to wait.
Rèn (任),
pronounced *rén*.
He was the son of Hè (賀).
Yuán Hè (源賀) was the son of Túfà Rǔtán (禿髮傉檀);
upon entering Wèi (魏),
he was granted the surname Yuán (源).
Dōngyùzhōu Cìshǐ Tián Yìzōng (東豫州刺史田益宗) submitted a memorial, saying:
"The Xiāo (蕭) clan is in disorder,
ruler and subjects are in conflict.
The prefectures and garrisons outside the Yangtze [Jiangnan],
are divided into two.
It is said that all regions west of Xīyáng (西陽) have submitted to Xiāo Yǎn (蕭衍),
while those from Lìyáng (歷陽) downwards still belong to Jiànkāng (建康).
This has lasted for a year.
The common people are exhausted by transportation,
and the soldiers are weary from fighting.
Matters are addressed only in the immediate present,
and strength is depleted within their own command,
leaving no time to manage outer prefectures and garrisons,
or regulate various regions.
The vassal cities stand like isolated chess pieces,
existing only in solitude.
If we do not seize this opportunity to sweep them away swiftly,
and clear that barbarian territory,
I fear that future strategies
will not be as easy as this one.
Furthermore, although Shòuchūn (壽春) has been pacified,
three sides are still blocked.
The necessities of defense
truly require prior arrangements.
Yìyáng (義陽) is relatively close to the source of the Huái (淮) River,
a strategic crossing point.
The imperial court's army,
will certainly pass this way.
The *Shuǐjīng* (水經) says: The Huái (淮) River originates from Tāizānshān (胎簪山) in Píngshì (平氏) County, Nányáng (南陽);
it flows northeast past Tóngbóshān (桐柏山),
then east past Yìyáng (義陽) County.
Hence it is said that Yìyáng (義陽) is relatively close to the Huái (淮) River source.
The source of the Huái (淮) is shallow and narrow,
the Wèi (魏) people consider this area a strategic crossing point for their armies.
If there are affairs outside the Huái (淮) [River],
meaning if Xiāo Yǎn (蕭衍) pacifies Jiāngnán (江南),
he will inevitably use troops outside the Huái (淮).
They would array boats along the long Huái (淮);
this refers to the common military strategy in Jiāngnán (江南).
Fàn Cháng (汎長) is [pronounced] *zhī liǎng fān* (知兩翻).
We must proceed from north of Yìyáng (義陽);
this refers to the Wèi (魏) army's route to Shòuchūn (壽春).
Wèi (謂) means Yìyáng (義陽).
The destruction of Yìyáng (義陽),
is indeed the right time now.
I estimate that they would require no more than twelve thousand elite soldiers;
however, the art of warfare
values creating a formidable display.
I request that the forces of the two Jīng (荊) prefectures move west to threaten Suí (隨) and Yōng (雍),
The two Jīng (荊) prefectures refer to the Jīngzhōu (荊州) established by Wèi (魏) in Rángchéng (穰城) and Dōngjīngzhōu (東荊州) in Bǐyáng (沘陽).
Suí (隨) and Yōng (雍) refer to Suí Jùn (隨郡) and Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Yōng (雍),
pronounced *yú yòng fān* (於用翻).
This would prevent reinforcements from the Three Passes;
then the armies of the two Yù (豫) prefectures would advance directly to the South Pass,
confronting Yántóu (延頭).
The two Yù (豫) prefectures refer to the Yùzhōu (豫州) established by Wèi (魏) in Rǔnán (汝南) and Dōngyùzhōu (東豫州) in Xīnxī (新息).
The South Pass refers to Yīnshān Guān (陰山關).
Yántóu (延頭) is in the territory of Ānlù (安陸).
If we advance the army in the last month of winter,
and continue until late spring,
no more than ten *xún* (旬) [a period of ten days],
victory will be certain."
*Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The biography of Yìzōng (益宗) says:
"Shìzōng (世宗) adopted his suggestion,
and sent Yuán Yīng (元英) to attack Yìyáng (義陽)."
According to records, Yīng's (英) attack on Yìyáng (義陽) took place in the eighth month of Jǐngmíng (景明) 4th year.
This memorial states that the ruler and subjects of the Xiāo (蕭) clan were in conflict,
which means it was when Liáng Wǔdì (梁武帝) attacked Dōnghūn (東昏).
Therefore, Yìzōng (益宗) made this proposal now,
but it was carried out in a later year.
"Now Bǎo Juàn's (寶卷) own kin are slaughtering each other,
and the vassal garrisons stand in a tripartite division.
Yìyáng (義陽) is isolated and cut off,
close to the royal territory,
with no internal military provisions,
and no hope of external aid.
This is like a bird about to be burned,
one should not remove the firewood;
a bandit surrendering his head,
how can one delay the axe!
If we lose this opportunity and do not take it,
not only will later endeavors be difficult to plan,
but I also fear it will become an even greater problem.
Now Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Sīmǎ Yuè (豫州刺史司馬悅) has already declared an emergency and is about to depart,
and Dōngyùzhōu Cìshǐ Tián Yìzōng (東豫州刺史田益宗) is garrisoning the Three Passes.
I request that a Jūn Sī (軍司) be dispatched to direct them."
The Wèi (魏) ruler then sent Zhíqǐn Yáng Língyǐn (直寢羊靈引) as Jūn Sī (軍司).
Zhíqǐn (直寢) was
an official title derived from guarding the private chambers of the palace.
Jiànníng Tàishǒu Huáng Tiāncì (建寧太守黃天賜) fought Yìzōng (益宗) at Chìtíng (赤亭).
Sòng (宋) had a Left Commandery of Jiànníng (建寧).
In Xiàowǔ (孝武) Dàmíng (大明) 8th year,
the Left Commandery of Jiànníng (建寧) was abolished and became Jiànníng (建寧) County,
subordinate to Xīyáng (西陽) Commandery.
Later it was restored as a commandery.
*Suí Zhì* (隋志) says: Huángzhōu (黃州) Máchéng (麻城) County,
formerly had Jiànníng (建寧) Commandery established there.
Also,
in Sòng Wéndì (宋文帝) Yuánjiā (元嘉) 25th year,
twenty-eight counties were established for the barbarian peoples of the Yù (豫) region,
Chìtíng (赤亭) being one of them.
*Shuǐjīngzhù* (水經註) says: The Jǔ (舉) River flows south from Húpōchéng (湖陂城),
passing below Chìtíng (赤亭),
hence called Chìtíng Shuǐ (赤亭水).
Among the Five Waters barbarians of Xīyáng (西陽),
Chìtíng (赤亭) was one.
*Kǎoyì* (考異) states: *Wèi Dìjì* (魏帝紀) says:
"In the seventh month, on the *yǐwèi* (乙未) day,
Tián Yìzōng (田益宗) defeated Xiāo Bǎo Juàn's (蕭寶卷) general Huáng Tiāncì (黃天賜) at Chìtíng (赤亭)."
Tián Yìguāng's (田益光) biography says:
"At the beginning of Jǐngmíng (景明) era,
Xiāo Yǎn (蕭衍) sent army commander Wú Zǐyáng (吳子陽) with a multitude to raid the Three Passes.
Yìzōng (益宗) sent Guāngchéng Tàishǒu Méi Yǔzhī (光城太守梅與之) to hold Chángfēngchéng (長風城) and intercept Zǐyáng (子陽),
severely defeating him,
beheading and capturing over a thousand.
However, Wú Zǐyáng (吳子陽) was a general of Dōnghūn (東昏),
not a general of Yǎn (衍).
Furthermore, Yǎn (衍) was then fighting Dōnghūn (東昏),
how could he have time to raid Wèi's (魏) Three Passes!
This must be an error in Yìzōng's (益宗) biography.
"*Yìguāng Zhuàn*" (益光傳)
should be written as
"*Yìzōng Zhuàn*" (益宗傳).
When Cuī Huìjǐng (崔慧景) was pressuring Jiànkāng (建康),
Dōnghūn Hóu (東昏侯) appointed Jiǎng Zǐwén (蔣子文) as Jiǎhuángyuè (假黃鉞), Shǐchíjié (使持節), Xiàngguó (相國), Tàizǎi (太宰), Dàjiàngjūn (大將軍), Lùshàngshū Shì (錄尚書事), Yángzhōu Mù (揚州牧), and Zhōngshān Wáng (鍾山王).
When Yǎn (衍) arrived,
he again honored Zǐwén (子文) as Língdì (靈帝),
bringing his divine image into the rear hall,
and making shamans pray and offer sacrifices for blessings.
When the city was closed,
all military affairs within the city were entrusted to Wáng Zhēnguó (王珍國).
Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Zhāng Jì (兗州刺史張稷) entered to defend the capital,
and Jì (稷) was made Zhēnguó's (珍國) deputy.
Jì (稷) was
the younger brother of [Zhāng] Huái (張懷).
Zhāng Huái (張懷) was then Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫).
At that time, there were still seventy thousand armored soldiers in the city.
Dōnghūn had always been fond of military formations.
He practiced combat with eunuchs, imperial guards, and palace women in front of Huáguāngdiàn,
feigning being wounded
and having people carry him away on a board
for apotropaic purposes.
He often wore military attire and rode horses in and out of the palace hall.
He made armor and helmets of gold and silver,
adorned with peacock and kingfisher feathers.
Kǒng and Cuì
refer to peacocks and kingfishers.
Kǎi
is pronounced Kǔhài.
All was as usual.
Hearing the drums and shouts from outside,
he put on a large red robe
and ascended to the roof of Jǐngyánglóu to observe.
Today, the Fǎbǎosì in Jiànkāng
is the former site of Jǐngyánglóu.
Bèi
is pronounced Píyì.
At first,
Dōnghūn consulted with his attendants,
believing that Chén Xiǎndá was defeated in a single battle,
and Cuī Huìjǐng besieged the city and then fled.
He thought Xiāo Yǎn’s troops would do the same,
so he ordered the Imperial Kitchen to prepare firewood and rice for only a hundred days.
However, after the defeat at Dàhéng,
public sentiment became fearful.
Rú Fǎzhēn and others, fearing that the soldiers and civilians would desert,
closed the city gates and no longer sent out troops.
Soon after, a long siege had been established,
with solid trenches and palisades.
Only then did they sally forth to fight,
but they were repeatedly unsuccessful.
Dōnghūn especially treasured gold and money
and refused to bestow rewards.
Fǎzhēn kowtowed and pleaded for them,
but Dōnghūn said:
"Will the rebels come and take only me?!
Why do you come to me for things?!"
There were several hundred scaling ladders stored in the rear hall.
They were requested for city defenses,
but Dōnghūn wanted to keep them to make a palace
and ultimately did not give them.
intending to use them to clear out the palace after the siege was lifted.
The gold and silver carvings and miscellaneous items
were twice as urgent as usual.
Everyone was resentful and lazy,
putting no effort into their work.
As the outer siege continued for a long time,
everyone in the city wished for an early downfall,
but no one dared to act first.
Rú Fǎzhēn and Méi Chóng'ér said to Dōnghūn:
"The high officials are not paying attention,
causing the siege not to be lifted. They should all be executed."
Wáng Zhēnguó and Zhāng Jì feared disaster.
Zhēnguó secretly sent a trusted associate to offer a clear mirror to Xiāo Yǎn,
and Yǎn returned it with a gold piece.
A mirror is used to reflect objects;
by offering a mirror,
he wanted Yǎn to see his true intentions.
The Dàzhuàn of the Yìjīng says: "If two people are of one heart,
their sharpness can cut through metal."
Therefore, Yǎn used it as his reply.
Duàn
is pronounced Dīngluàn,
Wáng Sù pronounced Dīngguǎn.
Zhāng Qí,
Jì’s trusted confidant,
used Qí to secretly conspire with Jì
to assassinate Dōnghūn together.
Qí led Zhēnguó to Jì at night,
they knelt to finalize the plan,
and Qí personally held the candle.
He also informed Qián Qiáng, the Imperial Secretary of the Rear Chamber.
The Imperial Secretary of the Rear Chamber
was a position established in the Jiāngzuǒ region,
responsible for the rear chambers of the palace.
According to records, the Imperial Secretary of the Rear Chamber
was always in the palace,
as can be seen from the affair of Xú Lóngjū.
On the night of Bǐngyín,
Qiáng secretly ordered someone to open the Yúnlóngmén.
Zhēnguó and Jì led troops into the palace.
Fēng Yǒngzhī, the Imperial Sword Bearer, acted as an inside accomplice.
Fēng Yǒngzhī
was a soldier of the Right Guard,
entrusted by Dōnghūn.
Xìngpǔ states: The Fēng surname
is descended from Fēng, son of Zhèng Qīmù.
Dōnghūn, not yet in a deep sleep,
heard the troops enter
and rushed out the north door,
intending to return to the rear palace,
but the gate was already closed.
The eunuch Huáng Tàipíng wounded his knee with a knife.
He fell to the ground,
and Zhāng Qí cut him down.
Dōnghūn was nineteen years old at the time.
They ordered all officials to sign a memorial,
and wrapped Dōnghūn's head in yellow oiled silk.
Yellow silk treated with oil could resist rain
and was called yellow oiled silk.
Wrapping an object in yellow oiled silk
made the inside visible from the outside,
probably to allow Xiāo Yǎn to inspect it easily.
The Kǎoyì states: The Nánshǐ biography of Wáng Liàng says:
"Zhāng Jì and others discussed establishing Xiāngdōng Sìwáng Bǎozhì.
The commander of the Imperial Guard, Wáng Yíng, said: 'The city has been closed for a long time,
and morale is disintegrating.
The Commander of the Expeditionary Force is nearby,
why not consult him!'"
According to records, Emperor Hé had already been enthroned at that time.
Jì and others knew that Jiànkāng could not be held,
so they assassinated Dōnghūn.
How could they dare to discuss establishing Bǎozhì again!
We follow the Qíjì here.
"Although the cap is old,
how can one put a foot on it!"
Wáng Liàng took tree leaves from the courtyard, kneaded them, and swallowed them,
feigning illness,
and did not sign his name.
Yǎn read the memorial and, seeing no name,
secretly admired him.
Liàng was Yíng's cousin;
Zhì was
Sēngqián's son.
Xiāo Yǎn appointed Wáng Yíng
as Minister of State and Chief Clerk of the Left.
Wáng Sēngqián,
at the beginning of Qí, held the position of Grand Chancellor.
Yǎn and Yún traveled together to the western residence of Jìnglíng.
See Volume 136, second year of Wǔdì Yǒngmíng.
Wáng Liàng, in Dōnghūn's court,
gained favor by being ambivalent.
When Xiāo Yǎn arrived at Xīnlín,
all officials sent secret messages of surrender through back roads,
but Liàng alone did not send any.
When Dōnghūn was defeated,
Liàng came out to see Yǎn,
and Yǎn said:
"If he falls and is not supported,
what use is that minister!"
Liàng replied:
"If he could have been supported,
would Your Excellency have taken this action today!"
The Lúnyǔ,
Confucius said:
"If in danger he is not held,
if he falls he is not supported,
then of what use will that minister be?"
Yǎn cited this to question Wáng Liàng.
Some were robbed and plundered.
Yáng Gōngzé personally led his troops and arrayed them at Dōngyèmén,
escorting nobles, officials, and common people.
Therefore, many who left did so through Gōngzé's camp.
Yǎn sent Zhāng Hóngcè to first enter and clear the palace,
sealing the treasuries and archives.
At that time, treasures were piled high in the city,
but Hóngcè strictly disciplined his subordinates,
not allowing them to take even a trifle.
Pān and the favored officials Rú Fǎzhēn, Méi Chóng'ér, Wáng Xuānzhī, and forty-one others were all handed over to the authorities.
36 In the beginning,
when the King of Hǎilíng was deposed,
the event is recorded in Volume 139, first year of Míngdì Jiànwǔ.
It was called Xuāndégōng.
On Yǐsì,
Xiāo Yǎn, by order of Empress Dowager Xuāndé, retroactively deposed the Prince of Fúlíng as the Marquis of Dōnghūn.
Empress Chǔ and Crown Prince Sòng were both demoted to commoners.
Yǎn was appointed Zhongshu Jian, Dàsīmǎ, Lù Shàngshūshì, Piàojì Dàjiàngjūn, and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Jiàn'ān Commandery.
Following the precedent of Jìn Wǔlíngwáng Zūn acting by imperial authorization,
all officials paid their respects.
Without waiting for an imperial decree from the Western Terrace, he used the Empress Dowager Xuāndé’s order to appoint himself to high positions.
Xiāo Yǎn’s intentions
were known to everyone,
so why would it be necessary for Fàn Yún and Shěn Yuē to initiate it?
The affair of Wǔlíngwáng Zūn
is recorded in Volume 113, third year of Jìn Āndì Yuánxīng.
On Rénshēn,
Jiàn'ānwáng Bǎoyín was re-enfeoffed as King of Póyáng.
On Guǐyǒu,
Sītú and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Jìn'ānwáng Bǎoyì was appointed Tàiwèi,
also serving as Sītú.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
Xiāo Yǎn entered and garrisoned the Yuèwǔtáng.
He issued an order for a general amnesty.
He also issued an order saying:
"Apart from corrupt decrees, erroneous taxes, cruel punishments, and excessive corvée,
all can be thoroughly inspected from their previous origins,
and completely abolished.
'原' [yuán],
in the *Nán Shǐ* (History of the Southern Dynasties), is written as
'源' [yuán]."
"Previous origins" [qián yuán],
refers to the origins of things initiated recently.
The character '盪' [dàng]
is written as
'蕩' [dàng],
pronounced *tú-lǎng* fan.
Meticulously establish regulations [kētiáo],
and all shall follow the original precedents."
"原" [yuán],
means amnesty.
"守" [shǒu],
pronounced *shì-yòu* fan.
"Thoroughly inspect all departments of the Shangshū.
For all disputes and lawsuits that lost reason during the time of Dōnghūn [hūnjūn]
and those that the responsible officials procrastinated on and did not implement in a timely manner,
meticulously investigate and debate them,
and deliberate and memorialize according to the facts."
"訊" [xùn],
means to question.
The *Wáng Zhì* says: "Only after three interrogations is a punishment decided."
"辯" [biàn],
means to distinguish and clarify.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says: "If the son resigns,
the lord must clarify it."
"辯" [biàn],
pronounced *bīng-miǎn* fan.
"Collect and bury the loyal soldiers,
and inter the deceased of the rebellious faction."
Pān had the beauty of a state,
and Xiāo Yǎn wanted to keep her.
He asked the *shìzhōng*, *lǐngjūn jiāngjūn* Wáng Mào,
and Wáng Mào said:
"This woman caused the downfall of Qí.
Keeping her would likely invite external criticism."
So she was strangled to death in prison,
and favored officials such as Rú Fǎzhēn were also executed.
Two thousand palace women were distributed as rewards to the generals and soldiers.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Xiāo Hóng, *fǔguó jiāngjūn*, was appointed *zhōnghùjūn*.
When Xiāo Yǎn advanced eastward,
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Mǎ Xiānpǐn commanded troops and did not join Xiāo Yǎn.
Xiāo Yǎn sent his old acquaintance Yáo Zhòngbīn to persuade him.
Xiānpǐn first arranged wine for him,
then had him beheaded at the army gate to make an example.
Xiāo Yǎn again sent his clan uncle Huái Yuǎn to persuade him.
Xiānpǐn said:
"Great righteousness extinguishes family ties,"
and again wanted to execute him.
The army pleaded for him,
and he was thus spared.
When Xiāo Yǎn arrived at Xīnlín,
Xiānpǐn was still on the west side of the river daily raiding transport ships.
Yùzhōu was governed from Lìyáng,
which is west of the Great River.
"抄" [chāo],
pronounced *chǔ-jiāo* fan.
All the *zhōu* and *jùn* sent envoys to surrender,
but Wúxīng Tàishǒu Yuán Áng alone resisted at the border and refused to accept orders.
Yuán Áng
was the son of Yuán Yǐ.
Yuán Yǐ died during the chaos of Yìjiā.
Cáo Wèi established twenty-three *láng*,
of which the Jiàbù was one.
Dù Yòu said: "During Sòng and Qí, the Jiàbù was subordinate to the Zuǒ Mín Shàngshū."
(Xiāo Yǎn sent a letter to Yuán Áng saying:) "Since the foundation has been overturned,
how can the branches and leaves remain attached?
Now to exhaust one's strength for a corrupt lord [hūnjǔn]
is not sufficient to be called loyal;
for one's family to be slaughtered and annihilated
is not what is called filial.
How can this compare to suddenly changing one's plans
and inviting much fortune upon oneself!"
Yuán Áng replied in a letter saying:
"The three Wú are interior lands,
not a place for military campaigns.
Moreover, with a single remote commandery,
what can be accomplished?
Since your banners arrived,
none have failed to kneel and bare their chests at the army gate.
"膝袒" [xītǎn],
means to kneel and bare the chest.
"But as for my humble self,
with no achievements in military or civil affairs,
though I wish to offer my heart,
it would not increase the bravery of the grand army;
for me to remain silent in my foolishness,
would hardly hinder the might of the assembled forces.
Fortunately relying on the general's great magnanimity,
I may be permitted to act at my leisure and with propriety.
I secretly think that even a small kindness of one meal
is repaid with one's life;
how much more so to eat a man's salary and suddenly forget it in a day.
Not only would public opinion deem it unacceptable,
but I also fear that *mínggōng* would despise it.
This is why I hesitate,
and have not yet had time to present my jade."
"薦璧" [jiànbì],
refers to presenting a jade disc and surrendering.
"薦" [jiàn],
means to advance.
(During the Wú dynasty, Yǒng'ān County was established by dividing Wūchéng and Yúháng;
in the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it was renamed Wǔkāng,
and belonged to Wúxīng Jùn.)
"At the end of Yuánjiā,
a situation unprecedented arose,
and the late *tàiwèi* sacrificed his life to uphold his integrity."
(Yuán Shú was granted the title of *tàiwèi*;
his death is recorded in Volume 127, in the 30th year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng.)
"It is unreasonable to seek to preserve oneself at all costs,
and therefore he disregarded danger to follow his principles of righteousness.
The *sītú*
refers to Yuán Áng's father Yuán Yǐ;
Yuán Yǐ's death is recorded in Volume 131, in the 2nd year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Míng of Sòng.)
"He never repented of his actions.
Jīng and Yōng acted in concert,
taking advantage of their upstream position,
the will of Heaven and man is clear.
I hope *míngfǔ* will consider deeply,
and avoid future regret."
When Jiànkāng was pacified,
Xiāo Yǎn sent Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Yuánlǚ to pacify and comfort the eastern regions.
He instructed Lǐ Yuánlǚ saying:
"Yuán Áng comes from a family of integrity,
his clan has always been known for loyalty and integrity,
(this refers to Yuán Shú and Yuán Yǐ).
Do not insult them with military might."
When Lǐ Yuánlǚ arrived in Wúxīng,
he announced Xiāo Yǎn's decree.
Yuán Áng also did not request to surrender,
merely opened the gates and withdrew his defenses.
When Mǎ Xiānpǐn heard that Táichéng had fallen,
he wept and said to his generals and soldiers:
"I have received a trust from others,
and it is against my righteousness to surrender.
All of you have parents;
I will be a loyal official,
and you will be filial sons,
is this not acceptable!"
Then he sent all the soldiers within the city to surrender,
retaining only several tens of brave warriors,
closing the gates and defending alone.
Soon after, the soldiers entered,
surrounding him in dozens of layers.
Xiānpǐn ordered his men to hold their bows at full draw,
and the soldiers dared not approach.
At dusk,
Xiānpǐn threw down his bow and said:
"Gentlemen, just come and take me.
It is against my righteousness to surrender."
He was then sent in a cage to Shítou.
Xiāo Yǎn released him,
and had him wait for Yuán Áng to arrive so they could enter together,
saying:
"Let the world see two righteous gentlemen."
Xiāo Yǎn said to Xiānpǐn:
"Shooting the hook and severing the sleeve
were praised by people of old.
Do not blame yourself for having killed my envoy and cut off my supplies."
Xiānpǐn bowed and said:
"A small man is like a dog that has lost its master;
if a new master feeds it,
it will serve again."
Xiāo Yǎn laughed,
and treated both of them generously.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
Xiāo Yǎn entered and garrisoned the Diànzhōng.
37 After Liú Xīzǔ had conquered Ānchéng,
he issued a proclamation to the Xiāngbù region.
Wáng Sēngcàn, the Nèishǐ of Shǐxīng, responded to him.
Sēngcàn proclaimed himself Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu,
and led his troops to attack Chángshā.
When he was over a hundred *lǐ* from the city,
all the commandery and county troops of Xiāngzhōu rose up like a swarm of bees to respond to Sēngcàn.
Only the four counties of Línxiāng, Xiāngyīn, Liúyáng, and Luó remained intact.
The two counties of Línxiāng and Luó,
since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Chángshājùn.
The Wú established Liúyángxiàn,
which also belonged to Chángshā.
In the second year of Yuánhuī, King Cāngwú of the Sòng dynasty, by separating Yìyáng, Xiāngxī, Luó, and the displaced people from Bāxiá, established Xiāngyīnxiàn,
which belonged to Xiāngdōngjùn.
The Suí changed Línxiāng to Chángshāxiàn,
which was the administrative seat of Tánzhōu.
The Táng abolished Luóxiàn, incorporating it into Xiāngyīn,
which belonged to Yuèzhōu.
Liúyáng still belongs to Tánzhōu today.
The character 'Liú' (in Liúyáng),
is pronounced *liú*,
and also *liǔ*.
The Xíngshì, Liú Tǎn, gathered all their boats and burned them,
and dispatched Jūnzhǔ Yǐn Fǎlüè to resist Sēngcàn.
After several unfavorable battles,
the former Zhènjūn of Xiāngzhōu, Zhōng Xuánshào,
(Note: At that time, officials of the prefectural administration had no title of Zhènjūn,
this must be an error in the *Liángshū*.)
set a date to revolt within the city and respond to Sēngcàn.
Tǎn heard of his plot,
feigned ignorance,
and prolonged legal proceedings until night,
thus causing the city gates to remain open, to make him suspicious.
Xuánshào had not yet acted.
The next morning,
he went to Tǎn to ask why.
Tǎn detained him for a long time, talking with him,
while secretly sending trusted soldiers to seize his family letters.
While Xuánshào was still seated,
the soldiers sent to seize had already reported back,
having fully obtained the details of his documents.
Xuánshào immediately confessed,
and was executed on the spot;
his documents were burned,
and no questions were asked of his remaining associates.
The multitude felt ashamed and submitted,
and the prefecture and commandery were thus pacified.
Fǎlüè and Sēngcàn were locked in a stalemate for several months.
When Jiànkāng city was pacified,
Yáng Gōngzé returned to the prefecture.
Sēngcàn and his group dispersed and fled.
Wáng Dān was killed by the local people of the commandery.
(Wáng Dān had earlier used Nánkāng to respond to Liú Xīzǔ.)
Gōngzé was self-restrained, honest, and cautious,
he lightened punishments and reduced taxes.
After a short while,
the population of Xiāngzhōu almost recovered to its former state.
Punctuated by Niè Chóngqí, collated by Wáng Chóngwǔ.
